item.title: Bonita Equestrian Center ramps up horse care during dangerous heat wave
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Score: 4.56
BONITA (KGTV) — A Bonita equestrian center is stepping up care routines, even canceling riding lessons for its horses, as a dangerous heat wave pushes temperatures above 100 degrees in parts of the South Bay on Wednesday. Mt. Miguel Equestrian Center is both a training and riding school year-round. It is home to about 70 horses and typically sees around 100 riders per week. It's also currently in the middle of show season. However, with Bonita experiencing triple-digit temperatures for the third consecutive day, horse trainer Emily Ruocco said the focus has shifted entirely to the horses' well-being, as well as the students' and staff's. "So in the middle of a heat wave of this degree, we will cancel [lessons] for safety reasons for both horse safety and rider safety," Ruocco said. Ruocco said their primary goal during the heat wave is to keep the horses active, while also preventing them from overheating. "The whole mission is not to raise the heart rates of the horses," Ruocco said. Ruocco said within the past week, one horse unfortunately passed away from an underlying condition exacerbated by the heat wave. Another horse was in surgery this week and is expected to make a full recovery. It shows how dangerous temperatures have been in Bonita for the horses, and how mindful the team at the equestrian center has had to be about the horses' health. "Horses don't have the reasoning side," Ruocco said. "When their heart starts elevating, they don't have this thinking side of 'I should stop and drink water,' and if you don't recognize the signs, it can often lead to health issues like colic (abdominal pain), dehydration, heat exhaustion and more." Ruocco said the signs they're constantly scanning for are lethargy and if the horses start pawing or rolling, because those could be signs of distress and perhaps signs that lead to colic. Assistant Instructor Cameron Nembach said another concern during a heat wave is the horses' digestive tract. Staff have been making sure horses stay extra hydrated and are getting at least a walk each day to keep their digestive systems moving. "That statement 'You can bring a horse to water, but you can't make them drink,' really does stand," Nembach said. Ruocco added that monitoring for a healthy amount of droppings per day is another way staff can tell if a horse's digestive system is functioning correctly in the heat. The center has also introduced additional supplements into the horses' routines. Assistant Jayme Engen said staff is mixing electrolyte powder into the horses' water to encourage them to drink more. Sometimes, the horses are also fed diluted Gatorade because it's safe for the horses to drink. Engen said the staff's routine has been revolving around the following steps: adding extra buckets of water in the horses' stalls, adding electrolyte powder, applying fly masks to the horses' faces, and spraying them with a protective spray to keep flies off the horses' faces, hooves, private areas and more. Ruocco said the humidity accompanying this heat wave has added another layer of concern. "The humidity has been a big game changer," Ruocco said. "The other part that a lot of people don't realize is that because our days are now shortening up, their winter coats are starting to grow in. They don't follow the trend of the weather. They tend to follow the trend of the sunlight." Which is why bathing the horses in cold water is also a part of the center's routine during the heatwave. Despite the canceled riding lessons for the week, Ruocco said there's still a teaching opportunity in the heatwave. She said her students are still expected to come to the center in the afternoons after school and learn how to take care of their horses in this heatwave. "So they don't rely on us to do everything," Ruocco said. "They have to learn their [horses'] behaviors and their habits."

item.title: As nation marks 25th anniversary of 9/11, San Diegans will honor lives lost
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Score: 4.23
Ceremonies, tributes and other events will be held throughout San Diego County Friday to mark the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. The day's observances will begin at 5:46 a.m. Friday, when U.S. Customs and Border Protection personnel will briefly halt northbound traffic at the San Ysidro, Otay Mesa and Calexico West ports of entry. The pause corresponds with 8:46 a.m. Eastern time, when American Airlines Flight 11 struck the World Trade Center's North Tower in New York City 25 years ago. In Chula Vista, businesses will provide appreciation meals to fire stations and police headquarters throughout the day in remembrance of the first responders who died in the attacks. Breakfast will be served from 6:30 to 8:30 a.m., lunch from 11:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. and dinner from 5 to 6 p.m. The University of San Diego will hold a 9/11 remembrance and interfaith prayer for peace at 8:30 a.m. at 5998 Alcala Park. Assemblyman Chris Ward, D-San Diego, Rep. Sara Jacobs, D-San Diego, and San Diego Fire-Rescue Department Capt. Brant Truver were scheduled to speak. The ceremony will also include an NROTC color guard, Taps and interfaith prayers for peace. At 9:30 a.m., USD's Epstein Family Military Center and Palomar Health Student Wellness Center will hold a 9/11 Memorial Stair Climb at the university's Palomar Health Student Wellness Center. Participants will climb the equivalent of 110 stories on stair-climbing machines, representing the height of each of the World Trade Center's twin towers. San Diego County Sheriff Kelly Martinez will join regional law enforcement leaders at 10:30 a.m. to discuss lessons learned from the attacks and cooperation among local, state and federal agencies in responding to threats. The event will be held at the Sheriff's Technology and Information Center, 5575 Overland Ave. One of the day's largest commemorations will begin at 2:30 p.m. aboard the USS Midway Museum, where retired New York City firefighters will join the San Diego Fire-Rescue Department, National City Fire Department, San Diego Firefighter's Emerald Society, Wounded Warrior Project and others for a ceremony on the flight deck. The ceremony will include honor guards, pipes and drums, the national anthem, a reading of the names of 441 first responders who died as a result of the attacks, tolling of the ship's bells, a San Diego Fire-Rescue helicopter flyover, a 21-gun salute, Taps and a Harbor Police fireboat water display. Admission to the USS Midway Museum, 910 N. Harbor Drive, will be free from 1:45 to 3 p.m. for people attending the ceremony. Also at 2:30 p.m., San Diego County Supervisor Joel Anderson will host a 9/11 remembrance ceremony at Gillespie Field in El Cajon. Jacobs and retired New York City firefighter David Blacksberg, who responded to the Sept. 11 attacks, are scheduled to attend the ceremony at Hangars G and H, 1860 Joe Crosson Drive. At 6 p.m., Punches in the Piazza will be held at Piazza della Famiglia in Little Italy in remembrance of boxing promoter Bobby DePhilippis and the victims of 9/11. "Punches in the Piazza is a celebration of community, resilience and generosity," said Michelle DePhilippis, founder of The Bobby D. Foundation. "This year, as we mark the 25th anniversary of 9/11, we have an opportunity to come together to honor those we lost, recognize our first responders and support organizations making a meaningful difference in people's lives." Proceeds from the event will benefit the Washington Elementary School Foundation and the Tunnel to Towers Foundation, a nonprofit that honors military service members, veterans and first responders and supports their families through housing assistance programs. Nearly 3,000 people were killed when 19 al-Qaida terrorists hijacked four commercial airliners on Sept. 11, 2001. Two planes struck the World Trade Center towers in New York, a third struck the Pentagon and a fourth, United Airlines Flight 93, crashed in a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania, after passengers and crew members attempted to regain control of the aircraft. The attacks killed 2,977 victims, including 343 New York City firefighters and 60 police officers in New York and at the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey. The San Diego area's commemorations will continue Sunday with the Travis Manion Foundation's 9/11 Heroes Run at NTC Park in Liberty Station. The 5-kilometer run, walk and ruck will begin at 9 a.m. and honor those killed in the attacks and military service members who served in the wars that followed.

item.title: DA will not charge officer who shot & killed 16-year-old Konoa Wilson at Santa Fe Depot
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Score: 3.86
SAN DIEGO (KGTV) — San Diego District Attorney Summer Stephan has decided not to charge Officer Daniel Gold in the shooting death of 16-year-old Konoa Wilson at the Santa Fe Depot. The decision closes a case that resulted in a $30-million settlement between the city of San Diego and the Wilson family — the largest of any police killing in U.S. history. Wilson was shot twice in the back by Gold in late January last year. Surveillance cameras captured Wilson sprinting away after shots were fired at him by another person. Wilson turned a corner where Gold was waiting and was shot within seconds. He died at the hospital. Stephan released a 14-page report detailing her findings after a review of the case. The report says Gold and another officer, referred to as LE1, responded separately to the area after reports of an assault. As LE1 and an Amtrak police officer discussed the call, they heard gunshots — which we now know, based on surveillance footage, were aimed at Wilson by another person. After those initial shots rang out, LE1 broadcast "I've got shots fired. Again, shots fired" over his radio. The report says that word choice is key, noting LE1 acknowledged the phrase "shots fired" might lead other officers to believe he was involved in a shooting, rather than using police code 11-6, which is more commonly used when shots are heard in the area. In his statement, Gold said he believed LE1 had been injured, shot, or ambushed, and Gold believed there was a need to preserve LE1's life. A use of force expert cited in the report said, although Gold's response did not follow traditional training protocol or have the desired outcome, his actions may be viewed as reasonable by peers faced with the same set of circumstances. Stephan relied on that reasoning in her decision not to file criminal charges. Nick Rowley, the attorney representing the Wilson family, pushed back sharply on that conclusion. "Their reasoning is bullsh*t," he said. "This was negligent discharge of a firearm. You've got to know what you're shooting at." Rowley said the $30 million settlement does not deliver the accountability the family sought. "That's separate. The criminal liability here, the criminal liability, which there is none, that would have held the cop responsible, and that would have ensured that he never does anything like this again, and it would have set an example for other police officers," Rowley said. Rowley said the DA's decision raises a broader concern about what it signals going forward. "If there's no consequence when you kill a 16-year-old by shooting him in the back to the individual, then what's going to prevent that individual or others like that person from doing it again?" Rowley said. Rowley said he was not surprised by the outcome. "Very disappointed, but not surprised." The DA's decision cannot be appealed by the family, bringing the criminal case to a close. Follow ABC 10News Anchor Max Goldwasser on Instagram, Facebook and Twitter. This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. item.title: San Diego has avoided rotating outages since 2022 — battery storage is why
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Score: 3.81
SAN DIEGO (KGTV) — Battery storage facilities have played a central role in keeping San Diego's power on during periods of high demand, even as California's grid relies increasingly on renewable energy sources that fluctuate with the weather. California's grid has a capacity of around 70,000 megawatts. About three-fourths of that comes from renewable sources like solar and wind power, according to California ISO. Because those sources depend on weather conditions, storing renewable energy has become critical. Battery storage facilities have come online and expanded over the years to meet that need. SDG&E owns 600 megawatts of battery storage and draws on an additional 750 megawatts owned by other companies, just in San Diego County alone. That stored energy kicks in during peak usage hours, reducing the need for customers to cut back on power consumption. Jayme Ackemann of CAISO said the expansion of battery storage has been a turning point for grid reliability. "Capturing that solar energy with our battery storage resources, which is not something we were able to do in 2020 has been really vital to helping strengthen the grid and avoid issues during stressed grid conditions." California has not asked San Diegans to reduce power usage since 2022. Ackemann said there hasn't been a rotating outage since 2020. When San Diego neighborhoods lost power during recent heat events, it was not because the grid lacked capacity. Outages were caused by individual neighborhoods' equipment failing after record-high evening temperatures and greater overall usage, according to a spokesperson from SDG&E. Battery storage facilities have been a key factor in keeping air conditioning units and lights running across San Diego neighborhoods during periods of extreme heat and high demand. item.title: Oceanside teacher holds a specific and special lesson on 9/11 anniversary for students
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Score: 3.12
OCENASIDE, Calif. (KGTV) – For many, it’s hard to forget where they were on Tuesday, September 11, 2001. “I was actually in a high school classroom myself, and I remember, if I'm gonna go back, the teacher rolling in a TV cart and saying, 'Something's happening in New York City,” Jesse Kauric, an Oceanside High School social studies teacher, said. “I watched live in a classroom the second tower being hit and the school going on lockdown, unbeknownst to me, that another plane is going to be going down right outside of Pittsburgh, you know, not too far away from where our high school was.” Four planes, three cities, thousands of lives lost, and a country changed forever. “I started doing the lesson, right when I started teaching, even when I was substitute teaching. If I was substitute teaching on 9/11. I was doing a lesson plan.” Since 2016, Kauric has been doing a specific lesson about 9/11 for his students. “When I first started teaching, the students were, you know, babies or toddlers during 9/11. And now, since really 2020, we have no students that were alive in 9/11,” Kauric said. “I think it is incredibly important for the students to know what their parents and their grandparents and their aunts and uncles and so forth what they carry with them. This is a scar that we have.” The lesson is students fill out worksheets on what they know and didn't know about 9/11, seeing video clips, seeing a flag flown from Camp Pendleton, the cultural impact of 9/11, and front pages of newspapers the next day of what happened 25 years ago. “Learning about it in deeper detail today, learning about the boat lift, learning about how people stepped in and how involved the American people were,” Darone Redd, an Oceanside HS Senior, said. "It really moved my heart this year to want to appreciate 9/11 more, and you know, never forget, as they say.” 90 minutes to reflect on how a nation was changed at a time when these students weren’t even alive. “I think it's just best to once again never forget, to be able to not be desensitized to it as a lot of people are since it happened,” Adelyn Aguon, Oceanside HS Senior. As the lesson ends with the ringing of the bell and a final moment of silence, there’s a message Kauric hopes to get across to his students. “We promise to never forget, and part of never forgetting is telling the story,” Kauric said.

item.title: El Niño is coming: Here's how to protect your home roof
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Score: 2.91
IMPERIAL BEACH (KGTV) — A stronger-than-expected El Niño season is on the way, and experts say homeowners need to act now to protect one of their biggest investments: their roof. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration and the National Weather Service have issued a stark warning. "El Niño is strengthening, with a greater than 90% chance of a very strong event during the Northern Hemisphere fall and winter 2026-27." Realtor Deborah Vance, with Spirit Realty in Imperial Beach, said she is taking the threat seriously when it comes to her home listings. "This one is real and it's legit," Vance said. "I would highly advise everyone to consider servicing your roof and weatherproofing it for what's to come." That forecast has homeowners scrambling to prepare—and at least one local roofing company is seeing the uptick. Martin Carr, owner of RoofMaxx of Carlsbad, says he’s now getting at least two calls a day from homeowners looking to prepare their roofs for El Niño. That included a call from Vance. "So these homeowners are concerned. They want to make sure that their roof is sound so they don't have any problems with the leaks," Carr said. During a recent inspection at Vance's listing in Imperial Beach, Martin and his colleague Dillon identified several problem areas that El Niño conditions could exploit: a loose vent pipe, loose attachments, and loose shingles where rainwater can leak through. Carr added that heavy rain can wash granules off shingles and wear a roof down over time. He also pointed to a more immediate concern. Carr recommends homeowners also check their gutters for debris and look for loose attachments and loose shingles before the season arrives. "If those are flapping around, they're going to blow off in the high winds," Martin said. Vance said addressing those problems now can prevent far more costly consequences. The Imperial Beach home, listed at $989,000, illustrates the financial stakes. Vance was prepared to offer a $4,000 discount to account for needed roof updates, but a previous buyer requested a $20,000 credit instead — and the deal fell through. Vance said she plans to move forward with the roof treatment before relisting. "So with our next buyer we're gonna keep it at 989,000, and we're gonna have a five-year warranty on the roof," Vance said. RoofMax said treating the roof on that one Imperial Beach home will cost up to $3,600. Carr advised all homeowners and potential homebuyers to always get three quotes as a best practice for avoiding scams.

item.title: "I had to": Retired FDNY firefighter recalls going back to Ground Zero days after the 9/11 attack
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Score: 2.90
SAN DIEGO (KGTV) — The USS Midway Museum is lit up in red, white, and blue as San Diego marks 25 years since the Sept. 11 terror attacks — attacks that changed the lives of Americans forever and spurred one former New York City firefighter into action. Robert Allen is a proud New Yorker who served as a firefighter in his hometown for 8 years before an injury forced him to retire. He eventually moved to San Diego, where he currently lives. 24 years after leaving the job, Allen remembers the moment he watched the terror attacks unfold from across the country. "I was driving a school bus here in San Diego," Allen said. "It's unbelievable that it could be 25 years." After learning about the attacks and witnessing the harrowing scene on television, Allen and a group of fellow FDNY retirees returned to New York City. For 10 days, they helped in what would be months-long recovery efforts at Ground Zero. "I had to. It's just I didn't in my head, I didn't have a choice. I wouldn't have been able to live with myself if I couldn't go back," Allen said. "Every day we called and every day they said, "We'll fly tomorrow. Don't worry about it. We'll fly tomorrow and nine days later, [the airlines] are flying." In the midst of a horrific scene at Ground Zero, what stuck out the most to Allen as he worked the recovery efforts was the effort from the active firefighters, going through the rubble and working for 12+ hours a day. "I had to take it easy compared to them, and I felt really less, to tell you the truth. The energy these guys put out, it was absolutely incredible," Allen said. Allen says being a firefighter is like being a part of a brotherhood. It's that camaraderie he built with his crews in the '70s that took him back to New York to help after the attack. San Diego, National City Fire and other organizations will join Allen and other retired New York City firefighters at the USS Midway Museum for today's 25th anniversary ceremony. The ceremony begins at 2:30 p.m. Admission to the Midway will be free from 1:45 p.m. to 3 p.m. for people attending.

item.title: Escondido bans riders under 12 on e-bikes as crashes surge to 35 this year
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Score: 2.51
ESCONDIDO (KGTV) — Escondido has new rules for electric bicycle riders, including a ban on anyone younger than 12, as the city sees a dramatic rise in crashes. The Escondido City Council voted 4-1 last month to update its e-bike regulations. The new rules address where riders can operate e-bikes, require education, prohibit reckless operation as determined by the responding police officer, and ban multiple riders unless the bike is designed for it. Fines start at $50 for a first violation, $100 for a second, and $200 for each additional violation. The changes come as e-bike crashes in Escondido have spiked sharply. From 2022 to 2025, the city averaged fewer than 5 crashes per year. This year alone, there have been 35. Across San Diego County, e-bike popularity is growing — but so are the number of crashes and serious injuries. Reyna Swanson rides electric unicycles and skateboards with Personal Electric Vehicles, a community group in San Diego County that rides from San Marcos and Escondido to Oceanside. She said proper training is essential, especially for younger riders. "I don't think that there is much training or much aforethought. I mean, you're giving someone something with an electric motor. We might want to do some training," Swanson said. Swanson said a formal training requirement would set an important baseline for new riders. "If you're going to be handed a bike, you need to go through some sort of just formal training, whether they listen or not, whether they absorb the information or not, at least that benchmark is there," Swanson said. Councilmember Judy Fitzgerald supported the new regulations. "It is convenient but it is also dangerous if they are not educated and aware and know how to be safe," Fitzgerald said. The mayor cast the lone no vote, expressing openness to an alternative approach. "Totally understand the approach that we're taking but I disagree with it and I'm just curious if anyone else is open to an education program," Dane White said. Swanson said accountability starts with the adults making the purchase. "I think to me it starts with who's buying the vehicle and what are they buying it for," Swanson said. item.title: San Diego author uses love of art to spread literacy across the county
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Score: 2.50
SAN DIEGO (KGTV) — Award-winning author Salina Yoon said reading didn’t always come easy to her. Her parents came to the United States from Korea in 1976. "They came here to the US with only $400 in their pocket. My parents wanted to come here, settle, and prepare for having the kids come, and so I came two years later," Yoon said. Starting school in a new country was not easy. "I started kindergarten. I didn't speak a word of English, and so school was really uncomfortable for me,” Yoon said. As a little girl who felt out of place, books made her feel connected. "Because it wasn't something that I had to do with anyone. The scenes and the pictures, and that's what drew me in," Yoon said. Art came first, writing second. Her earliest works were concept books that relied more on illustration than text. "I always loved art as a child, and that is where I found my greatest joy. The writing part of it came a little bit later," Yoon said. Yoon said she has written nearly 190 books, although she stopped counting after about 180. More than 25 years into her career, Yoon continues to write and draw, reaching thousands of children around the world. She also visits schools to speak directly with young readers. "Books can spark curiosity and their imagination. It teaches them new things. It allows them to discover new things," Yoon said. Her message to kids is rooted in her own story. "If you have a passion for something, keep pursuing it, and you have no idea where life will take you," Yoon said. item.title: Nearly 500-pound bluefin tuna caught off San Diego feeds a local supply chain from boat to table
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Score: 2.44
A nearly 500-pound bluefin tuna caught off the San Diego coast is believed to be the largest ever taken by rod and reel on the West Coast — and the massive fish is now making its way through a local supply chain, from the boat to a fishmonger down the dock to Herb and Wood restaurant in Little Italy. amp-iframe "I think the biggest rod and reel bluefin tuna or any tuna that's ever been caught here on the West Coast," fisherman Markus Medak said. Chef Aidan plans to serve the fish for four weeks, preparing it every way possible until none of it is left. The price paid for the fish remains undisclosed. When asked, the fishmonger, Tommy Gones, was direct. "How much did you sell it for, can you tell me?" I asked. "No, it's business -- proprietary information," the fishmonger said. Fish of this size are typically caught off the coast of Japan, making this San Diego catch unusual, Markus says. Markus believes the fish's presence here reflects decades of responsible fishing practices in the North Pacific. "In the late '90s, bluefin tuna in the North Pacific were horrifically overfished... we have had fisheries managers that came together and actually worked to make some real changes... they have made an absolutely dramatic recovery across the North Pacific," Markus said. For Aidan Owens, the culinary director of Herb and Wood, the catch landing in his restaurant is representative of deep ties to San Diegans. "Now that it's here, it's a little daunting," Owens said. "... I think if you're able to support local and keep the money local... you really do find a lot of other people with the same mindset and then you end up getting better products." He planned to carve it for diners at 6:30 Thursday evening in the Herb and Wood dining room, then break it into steaks. He says he'll use even the bone marrow in the fish, not wasting a bite. item.title: National City's new short-term rental law takes effect next week
item.description:
Source: ABC 10News San Diego Score: 2.17
NATIONAL CITY (KGTV) — A new National City law targeting crime at short-term rental properties takes effect next week, requiring operators to obtain permits and maintain around-the-clock oversight of their properties. City Council unanimously passed the ordinance last September. It caps short-term rentals citywide in National City at 180 units — 45 per council district. New and existing operators must apply for permits on a first-come, first-served basis and comply with rules, including noise restrictions from 9 p.m. to 6 a.m. Councilmember Jose Rodriguez has been a leading advocate for the crackdown. He said unsupervised properties listed on platforms like Airbnb and VRBO had become locations for criminal activity. "We had short-term rental properties that were being used for illicit activities, including human trafficking, parties, shootings, stabbings, and sometimes drug consumption," Rodriguez said. Rodriguez said the new law is designed to hold property owners directly accountable. "This ordinance will make sure that the owners of the properties are responsible to who they rent to and make sure that there is somebody on-site or available 24 hours a day in case there are any issues," Rodriguez said. He also said the ordinance benefits operators who already run their properties responsibly. "I think this actually does a service to those that operate properties professionally," Rodriguez said. "I think this actually dissuades the bad owners from operating in our city." A woman who lives near a short-term rental property near Civic Center Drive spoke about what she has witnessed, asking to remain anonymous for safety reasons. She said she has never seen the property owner check on the rental in person. The rental was also recently the scene of a shooting. "There's a lot of partying, there's a lot of girls coming in and out of the cars, half-nude," she said. "Even though he [the owner] has cameras, it doesn't mean that he shouldn't come by and see visually what's going on." The permit application is expected to go live on the city's website next week. National City is using a third-party company called Deckard Technologies to process the applications. ABC 10News reached out to both Airbnb and VRBO for comment on the new law and is still waiting to hear back.

item.title: Residential air pollution linked to higher depression scores among 9/11 responders
item.description:
Source: ABC News: Top Stories Score: 4.72
Residential air pollution linked to higher depression scores among 9/11 responders: Study Approximately 39% of responders met criteria for probable PTSD. In the 25 years since 9/11, researchers have examined first responders' later-life exposure to fine-particle air pollution, known as PM2.5, as well as temperature and greenness in the neighborhoods where they lived. Researchers at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai analyzed data from 18,734 responders who live in New York City and are enrolled in one of the World Trade Center Health Clinical Centers of Excellence. Approximately 39% of responders met criteria for probable PTSD and 35% for probable depression, according to their study, published Thursday in the journal Nature Communications. The study is the first to examine how later-life environmental exposures may interact with World Trade Center-related chemical and psychological exposures to affect aging and mental health outcomes, according to Mount Sinai Health System. "We know that responders who took part in the mission after 9/11 suffer health consequences to this day," Maayan Yitshak-Sade, associate professor of environmental medicine at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, told ABC News. "We see higher rates of PTSD and mental health conditions, and higher rates of frailty despite the relatively young age of this population." She added, "We were interested to know how the exposures they experienced 25 years ago interact with their day-to-day environmental exposures in their residential environment, and how all these together shape their long-term health." Higher levels of air pollution and heat were associated with increased risks of depression, PTSD and frailty. For each 2.48 micrograms per cubic meter increase in annual PM2.5 exposure, responders had, on average, about 2.3% higher frailty scores, 2.1% higher PTSD symptom scores and 3.9% higher depression symptom scores. "This suggests that this initial extreme environmental exposure or stress exposure ... had a long-lasting impact, which then made them more vulnerable later in life [to] environmental exposures," Yitshak-Sade said. Neighborhood greenness showed the opposite pattern. For each 6.67-point increase in the study's Green View Index, which measures the amount of visible tree canopy surrounding a person's residence, responders had about 1.4% lower frailty scores, 1.9% lower PTSD symptom scores and 3.8% lower depression symptom scores. Researchers say there are several possible explanations for why greener surroundings may benefit health, including providing opportunities for physical activity and social interaction. "Some theories suggest that even being exposed to nature ... has this calming effect [on] stress levels," Yitshak-Sade said. "So, there is no one answer that we know that is the correct answer, but we do see that residential greenness has beneficial effects on reducing mortality rates, reducing the risks of cardiovascular diseases, metabolic diseases like diabetes, and of course mental health conditions and frailty." Greater neighborhood greenness, however, did not eliminate the harmful health impacts researchers observed with heat and air pollution. "Even if you do live in a green environment, we still see harmful effect of heat and air pollution," Yitshak-Sade said. Of all the environmental factors studied, temperature appeared to have the strongest association with responders' health outcomes, accounting for 98% of the overall association with frailty and 73% of the association with PTSD symptoms. "Temperature indeed emerges as the primary driver of the exposure mixture associations that we saw," Yitshak-Sade said. "We think it likely reflects the persistent physiological burden on the body that is ... harder for vulnerable populations to mitigate." The findings suggest that two people living in the same neighborhood and experiencing similar levels of heat or air pollution may not necessarily be affected in the same way, Yitshak-Sade said. People with a history of extreme environmental or stress exposures "may be more vulnerable" to everyday environmental conditions later in life, she said, adding that the study's findings underscore the importance of continuing to monitor the health of WTC responders decades after 9/11.

item.title: 25 years after 9/11, many first responders and survivors navigate health effects
item.description:
Source: ABC News: Top Stories Score: 4.05
After thousands of deaths, first responders are still navigating health effects 25 years post-9/11 More than 9,400 people have died from 9/11-related illnesses. When Michael O'Connell found out he had been accepted into the New York City Fire Department, he was elated. O'Connell had started his career as a police officer, but he always had more of an interest in becoming a firefighter. "It was more my speed," O'Connell told ABC News. "It was like camaraderie, team, unity. It's where I wanted to be." O'Connell was sworn into the FDNY as a probationary firefighter. Just four months later, he was deployed to lower Manhattan on Sept. 11, 2001, following the terrorist attack at the World Trade Center. For several weeks, O'Connell said he didn't go home. He went back-and-forth between his firehouse and ground zero, extinguishing fires amid the rubble and engaging in search-and-rescue operations. O'Connell started hearing about fellow firefighters who worked at the site being diagnosed with asthma or cancer but didn't experience any health problems himself until New Year's Day 2007, when he says he woke up in severe pain. "My body inflamed two times the size of what it was," O'Connell said. "I didn't know what was going on ... and I had like bruises and blisters all over my body." O'Connell said he was eventually diagnosed with sarcoidosis, a multi-system inflammatory disease that typically affects the lungs, skin and lymph nodes, and his doctors believe is linked to his exposure to toxins at ground zero. It's estimated that 400,000 people were exposed to toxic dust, smoke and debris; risk of physical injury; and physically and emotionally stressful conditions from 9/11 and the aftermath, according to the World Trade Center Health Program. At least 69 cancers -- including breast, prostate, skin and head and neck -- have been certified as being linked to 9/11 as have airway and digestive disorders, musculoskeletal disorders and mental health conditions, according to the WTC Health Program. More than 9,400 people have died from 9/11-related illnesses -- according to recently published data from the WTC Health Program -- which is three times higher than the 2,977 who died in the attacks in New York, at the Pentagon and in Shanksville, Pennsylvania. Data from the WTC Health Program shows about 50,000 cancer diagnoses have been certified. Many of these people are members of the FDNY and NYPD who responded to the attacks or assisted in cleanup operations, but they also include civilians -- those who lived, worked, went to school or passed through the area. "The truth is, 9/11 didn't end on 9/11," Michael Barasch, managing partner at Barasch & McGarry, a law firm that specializes in helping 9/11 responders and survivors get compensation and health benefits, told ABC News. "I personally lost dozens of clients, mostly firefighters and police officers, on 9/11, but I have lost thousands of clients since." "9/11 Tribute in Light: Live from Lower Manhattan," a one-hour ABC News multiplatform live special, premieres on Friday, Sept. 11, at 8:00 p.m. EDT across ABC, Disney+, Hulu, National Geographic, ABC Owned Television Stations livestreams and ABC News Live. Responding to ground zero On the morning of 9/11, Thomas Wilson, an NYPD sergeant, was investigating a burglary of an elderly couple in Brooklyn when calls came in over his radio that an object had hit the World Trade Center. Wilson replied that he was heading to the Williamsburg Bridge. "I said goodbye to that couple, 'I'll come see you later on to take that report,'" Wilson told ABC News. "Never did see them again." Wilson said he shut down the Williamsburg Bridge on the Manhattan side while his colleague shut down the Brooklyn side. The assignment went from facilitating the movement of vehicles over the bridge to securing it as people fled from Manhattan over the bridge on foot. "I don't know how many thousands upon thousands of people crossed the bridge that day," Wilson said. "I'm still haunted. Covered in dust. ... That mass exodus out of Manhattan still sticks with me." When O'Connell, the firefighter, got down to the site, he said he was instructed to help shut down the water mains, and then he climbed on the rubble to assist in search and rescue. Throughout the day, O'Connell remembers hearing alarms. He said that attached to the Scott Air-Pak, a self-contained breathing apparatus that firefighters wear, is a Personal Alert Safety System (PASS) Alarm, which sits on the chest and tracks movement. If a firefighter stays still for 20 to 30 seconds, it emits a loud beep to help colleagues locate them. "That's all you heard were those alarms when we first got there. Nothing but PASS Alarms," O'Connell said. "As a fireman, when you hear it, you're meant to act and try your best to get to that person. You couldn't. They were underneath that pile." John Feal, a demolition supervisor at ground zero who arrived on site on Sept. 12, also remembers the PASS Alarms going off. "I don't care who you are, you're not programed ... to see that kind of devastation of that magnitude," he told ABC News. "I've never witnessed anything like that in my life, nor do I wish I ever see anything like that again." Cleanup efforts Wilson said he contributed to recovery efforts at ground zero, where he says he spent about 350 hours, and later as a sifter at Fresh Kills Landfill on Staten Island, which was temporarily reopened as a sorting ground for some of the ground zero rubble. Wilson said he almost never thought about the dust and toxins he was inhaling. "My mindset was just get the job done," Wilson said. "... Got to do what you got to do to keep things moving along." At the landfill, Wilson said he was issued a disposable suit with boots, a hood, gloves and a respirator, but said the shifts were 12 hours, and that some respirator filters have an eight-hour limit. Ivonne Sanchez, former FDNY emergency medical technician, arrived at ground zero after the towers fell and said she spent about 20 straight hours at the site. She said the dust was so thick that she couldn't get her bearings. For the next several months, Sanchez worked on body identification and recovery efforts. She said she was motivated to continue responding at ground zero with the hope that she would find her friend, who died in the attacks. Sanchez said she didn't receive a mask until October, when the site was visited by Occupational Safety and Health Administration inspectors for mandatory mask fittings. O'Connell, the firefighter, said he didn't have a mask for the first few days until he received a painter's mask. "You'd put them on but, quite honestly, you can't work with a painter's mask on for 24 hours straight and be a part of Bucket Brigade and talk to your guys and drink water," he said. "You're always pulling it on and off. Nobody was thinking, 'What's coming of this? Are we gonna get sick because we're breathing this stuff in?' That wasn't in anybody's head." First responders begin falling ill New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said this week that more than 170,000 pages related to the attacks were being made public, including about air quality. Among the documents revealed is the "Harding Memo," an October 2001 memo from then-Deputy Mayor Robert Harding that indicated the city knew of the air quality dangers and the legal liability, even though the city publicly declared the air was safe. The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) also told the public at the time that the air around ground zero was safe to breathe. In an interview with The Guardian in 2016, Christine Todd Whitman, who was EPA administrator during 9/11, apologized for "whatever we got wrong" but denied that she knowingly lied about the air quality or knew at the time it was dangerous. In Lower Manhattan, the collapse of the Twin Towers led to a massive dust cloud that filled the air and blanketed city blocks with ash, debris, metal, glass, asbestos, benzene and other harmful particles, according to the WTC Health program. Fires within the debris pile burned through the end of December 2001 with flare-ups in 2002. The city did not immediately respond to ABC News' request on potential toxins first responders were exposed to in the aftermath or allegations by agencies at the time that the air was safe. Medical research is ongoing about the potential links between 9/11-related toxic exposure and certain cancers and illnesses. Dozens of cancers and conditions have a certified link, but scientists are still learning about the cumulative effects of breathing in a "toxic cocktail," how long it may take for certain cancers to develop -- if they do at all -- and how chemical exposure and trauma can accelerate physical decline and life expectancy. Sanchez, the EMT, said she would often go home after a day at ground zero coughing, bleeding from her nose or vomiting. Sanchez retired in 2002 after recovery efforts ended due to an injury at the site, which she said caused lower back pain and nerve damage that she said she manages to this day. In the years after 9/11, Sanchez said she developed chronic sinusitis and asthma. In 2014, in her early 40s, she said she began experiencing severe hot flashes. Sanchez said she went to the doctor four weeks later and was diagnosed with breast cancer that spread to her lymph nodes. "It was Stage II and ... it was very aggressive," Sanchez said. Sanchez said she had a lumpectomy in August 2014 and a mastectomy in December 2014. While Sanchez says her cancer is currently in remission, she said she has also developed seven or eight stomach ulcers that have caused gastrointestinal problems from her time at ground zero. Wilson, the police officer, said he also developed cancer. Wilson was diagnosed with an aggressive neck cancer that had spread to his tongue and skeletal muscle after going to the doctor for sinus issues and tongue pain, he said. Wilson said he underwent a procedure called a hemiglossectomy, which involved removing part of his tongue, along with a neck dissection to remove the neck tumor and 39 lymph nodes. Doctors used a skin graft from the wrist to replace part of Wilson's tongue as well as an artery from his arm to implant in his neck, he said. To this day, Wilson said he continues to take medication for his thyroid, experiences fibrosis in his neck, attends swallow therapy and sleeps with an oxygen machine due to severe asthma. He said he also suffers from osteoradionecrosis in his jaw, a serious condition in which bone dies after being exposed to radiation therapy. Wilson said he also started seeing a mental health specialist two years ago. "I had a lot to unpack," he said. "It eases me and it helps me get back, and I know I had a lot of anxiety; I still do." O'Connell, the firefighter, learned he had developed sarcoidosis when his wife was pregnant with the couple's first child, he said. "I just [thought], this is the first child I'm gonna have. Maybe the only. I just want to get to that day. Get me to the day so I can see this baby and see you and her together, and then I'm good," O'Connell said. O'Connell said he received drugs, including cancer medications and steroids as treatment. He said he was told there was never a case of sarcoidosis in the history of the FDNY until he was diagnosed but, since then, there have been many more cases, according to O'Connell. O'Connell returned to work but said he had to retire as a lieutenant in 2010 after experiencing flare-ups while he was in the line of duty. "That's your family. ... It's a house of 50 guys, and we do everything together," he said. "It's a family and leaving that is one of the worst things that's ever happened in my life." Many first responders have died from their illnesses, including William Gormley, a firefighter with the New York City Fire Department. His daughter, Bridget Gormley, said from 9/11 until his death, he had a persistent cough. She said her father was also riddled with skin cancer following his time at ground zero and was going to the doctor two or three times a year to remove cancerous tissue from several areas including his back, arms and nose. In Christmas 2016, William Gormley was diagnosed with bladder cancer. The cancer spread to his lungs, and he died in June 2017. "I think my father was well aware that it was caused from being downtown, ground zero, in the pit, in a pile," Bridget Gormley told ABC News. "He and his friends would joke, 'This is all going to kill us one day.' Very gallows humor, but I think they knew." "I couldn't wrap my head around it': Civilians develop illnesses as well 9/11-related illnesses didn't just affect the first responders but also civilians, including people who were working in the area at the time. Barbara Mohan, office administrator and paralegal at Barasch & McGarry, said she first realized something was wrong in 2016, when she tripped on an uneven sidewalk walking across City Hall Park on her way to the office and fell on her knee. Mohan said she went to a hospital, where doctors determined she hadn't broken or fractured any bones. Within a week or two, Mohan said she started to get pain in her hip. She said she went to an orthopedist, who diagnosed her with bursitis -- inflammation of a small fluid-filled sac that cushions the bones, tendons and muscles near joints -- and recommended physical therapy. "The more I went to physical therapy, the more it hurts," Mohan told ABC News. "Another X-ray, and then [the orthopedist] sent me for an MRI, and it showed a lesion on my hip bone, kind of the top of the femur." The doctor referred Mohan to Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, she said, where she was diagnosed with large B-cell lymphoma, a subtype of non-Hodgkin's lymphoma that affects the lymphatic system. Mohan, who had been working in an office just blocks away from the World Trade Center since 1996 -- and returned to work three weeks later -- was told by colleagues at the firm that they believed her cancer was linked to her 9/11 exposure. "I just couldn't wrap my head around it," she said. "I just got cancer. I guess I never associated it to [9/11] ever, not once. And I work here, two blocks away." Barasch, the attorney, said he also developed cancer. In 2018, he was diagnosed with prostate cancer, which is the second most common cancer in the 9/11 community, and then years later, he was diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma, a skin cancer, when doctors noticed irregular coloring under his thumb. "Of course, I knew right away it was caused by my exposure," Barasch said. "I was here on 9/11, caught in the dust cloud, moved back three weeks later. ... So, I knew, because this is what I do for a living, I suspect the average civilian has no idea." The fight for benefits Feal, the demolition supervisor, said he was injured at ground zero on Sept. 17, 2001, when a falling piece of steel landed on his left foot. He said he developed gangrene, then sepsis, and eventually required a partial amputation. He said he was denied compensation from the first 9/11 Victims' Compensation Fund (VCF) created by Congress because his injury occurred outside of a 96-hour window of eligibility for rescue workers. Feal was injured about 123 hours after the attack. A spokesperson for the VCF told ABC News that questions about denied compensation under the first VCF "should be directed to those who implemented the program and formulated the regulations," and pointed to remarks VCF Special Master Allison Turkel provided during a press briefing last week. The denial spurred Feal to become an advocate for 9/11 first responders. Feal founded the FealGood Foundation to help ground zero workers receive assistance, spread awareness and advocate, including lobbying members of Congress. "I had nothing to prove. I had a documented injury," Feal said. "All of those men and women, uniform and non-uniform, and those people that [went] to work, that went to school in lower Manhattan, they had to prove they got sick from 9/11." Feal and several first responders suffering from 9/11-related illnesses lobbied Congress in the late 2000s to help pass the James Zadroga 9/11 Health and Compensation Act of 2010, which provides health monitoring and aid to the first responders, volunteers and survivors of the attacks. This also led to the establishment of the WTC Health Program. James Zadroga was an NYPD officer who responded to recovery efforts at ground zero and died in 2006 of a respiratory disease. Two separate autopsies reportedly linked his death to inhaling toxic substances at ground zero and he was the first NYPD officer whose death was attributed to exposure at the site. Turkel said during the press briefing last week that the VCF has received more than 112,000 claims and has awarded more than $18.56 billion to over 77,000 claimants since reopening in 2011. The Zadroga Act expired in 2015, and Feal and first responders went down again to Washington, D.C. O'Connell, the firefighter, testified before Congress, as did late night host Jon Stewart in a clip that went viral. "What Jon did in those eight-and-a-half, nine minutes in front of Congress that America saw really moved the needle," Feal said. In December 2015, the James Zadroga 9/11 Health and Compensation Reauthorization Act passed, which extended medical benefits to affected individuals until 2090. 25 years later The first responders -- O'Connell, Wilson and Sanchez -- often conduct outreach, including speaking at schools, sharing with students their experiences at Ground Zero and their work to ensure first responders receive health care and compensation. "I think [9/11 is] an historical event, but also, we're still living with ... many of the repercussions that happened that day," Wilson said. "So, I would like to see more schools make sure they're teaching about it." The 9/11 Memorial & Museum announced earlier this year it will add a seventh moment of silence and a bell toll at this year's 25th commemoration ceremony to honor those who have died of illnesses related to their time at or near the World Trade Center site. For the past 24 years, there have been six moments of silence followed by bell tolls: two to mark the times when the planes struck the World Trade Center towers; one to mark when a plane struck the Pentagon; one to mark when a plane crashed in Shanksville, Pennsylvania; and two to mark the collapses of the Twin Towers. Knowing what they know now, and having suffered their various illnesses, O'Connell, Wilson and Sanchez all said they would respond to ground zero the way they did a quarter-century ago. "I wouldn't change a thing," O'Connell said. "I can't say anything else but that. Nothing, not a thing."

item.title: Triplets carry on father's FDNY legacy after 9/11
item.description:
Source: ABC News: Top Stories Score: 3.34
Brothers pursue firefighting careers inspired by late FDNY father who died from 9/11-related illnesses A firefighter father's 9/11 sacrifice is inspiring his triplet sons to serve. NEW YORK -- The triplet sons of an FDNY firefighter who responded to the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks are not identical, but they share a common past and will soon share a common future. They're three of the thousands of children who lost a parent 25 years ago on Sept. 11 or in the years after due to 9/11-related illnesses. William Gormley's sons - Raymond, Billy and Kevin - were just 3 years old when their father rushed to the twin towers on Sept. 11, 2001. While many children lost parents that day, the brothers grew up with their father, only later learning the toll his work at Ground Zero had taken on his health. "We all, for the most part, have the same lives in a lot of ways," Raymond said while sitting on a couch between his two brothers. "The same trauma, the same upbringing, the same everything. No one understands me like these two understand me." But for Kevin, Raymond and Billy didn't learn about what happened from the history books, they lived it and they always had each other to rely on. "This is a huge point my father always made, he said, 'These are your people. You were born with them, and this is what you got til the end,'" Kevin said. They don't remember what happened on Sept. 11, since they were so young. "Now, 25 years later, we're understanding the full grasp of what happened that day," Raymond said. William Gormley rushed to the twin towers after they were struck. Unlike many children, they didn't lose their dad that day. The reality of the work he did hit later in life. Firefighter Gormley worked on the pile for months, looking for survivors and later, for the remains of victims. "It makes you feel some pride knowing your father went in there selflessly to help others and do the best he could," Kevin said. The family said the long-term effects of his work became apparent over time. Growing up, the brothers accompanied their father to numerous doctor appointments but did not fully understand the severity of his health problems. "They never really told us anything really," Billy said. "But as kids we'd go to hospital waiting rooms in summer for doctors' appointments. But not knowing the severity." Raymond added, "Growing up he had skin cancer, sinus issues. So growing up as a kid, I personally never really understood what that came from. It wasn't until he was diagnosed with bladder cancer in 2016 that we put two together and realized it was from his time spent at Ground Zero." William Gormley died of bladder and lung cancer in 2017. According to a report, he was one of more than 400 fire and EMS workers who have died from 9/11-related illnesses. Asked whether his father would have made the same decision knowing what is now known about the dangers faced at Ground Zero, Raymond said there was no doubt. "One hundred percent, without hesitation," he said. "Not only him, but every single person he went down with that day would go down to the pile again, without a doubt." Today, a street in Brooklyn bears William Gormley's name, near the firehouse where he worked. Despite their father's advice to seek work outside the fire service, the brothers found themselves drawn to the profession. "My father would always say, 'When you get older, get a job where you sit behind a desk and write checks for people,'" Kyle said. "He'd always say, 'Work with your brain, not your hands,'" Raymond added. He went on to say, "So I'm a firefighter right now, an FDNY firefighter working at the same house he worked at, Ladder 174. So it's full circle really, it's crazy from him telling me to work with your brain, not your hands, and it's crazy I'm sleeping in the same bed he did 20 years ago." Billy hopes to join the fire service soon. "So I'm an EMT with the fire department at the moment," he said. "Waiting to join fire as well." Kevin has also applied to become a firefighter. "You hope one day, you can fill those shoes," he said. The report said Billy and Kevin could join the fire academy as soon as this month. The brothers said they were inspired not only by their father, but also by the support they received from firefighters after his death. "Once I saw the camaraderie, everyone coming together, people driving us around, his old coworkers taking care of us, the laughs, the tears," Raymond said. "After that in my mind, it was something I would really like to do." "Yeah, what they did was incredible how they took care of us, made sure everything was in order," another brother added. And this didn't just have an impact on the three brothers, it impacted the entire family, including their big sister, Bridget. "I think there's a beauty in that it was never forced down their throats," said Bridget. "My dad was never like, 'You're going to be a fireman!' Our dad was like, 'You're NOT going to be a fireman!'" Bridget has also dedicated her work to preserving the stories of those affected by Sept. 11. She works with 9/11 survivors and produced a documentary about the dangers of toxic dust exposure. It's called, "Dust: Lingering Legacy of 9/11." "Along the way, I got to know my father's friends better," she said. "I mean, I lost my dad, but I've got [sic] thousands of uncles now." For the Gormley siblings, the events of Sept. 11 continue to shape their lives and careers. They say their shared experiences and bond have helped them navigate a loss that has defined much of their lives. "Just being there for someone on their worst day, being their hope when there's no hope is really something special, something we take a lot of pride in," Raymond said. "We all, for the most part, have the same lives in a lot of ways, the same trauma, the same upbringing, the same everything, no one understands me like these two understand me," one of the brothers said. As they continue their careers in public service, the brothers say they are carrying forward the values their father exemplified, together.

item.title: Students with President Bush on 9/11 look back on day: 'You could see it on his face'
item.description:
Source: ABC News: Top Stories Score: 3.33
Students with President George W. Bush on 9/11 reflect on the day: 'You could see it on his face' Bush was visiting the school when he received news the nation was under attack. Former Sarasota, Florida, second grade student Krystal Davis remembers a wave of confusion washing over her and her classmates on the morning of Sept. 11, 2001, after a suited man whispered into the ear of the president of the United States, who was seated just in front of the students. Then-President George W. Bush was visiting Emma E. Booker Elementary School and had been listening intently to the children in Mrs. Sandra Daniels' second-grade class flexing their reading skills, when the look of admiration on his face suddenly gave way to an expression of concern. Chief of Staff Andrew Card had just relayed to Bush that a second plane had crashed into the World Trade Center in New York City. "America is under attack," he later recalled whispering to the president. 9/11 Tribute in Light: Live from Lower Manhattan,” a one-hour ABC News multiplatform live special, premieres on Friday, Sept.11, at 8:00 p.m. EDT across ABC, Disney+, Hulu, National Geographic, ABC Owned Television Stations livestreams and ABC News Live. "You could see the shift with [the president] once he got the message, and then you could see it on his face," Davis said in an interview with ABC News commemorating 25 years since the 9/11 attacks. "And then the shift of him going back to his normal self and smiling like, 'I don't want to alarm the kids.'" Teacher Daniels told Sarasota ABC affiliate WWSB in an interview published Tuesday that she "immediately knew something was wrong" at that moment. "His entire demeanor changed," she recalled, referring to Bush. Davis described the concern among the students as Bush was escorted out of the room, once the reading lesson concluded. "And we're just like, 'OK, in the middle of reading, what happened? What did we do? Like, did we do something wrong? Did he not like us reading or whatever?'" Davis recalled. Though unaware at the time, Davis and her classmates had a front-row seat to history. Meanwhile, 10-year-old Stevenson Tose'-Rigell, son of principal Gwendolyn Tose'-Rigell, was in the school's library eagerly awaiting the president's arrival, where Bush was slated to deliver a speech on his signature education policy, the No Child Left Behind Act. "I'd probably say it was a couple of hours at least we were out there on the podium waiting around. We didn't know what was going on at the time," he said. He continued, "They were trying to entertain us a little bit and, you know, keep, everybody feeling kind of excited … but we're waiting around for hours, you know, it's like, 'Man, this is this a long time waiting around for someone.'" Tose'-Rigell said Bush did eventually enter the room, but the 10-year-old quickly realized the speech Bush was delivering would not touch on education policy. Instead, Bush delivered an address to the nation, confirming reports of "an apparent terrorist attack on our country." "We're pretty much [thinking], 'Sounds like we're under attack,'" Tose'-Rigell recalled. "So yeah, it was definitely far off from the script." Back in Daniels' classroom, Davis said the children were moved into another room, where a teacher tried to explain what was going on. Davis said it was at that moment the students watched the images of the World Trade Center's Twin Towers crashing down on a television. Tose'-Rigell said he was not able to leave school right away, as his mother was the school's principal. Instead, he said he watched the devastation unfold on a small TV in the school's front office. From Sarasota, Bush boarded Air Force One, departing Florida for military bases in Louisiana and Nebraska before arriving back in Washington, D.C., that night. By day's end, nearly 3,000 people had died in terror attacks at the World Trade Center in New York City; the Pentagon building in Arlington, Virginia; and in Shanksville, Pennsylvania, the crash site of United Airlines Flight 93. A quarter century later, as the country continues to grapple with the ramifications of that day, so too do the alumni of Emma E. Booker Elementary who were at the school the day of the attacks. In May, the school commemorated the 25th anniversary of 9/11 by welcoming a steel beam from the World Trade Center, brought by the Tunnel to Towers Foundation, which allows the public to "put their hand on that steel and feel the loss and sacrifice that was made that day." Stephen Siller Jr., whose father Stephen Siller was one of the 343 New York City Fire Department members killed on 9/11, said bringing the steel beam to Emma E. Booker Elementary was one of the most impactful visits he's made with the foundation's Steel Across America campaign, out of dozens of similar trips. "Little kids ... understand that, you know, this is a sacred piece of history," he said. "...It once held up the Twin Towers, it once held floors and walls, and now it holds the gravity of that day." In a statement to ABC News, Sarasota County Schools Superintendent Terry Connor reflected on the impact 9/11 had on the district. "For Sarasota County Schools, the legacy of Sept. 11 carries a uniquely personal connection," the statement read in part. It added, "On this 25th anniversary, we honor those who were lost, remember those who answered the call, and express our gratitude to all who continue to serve our communities and our country." Speaking with ABC News, the former students of Emma E. Booker Elementary reflected on their intersection with history, recognizing the grave impact on those directly affected by the tragedy while also considering the mark it left on their own lives. "You realize, 'People really lost they live[s] yesterday,'" Davis said, recounting the days following 9/11. "And we were right in the midst of everything. [The president] was right here in Sarasota, Florida, [when it happened]." Davis, who currently works in healthcare but said she aspires to be a police officer, said the events that day inspired her to pursue a career serving others. "As a second grader, I couldn't really explain," Davis said, adding that she would later realize her experience left her "wanting to do more for my community, wanting to do more for myself and my kids." "That day is going to always be something I never forget," she added. Tose'-Rigell said he also carries complex feelings surrounding his memory of that day, including sadness and a sense of pride. His mother, the school's former principal, died in 2007 after a battle with cancer. "I always knew my mom was a rock star, you know? In my mind, you know, she was my superhero," Tose'-Rigell said, describing seeing his mother on the world stage on Sept. 11, 2001, and the "national recognition" she received. He added that seeing her in archival footage from that day brought back memories of her each year on the anniversary of 9/11. "It feels like she comes back," he said. "You know, like, once a year, [she] reincarnates right onscreen again."

item.title: A 9/11 widow reflects on 25 years of grief and what comes next
item.description:
Source: ABC News: Top Stories Score: 3.01
When the 9/11 attacks unfolded, 25 years ago, most Americans remember exactly where they were at the moments hijacked planes crashed into the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and in a remote field in Shanksville, Pennsylvania. Marian Fontana was in Brooklyn and had plans to celebrate her eighth wedding anniversary that day with her husband, Dave Fontana, a New York City firefighter. He stayed past his shift and like so many other firefighters, rushed to Lower Manhattan when the first plane struck, she said. "And I dropped my son off for his second day of kindergarten," Marian Fontana said. "He was five. And I sat, I called [Dave] and said, 'you know, are you ready to go?'" Fontana said there was a change of shifts around the time of the attack. After the attacks, rows of media trucks were set up along West Side Highway, more than a mile from Ground Zero where first responders and crews searched for victims. Frank Schramm, a professional photographer, says he grabbed his camera and began documenting scenes around the city. Looking back, he says it was one of the few ways to mark history before the era of smartphones and social media. Reporters and photographers were often the "first witnesses of 9/11," he said, "and in a way they, by being there, were speaking to the world about what was going on." For millions of Americans, the attacks were not something they experienced directly but witnessed on a TV screen. Regardless, the experience still left its mark. Mindy Notheis says she was getting ready for work at her home in St. Louis, Missouri. "And the first plane hit, there was tons of confusion and then the second plane hit and everybody knew that something was drastically wrong and then you just saw --within a matter of what, an hour? -- the towers fall," she said. Notheis says she recently visited the 9/11 Memorial in Lower Manhattan with her niece -- who wasn't even born when the attacks happened -- paying their respects to the thousands of names inscribed in the bronze around the twin reflecting pools where the towers once stood. She says she has made it a point to bring her other nieces and nephews to see the 9/11 Memorial and Museum over the years. New York City, its residents and families who lost loved ones showed resilience in those initial days, weeks and months that followed. After the attacks, relatives of victims, political leaders and the public have gathered at the 9/11 ceremonies in Lower Manhattan. But many other families have marked the anniversary in private. Marian Fontana and her son, Aidan, who's now 30, say they will go to the beach to pay tribute to Dave. "It's a mixed bag because I'm grateful that people remember, and yet sometimes it's really hard to go back there," Marian Fontana said. "It's very traumatic. And so I've really always let my son decide what we do on that day, and I think because it's been such a public event that we've been part of, he always chooses a very private." Marian Fontana says after 25 years of raising her son and grieving, she can start thinking about what's next. She says that includes getting back to activities like comedy and writing, along with launching a podcast called "Firehouse Files," which features firsthand accounts from firefighters and first responders. "I wanted to give back for the huge generosity that was shown to me after 9/11 and this overwhelming flow of generosity from the world," she said. "And I felt this duty to give back, and I still do. But there was a point at which I was kind of sacrificing my own, you know, my own well-being. So I'm kind of spending this next chapter kind of focusing on myself, returning to theater, returning to the things I love, and really trying to make this last chapter a happy one." Michelle Franzen is a correspondent and anchor for ABC News and ABC Radio

item.title: 9/11 firefighter's son spends months bringing steel from World Trade Center across US
item.description:
Source: ABC News: Top Stories Score: 2.78
The steel 'embodies his soul': 9/11 family takes World Trade Center beam across US Stephen Siller Jr. was just 9 months old when his firefighter dad died on 9/11. On the morning of Sept. 11, 2001, 34-year-old New York City firefighter Stephen Siller had just finished his overnight shift when he heard a call come in on the scanner. "He immediately knew something was awry," so he drove to his firehouse in Brooklyn, his son, Stephen Siller Jr., told ABC News. "When he got there, he realized his whole unit had responded [to the World Trade Center]," Siller Jr. said. "So he grabbed his gear, threw it in his truck and started to make his way to the World Trade Center. But on 9/11, they shut down every entryway into Manhattan." He parked his car by the Brooklyn Battery Tunnel, Siller Jr. said, put about 60 pounds of gear on his back, and ran through the tunnel to the South Tower of the World Trade Center. Stephen Siller was among 343 New York City Fire Department members killed on 9/11. He was survived by his close-knit siblings, his wife Sally, and his five children, including Stephen Jr., who was 9 months old. Siller Jr., now 25, doesn't have his own memories of his father, but he's poured his energy into honoring those who died on 9/11. And to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the terror attacks, he spent the last four months bringing a 16,900-pound steel beam from the World Trade Center to dozens of cities across the U.S. in hopes that seeing a piece of history up close will help Americans remember, learn and be inspired. The Steel Across America campaign allows the public to "put their hand on that steel and feel the loss and sacrifice that was made that day -- the sacrifice of first responders and their loss, the loss of innocent people who just went to work," Stephen Siller Jr.'s uncle, Frank Siller, told ABC News. "9/11 Tribute in Light: Live from Lower Manhattan," a one-hour ABC News multiplatform live special, premieres on Friday, Sept.11, at 8:00 p.m. EDT across ABC, Disney+, Hulu, National Geographic, ABC Owned Television Stations livestreams and ABC News Live. Siller Jr. described the entire tour as "incredibly powerful." At the first stop, ground zero, a firefighter whose entire unit was killed on 9/11 "walked up to the steel and he put his hand on it, and he was overcome with emotion," Siller Jr. recalled. "You could just immediately see tears rushing down his face. And he started to hug the steel like he was hugging his friends he lost 25 years ago." To Siller Jr., the steel represents the more than 1,000 bodies never recovered from the World Trade Center -- including his father's. "Who they are is ingrained in that steel, what they did is ingrained in that steel. It holds the memory of that day," he said. "It's the most overwhelming piece of history I've ever come across." The beam represents "resilience, strength, but also sacrifice," Frank Siller added. "... Ground zero is my brother's burial place, obviously. But the steel has his -- embodies his soul, and the souls of so many." As Siller Jr. spent his summer traveling the U.S., from Oklahoma to California to Mount Rushmore in South Dakota, he said he was surprised by how many people had personal connections to the terror attacks, like the police officer he met in Seattle whose uncle was killed on 9/11. "And we had thousands of people show up to 35 events across the country who may not have had a connection to 9/11," he added, "but for them, they wanted to mourn that day, they wanted to make sure they never forgot." "Everywhere we went was incredible -- the support, it was mind-boggling," Siller Jr. said. "In Texarkana, a small, little town in Texas, we had about 1,000 people show up to an event. It was unbelievable. You know, companies letting all their employees out of work to go see this piece of steel." Siller Jr. found one of the most memorable stops to be Emma E. Booker Elementary School in Florida, where President George W. Bush was reading to students on the morning of Sept. 11, 2001, when he learned of the attacks. "We normally have stairs that go up to the steel truck," Siller Jr. explained, but on this May visit to the school, it was pouring rain. Still, the children "were begging the firemen, 'Hey, can we get up? We just want to touch the steel,'" Siller Jr. said. As the kids were lifted up, they began "praying over this steel," he recalled. "Little kids who understand that, you know, this is a sacred piece of history ... it once held up the Twin Towers, it once held floors and walls, and now it holds the gravity of that day," he said. "I was really shocked at how interested they were," he said. To Frank Siller and Siller Jr., educating the next generation was a key goal of the Steel Across America campaign. "These kids were incredible; they were patient ... and they consistently showed up," Siller Jr. said. "No matter where we were in the country, there were families there, which was beautiful -- fathers and mothers wanting to teach their kids." "I was 9 months old on 9/11 -- if you were born after me, and not in New York City, you know, there's a high chance that you have no real understanding of that day," he continued. "It's important that that lesson is taught to these kids -- there's so much to be pulled from the sacrifices made." The Steel Across America campaign is part of the Tunnel to Towers Foundation, started by Frank Siller in honor of his brother's run from the Brooklyn Battery Tunnel to the World Trade Center. The foundation supports military members, first responders and their families across the U.S. The foundation is currently providing wounded veterans and first responders with mortgage-free, specially-adapted smart homes. "We didn't let Stephen just perish in that rubble and let that story end there. No, we took his act of courage and sacrifice and said, 'We're going to do good with it,'" Frank Siller said. "Would Stephen make that run again through the tunnel, knowing he was gonna die? I think he knew he was gonna die," Frank Siller said. "At the very least, he knew it was a strong possibility that he might not be coming home. And to think that he did that, knowing how much he loved Sally and his kids, people like that are few and far between. ... And it's got to be recognized and never forgotten."

item.title: Remembering the FDNY chaplain who raced to the Twin Towers on 9/11 to pray
item.description:
Source: ABC News: Top Stories Score: 2.29
Remembering the FDNY chaplain who raced to the Twin Towers on 9/11 to pray As chaos unfolded on Sept. 11 FDNY Chaplain Father Mychal Judge ran toward it. NEW YORK -- FDNY Chaplain Mychal Judge raced to the twin towers on Sept. 11, 2001 from his midtown Engine Company One / Ladder Company 24. As the chaos unfolded, he prayed for the people trapped, for the rescuers and for humanity. His legacy of hope and service live on a quarter century after his death when the south tower collapsed. "Today we will bury Mychal Judge," Father Michael Duffy said in a homily delivered after the chaplain's death. "We will bury his body, but not his spirit." Judge, described as a close friend of Duffy and the first official victim of the 9/11 terror attacks, raced to the twin towers as the chaos unfolded. "I pray for him every day," Duffy said. "And I think whenever there's excitement around or a fire truck or an ambulance or somebody need consolation, I think, 'Mychael Judge would be right there with them.'" A French film crew happened to be profiling the FDNY that day and captured Father Judge's final moments inside the lobby of the north tower. He was praying for people jumping from the fire and smoke on the upper floors when the south tower collapsed, sending forth a tsunami of concrete and steel. Duffy recalled learning of Judge's death while at his soup kitchen in Philadelphia. "I had no doubt that when the plane hit the building, that he would be there," Duffy said. An image of Judge's body being carried from the rubble became one of the enduring symbols of the attacks. "That kind of is an icon that represents 2,000 people," Duffy said. "And the helplessness of goodness being overcome by evil and all those 2,000 people who died and how they were loved by their friends and families." He went on to say, "I think that that picture symbolized it, that brought it concretely, that's why we feel empty." The two men first met in the 1970s as Franciscan priests assigned to the same parish in East Rutherford, New Jersey. Duffy said Judge became a mentor without officially being a mentor. Duffy also remembered Judge's humility. "He had no airs about him, like he was better or standoffish," Duffy said. "So if you want to share what's really going on in your life, you want to gravitate to the most receptive person and that was him." Born in Brooklyn, Judge shined shoes near the Church of St. Francis of Assisi on 31st Street before joining the Franciscan order. He was appointed FDNY chaplain in 1992 and ministered to people from all walks of life. "There's another part of him that I don't know if too many people know that about him, he loved to be where the action was," Duffy said. Four days after Judge's death, Duffy traveled to New York to deliver the homily at his funeral, as Judge had wanted. Thousands gathered at the church on 31st Street.
