item.title: A billionaire wanted $125 million for his Aspen compound. He got $33.5 million.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.23
Billionaire and member of the famed Koch family Bill Koch tried to offload his massive compound in Aspen for nine figures, but ended up selling it at auction for nearly $100 million below the listing price. The founder of Oxbow Carbon bought the ski-town property in 2007 for $26.5 million and later added 31 acres. The compound hit the market in 2015 with an asking price of $100 million. Koch eventually dropped the price to $80 million the following year. In 2020, he sold the additional 31 acres he added for $14.5 million, but held on to the lodge and the rest of the 52-acre property. In 2025, Koch relisted the property at $125 million, but it didn't sell. In 2026, Koch went the auction route — a tactic sometimes employed for notable properties. The property finally sold in July, but for a fraction of its original listing price. The Wall Street Journal reported that the winning bid was $33.5 million — a 73% decrease from its peak listing price. Koch's lofty $125 million price would have been the most expensive sale in Colorado history, beating Palatir Alex Karp's recent $120 million ranch purchase in nearby Snowmass, Colorado. Koch, who has a net worth of $2 billion, according to Forbes, sold his stake in Koch Industries to his brothers for $470 million in 1983. That left him with plenty of money to make renovations to his Colorado ranch. The recently sold main lodge spans 16,600 square feet and is accompanied by seven cabins — one of which is a home gym. The property also includes hot tubs, hiking trails, and an altitude-acclimation room. See what else awaits the new owner of this massive compound. He later added about 31 more acres to the property. He eventually sold those extra acres for $14.5 million in 2020. In 2015, Koch listed the entire property for $100 million. He dropped the price to $80 million in 2016, but it didn't sell. The property was delisted and relisted various times. Ten years after the original listing, Koch listed the property again for $125 million at the beginning of 2025. Before then, he tried renting out the main lodge for $300,000 a week. The price was dropped one final time to $99 million at the end of 2025 before eventually heading to auction. The property went to auction through Concierge Auctions in July. This 52-acre compound sold for $33.5 million at auction. The auction went on from July 7 to 17. Eight structures are spread out across the compound. The main lodge is 16,631 square feet. Counting the other buildings, there are 14 bedrooms and 17 bathrooms. The other buildings bring the total square footage to 25,277. The lodge, also known as the primary cabin, is two stories with 30-foot ceilings. It has a dining room that seats 20 people, a screening room, and a living room with a wall of windows that faces the mountains. Other amenities around the property include a gym, hiking trails, two hot tubs, and an altitude-acclimation room. And if there's not enough to do on the grounds, the estate is 11 miles from Aspen by car. Correction: February 28, 2025 — Bill Koch's Aspen property was once on the market for $300,000 a week, not $300,000 a month. It's also unclear when Koch acquired 30 additional acres that he sold in 2020. An earlier version of this story said he added them in 2015.

item.title: Brooks Brothers was steps from the World Trade Center on 9/11. Its creative director still can't look at the pictures.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 4.13
Like many people, Brooks Brothers creative director Michael Bastian remembers exactly where he was on the morning of September 11, 2001. "9/11 is personal for me," he told Business Insider during New York Fashion Week on Thursday as Brooks Brothers presented its Spring/Summer 2027 collection. "I was in the air on 9/11. I was flying back from a trade show in Paris. I was working at Bergdorf Goodman at the time. And I ended up in Nova Scotia in Halifax, Canada." After hijacked planes hit the World Trade Center and the Pentagon, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a full national ground stop, shutting US airspace for the first time in history. It took Bastian four days to get back home to a New York City that was no longer recognizable. "It really changed everyone's life," Bastian, who joined Brooks Brothers as creative director in 2020, said. Brooks Brothers, a 208-year-old menswear brand founded by Henry Sands Brooks in New York City, is also part of the history of that terrible day and the recovery efforts that followed. In the immediate aftermath of the September 11 terrorist attacks, a Brooks Brothers store, located next to the World Trade Center at One Liberty Plaza, served a different, tragic purpose: a makeshift morgue. Once a place where job candidates deliberated over ties ahead of interviews in the Twin Towers, the men's shirt department at Brooks Brothers transformed into a holding area for bodies — and body parts — pulled from the rubble of the World Trade Center. Victims' remains were held there until they could be moved to New York City's Office of the Chief Medical Examiner for identification. The Brooks Brothers location at One Liberty Plaza sustained heavy damage when the Twin Towers collapsed, but reopened exactly one year after the attacks. While the store is no longer there — it closed in 2018 amid planned renovations and relocated a few blocks away — the memories stay with Bastian 25 years later. "I still can't look at the pictures," he said. "If you were here, it really affected you, as a New Yorker, as an American."

item.title: 5 jewelry trends that are in right now and 4 that are out, according to jewelers and stylists
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.91
From a diamond necklace to a pair of gold hoops, a simple touch of jewelry has long been an easy way to add just a little something to any outfit. But this fall, straightforward and understated styles seem to be taking a back seat to pieces with more personality. That's why Business Insider asked two jewelers and a stylist to share the trends they're seeing take off this autumn and the ones that are starting to fade. Here's what they said. Men's statement jewelry is on the rise. Nishit Mehta, president and CEO of La Joya Jewelry, said he's seeing men wear more expressive jewelry, including thicker rings with stones, as well as brooches. JesseRay Vasquez, jewelry designer and the founder of the brand Nickho Rey, also said statement rings are an especially strong trend for men right now. "I've never had this much of an interest from guys," Vasquez told BI. Color is showing up more. This summer's jewelry trends embraced plenty of color through beaded necklaces and other styles. And according to Kendra Sharpe, a stylist and founder of Kendra Sharpe Styling and Creative, that theme is continuing into fall. However, she recommended shifting toward jewel tones, browns, and deeper purples to complement the new season. Vasquez also said he's seeing pops of bright color, specifically paired with classic metals like silver and white gold. Statement cuffs can make any outfit pop. According to Sharpe, statement cuffs are a growing trend. Part of their appeal is their simplicity: rather than stacking several smaller pieces of jewelry, wearing a single large cuff can stand out on its own. "The larger the cuff, the better," Sharpe told BI. She also recommended experimenting styling options, like wearing the cuff over a long sleeve rather than directly on your wrist. Pearls are getting bigger and more irregular. Sharpe said pearls are trending this fall season, but with a fresher, less traditional feel. She told BI these iterations will be supersized, multistrand, more irregular, and natural-looking. "I think the more unique the shape is, the better," Sharpe said. She also noted there are a variety of ways to wear pearls this fall, whether as a single pendant, a strand, or an uneven set of earrings. Oversize pendant necklaces and collars are having a moment. The experts told BI that oversize necklaces are trending this season — specifically large pendants that hang lower and create a dramatic look. Vasquez said he's seeing larger collar necklaces, in particular, gain popularity. These styles are typically bulkier than traditional link necklaces and can be layered with fine jewelry. On the other hand, smooth metals are being replaced by textured materials. Vasquez said he's seeing a shift from smooth, polished metals to textured styles that add detail in unexpected ways. He said the style can include faceted links, engraved swirls, or other dimensional details that add more interest to the jewelry. Matching jewelry sets won't be as popular. Sharpe said perfectly matching your necklaces, rings, and earrings is starting to feel too safe for today's more playful styles. Instead, the stylist recommends thinking outside the box with asymmetrical or dramatic statement earrings, sculptural pieces, or unexpected textures. Thicker engagement bands and large statement stones are replacing dainty rings. Mehta said minimal, thin engagement bands are being replaced by chunkier, gold alternatives. He pointed to Miley Cyrus' engagement ring as one celebrity example of this shift. The jeweler also said he's seeing less interest in halo settings with clusters of small stones, in favor of one large statement stone. "People want one big statement stone that really catches attention, and it becomes a talking point," Mehta told BI. Rose gold is not as popular as it once was. A few years ago, rose gold was having a major moment, but according to Sharpe, it's not shining quite as brightly anymore. Instead, she said people are leaning more into mixing yellow gold and silver to create more dimension — especially when wearing a monochromatic outfit.

item.title: Apple's new CEO was asked about 'pervert glasses.' Here was his response.
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 3.37
Apple would kindly like to stay far away from Meta's ongoing reputational challenges with AI glasses. Apple CEO John Ternus was recently asked about how the company thinks about privacy in the age of AI wearables in light of backlash around AI glasses like Meta's. After all, Apple is rumored to be cooking up some AI glasses of its own in its labs. "I know you can't talk about unannounced products, but what do you think about the backlash around what people are calling, you know, 'pervert glasses,'" Tom's Guide editor in chief Mark Spoonauer asked. Before Ternus could answer, Greg Joswiak, Apple's senior vice president of worldwide marketing who also being interviewed, quipped: "That's quite a marketing slogan." The remark drew laughter from Ternus. Meta is actively fighting back at that perception with a marketing blitz that emphasizes the AI glasses' light that alerts people when the recording feature is activated. It's also taken steps to thwart users who tamper with that light and pledged to remove "harassing" videos recorded by the AI glasses from Instagram (Business Insider has found those moderation efforts are off to a bumpy start.) Meta declined to comment on the Apple executives' remarks. Beyond some laughter at a rival's expense, the pair of Apple execs instead looked to explain how the company hopes to address privacy concerns when it releases two new AI-enabled listening features alongside the next generation of Apple Watches. "We wanted to do this in a way that people feel comfortable using it, and people around the user feel comfortable about its existence," Ternus said. While its first foldable phone, iPhone Duo, stole the show, Apple also announced that Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 will come with optional "audio intelligence" features that, depending on a user's preference, can mean Siri is always listening to your conversations throughout the day. Apple says the features don't start working until the on-device AI detects speech and that no audio is recorded or stored. One feature, "Siri Recap," can listen to meetings or even your whole day and generate what the company calls "high-level" notes on what happened. Another feature, Live Rewind, shows a text snippet of the last 15 seconds of what was just said around you on the Apple Watch's screen. Ternus and Joswiak emphasized that neither feature includes speaker attribution. There's also no audio recording that the user could store for later playback. Apple also says it doesn't have access to the raw audio files. Joswiak also said this means Apple can't be compelled to turn over an audio file. "It's just those higher-level notes to remind you of that without getting into all the stuff that really is privacy concerning which a lot of other products are doing," Joswiak said. While they did not mention it, the Live Rewind feature also includes audio and visual cues on the Apple Watch's screen — similar to the recording light on Meta's AI glasses — to alert those around the watch wearer that the last 15 seconds of conversation is being processed. Apple says "Live Rewind" and "Siri Recap" will be available in beta later this year. Both Apple execs also said that current apps have long allowed users to record themselves and those around them. While they didn't mention anything in particular, AI-enabled apps and devices like Granola and Plaud are also designed for such use cases. But the Apple execs' response to the question highlights that Apple is seeking to differentiate its approach to information-gathering on AI devices. Whether or not people ultimately feel comfortable about Apple Watches listening in on their conversations is another question altogether.

item.title: Confluent cofounder says believing in AI's upside means reckoning with its 'dark side'
item.description:
Source: Business Insider Score: 2.89
AI safety fears have recently moved from an abstract Silicon Valley argument to a series of unnerving real-world episodes. Jay Kreps, a former Anthropic board member and a cofounder of data-streaming software company Confluent, says it is important to take them seriously. In a Thursday night X post, he argued that AI backers need to contend with the technology's downside risks as its capabilities improve — and that fears about those risks are not merely a cynical marketing ploy. "Most positive use cases for AI have a corresponding 'dark version,'" Kreps wrote. A system that is superhuman at coding could also be superhuman at hacking, he said. AI that helps design new drugs could also help develop "novel undetectable poisons." As AI's capabilities have improved, Silicon Valley has faced several unnerving headlines over the past couple of months. On Tuesday, Jacob Coxon, an Anthropic researcher who previously worked at OpenAI, announced his resignation, writing on X that the labs are "gambling with our lives." Geoffrey Hinton, the so-called "Godfather of AI," said a 10% chance that AI could wipe out humanity within a decade was "not unreasonable." Their warnings have received pushback from big-name AI backers. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, for example, has called the wave of warnings a possible "setup" and a "psy op" in X posts. There have been several high-profile incidents that have highlighted AI's alignment issues. In July, an internal OpenAI research model circumvented the test environment's controls, accessed the internet, and compromised parts of another company, Hugging Face. Anthropic, meanwhile, disclosed this week that Claude models, during closed cybersecurity exercises, accessed the real internet and went beyond the scope of their tests. In his Thursday X post, Kreps said he is confident the industry can build better guardrails — but warned that it has not yet done so. "Talking about these issues is just common sense. It's not a sign of some kind of neuroticism or pessimism," he wrote. "Mocking people who are worried about this or talking about it, without anything substantive to say about how we can be sure these problems won't arise, is not really a very helpful contribution."

item.title: Why we're still looking for dark matter
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.71
On September 1, 2026, scientists at a dark matter detector called LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) reported they had observed an event, a particle interaction, that they were unable to explain. The team, based in South Dakota in the United States, said the event resembled what they think a dark matter particle should produce when it collides with liquid xenon, one of a range of materials used for detecting dark matter. They stopped short of calling it the discovery, or proof of dark matter, that many in the field have been hunting for almost 100 years. The term "dark matter" was coined by physicist Fritz Zwicky in 1933 as a means to describe unseen matter that would explain fast-moving galaxies. The LUX-ZEPLIN observation came just days after the release of the second season of Dark Matter, a sci-fi thriller starring Joel Edgerton and Jennifer Connelly. Both events pushed the term "dark matter" back into people's minds. Here's what you need to know, with the science separated from the series. What is dark matter in simple terms? Dark matter is often described as an "invisible" substance. But it may be better described as "transparent" because it can be seen, or detected, by the gravitational attraction it exerts. That said, it neither emits nor reflects light and has never been observed directly. So, in that sense, it is invisible. Is it true that 95% of the universe is invisible? Yes, roughly. Ordinary matter — everything that can be seen or touched — accounts for about 5% of the universe. Dark matter accounts for about 27%, and dark energy, a separate force linked to the accelerating expansion of the universe, about 68%. Together they account for about 95%. A different figure of 85% is dark matter's share of matter alone. But does dark matter really exist? The strongest evidence that dark matter exists comes from the so-called Bullet Cluster, which formed when two galaxy clusters collided. The collision produced hot gas clouds that interacted. This interaction revealed mass in the gas clouds that distributed differently from the gas. Researchers said that mass could be dark matter. How do scientists search for dark matter on Earth? Scientists use detectors like the LUX-ZEPLIN that passively wait for interactions between naturally occurring particles and detect radiation. They tend to be buried deep underground, where the surrounding rock blocks cosmic radiation that would otherwise distort signals. They are built from materials chosen for their very low levels of trace radioactivity, so a genuine detection is not lost in background noise. The LUX-ZEPLIN detector specifically works by watching for a faint flash of light and pulse of electric charge released when a passing particle strikes a liquid xenon particle. Liquid xenon, a noble gas, has good properties for detecting radiation. What is dark matter made of? These are leading candidate particles: WIMPs, or weakly interacting massive particles, are the longest-standing theory. They are heavy and interact only rarely with ordinary matter. Axions, which are lighter and behave more coherently than WIMPs. A team at Kyoto University, Japan, say data from Earth's magnetic field could be used to search for axions. What does dark matter do to humans? Dark matter passes through the body constantly without measurable effect. Billions of candidate particles cross through a person every second but only about 10 strike a nucleus in the body over a year. The resulting radiation exposure is far lower than what people receive from radon or cosmic rays. Edited by: Zulfikar Abbany

item.title: The 'end of an era' as Goethe-Institut in Russia closes
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.64
In recent years, Moscow has declared numerous foreign foundations and organizations "undesirable" and banned them from operating in the country. However, despite the significantly deteriorated relations between Russia and the West as a result of Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine, the Goethe-Institut, which opened in Russia in 1992, had been able to continue operating. But that's no longer the case. Employees of the Goethe-Institut must stop working on September 13 — and staff members sent from Germany must leave the country by that date. According to Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, the closure of the Goethe-Institut's three locations in Moscow, St. Petersburg and Novosibirsk comes as a response to the announced closure of the Russian House in Berlin, the minister said. Germany intends to terminate its contract with the cultural and events venue as a punitive measure. The German government holds Russia responsible for the attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport. "The announcement by the Russian foreign minister marks the end of an era in German-Russian cultural relations," wrote Gesche Joost, president of the Goethe-Institut, in a press release. She said it was bad news for people in Russia and that the Goethe-Institut had connected the two countries through culture and language. As early as 2023, the Russian Foreign Ministry had demanded the Goethe-Institut's staff be significantly cut. Cultural exchanges with German artists were limited extent and kept to digital formats. Nevertheless, interest in German-language courses remained high, with around 10,000 students taking part. "Our work in Russia was and remains important," Joost said, referring to learning the German language, the many encounters and mutual understanding between people. A fresh start after World War II For the past 75 years, the Goethe-Institut has represented Germany abroad, promoting the German language and sharing German culture with people around the world. It was founded in 1951, at a time when Germany was seeking to rebuild international trust in the aftermath of World War II and the crimes of the Nazi regime. Originally established as the "Goethe Association for the Further Training of Foreign Teachers of German," the organization initially focused on inviting foreign teachers to Germany for language training. Its mission soon expanded, however, to promoting the German language abroad. The first Goethe-Institut opened its doors in Athens in 1952, and just a decade later, the organization had already established 54 branches around the world. Today, the Goethe-Institut operates a global network of 154 institutions in 100 countries, employing nearly 4,500 people. Around one million people take an official German exam at a Goethe-Institut or one of its partner organizations each year. In a speech honoring the institute's 75th anniversary, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier emphasized the significance of promoting German culture abroad, stating, "For countries like ours, which are not great powers, our foreign policy will continue to have to rest on four pillars: yes, military strength, so that we are taken seriously, but also smart diplomacy to devise solutions and forge alliances; wherever possible, an international legal order to provide a framework and direction in addition; and, fourthly, culture and science as soft power, as something we offer to the wider world." From classical music to jazz One element that proved crucial to the institute's success from its founding onward is its credibility as an independent association. Although two-thirds of its funding stems from the German Foreign Office, the organization itself determines its programs — and over the decades, these programs have regularly been adapted to be in step with the prevailing political and social climate. The institute promptly made its ambitions clear to expand its scope beyond mere language instruction by striving to provide a more comprehensive picture of Germany through a range of cultural and informational programs. "And it was also very clear that this was not about exporting so-called German culture to the world," explained Gesche Joost, president of the Goethe-Institut since 2024. "On the contrary — the aim was to reflect on how we could have a fresh start and how we want to shape society and the future together." In its early years, the institute's cultural programs deliberately drew on Germany's rich heritage in the areas of classical music and literature. Figures such as Schiller, Bach and Beethoven had lost none of their international appeal despite the Nazi era. Then, in the 1960s, German jazz was a hit among the institute's cultural exports — with musician and composer Klaus Doldinger and his band touring the globe. Over the decades, Nobel Prize-winning authors Günter Grass, Heinrich Böll and Herta Müller also traveled internationally on behalf of the Goethe-Institut. With the spirit of change ushered in by the generation of 1968, with flower power and student protests, the institute's profile changed once again, and it increasingly incorporated critical viewpoints on social issues into its programs, including efforts to critically examine Germany's Nazi past. A space for dialogue In this period, West Germany was redefining itself under Social Democratic Chancellor Willy Brandt. In 1970, sociologist Ralf Dahrendorf, then parliamentary state secretary at the foreign office, announced a new set of guiding principles. Cultural policy was to become the "third pillar of foreign policy." But Dahrendorf didn't simply wish to give culture a higher profile — he advocated for a new way of thinking. "What we give is worth only as much as our willingness to receive," he said. "Openness toward others is thus a principle of our foreign cultural policy." As a result, the Goethe-Institut moved away from the idea of simply exporting culture and toward dialogue, cooperation and reciprocal learning. That approach continues to guide the organization's work today. While Germany was divided, East and West also competed to forge political alliances abroad through their foreign cultural policies, especially during the Cold War. In the 1970s, the East German press even spread rumors that Goethe-Instituts were being used to conduct espionage. After the Iron Curtain fell in 1989, the Goethe-Institut opened numerous new locations in Eastern Europe and the former Eastern Bloc, including in Moscow in 1992. Despite turbulent times, its doors had remained open there until now. For its part, the Kyiv branch, in Ukraine, has also remained open throughout the war. The institute offers a flexible hybrid scheme for its German courses there: When an air raid alert sounds, in-person classes are moved to a shelter. A range of digital and hybrid options are also available if necessary. The 'turning point' has already come "I have the impression that working under crisis conditions has become the norm in many regions," Gesche Joost explained. "Either because democracy is being pushed back, because colleagues are working under censorship or because they are being threatened by armed conflicts." In many Goethe-Instituts, she said, the much-discussed Zeitenwende — or "turning point" — has long been reality. This term entered public discourse after a famous speech by former German Chancellor Olaf Scholz after the war in Ukraine broke out in 2022 and refers to the dawn of an era marked by geopolitical turmoil in Europe. "We've recognized that we're important partners for civil society in crisis regions. At the same time, we have to make sure that we act sensitively and diplomatically so that we don't get expelled," added Joost. In times where freedom of cultural expression, freedom of speech as well as science and education are increasingly coming under pressure, the Goethe-Institut plans to continue providing spaces for dialogue where open debate, critical reflection and cultural exchange remain possible. Meanwhile, Germany's position on the Middle East conflict is currently making the organization's work more challenging in many countries. Some partners in the Arab world have suspended their cooperation as a result, while Goethe-Institut events have seen boycotts elsewhere. "Our task then is to explain the German position and the history behind it, but also to show the debates taking place on the issue within Germany," Joost said. "At the same time, we also convey the criticism coming from many countries back to Germany." The Goethe-Institut's work has also been made more difficult in recent years due to deep cuts in federal funding, forcing it to restructure and even shut down some locations. At the same time, integrating Germany's growing number of foreign skilled workers presents new challenges; Joost feels her institute plays a crucial role here. "We see that many foreign skilled workers see a future for themselves in Germany. But settling into life in Germany is not always easy," she said. "To support them, we have our welcome coaches who are available to answer questions about living and working in Germany and provide guidance, especially in the early stages. That is an important contribution the Goethe-Institut can make in Germany." This article was originally published in German on June 22 and updated on September 10, 2026, ahead of the closure of the Goethe-Institut in Russia.

item.title: The Bayeux Tapestry in London: What's behind the hype?
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.44
First, let's start with a clarification: Strictly speaking, it's not actually a tapestry, since tapestries are woven, whereas this artwork is an embroidery on linen. Nevertheless, it is commonly referred to as such. This pictorial narrative which is approximately 70 meters (230 feet) long, depicts the events surrounding the Norman Conquest of England in 1066, culminating in the Battle of Hastings and William the Conqueror's victory over Harold II. The Norman Conquest radically changed England: Politics, laws and culture all came under the influence of Norman rule. The Bayeux Tapestry bears witness to this event; at the same time, it is an outstanding example of English craftsmanship from the Middle Ages and is seen by many Britons as one of the most important symbols of British identity, alongside the works of Shakespeare or Stonehenge. The tapestry is thought to have been commissioned by the Bishop of Bayeux, William's half-brother, who was present at the battle, from embroiderers in southern England for the opening of his cathedral in 1070. Anglo-Saxon embroiderers were famous throughout Europe at the time for their skills. The work then made its way to France, where it remained for almost a thousand years — until now. Why is the Bayeux Tapestry so important? The Bayeux Tapestry is considered one of the most important pictorial monuments of the High Middle Ages. Many researchers view it as an elaborately crafted piece of propaganda that showed and explained William the Conqueror's victory to people at the time. Its scientifically disputed message is that Harold Godwinson, then Earl of Wessex, had sworn a sacred oath on relics to support William's claim to the English throne. He broke this oath when he had himself crowned king. The war is therefore portrayed as his just punishment. The fact that Harold had probably not taken the oath of his own free will is irrelevant to this woven narrative. The embroidery is part of the UNESCO Memory of the World Register and, because of its 58 pictorial scenes, is sometimes referred to as "the world's oldest comic." Accompanied by Latin inscriptions, the pictorial narrative depicts the horrors of war — including massacres, rolling heads and the death of a king. But it is also a valuable historical document for researchers. The tapestry illustrates shipbuilding and military equipment in surprising detail, as well as everyday medieval life. Even Halley's Comet is shown in it — the comet was visible in the sky in 1066 and was interpreted by the Anglo-Saxons as a bad omen in the pictorial narrative. Why did it take so long to get the tapestry on loan? The tapestry is owned by the French state and had been placed on deposit with the City of Bayeux for display at the Musée de la Tapisserie de Bayeux. Britain had already tried to borrow the tapestry for the coronation of Elizabeth II in 1953, as well as for various historical occasions afterwards, but France had always refused. The artefact was considered too fragile and the journey too risky. Finally, President Emmanuel Macron gave the green light last year for an exhibition at the British Museum — overriding the concerns of his experts. Last September, the tapestry was taken down, packaged and initially placed in storage in a highly elaborate, six-hour procedure. On July 9, it finally arrived in London in a secret transport operation, enclosed in a high-tech container that shielded it from all vibrations while maintaining a constant temperature and humidity level. The British government has also insured the artwork for £800 million (around €932 million or $1 billion). Where can you get tickets? The British Museum has divided ticket sales into three phases. The first, covering September to December, began on July 1. All tickets sold out quickly, with up to 80,000 people reportedly trying to secure a slot at the same time. Many had to wait up to nine hours. For those who missed out, there will soon be another chance — tickets for January to March will go on sale on October 21, and tickets for April to July in January. The exhibition is being marketed as a "once-in-a-generation" event, and an extensive educational program is intended to involve schools across the country. The British Museum is optimistic that the Bayeux Tapestry will help it set a new visitor record. The most popular exhibition in the museum's history to date is the 1972 "The Treasures of Tutankhamun," which attracted almost 1.7 million visitors. No ticket? Here's an alternative If you're now eager to see the tapestry but unsure if you'll land a ticket, you can also head to the town of Reading, around two hours west of London. There, you can see a faithful replica of the tapestry, which is itself already 140 years old. Even back then, there was a strong desire in England to have this artwork in the country. In 1885, 35 embroiderers set to work for around a year. Using colored photographs as a reference, they reproduced the tapestry on a one-to-one scale. However, they did change one detail: Some figures on the original border are naked and in suggestive poses. Apparently, this was considered too scandalous in Victorian England. One figure was retouched in the corresponding photograph — and the embroiderers copied the alteration. As a result, the figure is depicted wearing underwear. This article was translated from German.

item.title: Are electric cars really bad for the environment?
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 5.28
"The EU's car lie" — Germany's Bild tabloid newspaper didn't mince words when it reported on what it called the European Union's "dangerous" claim that electric vehicles were carbon neutral. Markus Söder, the conservative state premier of Bavaria — home to major automotive brands like Audi, BMWand Mercedes-Benz — was equally direct. Writing on social media, he called for an end to "the EU's phaseout of internal combustion engines" set for 2035. Stepping away from the phaseout, he said, would now be backed by "science." Söder and Bild were reacting to a new report by the Technical University of Munich (TUM), which outlined what it considered to be a major flaw in the EU's climate strategy: the fact that its vehicle emissions regulation only focuses on CO2 emissions from exhaust gases and that battery-electric vehicles are considered "climate-neutral." The report stated that battery-electric vehicles reduce carbon emissions by only "41% on average" over combustion engine vehicles, with the EU regulation failing to take into account emissions generated by other factors like manufacturing and electricity mix. Gas-powered vehicles were at a disadvantage, the report concluded, suggesting emissions should be counted over a vehicle's entire life cycle, from the materials used to build a car to the fuel that makes it run. Credit could be given for the use of green steel, for instance, or recovering raw materials through recycling. It highlighted several major car manufacturers that support this approach, including BMW, Audi and Volkswagen — all major institutional donors at TUM. No new insights in TUM report Georg Bieker, who researches the environmental impact of electric and gas-powered cars at the US-based International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT) think tank, said TUM's analysis didn't offer any new insights. He, and other climate and mobility experts, pointed out that the importance of life-cycle assessments was already well known. Bieker co-authored a 2025 study examining the global warming potential of passenger cars sold in the EU which took into account their entire life cycle, from the production of the vehicle to its fuel consumption and maintenance. It found that the emissions generated by battery-electric vehicles are on average 73% lower than gasoline cars, and up to 78% when using only renewable electricity. Similar studies, including from the EU and the International Energy Agency, came up with emissions reductions of between 60%-66%. The Germany Environment Ministry said modern vehicles could even achieve reductions of up to 80%. Hybrid vehicles, meanwhile, which combine a combustion engine with an electric motor and battery charged by the car's brakes and an internal generator, generate fewer emissions than traditional cars, but still don't match fully electric vehicles. Bieker said the full EV advantage will only grow as production and operation becomes less carbon intensive. Even today, he added, production emissions for gasoline internal combustion vehicles only account for around 13% of the total climate impact; most of the emissions come from the tailpipe. Batteries have a high environmental cost Bieker confirmed batteries were still one of the main environmental challenges facing electric cars. The mining of key resources like cobalt and lithium has been linked to habitat destruction and water depletion; mining 1 ton of lithium, enough for around 125 EVs, requires some 2 million liters of water. Bieker's ICCT study found that while battery-electric vehicles had an estimated 40% higher production emissions than gas-powered vehicles due to battery production, these additional emissions were offset after driving about 17,000 kilometers (10,500 miles), or in one or two years. And, Bieker pointed out, most of those batteries could eventually be recycled — unlike the gasoline burned in a combustion engine. "We see a trend of emissions decreasing for battery production," Bieker told DW, pointing out that technology was still being developed. The production of lithium-iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, for example, generates fewer emissions than the nickel manganese cobalt variety. LFPs are increasingly becoming the battery of choice for the industry — they're generally safer, last longer and are cheaper to manufacture. Bieker said batteries were also increasingly being produced in Europe in larger, more efficient factories, which also helps reduce emissions generated by importing them from abroad. Though Europe still ranks second behind China when it comes to battery cell manufacturing, the European Commission has committed to boosting the sector with financial support, including a recent €1.5 billion in interest-free loans. Renewable energy making the case for EVs The other major factor contributing to EV emissions is the electricity mix — how the power charging the batteries is actually generated. While electric cars don't produce emissions during driving, they can generate them indirectly when charged using electricity produced by burning fossil fuels like coal and gas. But the rapid expansion of renewable energy in recent years — especially solar, including a growing popularity of home installations — is increasingly tipping the scale in favor of EVs. "Europe's electricity grid is currently more than 70% decarbonized and expected to be almost fully decarbonized by 2040," said Gabrielle Clark, a policy officer at European trade federation Eurelectric focusing on energy, climate and sustainability. "As the production of green steel and battery recycling capacity also ramps up as expected, this will only strengthen the case even more." Clark said it wasn't necessary to replace the EU's current tailpipe emissions regulation, which plans to phase out combustion engines entirely by 2035, with more complex regulations and green accounting rules. "Whether assessed through [life-cycle assessment] or tailpipe emissions, [battery-electric vehicles] are always the preferred technology for carbon emission reductions in the road transport sector," she told DW in an email. "Their replacement of [internal combustion engine] vehicles must be accelerated, not delayed." Rising fuel prices, climate concerns push EV growth Bieker said that in the end the market will decide, not policy. "The future will be electric, no matter what European policymakers or German carmakers think," he said, highlighting the global growth of EV sales in recent years, especially in China and Southeast Asia. EVs are also taking off in Europe. In Germany, for example, a new survey by research firm SBD Automotive and Here Technologies showed that 54% of respondents were more likely to consider buying an electric car as their next vehicle, citing technology advances, rising fuel prices and environmental concerns. "We cannot win the race by ignoring it," said Bieker. "[For climate,] for competitiveness and economic development, we need to double down on electrification and not slow it down." Edited by: Tamsin Walker

item.title: Yemen: Houthis tighten control of strategic Red Sea towns
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.90
Yemen's Houthi militia have captured strategic points on the Bab el-Mandeb strait, one of the world's most important shipping routes. In addition to the Iran-backed group's takeover of the port city of Mokha on Thursday, Yemeni government sources told several news agencies on Friday that the Houthis have now also captured the island of Perim, also called Mayyun in Arabic. Reuters reported that Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces said they had withdrawn from Perim, and that the Houthis had also taken the mainland Red Sea coastal town of Dhubab, located south of Mokha and closer to the narrowest part of the strait. Mokha is located 80 kilometers (50 miles) up the Red Sea coast from the Bab el-Mandeb strait, while Perim Island is located in the strait itself. Vital Red Sea transport route vulnerable? The Red Sea has served as a key alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where shipping has been disrupted amid the United States' war with Iran, sending global oil prices skyrocketing. Houthi spokesperson Abdulsalam was cited by the Reuters news agency as saying that freedom of navigation and international trade in the Red Sea and the Strait remain safe and operations are limited to specific targets. The Houthis have in the past targeted international shipping in the Red Sea, saying it is in solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza. Saudi Arabia closes oil pipeline after attack Saudi authorities said that they temporarily closed the East-West oil pipeline near Riyadh and Medina on Thursday after it came under attack. The pipeline runs across the Arabian Peninsula, from the Persian Gulf coast to the Red Sea, and is a key part of the route bypassing the Strait of Hormuz. "The East-West pipeline in the Riyadh and Medina regions was subjected to several attacks," the official told the SPA news agency on Friday. "The pipeline was stopped as a precaution, and the attacks resulted in some injuries." The Foreign Ministry said the drones involved in the attack were launched from Iraq. Meanwhile, Houthi rebels accused Saudi Arabia of launching strikes on the southwestern province of Taiz. "The Saudi enemy launched 10 strikes on the Dhubab district in western Taiz," the Houthis' Al-Masirah TV channel was cited by AFP news agency as saying. Dhubab lies just south of Mokha. Fighting intensifies between Houthis and Yemeni government Fighting has intensified between the Houthis and Yemen's internationally recognized government in recent months after four years of relative calm, with rebels stepping up efforts to solidify their control over the country's coastline. The capture of Mokha is the Iran-backed militia's biggest territorial gain since a UN-brokered truce signed in 2022. The Iran-backed Houthis control the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, as well as much of the more populous areas in the country's north and west. The internationally recognized government is headquartered in the southern city of Aden and receives considerable support from Saudi Arabia. Yemen's civil war has killed over 150,000 people and brought others to the brink of famine. Edited by: Wesley Rahn, Dmytro Hubenko and Wesley Dockery If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first.

item.title: Why are European banks moving gold out of United States?
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.68
Fort Knox, the fortified complex in the state of Kentucky where about half of the US government's gold reserves are held, is a byword for security. To be "like Fort Knox" means to be extremely secure and well-guarded. Yet the perception of the United States as a whole as a secure location to store gold is clearly on the wane. The decision by the Dutch central bank recently to move about 86 tonnes (95 US tons) of gold from New York to London highlighted growing concerns among some governments over storing strategic assets in the US and whether they could be readily accessed in a crisis. The De Nederlandsche Bank (DNB) cited "geopolitical unrest" and said moving its gold across different jurisdictions would improve its "crisis preparedness." France also removed its remaining gold exposure from the New York Federal Reserve between July 2025 and January 2026, although Bank of France Governor François Villeroy de Galhau said at the time that it was not politically motivated. Several politicians in Germany and Italy — which hold the world's second- and third-largest gold reserves, respectively — have called for their countries' gold to be also taken out of the US amid concerns about the Trump administration's unpredictable policymaking and its growing antipathy toward the European Union, including threats to annex part of Greenland. The gold rush Sebastien Tillett, an analyst with Oxford Economics, told DW the outright seizure of assets is an "extremely remote risk" for European central banks. However, he said, there are growing concerns about ease of access in an age of geopolitical uncertainty. "The more relevant concern is that assets held in another jurisdiction could become temporarily inaccessible in an extreme sanctions, legal or geopolitical scenario," he said. In general, said Krishnan Gopaul, of the World Gold Council, central banks around the world have been buying more gold since the 2008 global financial crisis and are increasingly focused on where and how they store it. As a result, gold prices have soared to record highs. A recent survey by the World Gold Council found that central banks have accumulated an average of 1,000 tonnes of gold over the past four years, up from the 500-tonne average over the preceding decade. Because the 2008 global financial crisis was followed by the euro sovereign-debt crisis and then a variety of political crises, a pandemic, and sustained geopolitical upheaval and conflict, gold has come into sharper focus as a safe haven asset, Gopaul said. "As we've gone through the last two decades, there have been questions and concerns around the global financial system and the state of geopolitics in one form or another," he said. The decisions by the Dutch and French to move their gold out of the United States and back to Europe highlight the new focus on where exactly the gold is held so that it can be easily and quickly leveraged in the event of a new crisis. Central banks, governments and sovereign wealth funds hold physical gold in different locations. Moving it can be extremely complex, risky and costly, while the ease of selling it or trading it for currencies or other assets depends on the location. "Central banks are paying greater attention to where reserves are held as well as what assets they hold, mainly to maximize resilience and flexibility of reserve holdings," Tillett said. Gopaul said reserve management had become "incredibly important" and that, while it might seem obvious to focus on the possible negative risks associated with a certain jurisdiction such as the US, part of the rationale behind such decisions is making sure that the gold is as close to home as possible and in a trading hub that moves fast. He highlights the fact that the Dutch central bank moved its gold to London rather than to the Netherlands because the United Kingdom is "one of the most liquid trading hubs in the gold market." "The idea is that in the event of a crisis, in stress periods, that gold can be potentially mobilized," he said. "London is pretty much the heart of the gold market, and there is so much activity there, and it's such a liquid market, that in a time of crisis that is where you want your gold." The Bank of England is a major global gold holder and custodian. There are estimated to be around 400,000 gold bars in its possession, worth around $270 billion (€232 billion). The US question While moving gold to a location such as London has an attraction of its own for European entities, it is clear that doubts over US reliability in the Trump era and over the US financial system as a whole is driving decision-making. Last week, the manager of Norway's massive $2.3 trillion sovereign wealth fund said the fund needs to significantly cut its exposure to US treasuries. That decision seems to be driven by concern about US government bond markets, with soaring inflation and government debt driving up borrowing costs and spooking investors. Tillett said gold remained sensitive to decisions by the US Federal Reserve and general concern about US financial markets meant that gold holders are looking to move their assets. As well as those specific financial market concerns, Trump's rhetoric about Greenland and continued veiled threats toward the EU has added to the reasons for European institutions to want to move their assets around. Yet the United States, and the New York Federal Reserve in Manhattan, in particular, remains a key custodian of much European gold, not least from Germany. Although the Bundesbank moved about 300 tonnes of gold back to Germany from the US between 2013 and 2017, it still holds well over 1,000 tonnes in the United States. Last year in a statement it said: "We have no doubt that the New York Fed is a trustworthy and reliable partner for the safekeeping of our gold reserves." Edited by: Kristie Pladson

item.title: India's BRICS strategy tested with Xi, Putin set to visit
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.53
India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi will host the 18th BRICS summit this weekend in New Delhi, welcoming Chinese President Xi Jinping to India for the first time since 2019. The summit comes at an important moment for India. As New Delhi's year-long BRICS presidency draws to a close, India is stepping up engagement with China and Russia, and its relationship with Washington remains difficult. Modi met both Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, on August 31 and September 1. Just two weeks later, Modi is set to see them again in New Delhi for the BRICS summit. But with BRICS both growing in size and increasingly troubled by internal divisions, the forum might limit Modi's diplomatic gains. New Delhi and Beijing locked in 'armed coexistence' and competition Indian diplomats are trying to protect their room for maneuver in a changing international order. Ashok Kantha, a former Indian ambassador to China, said India's engagement with BRICS and the SCO is part of New Delhi's longstanding strategy of strategic autonomy. "These groupings give India a seat at the table and allow it to pursue its own interests while maintaining relationships with different major powers," Kantha told DW. However, as Modi prepares to host Xi in New Delhi, ties between India and China are less than ideal. Both countries reached a border patrol agreement in 2024, ending a four-year military standoff along their disputed frontier. International flights have resumed, the Kailash Mansarovar pilgrimage has reopened and some visa restrictions have eased. But major problems remain between Beijing and New Delhi — India is reporting a trade deficit of over $112 billion (€96.5 billion) with China, and the two countries argue over market access. The Modi-Xi meeting will therefore be watched for signs of a major diplomatic thaw, particularly on trade and investment. Kantha said the visit could bring some stabilization but should not be mistaken for a reset. "The border remains heavily militarized and major differences over trade, investment and security remain. India needs a stable and predictable relationship with China, but without lowering its guard," said Kantha. "It is a relationship of armed coexistence and managed competition. We should not reduce it to a simple 'elephant and dragon' story," he said, referring to traditional symbols of the world's two most populous nations. BRICS gets bigger, divisions grow India's presidency has already exposed the difficulty of reaching agreement within BRICS, which has grown from its original five members to 11. With nations such as Brazil, South Africa, Indonesia and Egypt all part of BRICS, its leaders struggle to reconcile its very different relationships with the US and different interests in conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine. The group now also includes Iran and the UAE, countries that have found themselves on opposing sides of the war in Iran. Earlier this year, BRICS foreign ministers failed to agree on a joint statement on the Middle East crisis, forcing India to issue a unilateral chair's statement instead. With Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian expected at the Delhi summit, this diplomatic divide is likely to take center stage. "Differences between members such as Iran and the UAE show how difficult it can be to find common ground," says Harsh Pant, vice president for Studies and Foreign Policy at the Observer Research Foundation. "BRICS can still work on areas where members share interests, such as reforming global economic governance. But such disagreements are likely to become more common," he added. Fears of Chinese dominance The future of BRICS will also be impacted by the rivalry between India and China. India wants BRICS to give greater weight to the concerns of developing countries and to support reform of other global institutions such as the United Nations, IMF and World Bank. However, New Delhi does not want the grouping to become a China-led challenge to the West. India has been pushing for easier cross-border payments between BRICS countries and greater use of national currencies in international trade. At the same time, the Modi government has also been careful not to present this as an attempt to replace the US dollar or create a common BRICS currency. "Local-currency transactions are likely to become an important area of cooperation," Pant said, but stressed that India and other BRICS countries are not necessarily seeking 'de-dollarization.'" "Instead, they are looking for greater resilience and alternatives to dollar-based financial arrangements." India's 'America Plus' strategy Despite its disagreements with the Trump administration, New Delhi still wants stronger economic and strategic ties with the US, while also maintaining its longstanding relationship with Russia and improving relations with China. India's diplomatic course is not a pure "multi-alignment" approach but an "America Plus" strategy, strategic affairs analyst C Raja Mohan told DW. "India remains dependent on the West for capital, technology, markets and security, while deepening ties with Russia and China for strategic reasons," said Mohan, a professor of American studies at Jindal Global University. But this balancing act will become harder as great-power rivalry intensifies, Mohan warns. "A US-China accommodation could leave India exposed, while Russia's growing dependence on China is changing the Eurasian balance," he said. In this calculation, a more anti-Western BRICS could put pressure on India over its continuing dependence on the West. The upcoming Delhi summit is likely to show the extent of India's power — especially as it wraps up its BRICS presidency. For Narendra Modi, the test is whether India can advance its priorities for BRICS and give itself more room to maneuver internationally, without allowing the grouping to become dominated by China or reduced to an anti-Western platform. Edited by: Darko Janjevic

item.title: Uber leaves two key African markets — and their drivers in despair
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 4.20
A week ago, Uber unexpectedly announced its departure from the Nigerian market after spending more than a decade building up its presence in Africa's most populous country. The ride-hailing platform also said it would be winding up its operations in Uganda — also with immediate effect. With the exit from both Nigeria and Uganda, Uber now remains operational only in a handful of African countries — namely Egypt, Ghana, Kenya and South Africa. "This decision is limited strictly to these two markets and does not impact our operations across the rest of the continent," Uber said in a statement, adding that their "immediate priority is supporting drivers, riders, and local team members throughout this transition," without sharing details on what this assistance would entail. In the last year, the multinational company also closed shop in Ivory Coast and Tanzania, while also cutting its global workforce by 10%. Africa a difficult market to crack Uber has not managed to grow across much of the African market despite its massive global scale. The profit-driven ride-hailing app faces stiff competition from rival platforms, including Bolt, inDrive and SafeBoda, which operate in the Nigerian and Ugandan markets and beyond. However, it's not only Uber that is having to deal with its frustration over the current situation: Many of its drivers across Africa have been raising complaints about shrinking profit margins amid rising fuel costs, inflation and currency volatility, especially in markets like Nigeria. In their view, Uber's business model of pocketing around 20% — 25% of any trip fare in commissions is no longer tenable. Discontent, discombobulated and disregarded drivers Abbas Olamide, an Uber driver in the Nigerian capital Abuja, said the company's overall service was "good," while firmly stressing that the high commission rates were adding greatly to his existing woes. He told DW that a ride of 30,000 Naira (€20) "to the airport means the ride-hailing app would deduct 6,000 Naira as commission," still leaving him to "then pay a gate fee at the airport." "Probably because you do not want to go back to town empty-handed, we also pay to park at the airport [to pick up another client]," he explained. "At the end of the day, what's left is no longer enough." Samuel Olatunji, an Uber-driver in the megacity Lagos, also shared his concerns with DW following the abrupt announcement of Uber's exit, saying he will now have to recalibrate his own business model. The 43-year-old driver says he'll have to join hundreds of other drivers who "have to depend on other [ride-hailing] apps now" to ensure any steady stream of income. "But the amount I take home won't add up like before again." In recent years, drivers like Olamide and Olatunji have staged several strikes and protests over soaring operating costs, low fares and working conditions, as well as Nigeria's fuel hikes, which this year have also been worsened by the surge in prices at the pump following the war in Iran. Their pleas and concerns, however, remain largely unheard, as they find themselves having to prepare for a bumpy ride ahead. Dollars versus naira Uber meanwhile did not provide a detailed explanation for its decision; however, it comes against the backdrop of double-digit inflation in many places across Africa, which has eroded the purchasing power of millions of people while pushing them deeper and deeper into poverty. This also makes consumers less likely to use the transport company. Ikemesit Effiong, partner at SBM Intelligence, a consulting firm based in Lagos, explained that "[r]ising costs for such things as fuel, vehicle maintenance, insurance, coupled with a currency that is less valuable now than in 2014 means that fares were climbing faster than the average Lagos or Abuja rider's willingness or ability to pay for the convenience." Effiong added that while Uber's cost base is dollar-linked, the drivers' revenue is the shrinking naira, leading to the overall maths not working anymore, and forcing Uber to operate under unsustainably thin profit margins. This is despite the fact that Nigeria's ride-hailing market alone is estimated to be worth around $450 million per year. "These platforms are trying to hold fares low enough to retain price-sensitive riders, while the driver take-home shrinks in real terms. This pushes drivers toward multi-apping, off-platform negotiation, or exit altogether," he noted. Effiong further highlighted that one of Uber's local competitors, InDrive, does actually operate under a negotiated-fare approach, resulting in "less reliance on the capital-heavy, standardized-fare template that works in wealthier markets." The complex economics of ride-hailing There are some striking similarities between the Nigerian and Ugandan markets: Both countries have huge populations and a growing demand for more transport solution. But both across both Kampala and Lagos, Uber's exit also creates a loss of a service many users had considered a safe and reliable option — more so than some of the other options. Mary-Esther Anele, a Lagos resident, told DW that she knows that she is "going to start looking for alternatives." "But most importantly, I'm going to travel less anyway now because transportation costs are going to increase," she added. There also are questions about any knock-on effects beyond the current decision by Uber: Will the California-based multinational leave its remaining African markets? Will its pricing dynamics change in order to bring in more money from the continent? And how will competitors respond? In some other African countries like South Africa, ride-hailing apps like Uber have also long been a thorn in the side of taxi companies and minibuses, whose operators say they don't want to compete against those drivers, even resorting to violence at times as part of ongoing local taxi wars. Will Uber's shrinking footprint in Africa impact these kinds of developments in other markets? As countless drivers prepare for an unknown future, the end of their partnership with Uber might — for many — spell their journey's end. Frank Yiga from Kampala contributed to this report. Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

item.title: Philippines ferry fire: Search continues for dozens missing
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.59
Philippine firefighters on Friday managed to enter a smoldering ferry in a search for dozens of people still unaccounted for after the vessel caught fire on Wednesday evening, with rescue work complicated by heavy smoke and extreme heat. The Philippines Coast Guard said that rescuers recovered 30 bodies from a ferry, raising the death toll from the incident to 35. Earlier, firefighters reported that five people had died, 43 had been rescued, and more than 80 were missing. On Friday, Coast Guard spokesperson Commodore Noemi Cayabyab said that charred remains had been found in the economy accommodation area, but added that the exact number of those found would need to wait for police forensic investigators to examine the remains for recovery and identification. "We can't provide exact numbers yet on what we saw today," Cayabyab told AFP news agency. "We will be providing it once we conduct retrieval and recovery," she added. The ferry "MV June Aster" had originated in Manila, and was nearing its destination, the tourist hotspot of Coron in the western Philippine province of Palawan, when it caught fire just off the coast. The Philippine Coast Guard updated the number of missing people from 86 to 84 after confirming that two people originally listed on the manifest had not been on board. Ferry fire spread 'in seconds' Cayabyab told a radio interview earlier Friday that the fire broke out in "seconds." "From the time that they heard the loud explosion, the appearance of smoke, and then fire. It spread very quickly," she said, citing survivor accounts. Cayabyab said some of those who made it off the ship did not have time to put on life jackets. The Coast Guard has deployed several vessels and divers to the incident, while army rescue boats, fishermen and private resort owners have also provided assistance in the search. Investigation ongoing The fire began in the cargo hold, and may have moved even more rapidly due to strong winds, Cayabyab added later. Although the exact cause of the accident has yet to be officially determined, survivors reported hearing explosions inside the ship. They later said that a small fire quickly escalated and engulfed the vessel. Some passengers jumped into the sea, where they remained afloat until they were rescued. The vessel caught fire some 7 kilometers (4.5 miles) off the village of Turda. The ferry was carrying electric cars, motorcycles, cargo, and heavy-duty equipment, as well as provisions for the crew and passengers. Ferries are one of the most widely used forms of transport in the Philippines, an archipelago made up of 7,600 islands. The country has a history of maritime accidents, some of which are caused by overcrowding, adverse sailing conditions, and lax safety standards. Edited by: Wesley Rahn Don't let the algorithm hide the news. item.title: PISA 2025 results: Reading and math scores plummet worldwide
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.28
The results of the 2025 PISA study, published on September 8, show a dramatic drop in performance in reading and mathematics around the world. The Program for International Student Assessment, better known as PISA, is a global study that measures how well 15-year-old students can apply their knowledge and skills in reading, mathematics and science to real-life situations. The test is designed to measure problem-solving skills rather than evaluate students on memorized school facts, which means they cannot revise in preparation for it. First administered in 2000, it is considered the world's most influential measure of educational performance. In 2025, more than 760,000 students in 91 countries and economies took the test. The study always includes in its ranking the average of the international group of 38 advanced, high-income countries that are part of the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, the OECD. Downward trend in students' performances Between 2015 and 2025, reading skills have seen the most significant decline, decreasing by 28 points in OECD countries, and by 16 points in the other participating countries and economies. Scores in math have dropped by 22 points across the OECD on average, compared to a decline of 8 points in the rest of the world. In science, the focus of the 2025 PISA assessment, a seven-point decline was measured in OECD countries, while the performances in other countries and economies remained broadly stable. Nearly a third of OECD students considered 'low performers' The latest PISA study reveals that around 29% of 15-year-olds in OECD countries are now estimated to be "low performers" across all three subjects. What does this mean? In science, they struggle to interpret simple data or decipher a graph. In reading, they find it hard to find information in simple texts. In mathematics, they might be unable to understand, for example, the relationship between units and price — basic skills needed for grocery shopping. Drop in global reading scores most concerning Across the OECD, reading scores fell by 25 score points on average. The study points out that 20 score points are about equivalent to a year of learning. This implies that most 15-year-old students were performing at the level typically expected of 14-year-olds. Among the OECD countries, the drops were most extreme in Iceland and Slovenia, with scores going down by more than 50 points. Reading scores improved in five countries only: Qatar (up 11 points), Brunei Darussalam (18), Cambodia (26), the Philippines (27) and Zambia (50). Even though these education systems are still below the OECD average, they "deserve recognition for achieving measurable gains despite the broader global decline," notes the study. Not all schools are equal in Germany In some countries, such as Iceland, Cambodia and Finland, for example, there is very little variation in performance among schools, showing less than 10% overall variation in student achievement. But in 10 countries, including Germany, differences among schools account for at least 50% of the total variation in performance. The study notes that these countries' systems presumably have schools reserved for higher-achieving students, leaving disproportionately large numbers of lower-achieving students enrolled in the other institutions. For the authors of the PISA study presentation, this is a problem that needs to be taken seriously: "Where such academic segmentation compounds with social background, it can amplify inequalities, producing pockets of excellence while failing to ensure consistent learning outcomes across the education system as a whole." Germany's PISA shocks The very first PISA study was held in the year 2000. As one of the 31 participating countries, Germany was shocked to discover that its 15-year-olds scored below the international average. In the last PISA test, held in 2022 and published in 2023, the scores of German students had dropped to a new low. In the latest study, scores have plunged even deeper. Between 2022 and 2025, reading scores plummeted by 15 points and math scores by 11 points, while science scores have gone down by seven. The top six rankings in reading skills are held by Asian countries. Germany barely remains above the OECD average, coming in 24th. The United States comes in 13th position, Poland ranks 14th and Turkey 18th. In math, Germany is below the OECD average, coming in 26th, just a rank above the United States. All top seven positions are held by Asian countries, followed by Estonia in the 8th spot. In science, Germany is only two score points above the OECD average, ranking 23rd. Turkey made important progress in this field, now ranking 19th, with an increase of 18 score points since the 2022 study. Why is educational performance falling globally overall? The data itself cannot explain the decline in reading skills, but the authors of the study note that while school closures due to COVID-19 may be one factor, there is no direct relationship between how long schools closed during the pandemic and the students' performances in reading. There was already a downward trend in many countries long before the pandemic struck, the study notes. These long-term declines in skills "suggest deeper structural issues within education systems, with challenges at the school and system level," according to the study. These challenges include the impact of digital distractions on students and growing disinterest towards reading books. AI has had an immediate impact on learning. The 2025 PISA study asked students about their use of AI in schoolwork; more than 40% said they used it to draft texts for writing assignments once or twice a week, or even every day. Students who reported using AI chatbots got lower scores in science, on average, than those who didn't use AI. "Overall, the data suggests weaknesses in how education systems are adapting to social, technological and economic change," states the study's summary. "Looking ahead, the challenge for policymakers is not simply recovering lost ground, but to ensure schools meet the rapidly changing demands of the world. As PISA shows, it is not an easy task." While waiting for policymakers to react, the study suggests that parents can contribute to children's potential by being supportive and curious about their studies and helping them develop positive attitudes towards school. "Even something as simple as asking children what they learned or did at school, about once a week or more, is associated with an average 26-point increase in science performance, after accounting for socio-economic status." Edited by: Brenda Haas

item.title: Putin rejects mobilization rumors, many Russians unconvinced
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.25
Twice within the first week of September, Russian President Vladimir Putin publicly dismissed rumors of a looming mobilization campaign in the country. On September 1, Putin called the rumors "complete nonsense" and described them as an "information attack" against Russia. Two days later, on September 3, at the Economic Forum in Vladivostok, Putin said that "there is no scenario today that would require mobilization." Summons are cause for unease among Russian DW users DW's Russian service asked readers in Russia, on condition of anonymity, whether they see signs of an impending mobilization. The most common response from DW readers concerned receiving summonses from military enlistments offices. "My nephew received a summons for data verification," wrote a reader from the industrial city of Naberezhnye Chelny. "I received a summons ordering me to appear for data verification. I'm self-employed. What should I do?" wrote a user named Maxim. "One of my friends, a school teacher, received a summons through the government services portal [Gosuslugi] on July 9 to update his records," said another reader, Sergei. People fear that they may be called up for military service or lose the ability to leave the country freely. As a result, some of those who have received draft notices are seeking to travel abroad as quickly as possible, while restrictions on leaving the country have not yet taken effect. "One acquaintance of mine left Russia two months ago after receiving a summons for data verification from the military enlistment office," one reader wrote. Emigration as 'a fantasy' Not everyone, however, sees emigration as a realistic option in the event of mobilization. "As for leaving, that's a fantasy. Where would you go, and more importantly, with what money?" one DW reader wrote. In June, reports emerged from Russia's Penza region that men were forcibly taken to military enlistment offices and pressured into signing military contracts. According to local reports, the practice became widespread enough that residents organized protests in support of relatives and neighbors. Journalists reporting on the issue say such raids are continuing. "People are being detained, particularly near the entrances to their apartment buildings," Lena Lemyasova, a journalist with news outlet Important Stories [Vazhnye Istorii], told DW. "Often men who have been drinking. Unknown individuals approach them, or vehicles pull up — often cars provided by local authorities. The men are simply seized and taken away, then their families and neighbors hear nothing more. Later, information sometimes emerges that they were transported to military units. They are often held there before being sent to the front." Important Stories specializes in investigative journalism. Its publisher, Roman Anin, spent ten years as investigations editor at well-known independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta. What do Russian lawyers say about the summonses? Does receiving a military summons mean a person will be sent to war? According to lawyer Artem Klyga, a summons issued "for data verification" does not in itself mean that someone will be drafted, mobilized or deployed. Data verification notices are one of several legally established reasons for calling someone to a military enlistment office. "These summonses only show that military enlistment offices have significantly improved their military registration procedures. If mobilization begins, such records would help authorities quickly summon the people they need," Klyga explained to DW. Russians have also increasingly reported receiving mobilization orders issued in advance. In peacetime, such orders do not oblige individuals to take any action. However, if mobilization is declared, recipients are required to report to their designated military enlistment office. "They were issued before the war and during the war [against Ukraine] as well. But what changed in the first half of 2026 is that, judging by all indications, they began to be distributed in the hundreds of thousands," Russian lawyer Timofei Vaskin told DW. "We do not know the exact figures because the information is classified. But judging from social media reports and the number of inquiries we and our colleagues received, the increase was dramatic, by dozens of times." At the same time, the 2022 decree on partial mobilization in Russia has never been formally revoked and technically remains in force. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has repeatedly described reports of a new mobilization wave as "fake stories." Yet critics note that Peskov also denied reports of a possible mobilization beginning in May 2022. Just eight days before the announcement of partial mobilization, he said: "At the moment, this is not being discussed." Growing demand for mobilization specialists As of August 8, DW found several vacancies on the Russian job platform HeadHunter seeking specialists in "mobilization preparedness." 40 such vacancies are available in Moscow and the surrounding region and 13 in St Petersburg. For example, some companies are looking for specialists responsible for ensuring that the organization has a mobilization plan in place and knows how it would operate if the state were to place the economy on a wartime footing. Their duties also include preparing the company for emergencies and civil defense measures, as well as helping to transition the organization to a special operating regime in the event of wartime conditions. The positions were advertised by both private companies and state institutions. Summonses, military training exercises, the expansion of military registration systems and active recruitment efforts help explain why official denials have failed to put the rumors to rest. Preparing for ‘any decision Putin might make' "The way to look at this is that bureaucrats have been tasked with preparing the system for any decision Putin might make. And if that decision is mobilization, they are expected to be ready," Artem Klyga said. In late July, the independent outlet Agentstvo counted 197 vacancies around Russia containing the term "mobilization preparedness" and more than 2,600 vacancies related to "military registration" on the same recruitment platform. Edited by: Carla Bleiker
