item.title: Why North Korea's Kim Jong Un doesn't need a US deal
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.16
In August, US President Donald Trump revived a charm offensive aimed at Pyongyang by drastically scaling back joint US military exercises with South Korea and heaping praise on North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.The US president said the North Korean dictator "has always treated me with great respect." North Korea's response to Trump's overtures has been markedly less enthusiastic, ranging from firing a barrage of missiles to publicly denying Trump's claims that Kim has responded "very positively" to a request for talks. This week, as the US and South Korea, along with Japan, kicked off a five-day military drill, there was no mention of any pullback from Washington, nor any sign of diplomatic progress with Pyongyang. Instead, Kim on Monday commissioned a naval destroyer, while again emphasizing North Korea must establish a "powerful and reliable nuclear war deterrent" and strengthen "maritime defense." Kim also said North Korea would soon unveil a "significant" naval advancement. No urgency for deal with US Unlike the summit diplomacy of Trump's first term, Kim's dismissive stance comes at a time when North Korea has alternatives to a grand bargain with the United States. "For Kim, the stakes are simply lower than they were in 2019. There is no longer the same sense of urgency in Pyongyang to get back to the negotiating table with Washington," Joon Ha Park, a correspondent at Korea Risk Group in Seoul, told DW. "North Korea now has a treaty-based alliance with Moscow and is drawing closer to Beijing, while its military capabilities have expanded significantly. That's why a single reduction in ROK-US military exercises is not enough for Pyongyang to be swayed," he added, referring to military ties between South Korea and the US. Kim rides high Park agrees that Kim is arguably in his strongest position since taking power in 2011. Just six years ago, amid crippling sanctions and the coronavirus pandemic, an emotional Kim stood at the lectern marking the 75th anniversary of the Korean Workers' Party and expressed regret for having failed the North Korean people. Fast forward to today, and North Korea's economy appears to be on a stronger footing. Estimates released last year by South Korea's central bank showed the economy expanded by 3.7% in 2024, its fastest rate of growth in eight years. Kim has brought North Korea closer to Russia and China than the traditionally isolated country has been in decades. This week, both Moscow and Beijing sent messages marking North Korea's 78th founding anniversary and praising the strategic importance of their deepening partnerships with Pyongyang. Kim's recent spate of good fortune began in 2023, after a summit with Vladimir Putin in Russia's far east. The meeting opened the door for North Korea delivering arms to help Russia fight the Ukraine war, with Moscow sending back aid. Since then, Pyongyang has heavily ramped up industrial military production, buoyed by fresh financing that skirts international sanctions. Beijing responds to the Russia-North Korea alliance China, North Korea's traditional benefactor, quickly took notice of the growing alignment between Moscow and Pyongyang, but initially kept its distance. "The war in Ukraine has opened up a crucial lifeline for the [North Korean] regime, delivering weapons, ammunitions and soldiers to Russia in return for cash, foodstuff and ostensibly advanced military technology," Alexander Lipke, policy fellow with the Asia Program at the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR), told DW. "These warming ties with Russia have also alarmed China, which is also actively attempting to cement its position as Pyongyang's preeminent partner," he added. By 2025, Russia and North Korea's ever closer ties forced Beijing to pivot and showcase its leading role among the three countries. In September that year, Kim was invited to the "Victory Day" celebrations in Beijing, and for the first time, stood publicly on stage alongside Xi and Putin. For a regime known for its international isolation, Kim standing shoulder to shoulder with the leaders of Russia and China was a major milestone. This was again the case when in June 2026, Xi's first foreign trip of the year took him to Pyongyang. Denuclearization off the table? Notably, any mention of "denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula" was omitted from communiques following these high-level meetings, despite the phrase previously being part of boilerplate diplomatic language from Beijing and Moscow. This diplomatic softening comes as North Korea aggressively takes steps to ramp up its nuclear program. In February 2026, Kim said North Korea's status as a nuclear weapons state was "irreversible," while calling for the country's nuclear force to be expanded. Recent analysis of satellite imagery suggests increased activity at known North Korean nuclear sites. Pyongyang has also insisted on US recognition as a nuclear weapons state as a precondition for any talks with Washington, while emphasizing that any future summits must omit language on "denuclearization." North Korea is estimated to have nearly 60 nuclear warheads, which is double the 20-30 warheads Pyongyang is thought to have possessed during Trump's last diplomatic episode with Kim in 2018 and 2019. "North Korea is no longer looking for talks centered on denuclearization or even traditional arms control. It increasingly wants recognition, implicitly or otherwise, as a nuclear weapons state," said Park from the Korea Risk Group. He added that any Trump summit without denuclearization included as part of the official agenda "could be portrayed by Pyongyang both domestically and internationally as implicit US acceptance of North Korea's nuclear status." Sanctions don't matter anymore? Since its first nuclear test in 2006, North Korea has been subject to a strict sanctions regime, with the UN Security Council having passed nine sanctions resolutions aimed at restricting exports, along with asset freezes. The last package was passed in 2017. At that point, it was combined with pressure and fiery rhetoric from the first Trump administration, raising tensions on the Korean Peninsula. Kim was under heavy economic pressure and seeking sanctions relief in return for concessions on his nuclear program. But that moment has now long passed. "North Korea's diplomatic situation has vastly improved, reducing the pressure to come to the table to cut a deal with the US," said Lipke, adding that "independent sanctions enforcement has widely collapsed," with Russia and China no longer actively pursuing their non-proliferation stance of previous decades. Lipke said North Korea no longer needs a bargain with the US regarding sanctions relief in return for partial denuclearization. "But the bargain now on the table could potentially be much larger for North Korea, a freeze in nuclear development in exchange for the recognition by the US as a de-facto nuclear state in front of the whole world." Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

item.title: 9/11 conspiracy theories that continue to circulate
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.08
The terrorist attacks on September 11, 2001, also known as 9/11, were the worst such attacks in history. Twenty-five years on, they have been thoroughly investigated and analyzed — yet many people still believe the conspiracy theories that swirl around the suicide attacks in the United States. First, a reminder of the event itself. On September 11, 2001, the Islamist terrorist network al-Qaeda hijacked four passenger planes. Two were flown into the twin towers of the World Trade Center in New York City. A third crashed into the Pentagon, just outside Washington, D.C., the headquarters of the US Department of Defense. The fourth airliner is believed to have been heading for the Capitol in Washington, the seat of the US Congress, but it crashed in rural Pennsylvania after passengers staged an intervention to prevent the hijackers from reaching their target. The suicide attackers killed almost 3,000 people that day, and injured thousands more. Live footage of the attacks was broadcast all around the world. September 11 was an event that changed the world — not only in terms of terrorism, but also conspiracy theories. "September 11 was a trigger point that led to so many things: debates in society as a whole that hadn't happened before, security problems no one had had to deal with before," historian Claus Oberhauser explained in an interview with fact checkers from BR-Faktenfuchs. Daniel Jolley is a professor of social psychology at the University of Nottingham who researches the societal repercussions of conspiracy theories. He told DW that conspiracy theories often spring up around events like this. Even today, many people still wonder how it was possible for the most powerful country in the world to be so utterly blindsided — and some believe conspiracy narratives provide the answer. 20% of Americans believe the government was involved According to a 2023 YouGov survey, one in five Americans believe the US government was behind the 9/11 terrorist attacks. It's a claim that has been circulating for decades. Jolley said it shows that many people mistrust institutions and "those in power." A conspiracy narrative that bolsters this myth is the claim that the twin towers and other World Trade Center buildings were brought down not by two passenger jets — or not by these alone — but with controlled explosions. Not only does this allegation continue to spread on social media, it is also based on the assertions of a small number of scientists. For example, one of their arguments is that the horizontal clouds of smoke seen when the towers collapsed supposedly indicate controlled explosions in lower floors. However, there is no evidence whatsoever that explosives or bombs were found at the site. Investigations like the one carried out by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) explain how the two passenger planes crashing into the twin towers caused them to catch fire and collapse. According to the NIST, videos of the attack support the scientific evidence. Other analyses, like those done by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) or the consultancy firm Weidlinger Associates, reached the same conclusion. Why do people believe conspiracy theories? Events like 9/11 can leave certain psychological needs unfulfilled, Jolley explained: "The needs being: to want to feel in control, to want to feel certain, to want to not feel anxious." Initially, especially with sudden, expected events like this, there are many unanswered questions and gaps in our knowledge. How did the attack happen? Who was behind it? "These gaps in our knowledge are precisely what encourage conspiracy theories to spring up," said Oberhauser. And then some people start to entertain the possibility that an even bigger conspiracy is behind it all. Karen Douglas, a professor of social psychology at the University of Kent, confirmed this. "Anyone can fall into conspiracy theories if the circumstances are right," she told DW. However, Jolley added that it's not the case that a person wakes up one day and suddenly distrusts the world. "Rather, this may have been a journey based on their life experience; for example, the adversities in their life," he said. The way a person generally deals with crises is also relevant. An anxious person is more likely to succumb to conspiracy theories, he added. Social networks in particular contribute to the rapid spread of myths. Social media already existed before September 11, 2001, but its big breakthrough came with Facebook in 2004. Apps like Instagram, WhatsApp, Telegram and YouTube are now used by billions of people. They're used to share false information and conspiracy narratives, and the platforms don't always act swiftly to take them down. "They become part of our everyday content, whether it's on our phones, on TikTok, on other social media platforms, where we can kind of come down that rabbit hole very, very quickly," said Jolley. "Going down a rabbit hole" means taking a very intense interest in a subject, clicking from one link to another, and "falling" ever deeper — like Alice in Wonderland. Why are conspiracy theories problematic? There are three main reasons why conspiracy theories are so dangerous. - Conspiracy narratives hold out the promise of making people feel less anxious and more secure. But as Jolley explained, the opposite is more likely to be the case. This can result in even greater mistrust of the government, and of other people, resulting in social isolation. - A conspiracy theory mixes reality and misinformation; and, unlike disinformation, it cannot easily be exposed as false as it is not based on clear statements that can be verified or disproved. The very essence of a conspiracy theory is the idea that a group of conspirators are acting in secret and the general public are not supposed to know anything about it. - Conspiracy theories have consequences, and can influence how people act, said Douglas. "Conspiracy theories historically have been linked with prejudice, genocide, risky health behavior, climate denial, and more recently some disturbing behavior related to QAnon and COVID-19 conspiracy theories." One group has been a particular focus of conspiracy theories around 9/11: Jews. The myth that Jewish people were behind the attacks has been widely shared on social media. This claim can be traced to the antisemitic trope that "the Jews" are a collective supposedly seeking world domination or to control the world. There is no evidence whatsoever to support this conspiracy theory, either. According to Jolley, certain groups — including Jews, Muslims and LGBTQ+ people — are often blamed for crimes they did not commit. Throughout history, Jews in particular have often been the focus of conspiracy myths, and this continues to this day. An example from Germany is that of the right-wing extremist who tried to storm a synagogue, then killed two people at a nearby kebab shop in Halle in 2019. He had been sharing antisemitic conspiracy theories online. How can societies respond to conspiracy narratives? In Germany, nongovernmental organizations like the Amadeu Antonio Foundation or the Federal Agency for Civic Education (bpb) give advice on how to deal with friends or family who believe conspiracy theories. For example: Communicate with each other on equal terms, and conduct research together to find reliable information, and call out antisemitism, racism and other extreme positions, and make it clear that you oppose them. The historian Oberhauser stressed that people need to learn to go back to trusting facts and science. This article, translated from German, was written as part of a collaboration with the ARD public broadcaster's fact-checking network.

item.title: Iran war: Saudi-Houthi escalation intensifies Yemen conflict
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.03
Fighting between the Houthi militia and Yemen's internationally recognized government escalated further this week as the Iran-backed group seized territory and exchanged missile and drone attacks with Saudi Arabia. On Thursday, the Houthis seized the port city of Mokha and by Friday had taken control of the town of Dhubab and the island of Perim, Yemeni government sources told the news agency Reuters. Mokha, Dhubab and Perim had been held by forces aligned with Yemen's government. All three are strategically located near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. With Iran having blockaded the nearby Strait of Hormuz, the narrow Bab el-Mandeb Strait has become increasingly important as an alternative route for Saudi oil exports. As the Houthis are aligned with Iran, control of and potential attacks on shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait gives Iran additional leverage in its war with the United States. The government-aligned National Resistance Forces announced on Thursday that troops were reorganizing and consolidating their defenses in Mokha in coordination with other anti-Houthi forces. The conflict has also spilled into Saudi Arabia, a close US ally and regional rival of Iran's. This week, the Houthis launched dozens of ballistic missiles and drones at four cities in Saudi Arabia. The Houthis said Saudi Arabia responded with dozens of airstrikes across four Yemeni provinces. "This is actually a full-scale war," Farea Al-Muslimi, a Yemen researcher at the London-based think tank Chatham House, told DW. "It hasn't been given that name yet but we are marching there full time," Al-Muslimi said. Houthis 'much stronger' The latest escalation, which started in July, ended a period of relative calm after years of war. A Saudi-led coalition intervened to support Yemen's government in 2015 following the 2014 Houthi insurgency. The war between the Houthis — which the United States redesignated as a foreign terrorist organization in March 2025 — and the Saudi-backed government ended in 2022 with a UN-brokered truce. However, the country remains de facto split. The Houthis control Yemen's capital, Sanaa, and most of the country's north, as well as parts of the center, and now also much of the western coastal stretch, including Mokha, Dhubab and Perim. The internationally recognized government, represented by the Presidential Leadership Council, is based in Aden. Many senior officials operate from Saudi Arabia. Government-aligned forces control parts of the south and east, while tribal groups retain significant influence in parts of the east. The political landscape was further fragmented in December, when secessionists backed by the Southern Transitional Council (STC), backed by the United Arab Emirates (UAE), seized areas in the south and east. The fallout between Saudi Arabia, which aims to keep Yemen united, and the UAE-backed secessionists ended with the termination of Yemen's joint defense pact with the UAE and the withdrawal of Emirati forces from the country. The STC was dissolved in January. Elham Manea, the director of the Middle Eastern and Gulf Studies Research Competence Area at the Institute of Political Science at the University of Zurich, told DW that the current situation is very different from that of 2015. "The Houthi movement is militarily and institutionally much stronger," Manea said, "while the camp opposing it, that is, the internationally recognized government, remains more fragmented." What's Pakistan's role? Manea said Saudi Arabia had changed its approach. In 2015, Riyadh joined the war in support of Yemen's ousted government. "Now, it is providing greater military, technical and logistical support to the internationally recognized government and forces aligned with it," Manea said. The key question is whether Saudi Arabia is preparing for a war aimed at defeating the Houthi group or seeking to change the military balance, restore deterrence and eventually negotiate from a stronger position. "At present, I consider the second scenario more likely," Manea said. Al-Muslimi offered a similar view: "The Saudis would like to avoid war at any cost." The Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, recently signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, has not yet been invoked. Reuters reported on Thursday that Pakistani officials said no military response under the agreement was currently being discussed, but the government would act when the time came. Alice Gower, director of geopolitics and security at the London-based political consultancy Azure Strategy, told DW that she doubts Pakistan would join the conflict directly. "But the escalation in Yemen will increasingly test its ability to stay out," Gower said. "Islamabad does not want to antagonize neighboring Iran," she added, "and will try to preserve its role as a mediator, while meeting its growing security commitments to Saudi Arabia through intelligence, advice and other forms of military support short of direct participation." Humanitarian toll rises Hans Grundberg, the UN envoy to Yemen, said the country was facing the "harsh reality" of a return to war. The UN Development Programme estimated that 377,000 people had died as a result of Yemen's conflict between 2014 and late 2021. Of these, approximately 154,000 deaths were directly caused by combat and violence. The current conflict has already killed nearly 200 people, according to the World Health Organization. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) also warnedthat around 18,500 people have been displaced. "Families are arriving with nothing: no shelter, no food, no way to know if it's safe to go back," Abdusattor Esoev, IOM Yemen's chief of mission, said in a statement. "Many of these are people who have already been displaced once, twice, even four times before," he said. "Every time fighting flares up, they lose whatever little they had managed to rebuild." This view is echoed by Niku Jafarnia, a Yemen researcher at Human Rights Watch. "When you have a country in which nearly two-thirds of people are in need of aid, any additional precarity and displacement will have a real civilian cost," she said. "Thousands of civilians were killed in the fighting between the Saudi-led coalition and the Houthis between 2014 and 2022, and warring parties repeatedly demonstrated extreme disregard for civilian life," she said. "The renewed fighting now threatens to repeat the devastating civilian casualty events of the earlier years of the war," she added. Edited by: M. Gagnon

item.title: Conspiracy theories can provide answers but not peace
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 3.00
Psychology is not an exact science. That may irk a few researchers in the field. But it is important to mention upfront: Researching the psychology of conspiracy theories — why people are drawn to believing them and the effect they have on those people — is a complicated field of research, and conclusions are difficult to derive. That is due, in part, to one of the basic problems with psychology, whether it's in treatment or in research, and that is that it relies on people's self-awareness. If we take the example of the 9/11 terrorist attacks, some people continue to maintain it was "inside job," orchestrated by a secretive and powerful club of evil doers in the US government, intent on controlling citizens' lives by fear. And that may be true. But it may also be true that you, as a believer in such a theory, have always felt powerful people — your parents or teachers — have controlled and curtailed your agency in life. You may even have a false memory of how the terrorist attacks evolved on that day in 2001. Then, if someone asked you, "What really happened?", could you really say it for sure? I couldn't. Self-report data are an issue in conspiracy research Whether as patients or participants in a study, we may be asked to "self-report" — to look inside ourselves and express how we feel and why. Self-reporting is an established way of measuring conspiracies, said Neil Dagnall, a professor of psychology at Manchester Metropolitan University, in an interview with DW. But self-report data are "not perfect," he added. They can be difficult data to handle because each judgment a person makes about themselves is relative, inherently subjective and open to outside influence and bias. People's answers can change from day-to-day, especially when they involve emotions or feelings about mental state, depending on a multitude of events and experiences in our lives. In addition, there is no common scale. Say, for example, you and a friend were asked, "Are you happy?" You may both say "yes," but your reasons for doing so may be completely different and be subject to different variables. The same goes for a question like, "Do you believe in conspiracy theories?" "The judgment I'm making is a relative one. What's my norm? Am I comparing it to my friends who don't believe in conspiracies, or am I in a group of people who do believe in conspiracies? We're always making relative judgments about our psychological propensities," said Dagnall. Which suggests we're unlikely to ever get a definitive answer. Self-report data suggest correlations, not causation. In a study on conspiratorial beliefs and well-being, which Dagnall co-authored and published in May 2026, "self-report data" was specifically highlighted as a limitation. This makes it very difficult to assess whether "conspiracy belief" or "conspiracy ideation" is good or bad for people and their sense of well-being. Especially as people who seek and believe in conspiracy theories often start out with a skewed view of reality. Observing behavior can offer clues There are ways of "triangulating" self-report data, as the authors of the study put it, to get a more reliable, objective reading of a person's emotional or psychological state. For example, psychologists use behavioral observations, like measuring heart rate variability or Galvanic Skin Responses such as the electrical conductance of a person's skin, which is affected by sweating under stress. You can also retest participants' self-reported data, and therefore its reliability, by asking the same questions at different points in time. But there is another factor that complicates research into the psychology of conspiracy theories, and that is that they, and people who believe in them, are more common than we like to think or admit (even when we believe them ourselves). "The idea that people who believe in conspiracies in general populations are remarkable or different is not true," said Dagnall. The truth: 'conspiracies theories are common' Most of us, at some point in our lives, are bound to see something strange or stressful in society and question whether we, as individuals or as a member of a group, accept the accepted truth of how that thing or event came about. It can be a healthy sign of a questioning mind. There are positive examples of conspiracy theories that happened to kickstart investigations that then revealed the horrible truth of government corruption. Take Partygate during the COVID pandemic in the United Kingdom or — the mother of all conspiracies — Watergate during the Nixon Administration in the United States. And there are other conspiracy theories, such as the one that nobody has ever landed on the moon, which you can either take seriously or laugh about. It all comes down to "the degree to which we engage in conspiracies generally, and the extent to which they interfere and disrupt our everyday lives," said Dagnall. For Dagnall, who doesn't believe in the 1969 moon landing, it doesn't seem to disrupt his daily life — at least, that is what he self-reported to DW. But for some people, conspiracy theories are disruptive and can lead to a sustained sense of dissatisfaction. "Ample studies suggest that exposure to conspiracy theories or belief in them might lead to more negative emotions, heightened anxiety or even paranoid thoughts," said Zuzanna Molenda, a researcher at the Polish Academy of Sciences and lead-author of a 2023 study on emotion dysregulation and belief in conspiracy theories. Some people may be primed to more readily believe in conspiracy theories because they generally struggle to deal with psychological threat and distress. When they then seek answers in conspiracy theories, their pre-existing negative psychology may be enhanced. "If anything, the available evidence suggests that rather than help people manage difficult emotions, conspiracy beliefs may be accompanied by or contribute to further distress," wrote Molenda in an email to DW. No long-term benefit from conspiracy belief There may be some psychological benefit to conspiracy theories, said Molenda, but only in the short term. "Conspiracy beliefs can provide people with a sense of explanation and understanding when events feel uncertain or difficult to make sense of. For some people, they might also be a source of entertainment and fun. For others, they can provide a sense of belonging and connection with others who share the same beliefs, and they can be an important part of social identity," Molenda said. But these potential benefits do not necessarily translate into better well-being in the longer term, said Molenda. In the end, we're all searching for meaning and purpose in life. If we find a satisfactory answer, it gives us something that psychologists call presense — a direction in life, and that is good. But if your search only leads to more uncertainty, more anxiety and more doubt in your purpose in life, then that's bad. "And people who believe in conspiracies are asking questions but not getting answers," said Dagnall. Edited by: Kristie Pladson

item.title: BSW and AfD – a political love-hate relationship in Germany
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.96
Following the election in Saxony-Anhalt, there is no clear governing coalition because the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) with its 44% share of the vote has fallen just short of securing an absolute majority. That means the formation of a new government in one of Germany's 16 federal states is more difficult than ever. This is also partly due to the success that the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), which was founded only in 2024, has managed to achieve. Wagenknecht, a trained economist, was a longtime member of the socialist Left Party, formerly a communist who over time has distanced herself further from her political roots. Her party does not conform to traditional labels. Many people can no longer relate much to labels like "left" or "right," she says. From the very beginning, Wagenknecht also showed no reluctance to engage with the AfD. Her long-held credo has been that the party includes people who are treated unfairly if labeled as Nazis. Now, Sahra Wagenknecht and her followers are working towards seeking common ground with the AfD and can even imagine helping the party's lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund into the role of state premier by abstaining from the vote. Wagenknecht mentioned this scenario before the September 6 election. Both AfD and BSW oppose 'uncontrolled migration' A few days before the vote, Sahra Wagenknecht spoke on TV broadcaster ntv about overlapping policy preferences of BSW and AfD voters: "These are people who have similar concerns: They want controlled migration, they do not want this uncontrolled migration and they want above all that politics is again conducted in their interests, that their lives are the focus." However, there is also a significant degree of agreement on issues other than German immigration policy: both parties call for an end to German arms deliveries to Ukraine, which has been attacked by Russia in violation of international law. Or they claim that freedom of speech no longer exists in Germany. Whether the BSW will actually team up with the AfD remains completely open. AfD lead candidate Siegmund emphasized even before the election that he intended to govern only with an absolute majority of his own. When the BSW was founded in January 2024, it had a spectacular start: Formed as a splinter party from the socialist Left Party, the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) was swiftly elected to the European Parliament and in the same year received double-digit results in three state parliament elections. In the eastern German states of Brandenburg and Thuringia, the party entered straight into government coalitions. That would also have been possible in Saxony, but coalition negotiations with the CDU and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) failed. The BSW favors a tough approach to refugees. It opposes any form of military support, whether for Ukraine or for Israel. The party's leader, Sahra Wagenknecht, is an economist who grew up in communist East Germany. She has had no reservations about contact with the AfD from the beginning. As early as 2023, she stated that some people within the party were being labeled Nazis unfairly. From rising star to struggling party However, the BSW in Saxony-Anhalt has ruled out a classic coalition. Following elections in Brandenburg and Thuringia in 2024, the branches in those states went against the stated will of their founder and joined governments alongside established parties. The permanent conflict between the federal leadership of the party and its state branches led to the breakdown of the coalition with the Social Democrats in Brandenburg, starting in 2025. In Thuringia, led by a coalition of the CDU, SPD and BSW, most of the BSW lawmakers declared that they were leaving the party two days before the election in Saxony-Anhalt. However, they wanted to remain a part of the CDU-led state government. "We have not been elected to tolerate flirts with right-wing radicals," is how Finance Minister Katja Wolf explained this decision, referring to the rapprochement with the AfD initiated by Wagenknecht. The BSW's success in Saxony-Anhalt and accompanying key role in the formation of the government has given the party, at least for the moment, a largely unexpected significance. During the Bundestag federal election of 2025 the BSW narrowly failed to reach the 5% threshold needed to enter parliament and, also due to its many internal conflicts, it seemed to have little credibility among the population. Furthermore, its figurehead Sahra Wagenknecht has stepped back from the leadership of her party and is no longer running for its chairmanship. She continues to exert her influence in the background, though, and is a drawcard at BSW rallies, especially during election campaigns. Boost for upcoming state elections? Following their successful entry into Saxony-Anhalt's parliament, which according to pre-election polls was by no means guaranteed, Wagenknecht responded confidently. "The BSW's comeback has begun," she told German news agency dpa. How sustainable this upswing is will be revealed on September 20, when parliamentary elections will be held in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and the city-state of Berlin. This article was translated from German.

item.title: Serbia, the conflicted EU candidate
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.76
The state-supported funeral of Ratko Mladic in Belgrade this week has raised a pressing question in Brussels: Can a country seek EU membership while giving a hero's farewell to a convicted war criminal? For many, the event has shown that Serbia's accession process has not merely stalled. It has largely lost its political drive. "For too long, the EU has kept treating Serbia as a normal candidate country," Engjellushe Morina of the European Council on Foreign Relations told DW, despite Belgrade's continued backsliding on democracy and the rule of law. Naim Leo Besiri of Serbia's Institute for European Affairs adds: "The ruling majority in Serbia has not performed anything that was promised on the reform agenda during the last five years." A candidate moving away from Europe Both experts point out that Belgrade has refused to join EU sanctions against Russia. Democratic standards have deteriorated under nationalist President Aleksandar Vucic, while relations with Kosovo remain tense. Despite having been sentenced to life imprisonment by a UN court for genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes, Ratko Mladic was buried in Belgrade on Monday with military honors and the participation of government representatives. President Vucic stayed away, but facilitated and defended the public mourning. Brussels reacted unusually strongly. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the images shocking. European Council President Antonio Costa condemned the glorification of war criminals. Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos canceled a visit to Serbia. Has the EU been too lenient? But both Morina and Besiri say that this is not enough. They believe Vucic has been given too much room to maneuver for too long. In their perception, he has been treated as an indispensable partner who could secure stability in the Western Balkans and keep Serbia anchored to the West, despite disregarding basic European values. Besiri says Serbian civil society had warned Brussels for years about attacks on media freedom, the rule of law and democratic institutions. But, he adds, the EU largely turned a blind eye. Economic relations demonstrate the strong ties between the EU and Serbia. The bloc is Serbia's largest trading partner, investor and financial donor. Politically, however, Serbia has developed a close partnership with Moscow. A common argument for continuing relations with Serbia is therefore based on the concern that greater pressure could push the country further towards Russia or China. Strong economic ties, close relations with Russia Morina accepts that isolating Serbia would be dangerous, but sees other options between accommodation and abandoning relations altogether. The EU should remain engaged with Serbian society while forcing Vucic to make clear political choices, she argues. Besiri says Russia and China could never replace the European market. In his view, Vucic uses both countries as a threat to discourage Brussels from taking firmer action. Both researchers see strategies behind the current approach: Vucic benefits from cooperation without implementing the necessary reforms. Brussels, meanwhile, can continue to claim that Serbia remains tied to Europe. The limits of financial pressure The EU has not remained entirely inactive. It has started applying financial pressure. Further payments under the Growth Plan for the Western Balkans have been withheld because of concerns about judicial independence. Besiri doubts that this will change Vucic's calculations. Broad funding cuts could hurt the population more than the political elite, he argues. Instead, he advocates targeted measures against those responsible for the country's democratic decline and the misuse of its institutions. Could the election bring change? The early parliamentary election on October 25 could put Vucic's model to the test. After 12 years as president, he now wants to remain Serbia's dominant political figure by becoming the next prime minister. Besiri says that the political opposition in Serbia remains fragile and that "it is extremely difficult to win democratically in undemocratic elections." Neither expert expects one election to repair Serbia's institutions or fundamentally change its relationship with the EU. Reconciliation remains a distant prospect Reconciliation in the region appears even more distant. According to Besiri, Serbia would first have to acknowledge its role in the wars of the 1990s and accept established facts about the crimes committed. Instead, narratives portraying Serbs exclusively as victims remain deeply embedded in Serbian politics, education and the media. "What has been happening recently is basically the reverse of everything that has been built for so many years," Morina underlines. Mladic's funeral did not cause this development, she adds. It simply revealed once again how far Serbia currently remains from both regional reconciliation and EU membership. Edited by: Carla Bleiker

item.title: Iran pursues cautious escalation ahead of US midterms
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.67
The war with Iran "is going to end immediately after the [US midterm] election because they can't hold out any longer," US President Donald Trump said of Iran's leaders on Wednesday. Speaking at the Republican midterm convention, the first such event to be held at a massive arena in Dallas, Texas, Trump described the November 3 vote as "one of the most important elections of your lives," and once again defended the war against Iran. The US president restated his argument that he had launched the attacks to prevent Tehran from developing a nuclear weapon. He also promised that oil prices would fall as soon as the US had won the war. But even if Trump's promises are taken at face value, rising gas prices are sure to hurt Republicans' electoral prospects in the midterms. On Wednesday, Brent crude — the global benchmark for prices — jumped to over $100 (€86) per barrel. The fighting escalated again this week, with the US striking Iranian oil tankers in retaliation for Iran's targeting of a US warship. Iran's tightrope walk "Iran still appears to see escalation primarily as a controlled instrument of coercive bargaining, rather than as an end in itself," said Mohammad Ghaedi, a Middle East expert and professor at the Department of Political Science at George Washington University. "Iran is trying to impose costs on the United States without raising those costs so dramatically that Washington feels compelled to return to full-scale war," he explained. "That helps explain why the number of missiles fired at US naval vessels has remained relatively limited." The regime wants to demonstrate that it can threaten US forces and disrupt the maritime traffic in the region, the expert said, "but it also wants to keep the confrontation below a threshold that could trigger a much larger American response." A return to the Islamabad truce? Tehran's preferred outcome would be a return to the Memorandum of Understanding signed in Islamabad in June, Ghaedi said, referring to a preliminary deal that paused the full-scale conflict. At the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in late August, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian reiterated that, if the United States returns to the memorandum, Iran would return as well. From Tehran, however, this scenario seems increasingly unlikely. Ghaedi said the first provision of the memorandum presents a major obstacle, as it requires an Israeli withdrawal from Lebanon — "something Tehran sees as unlikely before Israel's elections." Trump reportedly urged to limit US response Israel is going to the polls to elect a new parliament on October 27, just days before the US is set to hold its midterm vote. In Tehran, many believe that a decisive turning point in the conflict will not come until after these two elections. On September 2, the Reuters news agency reported that senior advisers to President Trump were urging him to limit any escalation of the conflict, fearing political repercussions for the Republicans at the midterms. The White House is reportedly considering expanding the military action after the elections. Tehran, Ghaedi said, "has little interest in pushing the conflict into a much higher level of escalation." "If Democrats gain control of Congress and try to constrain Trump's conduct of the war, Iran would be even more cautious about doing anything that could create a rally-around-the-flag effect or push Democrats closer to Trump." Will Iran bend to economic pressure? While military developments are hard to predict, the US will likely continue to boost economic pressure on Iran. But Ahmad Alavi, an Iranian economics professor based in Sweden, warns that economic pressure alone would not result in political concessions. "If the leadership of the Islamic Republic concludes that the goal of the pressure is not to change its behavior but to weaken or overthrow it, it might view concessions as a greater threat to its survival and resort instead to escalating military actions," he told DW. Tehran would be more willing to make concessions if there were a genuine prospect of easing pressure and an established channel for negotiations, he added. Gulf states search for Hormuz solution Meanwhile, Oman and several other Gulf states are once again seeking a diplomatic solution to the conflict. The foreign ministers of the Gulf states are planning to meet with their Iranian counterpart in Salalah, Oman, next week, to try to reach a deal that would temporarily ensure the safety of commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the Financial Times reported. However, such an agreement would likely require Washington's approval, given the prolonged US naval blockade against Iran. Iran keeps up hard line in public Iran's leaders have continued to signal defiance as the conflict drags on. "We will continue the war until final victory," Ali Nikzad, deputy speaker of parliament, told reporters on September 9. Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesman for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), also demanded on September 8 that the US "completely cease hostilities" and refrain from further threats if it wanted to end the current situation. At the same time, he threatened a more comprehensive Iranian response should the US attacks continue. On September 10, the IRGC released a video that, according to Iranian sources, shows the capture of a US Anduril Dive-LD unmanned underwater vehicle in the Strait of Hormuz. The vehicle is said to have been deployed on a covert mine-clearing mission. This article was originally written in German.

item.title: BRICS Summit 2026: Putin, Modi reaffirm partnership
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.38
What you need to know - Putin and Modi discuss a wide range of issues, including the Ukraine-Russia conflict, energy cooperation and trade across several sectors - Modi again urges Putin to end the war in Ukraine - Modi calls for maritime trade to be protected during bilateral talks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in New Delhi - Pezeshkian warns Iran coming under 'critical, dangerous' US economic pressure Here is a roundup of some of the top headlines from the BRICS Summit 2026 in India: Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed. We are pausing our coverage It's past midnight in New Delhi, so we are pausing our coverage for tonight. We will be back on Saturday for the start of the two-day BRICS leaders' summit. IN DEPTH: India's BRICS strategy tested with Xi, Putin set to visit New Delhi's "America Plus" approach sees India deepening its ties with China and Russia, while also trying to keep BRICS from turning into an anti-Western platform. But with BRICS both growing in size and increasingly troubled by internal divisions, the forum might limit Narendra Modi's diplomatic gains. Find out more about India's diplomatic balancing act between BRICS members China and Russia and the West in this report by DW's Mural Krishnan. Modi urges Putin to end Ukraine war India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi again appealed to Russian President Vladimir Putin to enter negotiations to end the war in Ukraine. During their meeting in New Delhi on the eve of the BRICS summit, Modi told Putin that dialogue and diplomacy are the right way to resolve conflicts, the Indian Foreign Ministry said in a statement. Russia's war in Ukraine and its impact on shipping in the Black Sea have affected India, a major buyer of Russian oil and grain. Indian sailors have also been caught up in drone attacks. The war, which the Indian Foreign Ministry has referred to as conflicts "in the Black Sea region," is on the agenda for the two-day summit. India has adopted a typically pragmatic approach to the conflict, seeking to balance ties with the West and with Russia. However, during an August meeting of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) in Kyrgyzstan, Modi urged Putin to end the war, which was in its fifth year. IN DEPTH: India looks to steer BRICS away from anti-Western turn The BRICS summit 2026 takes place in Delhi this weekend. Unlike last year, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are expected to attend. Can India keep the expanded bloc united? Modi meets Iranian president Pezeshkian Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has met with Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian on the eve of the BRICS leaders' summit. According to a statement by India's Foreign Ministry, Modi thanked Pezeshkian for taking part in the summit "despite the challenging circumstances" for Iran, which remains at war with the US and Israel. Despite that conflict and economic pressure from the US to cut trading ties, India has sought to balance maintaining its relationship with Tehran and with Israel and Arab Gulf states. Modi called for regional peace and stability to be restored and maintained and for maritime trade routes to be protected, amid the US and Iran's competing blockades of the Strait of Hormuz. Iran facing 'critical, dangerous' pressure — Pezeshkian Iranis currently experiencing "critical, dangerous" levels of pressure, President Masoud Pezeshkian said. The pressure comes as a result of the US sanctions on the country, according to Pezeshkian. "Iran has been subjected to heavy sanctions in recent years," the Iranian leader said ahead of the BRICS summit in India. "This pressure has reached critical and dangerous stage in recent months following the military aggression by the US and Israel," he added. Pezeshkian also said that the world is going through a period of "unprecedented complexity." Putin blames West for attempting to reclaim 'former leadership' Russian President Vladimir Putin blamed Western countries for attempting to reclaim their "former leadership" in an "unseemly" fashion, According to Russia's leader, the West is focusing on destroying facilities and pipelines, as well as seizing vessels, in an attempt to maintain its economic leadership. Putin made these comments while speaking at the BRICS business forum in India. Modi, Putin reaffirm partnership on issues of mutual interest Indian PM Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin held bilateral talks on the sidelines of the BRICS Summit that will begin on Saturday. The two leaders "exchanged views on India-Russia engagement in the multilateral sphere, in particular in BRICS under India’s Chairship for 2026," a statement by India's Ministry of External Affairs said. In the meeting, the leaders also exchanged views on "key regional and global issues of mutual interest, including the conflicts in West Asia and the Black Sea region which have impacted maritime trade and the safety and security of Indian seafarers." Reaffirming their ties, the two leaders committed to "remain engaged in an effort to strengthen further the Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership between the two countries," the statement added. Pezeshkian arrives for BRICS Summit Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian landed in Delhi to attend the BRICS Summit. This is the first visit by an Iranian President to India in over eight years. Pezeshkian is scheduled to hold bilateral talks with Prime Minister Narendra Modi at 6.15 p.m. local time Friday to advance two-way trade and strengthen overall ties. His participation at the BRICS Summit and bilateral talks with Modi holds significance as it comes at a time when tensions are rife in the Middle East and energy market disruptions have shaken the economy worldwide. WATCH — India's difficult BRICS chairship With BRICS nations now representing nearly 3.7 billion people and close to 40% of global GDP, leaders are meeting amid rising geopolitical tensions, trade disputes and energy challenges. While the expanded bloc is seeking a stronger voice in the global economy, disagreements over an alternative payment system and China's dominant role could test unity. Renewable energy and green infrastructure financing are emerging as key areas to watch. Former UN diplomat: BRICS is 'voice of Global South,' but 'contradictions remain' Speaking to DW about the BRICS Summit, former UN diplomat Shashi Tharoor said that the expansion of the bloc has made it the voice of the Global South. The BRICS coalition started out with four member countries; Brazil, Russia, India and China but now has 11 members and partner countries after the economic bloc decided to open up membership for more countries in 2023. Tharoor noted that while Iran joined the coalition, US strategic partners Egypt and Ethiopia also joined "The expansion that took place in Johannesburg turned out to be one in which both sets of geopolitical points of view were accommodated," Tharoor noted in an interview with DW. He argued that, "in some ways the expansion has made it much more the voice of the global south." However, he also said that while the majority of the world is represented in the new 11-member BRICS, the chances of having a consensus has also decreased. "I would say that BRICS is functioning, but the contradictions remain, and some contradictions have become even more apparent," he said. He said that when BRICS leaders met this year, they "could not agree on any particular language, and so the chair, India, issued a chair statement instead… it wasn't just Iran, it was also Ukraine that they couldn't agree on." Tharoor noted that the bloc has a "built-in set of geopolitical divergences which will crop up whenever issues divide the members." Piyush Goyal proposes 'borderless' digital trade at BRICS Indian Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal on Friday urged BRICS member countries to link their payment systems, encourage trade in local currencies, and make digital trade more accessible globally. Addressing the opening ceremony of the BRICS Business Forum on Friday, Goyal highlighted India's digital payments ecosystem, including the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), as a potential foundation for deeper cross-border financial cooperation among BRICS economies. "Today, it is also accepted in 11 countries and I would urge the Brics member countries and partner countries to link our payment systems, trade in each other's local currencies, make digital trade global and build together for the future emerging technologies," Goyal said as reported by Indian newspaper Deccan Herald. Modi, Putin to meet on the sidelines of BRICS Russian President Vladimir Putin landed in Delhi on Friday to attend the BRICS Summit being held at the Bharat Mandapam on September 12 and 13. He will be meeting Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi in the afternoon. Talks are expected to focus on enhancing cooperation in a range of areas, including defence, energy, technology, pharmaceuticals and people-to-people exchanges. "Warmly welcome President Vladimir Putin of Russia for the 18th BRICS Summit. He was received by MoS K V Singh at the airport. India and Russia share multifaceted and longstanding ties anchored in Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership," Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said in a post on X. This is Putin's first in-person participation at a BRICS Summit held outside Russia since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Later in the evening, Modi will also be holding a bilateral talk with Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian. Welcome to our coverage Hello! This is Midhat from the New Delhi bureau, bringing you the biggest headlines emerging from across India. With just one day to go before the BRICS Summit kicks off, Delhi is all geared up and welcoming the dignitaries — several of whom have already arrived in the capital, including Russian President Vladimir Putin. From Friday onwards, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi will be holding bilateral talks with several leaders, including China's Xi Jinping, Iran's Masoud Pezeshkian and Crown Prince of Abu Dhabi, Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan. Security in the capital has been intensified with thousands of personnel deployed. All schools in Delhi, including government, and private schools will remain closed on September 11 due to the BRICS Summit. Commuters in Delhi will see traffic restrictions and diversions over the bext three days. Authorities have advised travelers to plan journeys and use the Metro where possible. Stay tuned as we bring you more on the BRICS Summit and everything else making a buzz in the country.

item.title: The billion-euro trade driving Europe's eels to extinction
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.36
In Plentzia, a small waterfront town close to bustling Bilbao, eel fishing has long been part of daily life. Now fisherfolk across Spain's Basque Country can no longer catch the animals, a prized delicacy at the center of what authorities describe as one of the world's most lucrative wildlife trafficking trades. The regional ban is meant to protect the European eel, a critically endangered species, which has seen population declines of around 95% since the 1980s. Yet local fishermen argue the regulations punish those who adhere to them, while criminal networks profit from a billion-euro trade in illegally caught eels. "So it's the Basque fishermen who will make the eel extinct when the rest are allowed to fish?" said Unai Eizaguirre, who's been fishing eels for 30 years and is now facing the prospect of income shorfalls. "It's ridiculous." Conservationists support the ban as an emergency response in the face of multiple threats from pollution and climate change. But marine biologist Estibaliz Diaz says longer-term measures, like removing hydroelectric dams that block migration routes and kill eels with their turbines are also needed. "The situation is so bad that we have to act on everything," said Diaz, who works with local marine research institute AZTI. Eel smuggling as lucrative as drugs Part of what makes European eels so vulnerable is their remarkable life cycle, which was, until relatively recently, a source of mystery. Scientists now know adult eels migrate thousands of kilometers from European rivers to the Sargasso Sea in the North Atlantic, their only known spawning grounds. They breed and then die, leaving their larvae to drift to Europe. By the time they reach rivers, they've transformed into tiny, transparent "glass eels." Today, the number of glass eels reaching the Gulf of Biscay and connected waterways is only around 12% of what it was before the 1980s, Diaz says. The young glass eels conservationists are trying to protect are the most valuable in the illegal trade, fetching up to €9,000 ($10,400) per kilogram. "You can compare it with drug trafficking. Every year they seize tons of illegally caught eel in Europe," said Eizaguirre. "The big business lies in trafficking them to Asia," adding that the huge profits and comparatively small fines for smaller infractions by local fishers make the risk worth it. However, when criminal organizations are involved, penalties can be substantial with fines up to 6 times the value of illegally smuggled eel. Demand in countries such as China, South Korea and Japan is driving prices. As is a biological peculiarity: So far, it's been exceedingly difficult to get eels to reproduce in captivity. This means fish farms — where the eels are raised before being sold to premium restaurants — need a steady stream of young from the wild. Sometimes, the same smuggled eels come back to Europe as fillets for the sushi market. Conservationists had hoped pressure on the species would ease when the EU banned export of the species outside the bloc in 2010. Instead, organized crime groups have increasingly muscled in on the market, with the illegal trade now generating an estimated €3 billion in profits in peak years. "Our estimated maximum was always 100 tons of glass eels smuggled annually. That's already around 300 million fish," said Florian Stein, head of policy and science at the German Angling Association. But information from his contacts in the illegal trade have led him to the conclusion that it was a "very conservative estimate." International law enforcement agencies are also cracking down, with Europol's Operation Lake seizing 22 tons of glass eels and arresting 26 suspects between 2024 and 2025. "There has been a lot of pressure from law enforcement throughout Europe," said Interpol's Sanchez Romero. "That's why the criminal groups always look for new routes." Eels smuggled in suitcases along complex routes Stein, who wrote his doctoral dissertation on international eel smuggling and advises the German government, said trafficking has increased since 2020, and illegal trade routes have become more complex. "Ten years ago, Madrid airport was still one of the biggest smuggling hotspots," he added. This was due to its proximity to fishing grounds in northern Spain and Portugal. Increased checks by Spanish authorities on flights to East Asia forced traffickers to adapt. Experts now say a new route running through North Africa via Morocco, Mauritania and Senegal has become increasingly important. Geography is one reason the route is attractive. The Strait of Gibraltar is 14 kilometers at its narrowest point and a busy maritime junction. "We know that many drugs are also transported through this strait," Moroccan investigative journalist Yassir Al-Makhtoum told DW. European eels also inhabit rivers and estuaries in Morocco. Though the country has banned the export of glass eels smaller than 12 centimeters (4.7 inches), it is building a legal domestic eel trading industry. Experts fear that's acting as a cover for trafficked animals coming in from Europe. From Morocco, smugglers then move eels along numerous routes to Asia. The means are not always sophisticated. Glass eels can be transported in ordinary suitcases on domestic flights. They're placed in bags filled with a little water and insulated to keep their temperature stable. They can survive for up to 48 hours in those conditions. Once in Asia, they go to the fish farms. A species running out of time Eels are an important indicator species for the health of ocean and riverine ecosystems because their long migrations across multiple habitats make them vulnerable to problems that could also harm other species. They also serve as important prey for herons, otters and larger fish. "But the impact of its disappearance is difficult to predict," said marine biologist Diaz. Under EU regulations, member states must undertake measures to allow 40% of adult eels to return to the Sargasso Sea to spawn. Diaz also wants to ensure at least 40% of glass eels make it back from the Sargasso Sea. But European eels are not the only eel species under threat. A proposal to protect all freshwater eel species from illegal and unsustainable trade was rejected at the 2025 CITES wildlife conference. For Stein such protection is key. "The proposal should be on the table again at the next conference. I just don't know how else we can get a handle on this problem," said Stein, adding more lobbying and coalition building is needed to advocate for a ban. “The eel for us is more than just a fish,” said Unai Eizaguirre. “It's been part of our identity for centuries.” For fishermen like him, better protection for the eel represents a chance at a sustainable future. Edited by: Jennifer Collins The research for this story was sponsored by: The Med Mosaic. This article was updated to clarify the fall in volume of glass eels reaching the Gulf of Biscay and connected waterways is compared to figures from the 1980s.

item.title: Magyar vs. Moscow: Hungary toughens stance toward Russia
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.23
While Viktor Orban was in power, no other EU member state was as pro-Russia as Hungary. Indeed, the prime minister's apparent eagerness to be of service to the Russian president earned him the nickname "Putin's pinscher" or "Kremlin agent." For years, Hungary was seen as a security risk both in the EU and NATO. Russian spies were able to operate in the country largely unhindered for a long time. In February, it came to light that Peter Szijjarto, Orban's foreign minister from 2014 to 2026, had passed on confidential information from EU meetings to his Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov. All this came to an end in May, when the government headed by Peter Magyar took office. An unambiguous signal to Russia In a clear departure from the government line under Orban, Hungary's new prime minister has already heavily criticized Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine several times. The government also recently declared Russia a threat to Hungary's national security. This week, it took its biggest step yet against the Kremlin, expelling 10 Russian diplomats for engaging in activities "that are unacceptable for diplomats under the Vienna Convention," as announced by Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orban (no relation to the former prime minister). Although Orban did not provide any more details, the phrase is generally understood to mean that the diplomats in question were spies. Orban said the decision "protects Hungary's security and sovereignty." She added: "It does not imply breaking off diplomatic relations with Russia. Hungary intends to continue the necessary dialogue, based on mutual respect and adherence to the rules." Restoring old alliances The minister's brief announcement immediately generated a huge number of headlines and comments — hardly surprising given that this was not only evidence of a 180-degree turn on the government's policy toward Russia but also one of the toughest diplomatic sanctions targeting Moscow since the collapse of communism in 1989/1990. Speaking to Hungarian news website Index, secret service expert Peter Tarjani said this was "not a diplomatic conflict, but a serious secret service matter" and that with this decision, Hungary was simultaneously returning "to the mainstream of its allies' security policy." Political scientist and leading Hungarian Russia expert Andras Racz told the Hungarian national news agency MTI that Hungary was the only EU and NATO member not to have made such an expulsion in recent years. Racz said such a step "should really have been taken four and ahalf years ago." He added: "Hungary is now settling its old debt with its allies." Reliance on Russian gas? Under Viktor Orban, Hungary was the only EU country never to unreservedly condemn Russia's all-out war against Ukraine. Indeed, during the final two years of his rule, Orban even blamed Ukraine and the West for Russia's aggression. But long before that — even after he came to power back in 2010 — Viktor Orban took a markedly pro-Russia line, which he justified, among other things, with the claim that Hungary was more dependent on Russian energy supplies than almost any other country in the region. His government's repeated assertion that Russian gas was cheaper has long been disproved. What's more, the expansion of the Paks nuclear power plant with Russian support will cost Hungary dearly for decades to come. In the light of all this, Orban's close ties to Russia remain a mystery. Absurd situations For Hungary, this closeness to Russia often led to absurd situations in which the country's national security was put at risk. At the same time, Orban repeatedly told his critics that it was they who were a threat to Hungary's sovereignty. For example, Russian secret service agents for years took part in military-style training exercises in the far-right scene right up until 2016. Starting in 2012, Russian secret service operatives for years stole huge amounts of data from the Hungarian Foreign Ministry and other agencies without the government ever publicly condemning it. In 2019, Russia got permission to move the headquarters of the International Investment Bank (IIB) to Budapest. The IIB was known as the "spy bank" because its leadership was made up of individuals linked to or associated with Russia's FSB intelligence service. It was only after the United States imposed sanctions on the bank in 2023 that it left Hungary again. Investigative journalist Szabolcs Panyi has warned multiple times in recent years that Hungary had become a "logistical center and deployment zone for Russian secret services," thereby putting the whole region at risk. Rejection of Orban's pro-Russia course Orban's strictly pro-Russia course was laterally rejected by many Hungarians. The decidedly pro-EU orientation of Peter Magyar and his Tisza party had a considerable role to play in the party's election victory earlier this year. The EU flag was often seen and spontaneous cries of "Russians, go home" were often heard at election rallies last spring. Unlike Viktor Orban, Magyar and leading Tisza politicians are convinced that Hungary's place is exclusively in the European Union and that the country should only maintain pragmatic low-level relations with Russia. Nevertheless, many observers and experts are surprised at how radically the Magyar government has turned away from Russia. Andras Telkes, the former deputy head of Hungary's foreign intelligence service (IH), wrote in the newspaper Nepszava that the expulsion of diplomats shows that the presence of Russian secret services in Hungary obviously runs "very deep" and that the country has a serious problem. Telkes said the expulsion of 10 diplomats would help rebuild trust in Hungary in the eyes of the secret services of its NATO allies. He said the decision was significant. "Expelling two or three people would have been a sign," Telkes said. "Expelling 10 people already means war." Telkes said the expulsions create a serious security problem for Hungary. Will Moscow turn off the taps? A spokeswoman for the Russian Foreign Ministry condemned the expulsion of the diplomats in strong terms. She spoke of a "Russophobe lobby in Budapest" and announced a "hard and painful" response. Russian lawmaker Andrey Kolesnik, a member of the State Duma's Defense Committee, said the government would consider halting gas supplies to Hungary. Foreign Minister Orban knows more about such Russian threats than anyone else in the new Hungarian government: In 2007, she wrote her doctoral thesis on Russia's energy policy in Central Europe. A year later, she published a book: "Power, Energy, and the New Russian Imperialism." This article was originally published in German.

item.title: China angered by Taiwan VP's visit to EU democracy forum
item.description:
Source: Deutsche Welle Score: 2.18
China was angered by Italy and the EU on Friday, lodging "solemn representations" with both after news broke that high-ranking Taiwanese officials had traveled to the bloc to attend an annual democracy summit. Beijing's Foreign Ministry said it firmly opposes official interactions of any form with Taiwan by nations who have ties with China. Solemn representations is a literal translation of a Chinese term expressing diplomatic discontent. At issue is a visit by Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim and Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung, both of whom were welcomed to the Ventotene Conference for Freedom and Democracy in Italy. China sees democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory, which it has vowed to "reunite" with the mainland. Beijing has previously blasted Hsiao as an "independence diehard" and has criticized her Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) as a separatist outfit. Taiwan's government has not sought formal independence but Beijing has, nevertheless, threatened to take the island by military force. EU Parliament VP blasts Beijing 'regime' over interference European Parliament Vice President Pina Picierno announced Hsiao and Lin's attendance at the conference early Friday morning, adding that news of the visit had been kept under wraps until they arrived for safety reasons. The EU's Picierno, who called the visit a "very important message," was defiant on Friday, saying, "No one can decide who is hosted in Ventotene and who is not," and calling out the Chinese "regime" for seeking to interfere. Though Taiwanese foreign ministers travel abroad, it is rare for an official as high-ranking as the vice president to visit nations with ties to Beijing for fear of fallout for host countries. Other prominent pro-democracy advocates such as Russian Kremlin critic Yulia Navalnaya, the wife of the late Alexei Navalny, and Belarus opposition leader Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya are also in attendance. The conference began on Thursday and is scheduled to wrap up on Saturday. EU threading needle between support for Taiwan, ties with China Italy, like most nations, is not among Taiwan's 12 formal diplomatic allies, although the Vatican is. Still, both Italy and Taiwan have de facto embassies in each other's capitals. Italy's Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani will not meet with the visiting Taiwanese officials. Further details are expected to be made public after the conference concludes. The EU is walking a fine line between democratic support for Taiwan and relations with China. Beijing's support for Russia in its ongoing invasion of Ukraine — which also prompted Taiwan to seek closer ties with the EU in 2022 — has been a thorn in the side of EU nations and in Brussels. If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google, so you'll always see our verified news first. Edited by: Wesley Rahn

item.title: The Road Through Damascus
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 4.90
In early April, a convoy of 299 Iraqi fuel tankers crossed into Syria on its way to the Mediterranean port of Baniyas, one of the few remaining paths to international markets amid the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. It was the first time Iraqi oil had crossed through Syria legally since 2003, when the U.S. invasion of Iraq effectively shuttered the cross-border flow of oil from Iraq to Syria. In late April, Iraq expanded the route, reopening its northern Rabia crossing with Syria, a crossing that had been closed for more than a decade during Syria’s civil war. Between April and late July, more than 2.1 million metric tons of Iraqi fuel moved to the Syrian coast. Before Syria’s civil war began, in 2011, the country had served as a commercial crossroads between Iraq, Jordan, Lebanon, Turkey, and the Mediterranean, connecting Gulf states to European markets. But after 2011, Syria turned into a different kind of transit hub. Trade became dominated by Iranian weapons and logistics support on their way to Hezbollah in Lebanon, as well as fuel, narcotics, and other illicit trade that filled the coffers of the country’s dictator, Bashar al-Assad, but provided few benefits for Syrians. After Hayat Tahrir al-Sham, the militant group once led by Syria’s new president, Ahmed al-Shara, toppled the Assad regime at the end of 2024, regional trade began to trickle back in. By August 2025, as many as 327,000 trucks carrying over seven million tons of cargo crossed into Syria, according to estimates by Syria’s customs agency. Jordan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey began to normalize relations and do business in the country. Damascus’s new authorities moved quickly to restore the country’s ties with a wide variety of regional and international partners, with the aim of ending Syria’s economic isolation. Although significant, this is not nearly enough to rebuild the country after over a decade of civil war. In 2025, the World Bank estimated that Syria’s reconstruction would cost $216 billion, nearly ten times Syria’s projected GDP for 2024. Syria’s leaders are now positioning the country to benefit from a resurgence of regional turmoil. Since the outbreak of the Iran war, in late February, the opportunities for new foreign investment in Syria have proliferated. Because alignment with the United States and Israel and reliance on the Strait of Hormuz carry ever-greater risks of retaliation from Iran, many countries are turning to Syria, which has a variety of well-placed land and sea routes. Syrian authorities are using the potential rush of capital and trade to create a new source of revenue, allowing the state to recast the country’s image from a source of refugees, terrorism, and regional disorder to a transit power that plays a dominant role in regional connectivity. But the speed and scale of investment could also overwhelm the institutions needed to manage it. If not properly scrutinized or fairly distributed, the rush of new investment that seems so promising now may destabilize the country’s fragile recovery. AFTERSHOCKS The need for better and more diversified transit through the Middle East is not new, but for nearly 15 years, Syria’s civil war made transit through the country impossible. In 2009, the Saudi and Turkish governments began discussions around redeveloping the Hejaz Railway route, built by the Ottoman Empire and largely destroyed in World War I, but they abandoned these plans with the outbreak of Syria’s civil war. Between 2010 and 2021, Syrian exports fell by roughly 90 percent. Major transit routes through the country closed entirely as the state fragmented into competing zones of control. In 2023, India, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), the United States, and European partners proposed the India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor as a way to spur intraregional and interregional connectivity and integrate Israel, a node on the corridor, with its neighbors. Disruption in the Strait of Hormuz has made expanding these projects even more urgent. In April and June of this year, the Jordanian, Saudi, Syrian, and Turkish governments agreed to redevelop the Hejaz Railway within three to four years. Analyses of comparable regional rail corridors, such as that by the Atlantic Council, estimate that the railway could initially carry around 1.5 million containers annually, potentially rising to three million with track and port capacity expansion. This proposal resonates with Shara’s loose vision, laid out at an informal EU summit in April among leaders from Europe and the Middle East, for a Four Seas and Nine Corridors initiative that places Syria at the center of a network connecting the Persian Gulf, the Caspian Sea, the Black Sea, and the Mediterranean, facilitating ground- and sea-based trade in goods, electricity, and oil. Then, in July, Iraq and Syria agreed to rehabilitate the Kirkuk-Baniyas oil pipeline, which was destroyed during the U.S. invasion of Iraq in 2003, to create a permanent Mediterranean outlet for Iraqi oil. If the pipeline goes online within its four-year estimated timeline, it could transport two million barrels per day by 2030, equivalent to roughly 60 percent of Iraq’s crude exports before the Iran war and an estimated nine percent of the total oil that moved through the Strait of Hormuz. With new routes also planned through Turkey, Iraq is positioned to route more than 80 percent of its export volume around Hormuz, ending its near-total dependence on Gulf terminals. These trends, however, are not guaranteed to improve Syrians’ economic and political fortunes. Although Syria’s geographic position gives it geopolitical leverage with foreign actors seeking to diversify export routes, it also places the country in the middle of emerging rivalries, as Saudi Arabia and Turkey align on security, the UAE increasingly takes a commercial role in ports and logistics, and Israel attempts to prevent Turkey from establishing influence near its borders. Competition over who finances, operates, and protects these respective corridors could pull Syria into contests it is not stable enough to sustain. Syria could get pulled into contests over trade that it is not stable enough to sustain. Damascus has tried to limit this exposure by working with nearly every power willing to support its reconstruction and reintegration, including Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, the UAE, and the United States, as well as China and Russia. But this strategy is proving more difficult as time wears on. The influence of Syria’s greatest financial supporters is drawing Damascus toward a Qatari-Saudi-Turkish constellation. If competition over the corridors grows faster than Syria’s capacity to manage it, the country could fall victim to greater foreign control and extraction. Israel may also prove to be a significant obstacle to Syria’s reemergence as a reliable passageway for trade. The reconstruction of the Hejaz Railway, if successful, will decrease Israel’s importance to the India–Middle East–Europe Economic Corridor and as a Mediterranean gateway for Arab states. Israel may well try to resist this development.
