item.title: How al-Qaeda Ended
item.description:
Source: Foreign Affairs Score: 2.09
Al-Qaeda has ended. The organization that Osama bin Laden founded and led, that attacked the United States 25 years ago and killed 2,977 innocent Americans in the World Trade Center, the Pentagon, and rural Pennsylvania, no longer survives—and U.S. officials should say so, instead of burnishing the group’s legacy by acting and speaking as if it still exists. Terrorism has not ceased, jihadism has not gone away, and the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran may ignite more anti-American sentiment and violence. But the group that attacked the United States on 9/11 is finished. In the years following that assault, thousands of Americans dedicated their lives to avenging the victims. The nationwide horror of watching planes go into towers—innocent people crushed, burned, or jumping to their deaths—catalyzed a passionate response. And the cost to those who responded was high: in the post-9/11 wars, more than 15,000 U.S. military members and contractors died in combat, and some 1.8 million became disabled. And from 2012 to 2021, four times as many active-duty or veteran military members died by suicide as died in combat. Service members from loyal U.S. allies, especially Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, and the United Kingdom, joined the United States in combat; hundreds of them died fighting alongside Americans. They and their families deserve to know their efforts were not in vain. Washington and its allies lost the war in Afghanistan but succeeded against al-Qaeda. Jihadist terrorism persists as a threat, and not every group using the name “al-Qaeda” has been neutralized. Dangerous organizations operate in the Arabian Peninsula, the Horn of Africa, North Africa, the Sahel, and South Asia. They carry out attacks and hold territory, and some have come close to taking down governments, especially in Mali, Somalia, and Yemen. Jihadists of various stripes train in Taliban-governed Afghanistan—a development that must be closely monitored. But none of what are sometimes called “al-Qaeda affiliates” is centrally directed or led by bin Laden’s organization, and officials should cease suggesting they are, since doing so inflates the threat they pose without making it any easier to combat them. Indeed, it would be best to cease using the term “al-Qaeda affiliate” altogether. Studying the pattern of attacks tied directly to al-Qaeda shows how the central organization ran out of steam. Before 9/11, the core al-Qaeda organization kept up a steady pace of global operations against U.S. targets, with a track record that included the 1993 bombing of the World Trade Center (six dead, more than 1,000 injured), the 1996 bombing of Khobar Towers (19 killed, hundreds injured), the 1998 bombing of the U.S. embassies in Kenya and Tanzania (224 killed, thousands injured), and the 2000 attack on the USS Cole (17 killed). After 2001, core al-Qaeda’s efforts against the U.S. homeland included a fumbled 2001 attempt to ignite a bomb placed in a shoe on an airliner bound for Miami and a failed 2009 suicide bombing plot targeting the New York City subway. The group caused more pain for U.S. friends and allies than for the United States itself, with deadly attacks in Bali in 2002, Riyadh in 2003, and London in 2005. But following that spike in the first decade of the twenty-first century, the momentum shifted to other jihadist groups, and after 2009, core al-Qaeda’s global operations essentially ceased. For decades, I have studied how terrorist groups end, based on a dataset of 457 terrorist campaigns and organizations going back a century. By analyzing their makeup, targets, and intended audiences, one can identify common trajectories. Although not mutually exclusive, there are six major pathways such groups ultimately take: decapitation, negotiation, success, failure, repression, and reorientation to another mode of operation (such as ordinary criminality or insurgency). In the case of core al-Qaeda, although decapitation and military repression played important roles, the group ended primarily through strategic failure—just as bin Laden feared it would. A MOVING TARGET In the aftermath of the 9/11 attacks, the U.S. campaign should have been focused on destroying the perpetrators. But the United States failed to clearly define the threat. The Authorization for the Use of Military Force that Congress passed on September 14, 2001, did not mention al-Qaeda at all, instead vaguely identifying Washington’s enemies as “those nations, organizations or persons [the president] determines planned, authorized, committed or aided the terrorist attacks that occurred on September 11, 2001.” A few days later, President George W. Bush echoed that framing. “Our war on al-Qaeda begins with al-Qaeda but it does not end there,” he declared. “It will not end until every terrorist group of global reach has been found, stopped, and defeated.” With that, the United States declared war on a tactic, one that had shaped political violence in the modern world since anarchist terrorism swept through Europe before World War I. Washington had set itself a task it could never accomplish. Making the enemy “terrorism” meant its efforts would lack clarity and drag on endlessly. What followed was an ill-focused campaign in Afghanistan (which removed the Taliban from power in Kabul but allowed bin Laden and his cronies to escape) and then the war in Iraq, where al-Qaeda had not even operated until an affiliate emerged after the U.S. military occupation had been in place for a year. The invasion of Iraq did more to prolong the life of al-Qaeda than any other single event, drawing fresh recruits from Sunni populations all over the world, and eventually creating the conditions for the emergence of the Islamic State organization. Still, in the 25 years that followed, sometimes almost despite itself, the United States along with its allies did defeat bin Laden’s al-Qaeda—often with inadvertent help from the group itself. An important factor was the May 2011 killing of Osama bin Laden in Abbottabad, Pakistan, an event that undermined al-Qaeda’s coherence. U.S. forces stormed bin Laden’s compound, killed him, and then helicoptered his body to an aircraft carrier and buried it at sea, leaving no possibility for a memorial or focal point for his followers. The documents recovered in that raid were just as valuable to U.S. counterterrorism as bin Laden’s death, offering compelling evidence that he had not been centrally directing the group’s operations for some time. His death did not end al-Qaeda, but it was justice served, and it undercut the ability of his fans to rally around him. By September 2011, U.S. officials were claiming that the number of surviving people directly connected to carrying out the 9/11 attacks was no more than a couple of dozen. But instead of declaring victory over the group at that point and moving on, the U.S. drone campaign, which had begun in 2002 under Bush and accelerated in the early Obama administration, expanded its scope and target set. Instead of so-called personality attacks (which target known leaders), the campaign shifted to “signature strikes,” targeting unidentified individuals or groups who fit a particular profile, not just in Afghanistan and Pakistan but also in Somalia and Yemen. The drone campaign degraded al-Qaeda’s ranks and avenged attempted attacks—for example, by eliminating members of al-Qaeda’s Yemen affiliate who trained and equipped Umar Farouk Abdulmutallab, the would-be “underwear bomber” who tried to bring down a civilian airliner in 2009. But drone attacks also catalyzed terrorism: according to declassified FBI interviews, the 2013 Boston Marathon bomber, Tamerlan Tsarnaev (likewise inspired by al-Qaeda’s Yemen affiliate), told a friend that his killing of an eight-year-old in that attack was justified because children in Afghanistan and Pakistan had been killed by U.S. drones. The drone campaign had a strategic impact on U.S. allies: public attitudes in France, Germany, Spain, Turkey, and the United Kingdom hardened against Washington’s “global war on terrorism.” Drones were tactically important and probably saved lives, but they did not end al-Qaeda. More critical to that success was intelligence and law-enforcement collaboration among U.S. allies, which remains the bedrock of American counterterrorism. New measures to curb terrorist financing, biometric screening and databases, and new ways of sharing intelligence among allies helped Washington monitor threats beyond American shores. In 2006, for example, close cooperation between U.S. and British intelligence services thwarted an al-Qaeda-linked plot to smuggle the explosive TATP in beverage containers and take down U.S.-bound civilian aircraft over the Atlantic. THINGS FALL APART But much of the damage al-Qaeda suffered was self-inflicted. A key driver was a backlash against terrorist attacks that hurt Muslim civilians and a resulting loss of support among communities al-Qaeda supposedly represented. Bin Laden knew this was a weakness, and his frustration shows in the communications discovered in the Abbottabad compound. A May 2010 letter he wrote to one of his deputies warns, “This is when we lose the perception of the Muslims towards us, which is that we are the ones defending the Muslims and fighting their biggest enemy, the Crusader Zionist alliance…[and instead] killing those that the general public consider Muslims.” Al-Qaeda started building global franchises in 2004, but they typically emerged out of existing organizations, and their operational ties to core al-Qaeda could be hazy. According to bin Laden’s own assessment, rogue affiliates hurt al-Qaeda’s cause more than they helped it, since most victims of their violence were Muslim civilians, whose families and communities then blamed al-Qaeda. According to the Pew Global Attitudes project, between 2003 and 2011, support for bin Laden personally had dropped in Indonesia from 59 percent to 26 percent, in Jordan from 56 percent to 13 percent, and in the Palestinian territories from 72 percent to 34 percent. In Pakistan, where bin Laden was hiding, support for him plunged from 46 percent in 2003 to 18 percent in 2010. A decade after 9/11, bin Laden’s dream of a vanguard uniting Muslims had evaporated. Internal divisions also played a role in al-Qaeda’s demise. The most dramatic split was with the Islamic State, or ISIS, which had started out as an al-Qaeda affiliate before rebranding. In 2014, ISIS conquered major parts of Iraq and Syria, drawing some 15,000 foreign fighters from 80 countries to join its self-declared caliphate. This was a huge challenge to the original group: al-Qaeda had ideas, but ISIS had territory. ISIS’s trajectory reflected the core problem of dealing with affiliates who did not share (or necessarily even grasp) bin Laden’s strategy. In 2005, bin Laden’s chief deputy, Ayman al-Zawahiri, wrote to Abu Musab al-Zarqawi—the leader of what was then known as al-Qaeda in Iraq and would eventually become ISIS—advising him to stop killing Shiite civilians and beheading hostages in grotesque videos. “Among the things which the feelings of the Muslim populace who love and support you will never find palatable … are the scenes of slaughtering the hostages,” Zawahiri wrote. “We don’t need this.” Zarqawi ignored him. In 2006, a U.S. airstrike killed Zarqawi. But for the next decade, global jihadism shifted firmly in his direction, and against the comparatively more cautious approach of al-Qaeda. Much of the damage al-Qaeda suffered was self-inflicted. Even as ISIS swamped al-Qaeda, however, the limits of its approach became clear, vindicating Zawahiri’s warning. The first mistake ISIS made was to gather forces and materiel in a concentrated space, becoming a perfect target for conventional military force. Its second error was to enthusiastically embrace gruesome forms of brutality and sadism, antagonizing virtually everyone who did not belong to the group; by 2016, almost the entire world had united against it. Working with Iraqi, Kurdish, and Syrian forces, a global coalition to defeat ISIS had by 2019 recaptured the territory the group had seized and destroyed the caliphate. But for al-Qaeda, the damage had been done: it had lost its foothold in Iraq and split its recruitment base with a younger, flashier brand. Zawahiri’s response was to decentralize and focus on groups in South Asia and North Africa, such as al-Qaeda in the Indian Subcontinent and al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb, which primarily sought to overthrow local governments. In July 2022, nearly a year after the American withdrawal from Afghanistan, a U.S. drone strike in Kabul killed Zawahiri. The muted response to his death confirmed the weakness of core al-Qaeda. Today, the apparent head of al-Qaeda is Said al-Adel, who lives in Iran, a Shiite-majority country where, for a decade after 9/11, he and other al-Qaeda leaders and their families spent years living under a form of house arrest, and where his room to maneuver remains strictly limited. He has not even declared himself the group’s leader, perhaps because he fears assassination—but perhaps because there is, in reality, nothing for him to lead. Although the group could one day reinvent itself or carry out attacks sponsored or abetted by Iran, the al-Qaeda that attacked the United States 25 years ago has ended. The United States sometimes accelerated and sometimes slowed the group’s demise. But ultimately, al-Qaeda failed. item.title: Jamaica’s Reparations Push
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 4.57
Jamaica’s Reparations Push The country is asking the U.K. to consider compensation for the harms of slavery. Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Latin America Brief. The highlights this week: Jamaica petitions the United Kingdom for slavery reparations, Argentina renews its claims to the Falkland Islands, and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio tours South America. Welcome back to Foreign Policy’s Latin America Brief. The highlights this week: Jamaica petitions the United Kingdom for slavery reparations, Argentina renews its claims to the Falkland Islands, and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio tours South America. Redressing the ‘Gravest Crime’ Olivia Grange, Jamaica’s minister of culture, gender, entertainment, and sport, traveled to London this week to file what the island called a first-of-its-kind petition to King Charles III. The petition asks the highest court of appeal for Commonwealth countries to issue a decision on whether the British trafficking of enslaved Africans to Jamaica from the 17th to 19th centuries was unlawful—and whether the United Kingdom owes financial reparations. The petition made no specific monetary claim, though a lawmaker from Jamaica’s ruling party previously estimated that the U.K. owes Jamaicans around $10 billion. The Jamaican government has the right to lodge such a demand because it is a member of the Commonwealth, itself a vestige of the colonial era. Charles is still Jamaica’s head of state. Jamaica’s petition is backed by the rest of the Caribbean Community, or Caricom. Caribbean countries have played a leading role in the growing global movement for reparations. Since 2013, a Caribbean reparations panel has been refining its list of financial and symbolic demands to redress the harms of slavery. In March, Caribbean nations backed a successful United Nations General Assembly resolution deeming the trafficking of enslaved Africans as the “gravest crime against humanity” and calling for reparations payments. Argentina, Israel, and the United States voted against the resolution, while the U.K. and European Union countries abstained. Then, in June, Caribbean leaders including Barbadian Prime Minister Mia Mottley attended a conference in Ghana that demanded a formal apology for slavery. They also asked for reparations measures, such as debt relief, from countries involved in the slave trade. Jamaica’s reparations push is nonpartisan. The country’s conservative prime minister, Andrew Holness, who has otherwise taken a center-right stance on economic matters and worked closely with the International Monetary Fund, last year called the petition to the British crown a “watershed moment for Caricom and the broader global movement for reparatory justice.” Grange’s trip coincided with the anniversary of the Zong slave ship’s departure from West Africa to Jamaica in 1781. During that journey, the ship’s captain ordered enslaved Africans to be thrown overboard and later tried to claim insurance money for lost cargo. British law viewed enslaved Africans as property for centuries. When Parliament abolished slavery in the British Empire in 1833, the government borrowed funds equivalent to 40 percent of its treasury income to compensate slaveowners for their property losses. The formerly enslaved were never compensated for their stolen wages. Seeking reparations is part of an effort “to rewrite our history from the standpoint of the hunted, and not from the standpoint of the hunter,” St. Lucia’s reparations envoy, Earl Bousquet, told the Miami Herald. He described a push to break free from “mental slavery,” a nod to the words of Jamaica’s Bob Marley. Despite the growing international campaign for reparations, few governments or organizations have agreed to pay them. French President Emmanuel Macron made headlines in May by saying the matter should be addressed but provided no details as to how. In 2022, the Netherlands announced a $230 million fund to address the legacy of slavery, while the Church of England has pledged to set up a $135 million reparations fund. In response to Jamaica’s legal filing this week, a spokesperson for Buckingham Palace said it was working with the Jamaican government to ensure the petition was successfully lodged. But a spokesperson for British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the U.K. “does not and will not pay reparations.” If the U.K. court draws a similar conclusion, some observers believe that Jamaica could respond by severing its formal ties to the British crown, as Barbados did in 2021. Holness’s government introduced a bill to do so in 2024, but it has not yet advanced in the legislature. Upcoming Events Saturday, Sept. 12, to Sunday, Sept. 13: Brazilian Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira attends the BRICS leaders’ summit in New Delhi in place of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Tuesday, Sept. 15: The U.S. House of Representatives holds a hearing on policy toward Nicaragua. What We’re Following Education checkup. This year’s PISA scores are out. The test measures 15-year-olds’ proficiency in math, reading, and science in countries around the world. Many Latin American countries saw their scores decline in line with a global trend. The education and skills director of the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, which administers the test, told the Wall Street Journal that poor policies regulating smartphone and artificial intelligence use might be to blame. But the PISA exams also showed that certain uses of AI in education could be promising. In El Salvador, an additional school-level PISA test compared schools that were implementing reforms—including an AI tutoring program—with those that were not. Schools with the program had significantly better results. The World Bank, which is backing the reforms, praised them as a case to continue studying. Falklands flare-up. Argentine President Javier Milei gave a formal address last week claiming that the Falkland Islands, a British overseas territory, should be administered by Argentina. It was an effort to rally nationalist sentiment as his popularity wanes and households feel the economic pinch from Milei’s austerity program. This week, Argentina announced that it would impose sanctions on energy companies drilling for oil near the Falklands, which it calls the Malvinas. Milei said the companies could be blocked from operating at Argentina’s Vaca Muerta oil and gas fields. Unlike in the past, both U.S. President Donald Trump and a far-right Israeli cabinet member have signaled that they might support Argentina’s position, likely thanks to Milei’s alignment with Trump and new a U.K. ban on trade with settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank. Most countries across the global south support it as well. One major remaining obstacle, Antonio De Loera-Brust wrote in Foreign Policy in July, is the desire of the islanders themselves, who prefer being ruled by Britain. Pan-American humor. Chilean standup comedian Fabrizio Copano went on the pan-Latin America El Hilo podcast last week to discuss the role of humor in turbulent political times. Born in Chile’s capital, Santiago, Copano now lives in New York and does shows in both English and Spanish across the Western Hemisphere. “I think humor is still lucky enough to be able to make people laugh even when they don’t agree with what’s being said,” he said. Copano often tells his U.S. viewers that “Latin Americans come from the future”—they know what it’s like to get by when politics is dysfunctional, part of which includes being able to laugh. Copano naturalized as a U.S. citizen last year. He said in a recent comedy special that he really felt he was becoming American after taking his car in for a repair. The technician gushed about how much he loved Chile. He was thrilled. But the technician added that his favorite part about Chile was former dictator Augusto Pinochet. Copano thought for a moment about taking a stand for Chilean democracy, but then the man said he would give Copano a discount. He swallowed his dissent and accepted the lower price. Question of the Week FP’s Most Read This Week - Trump’s Venezuela Oil Deal Is a Farce by Keith Johnson - The World’s Only Real Hope of Maintaining Order by Charles A. Kupchan - Trump Has Peaked by Ravi Agrawal In Focus: Rubio’s South America Tour U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio traveled to Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru this week. All three countries now have right-wing presidents who have pledged close security cooperation with the United States and joined Trump’s Shield of the Americas anti-gang initiative. Washinton provided few details about the grouping when it was launched in March, though members vowed to support a militarized approach to fighting drug trafficking. Rubio’s trip delivered more specifics about the nature of that cooperation. In Ecuador, Rubio said there had been a recent shift in the U.S. approach to targeting alleged drug boats in the region. The United States was now carrying out more joint operations with South American countries in their own territorial waters, rather than unilateral U.S. strikes in international waters, he said. Rubio did not clarify when the change occurred. But in the last two weeks, the U.S. military has announced a series of interdictions off Ecuador’s coast of boats that allegedly served as refueling stations for drug runs. The crews were removed before the boats were bombed, in contrast with the previous norm. But the deadly strikes are continuing. The U.S. military announced one on Wednesday in the Caribbean but did not specify whether it took place in international waters. That brings the number of people that the United States has killed in its yearlong campaign to at least 230. Rubio said the United States would soon provide Ecuador with naval interceptor vessels; U.S. troops have already begun anti-gang land operations in the country. Speaking in Barranquilla, Colombia, Rubio said the country had not requested U.S. boots on the ground but rather equipment and training aid, which the United States planned to provide. item.title: What in the World?
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 4.21
What in the World? Test yourself on the week of Sept. 5: A German state votes, Philippine police make a high-profile arrest, and Nigeria appoints a new military commander. School is back in session in much of the world, so it feels appropriate to proctor a quiz for our readers. Find out if you’ve kept up with the globe’s latest developments! Have feedback? Email [email protected] to let me know your thoughts. School is back in session in much of the world, so it feels appropriate to proctor a quiz for our readers. Find out if you’ve kept up with the globe’s latest developments! 1. The far-right Alternative for Germany party won a state election on Sunday but fell short of the majority needed to form a government without a coalition. If the party succeeds in coalition-building, it would be the first far-right party to lead a German state since when? 2. Philippine police arrested a lawmaker and cousin of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Monday over his alleged involvement in a massive corruption scandal concerning what? 3. Jamaica’s culture minister traveled to London on Monday to petition King Charles III to refer a series of questions to a committee on the Privy Council, which serves former colonies. What topic did the questions concern? The petition asked the highest court of appeal of the Commonwealth countries whether Britain’s trafficking of enslaved Africans was unlawful and whether London owed financial reparations to Jamaica, FP’s Catherine Osborn reports in Latin America Brief. 4. On Tuesday, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced about $20 billion worth of tariffs on the United States as retaliation for what? 5. Which country did Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis attack on Tuesday? 6. Opposition lawmakers in Argentina called a special legislative session on Wednesday to consider a variety of measures intended to help Argentines do what? (Hint: One measure concerns interest rates.) Financial strains continue to mount for regular Argentines, despite the government negotiating numerous multibillion-dollar arrangements, including a credit line from the United States, which FP’s Keith Johnson wrote about last October. 7. Nigeria appointed a new military commander on Wednesday who is now responsible for doing what? 8. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Thursday that he expects that Russian forces will do what to weaken Ukraine? As the threat from Russia appears to increase across Europe, commentators have criticized Germany’s relatively muted response to a recent attempted drone attack that has been attributed to Moscow, FP’s John Haltiwanger and Sam Skove report. 9. A group of thieves broke into the Renoir Museum in France on Tuesday and escaped with what? 10. Scientists on Thursday reported that something is happening to the planet Mercury faster than expected. What is occurring? You scored It’s a big world out there! Brush up on global goings-on by subscribing to World Brief, Foreign Policy’s flagship daily newsletter. Have feedback? item.title: What India Gets Out of BRICS
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 3.80
What India Gets Out of BRICS Ahead of the group’s leaders’ summit, New Delhi is pulling out the stops. Welcome to Foreign Policy’s South Asia Brief. The highlights this week: India gears up for the BRICS leaders’ summit this weekend, Nepal’s youth movement marks its protest anniversary as the country reels from deadly floods, and Bangladesh’s energy crunch puts pressure on the government. Welcome to Foreign Policy’s South Asia Brief. The highlights this week: India gears up for the BRICS leaders’ summit this weekend, Nepal’s youth movement marks its protest anniversary as the country reels from deadly floods, and Bangladesh’s energy crunch puts pressure on the government. New Delhi Preps for BRICS Summit India’s government is pulling out all the stops ahead of the BRICS leaders’ summit hosted in New Delhi on Sept. 12 and 13. Commandos are staging security protocol drills; police are carrying motorcade rehearsals; and city officials are executing a makeover that includes fixing roads, planting flower beds, and deploying BRICS branding. BRICS—named after its original members of Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa—has long been a critical institution for India. New Delhi balances its membership in the grouping, meant to provide alternatives to Western economic institutions, with its close ties with the West; in doing so, it bolsters its strategic autonomy. The core goals and priorities of BRICS align with Indian ones: engagement with the global south, advocating for United Nations reform, embracing multilateralism. Most BRICS members are also top Indian partners, and India’s ongoing albeit modest rapprochement with China certainly helps. The grouping expanded in 2024, and aside from Iran, every new member is a close Indian friend. They include Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, and the United Arab Emirates. This year’s leaders’ summit, which follows a BRICS foreign ministers’ forum in New Delhi in May, is especially significant for India, though. The high-level summit offers the world’s fastest-growing major economy an opportunity to showcase its convening power and reassert its global leadership. India hasn’t regressed in this realm per se, but in recent months it has been somewhat upstaged in international diplomacy by its rival Pakistan, thanks to Islamabad’s lead mediation role in the Iran war and its increasing influence in the Middle East—from growing arms sales to participation in new bilateral and multilateral defense pacts with regional allies. Further, the BRICS summit provides India with an important space for deeper engagement with the global south amid rising discontent with the Western-led global economic order. New Delhi takes very seriously its goal of becoming a leader of the global south—an objective tied to both its great-power aspirations and historical leadership of the Non-Aligned Movement decades ago. But this effort faces obstacles, especially given India’s limited inroads in Latin America and Africa. Notably, China has a major investment presence in both regions and also seeks to assert itself as a global south leader. The upcoming summit gives Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi a chance to engage bilaterally with the leaders of Brazil and new member Ethiopia. Finally, this weekend’s summit provides India with a platform to make a strong pitch for freer markets and trade and more multilateralism amid U.S. President Donald Trump’s second-term policies, especially high tariffs. These policies probably inspired one of the themes of the summit, economic resilience. This theme is sure to resonate among all BRICS members, and India’s approach aims to ensure consensus for a strong joint statement—an outcome that New Delhi considers essential for a successful summit. The lead-up to BRICS leaders’ summits tends to produce contrasting commentary. One position dismisses the grouping as irrelevant, a talk shop incapable of producing anything of substance. The other celebrates it as a counter to the Western-led global order. Both arguments are flawed: BRICS has produced new initiatives, including its own development bank. At the same time, poor relations among some of the new members, heavy reliance on the U.S. dollar, and a lack of clarity around the group’s ultimate objectives constrain its ability to fully take on the West. Ultimately, BRICS is a significant grouping with considerable limitations. But for India, the calculus is simple: BRICS, warts and all, is a critical vehicle to advance its core foreign-policy interests. What We’re Following Nepal’s youth movement marks anniversary. A year ago this week, young people in Nepal took to the streets to denounce corruption and nepotism. The protests ousted the government in less than 48 hours, ushering in a caretaker government. Elections in March propelled to power the anti-corruption Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP), which had never held power before. The RSP-led government helmed by Prime Minister Balendra Shah, the popular 35-year-old former mayor of Kathmandu, didn’t take long to position itself as a very different kind of political player. It released a 100-point governance reform agenda and took unconventional positions; Shah initially refused to meet with foreign officials not of equal or similar rank before changing course. Six months after taking office, the government has been put to the test by the massive floods two weeks ago that killed an estimated 1,400 people in Nepal, with nearly 6,000 still missing. Even amid catastrophe, the government has acted like a maverick, initially declining foreign search-and-rescue teams, and now requesting $20 billion in climate change compensation. Nepal initially called on neighbors China and India to provide aid, but it has asked for support via the U.N. loss and damage fund. Unfortunately for Kathmandu, 119 countries have made similar requests totaling $2.8 billion; only $400 million has been provided. Bangladesh faces pressure on energy crunch. Bangladesh is grappling with a long-running energy crisis, and its new government is feeling pressure to address it. The opposition launched a long march in Dhaka over the weekend, with plans to reach Chittagong. On Monday, opposition leader Shafiqur Rahman, who heads the Jamaat-e-Islami party, said in parliament that Dhaka should establish a task force to tackle the crisis. The Bangladesh Nationalist Party government led by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman surely knew that energy would be one of its biggest initial policy challenges when it took office in February. Bangladesh has suffered serious shortages in recent years due to diminishing supplies of domestic fuel. The wars in Iran and Ukraine have worsened the crisis; Bangladesh relies heavily on foreign hydrocarbon imports. Recent industrial accidents, including fires at gas facilities, have made matters worse. Bangladesh has been less successful than many of its South Asian neighbors in embracing renewables to cushion the blow of oil and gas supply shocks. Dhaka recently vowed to expand domestic gas production and tap into clean fuels. But this hasn’t appeased the opposition or a restless public, and Rahman now faces the first major protest movement targeting his government. More violence on Afghanistan-Pakistan border. Last Thursday, Pakistan’s military said it had killed 15 militants attempting to enter the country from Afghanistan. Its statement identified them as members of Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), which carries out attacks in Pakistan and which Islamabad accuses the Taliban regime in Afghanistan of sheltering. The links between the TTP and the Taliban—and Pakistan’s contention that Afghanistan provides sanctuary to the militants—have sparked serious tensions between the two countries since the Taliban returned to power in 2021. The Taliban have not responded publicly to the Pakistani military’s recent statement. This silence is striking, given that the Taliban have repeatedly rejected claims that they shelter militants. The lack of response might indicate ongoing third-party efforts to ease tensions: Last week, the Chinese and Pakistani special envoys for Afghanistan reportedly met in Islamabad. However, previous external mediation efforts have failed to end the crisis. Islamabad continues to insist that the Taliban regime provide verifiable and written assurances that bases on Afghan soil won’t be used for terrorism against Pakistan. Under the Radar Last Wednesday, Sri Lanka announced that U.S. and Sri Lankan officials had busted a large drug smuggling operation that was attempting to use the country as a stop on the way to international markets. Sri Lankan police said anti-narcotics authorities from both countries seized about half a ton of crystal methamphetamine that arrived in a shipping container the previous weekend. Two Pakistani citizens were reportedly arrested in the sting. The U.S. Embassy in Colombo made a similar announcement, noting that $2 million worth of drugs were found hidden in bath towels in the shipping container. But this story has a curious twist. On Friday, Pakistan’s anti-narcotics agency issued its own statement announcing that Islamabad had worked with partners in the United States and Sri Lanka to bust a narcotics trafficking network. Pakistani officials said the raid in Sri Lanka was preceded by a Pakistani operation in Karachi in July. Additionally, while the U.S. and Sri Lankan statements described the drug ring as Pakistan-based, the Pakistani statement said it originated in Afghanistan. The reason for this discrepancy is unclear, though Pakistan would have an incentive to downplay drug trafficking on its own soil and emphasize the culpability of Afghanistan. Either way, trilateral cooperation between the United States and partners in South Asia is unusual. But in this case, it would make sense: Washington currently has warm ties with both Colombo and Islamabad, and Sri Lanka is one of Pakistan’s few close friends in the region. FP’s Most Read This Week - Trump’s Venezuela Oil Deal Is a Farce by Keith Johnson - Trump Has Peaked by Ravi Agrawal - Welcome to the New Defense-Dominant World by Stephen M. Walt Regional Voices In the Indian Express, journalist Aakash Joshi laments the killing of Chongtham Vikram Singh, a musician and member of an ethnic minority from India’s Manipur state. “Between the many whys and the single how of a murder in Delhi, there’s all the anger, inequality, bigotry and dehumanization that we accept every day,” he writes. A scathing Kathmandu Post editorial accuses Nepal’s government of reneging on its reform pledges a year after the Gen Z protests: “The most profound failure of accountability is the treatment of those who bled for this political change. A year later, wounded protesters are trapped in state neglect while new leaders thrive.” In the Daily Star, scholar Manzoor Ahmed argues that Bangladesh must adapt new strategies for combating illiteracy, which remains a persistent challenge. “Technology could help reshape how foundational skills are taught, moving away from rigid, under-resourced classrooms towards flexible learning environments,” he writes Michael Kugelman is the writer of Foreign Policy’s weekly South Asia Brief and a senior fellow for South Asia at the Atlantic Council. An analyst of the region for nearly two decades, he previously directed the South Asia Institute at the Wilson Center. item.title: Iran Launches Massive Attack on Global Shipping
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 3.65
Iran Launches Massive Attack on Global Shipping Such assaults put the Strait of Hormuz under growing pressure as global crude prices skyrocket. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at a massive Iranian attack on global shipping, Israel punishing the United Kingdom over its trade restrictions, and Europe’s fractured space strategy. Hormuz Under Fire Tehran claimed on Wednesday to have carried out its largest known wave of attacks on shipping since the start of the Iran war. Such assaults put the Strait of Hormuz under growing pressure, skyrocketing global crude prices and suggesting that recent efforts to gradually reopen the strategic waterway are at an impasse. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at a massive Iranian attack on global shipping, Israel punishing the United Kingdom over its trade restrictions, and Europe’s fractured space strategy. Hormuz Under Fire Tehran claimed on Wednesday to have carried out its largest known wave of attacks on shipping since the start of the Iran war. Such assaults put the Strait of Hormuz under growing pressure, skyrocketing global crude prices and suggesting that recent efforts to gradually reopen the strategic waterway are at an impasse. On Tuesday, U.S. Central Command (Centcom) claimed to have destroyed five Iranian oil carriers in the Gulf of Oman and near Iran’s Kharg Island, the latter of which hosts Tehran’s main oil export terminal. “Iran has used the tankers as part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] and its regional proxies,” Centcom said in a statement. The United States said that Tuesday’s strikes were retaliation for two failed IRGC ballistic missile attacks on a U.S. Navy warship. “Iran continues to try to hit U.S. naval ships, and for every time they do that or try to do that, they’re going to lose tankers,” U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday. In response, Iran said that it had attacked 10 ships—two U.S. ships and eight oil vessels—near the Strait of Hormuz as well as fired ballistic missiles at a military base used by U.S. forces in Jordan. At least one individual on the Gibraltar-flagged Hercules Star was killed, and several other ships reported fires onboard. U.S. officials told the Wall Street Journal that Iran has launched ballistic missiles at U.S. Navy destroyers, an aircraft carrier, and at least one Marine ship since Friday—marking a dramatic escalation in attacks on maritime vessels. Yet Centcom claimed on Wednesday that all of Iran’s recent attacks failed to hit U.S. military vessels. Jordan has similarly stressed that nearly all missiles fired at its military base this week were intercepted. However, such statements have done little to ease global market concerns. The price of Brent crude briefly hit $100 per barrel on Wednesday for the first time since July, and the price of West Texas Intermediate crude is up 41 percent since the start of the Iran war. Diesel costs have also soared and are now nearing $6 per gallon—more than 55 percent higher than on the eve of the conflict. U.S. President Donald Trump argued on Monday that the oil market will get better. “Oil prices will drop precipitously, like everything else is dropping (but more!), when we WIN the war with Iran,” Trump wrote on Truth Social, claiming that a gallon of gas will ultimately drop below $2. Yet crude prices continue to reach record highs even as the White House maintains that the Iranian navy and air force have already been destroyed and that the U.S. military has control of the Strait of Hormuz. Today’s Most Read - The World’s Only Real Hope of Maintaining Order by Charles A. Kupchan - Iran’s Regional Strategy Is Never Coming Back by Ali Hashem - 25 Years After 9/11, What Are We Failing to Imagine Now? by Colin P. Clarke and Clara Broekaert What We’re Following 30 days to leave. Israel on Wednesday gave the United Kingdom 30 days to close its consulate in East Jerusalem in retaliation for London announcing its intention to impose sweeping trade restrictions on Israel, including a ban on all Israeli goods produced in the occupied West Bank. Israel also barred 12 British politicians from entering the country, told British officials in the West Bank and at a Gaza coordination center to leave, and prohibited the United Kingdom from continuing to train the Palestinian Authority’s security forces in the West Bank. “The British move is morally distorted and constitutes blatant interference in the affairs of a sovereign state and its electoral process,” Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said, referring to upcoming Israeli elections that could challenge Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s hold on power. Notably, Israel did not announce similar punishments on Canada or France, which vowed to join the United Kingdom’s trade ban, nor on the nine other countries that endorsed Britain’s decision. British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband unveiled the measures the day before, citing Israel’s “unlawful” settlements and the alleged “ethnic cleansing of Palestinians” by extremist Israeli settlers. Although Miliband expressed disappointment with Israel’s decision to retaliate, he did not back down from his claims. “We weighed the costs and the benefits of acting,” Miliband told the BBC. “We thought that we couldn’t just simply stand by because we feared Israeli reaction.” Europe’s space ambitions. France and Germany kicked off the two-day International Space Summit in Paris on Wednesday with a bid for more European involvement in the competitive industry. But experts fear that the forum may have been doomed before it even began, as lower-than-expected turnout on Wednesday highlighted the lack of a unified space strategy among the continent’s biggest players. Organizers advertised the summit as an opportunity to advance global space cooperation and improve industry regulations, especially as the sector becomes increasingly privatized. However, the forum’s co-chairs, France and Germany, remain at odds over how best to address this. Whereas Paris has pushed for greater European autonomy from the United States, which has overwhelmingly dominated the private sphere, Berlin has shied away from abandoning the U.S.-based company SpaceX. The two have also disagreed on the best strategy for countering Starlink, with France supporting the European Union’s IRIS² secure satellite constellation and Germany investing in its own network. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz skipped the summit, citing other commitments. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni also chose not to attend. Meanwhile, representatives from U.S. space companies, including SpaceX and Blue Origin, withdrew from the event reportedly due to pressure from Washington, which opposes the summit’s pro-Europe agenda. A collapsing truce? Houthi rebels in Yemen accused Saudi-backed forces on Wednesday of conducting 54 overnight airstrikes across six Yemeni provinces. “These airstrikes and the ongoing aggression against our country will not go unanswered or unpunished, by the will and power of God,” said Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree, a Houthi military spokesperson. “And as the saying goes, the wheel turns against the aggressor.” No casualties or damages were immediately reported. However, rescuers on Wednesday continued to recover bodies from a strike earlier this week on a Houthi-run prison that killed at least 23 people. Wednesday’s overnight assault came less than 24 hours after the Iranian-backed proxy group launched a slew of missiles and drone strikes across Saudi Arabia, injuring more than 70 people and damaging critical civilian and military infrastructure. On Wednesday, the Saudi Civil Defense lifted its alert on the southern city of Khamis Mushait, where Houthi strikes hit the nearby King Khalid Air Base. Renewed violence between Houthi and Saudi-led forces in recent weeks has reignited fears that the two sides’ tenuous truce, established in 2022, could collapse into all-out war. “We call on the Houthis to cease their aggressive actions immediately,” Turkey’s foreign ministry said in a statement on Tuesday, warning that these attacks “disregard the safety of civilians,” escalate regional tensions, and “undermine diplomatic efforts aimed at bringing the conflict in Yemen to an end through a lasting political solution.” Odds and Ends Last Thursday marked the 125th anniversary of Australia unveiling its national flag. To commemorate the special day, Canberra planned to display 44 Australian flags outside of Parliament. However, in an embarrassing blunder, two of the flags raised were instead from New Zealand, prompting officials to quickly switch out the misidentified banners. To their credit, the Australian and New Zealand flags look quite similar, with the only big differences being the addition of a seven-point Commonwealth star on the Australian version and the stars being red instead of white. Still, Canberra only had one job. Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription. Subscribe Subscribe Already a subscriber? . item.title: Why 9/11 Baffles Us 25 Years Later
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 2.93
Twenty-five years on, it’s still hard to grasp the significance of 9/11 because it remains a moving target. The repercussions rippling out of that terrible day never seem to stop—or even slow down. The era of 9/11 began with one misbegotten U.S. war of choice in the Middle East, in Iraq. We are marking its 25th anniversary with another misbegotten U.S. war of choice in the Middle East, in Iran. In between, we’re not quite sure what we have learned, other than Americans never seem to get regime change right, whether we send in troops or not. And Washington still finds itself mired in a region that successive presidents have said they want to distance themselves from. Twenty-five years on, it’s still hard to grasp the significance of 9/11 because it remains a moving target. The repercussions rippling out of that terrible day never seem to stop—or even slow down. The era of 9/11 began with one misbegotten U.S. war of choice in the Middle East, in Iraq. We are marking its 25th anniversary with another misbegotten U.S. war of choice in the Middle East, in Iran. In between, we’re not quite sure what we have learned, other than Americans never seem to get regime change right, whether we send in troops or not. And Washington still finds itself mired in a region that successive presidents have said they want to distance themselves from. The Middle East quagmire only seems to grow deeper, the march of U.S. folly more self-destructive. After the expenditure of trillions of dollars and hundreds of thousands of American and Iraqi lives and limbs, a U.S. Army study concluded that “the only victor” to come out of the 2003 Iraq war appeared to be “an emboldened and expansionist Iran.” Now, in 2026, President Donald Trump’s latest war may have given Iran new advantages, at least for the moment. Though it has hit Tehran hard, the war has further weakened the U.S. role in the region while, once again, seriously draining its military firepower and piling on ever more debt. The prolonged conflict may also be reigniting the fading embers of al Qaeda. Beyond that, the downstream effects of 9/11 in both political and geopolitical terms are still so far-reaching that scholars will likely be debating them for a long time. How did a tiny, ragtag group of jihadists manage to provoke the world’s only superpower into a series of so-called forever wars—the post-9/11 global war on terror constitutes by far the longest war in U.S. history—that drained its power and prestige? What were the opportunity costs of this vast expenditure of blood and treasure over a quarter century—especially in terms of empowering China and, perhaps, encouraging Russia in its own bloody adventurism? As the military writer Elliot Ackerman has noted, “[W]hile Washington was repurposing the U.S. military to engage in massive counterinsurgency campaigns and precision counterterrorism operations, Beijing was busy building a military to fight and defeat a peer-level competitor.” Washington, suddenly alerted, is still trying to catch up to that strategic challenge after what one U.S. general described as the “era of the Great Distraction” following 9/11. Some analysts have argued that the botched response to 9/11 also helped to upend domestic U.S. politics. Did the fumblings of the preceding Republican president, George W. Bush—especially his disastrous invasion of Iraq—so discredit the traditional party agenda that it opened the way to a reckless demagogue, Trump, who has since turned the Grand Old Party into his chew toy? “Conservatism was never the same after the first improvised explosive device detonated in Baghdad,” Matthew Continetti wrote in his 2022 book, The Right: The Hundred-Year War for American Conservatism. Then there’s the question of whether Americans really knew who they were fighting—if they ever mastered the “metrics” of the so-called war on terror, as Donald Rumsfeld, Bush’s hapless defense secretary, once put it. Many strategic assessments conclude that, for all its costs, at least the war on terror prevented another large-scale attack on the U.S. homeland. But critical questions remain about how serious a threat that really was, and whether U.S. strategists mistook a marginal enemy—one that might have been quickly eliminated after 9/11—for an existential one. In his new book, All the Presidents’ Wars: Twenty-Five Years of America’s War on Terror, national security expert Peter Bergen takes the view that al Qaeda was a major strategic threat and the U.S. deserves credit for blunting it. Even so, Bergen eviscerates four different U.S. presidents and their administrations for badly mishandling that challenge. Bergen, who famously produced the 1997 CNN interview in which Osama bin Laden declared war on the United States, writes that he is attempting a full history of what he says “is as much a consequential epoch in American life as the Cold War was” on some levels. He gets most of that history right. It’s all here in a tight 400 pages, the long, ugly, almost farcical saga we’ve become familiar with: the missed opportunity to kill or capture Osama bin Laden and destroy al Qaeda quickly at Tora Bora, perhaps ending the war on terror in mere months; the fraudulently justified diversion into Iraq; and how that mistake in turn facilitated the Taliban resurgence in Afghanistan. Bergen recounts, in great detail, how the unnecessary invasion of Iraq—and the brutal U.S. occupation that ensued in the heart of the Arab world—dramatically inflated the number of jihadis Washington had to fight. This turned what should have been a narrowly targeted mission against “core” al Qaeda into the endless global war on terror—no doubt one of the flabbiest strategic concepts ever used to justify a major war. That last mistake was, in some ways, the most consequential. If the U.S. presidency once produced a Great Emancipator (Abraham Lincoln), history should remember George W. Bush as the Great Conflater. His administration, populated by cold warriors who never understood the transnational nature of al Qaeda-type terrorism, was constantly lumping together Islamists who generally had little or nothing to do with each other. The Bushies turned a war against a single, small group of terrorists into a war against supposed “state sponsors” of terror who, in the end, drew more U.S. resources and attention than the terrorists themselves. (We’ve since learned that al Qaeda couldn’t even agree among themselves if it was wise to attack the U.S. homeland.) This road to disaster began, Bergen writes, with the administration’s conflation of the Taliban with al Qaeda “even though the Taliban had no record of international terrorism.” Tragically, misunderstanding the Taliban—who were always uneasy about hosting al Qaeda—kept the United States from negotiating a stability deal with the insurgent group before it was too late. (By the time the Obama administration began seriously considering this approach more than a decade after 9/11, the Taliban had already recaptured large parts of Afghanistan and didn’t take negotiations seriously.) That was only the start of a tragicomedy of errors. Month by month, year by year, the Bush administration broadened the war on terror to include ever more peoples and countries—especially Saddam Hussein’s Iraq—relying on thinner and thinner evidence to do so. And what began as a hunt for a relatively contained group of self-declared murderers became a feckless global dragnet of tens of thousands of often innocent Arab and Muslim victims. Not only did Bush let bin Laden escape for another 10 years (he was finally killed during Barack Obama’s presidency in 2011), but by invading a major Muslim nation in the Middle East, Bush also managed to vindicate bin Laden’s warnings that the real threat was the “crusaders” of the “far enemy,” his term for the United States. Up until 9/11, many al Qaeda followers had argued that they should continue their traditional strategy of targeting the “near enemy,” the autocratic regimes of Saudi Arabia, Egypt, and other Arab nations. By occupying Iraq, the United States displaced these regimes as the main target for radical Islamists. Thus Bush inadvertently turned bin Laden into a revered prophet of jihad, even after his death. Bergen notes that Bush’s own National Intelligence Estimate from 2006 “concluded that the ‘Iraq conflict has become the “cause célèbre” for jihadists’” and was “shaping a new generation of terrorist leaders and operatives.” As Bush made the trumped-up case for his Iraq invasion, he declared in September 2002, in a typically muddled piece of rhetoric, that “you can’t distinguish between al Qaeda and Saddam when you talk about the war on terror.” The truth was quite the contrary: Not only could one distinguish between al Qaeda and Saddam, it was imperative that any responsible U.S. leader do so, and that he identify the enemy with precision of analysis as much as he targeted him with precision weaponry. Wars are won or lost on such issues of imprecision. Washington could not afford to let its soldiers see all Arab men as potential jihadis, all military-age male Iraqis as potential insurgents, and all post-9/11 enemies as “unlawful combatants” who did not even deserve the protection of the Geneva Conventions. Yet that’s exactly what happened—and it led directly to Abu Ghraib, Camp Bucca, and the nightmarish legal limbo that is Guantánamo today, where even the conviction of 9/11 mastermind Khalid Sheikh Mohammed is in doubt because of the torture used on him. As the late James Dobbins, the first U.S. envoy to post-Taliban Afghanistan and later the special representative for Afghanistan and Pakistan, put it to me on the 20th anniversary of 9/11 five years ago, the current era should be known as “the lost generation in American foreign policy.” That was because every president since Bush, he said, has been forced to spend most of his time trying to clean up Bush’s post-9/11 mess. But Obama, Trump, and Joe Biden didn’t do much better, Bergen writes. Obama improved the tactics against terror somewhat. But even as he denounced Bush’s “dumb war” in Iraq, Obama failed to plan for the “day after” when launching the ouster of Muammar al-Qaddafi in Libya. He also fumbled his Afghanistan surge, dooming it to failure by publicly committing to a withdrawal deadline. Then Biden blatantly lied about the withdrawal, denying that he’d received warnings from his military advisors (he had, multiple times) that the Taliban would swiftly reconquer Afghanistan if he removed the last 2,500 troops from the country. As for Trump, his justification for launching a new war with Iran in February was as flimsy as Bush’s had been for Iraq, writes Bergen, since “there was no evidence that the Iranian regime posed any pressing threat to the United States.” What’s puzzling about Bergen’s book is that even though all these compelling details add up to a strategic miscalculation of the first order—Bush’s hawkish team of so-called Vulcans, Bergen concludes, “were one of one of the most incompetent national security teams in American history”—he doesn’t dwell on the implications of this obvious conclusion. Instead, Bergen concludes that at least “the central aim of the war on terror was achieved: there were no large-scale lethal attacks in the United States carried out by foreign terrorist groups in the quarter century after 9/11.” That may be true. But what kind of achievement was this really, especially given the enormous costs? A great deal of evidence has been amassed suggesting that al Qaeda had one very lucky day on 9/11. This was in addition to two previous minor successes, when the terrorist group bombed U.S. embassies in Kenya and Tanzania in 1998, killing 224 people (including 12 Americans but mostly locals); and in 2000, when al Qaeda rammed the USS Cole with a small boat filled with explosives, killing 17 U.S. Navy personnel. Al Qaeda, in other words, had only one A-team, and only enough resources for one big roll of the dice. That was the 9/11 attacks, which took years to plan. As Nelly Lahoud, an al Qaeda expert at the U.S. Army War College, wrote in her 2022 book, The Bin Laden Papers: How the Abbottabad Raid Revealed the Truth About al-Qaeda, Its Leader and His Family, bin Laden’s “post-9/11 goals did not go beyond empty threats, unexecuted plans, and more than a little wishful thinking.” As a strategist, bin Laden “was sophomoric at best,” Lahoud told me in a recent interview. The thousands of documents left behind in bin Laden’s Abbottabad compound, which Lahoud pored over, “make it clear that bin Laden and his associates did not have a plan in place for what followed 9/11. By their own account, they were in ‘disarray’ and ‘afflicted.’ They never recovered.” So yes, 9/11 was an actual disaster, but Bush’s response, and the path he led his nation down afterwards, was a strategic disaster. In the middle of what should have been a tightly focused war of necessity against al Qaeda—really, just a series of special ops actions—Washington invented a new global war that sapped its military, credibility, economy, and moral standing; cost thousands of young Americans their lives and limbs unnecessarily; alienated much of the world; and diverted its attention from swiftly eradicating the chief culprit of 9/11. That is why Marine Gen. Anthony Zinni—the former Centcom commander who also served as a Bush envoy to the Middle East—has called the expansion of the war on terror beyond Afghanistan perhaps the worst strategic mistake ever made by a U.S. president. Bush mistook a singular if horribly tragic event, 9/11, for an existential threat, Zinni told me. And he mistook a nonstate actor that was in fact fairly small and weak for a huge state-sponsored terrorist menace. “This was not an existential threat,” Zinni said. “It was a band of maybe a thousand radicals. Yet we created an investment in this that was on a level of what we do for existential threats. … But this was not communism or fascism.” Indeed, the post-9/11 period was not even remotely comparable to the Cold War. Bergen argues that there was a persistent threat from al Qaeda after 9/11—for example the July 7, 2005, London bombings that killed 52 commuters—and he suggests that U.S. success can be measured by Washington’s dramatic improvement of its tactics against jihadists in the field, especially the Islamic State. “Politicians across the political spectrum often railed against the ‘forever wars,’ yet the war against ISIS ended the group’s territorial caliphate” with only a small force of 5,000 U.S. soldiers, compared to 150,000 a decade earlier, Bergen writes. He adds that U.S. officials also grew much more effective at detecting terrorist plots. All true. These were genuine tactical successes. But it’s hardly much of an achievement if Washington’s failed policies created most of the new jihadists the U.S. military was fighting, including those in the Islamic State—or if it was Washington’s errant strategy (in abandoning Afghanistan prematurely) that enabled those jihadists to operate in London and elsewhere in the first place. In his book, Bergen does capture some of this absurdity. He notes that Bush—in another nonsensical bit of rhetoric—once declared: “If we were not fighting these al-Qaeda terrorists in Iraq most would be trying to kill Americans and other civilians elsewhere.” This assertion, he writes, “was based on the faulty premise that the world contained a finite number of jihadist terrorists. … In fact, the pool of potential terrorists expanded quite dramatically because of the Iraq War,” leading to the rise of the Islamic State and new affiliated groups. Unfortunately, however, Bergen then returns to one of the familiar conclusions we’ve heard from him in previous work: that overall success should be measured by the fact that bin Laden failed in his main goal of pushing the U.S. out of the Middle East. Bergen is right to say that this was the original aim of al Qaeda laid down in its 1996 declaration of jihad. And he is right that bin Laden badly miscalculated what the U.S. response to an attack on its own soil might be. The terror chieftain saw the United States as a “paper tiger” because it withdrew from Lebanon in 1983 after a Hezbollah attack in Beirut killed 241 U.S. service personnel, and from Somalia in 1993 following the Black Hawk Down attack that killed 18 soldiers. But bin Laden failed to understand that Americans would respond to an attack on New York and Washington very differently. Yet bin Laden wasn’t a complete fool. He also sought to use the 9/11 attack to “destroy the myth of American invincibility,” Lahoud says. In that he calculated quite well. As bin Laden watched Washington fumble its response, one of his evolving goals was to pursue a policy of “bleeding America to the point of bankruptcy”—as he said in a 2004 video aired by Al Jazeera—through a long and draining conflict, just as his mujahadeen fighters did to the Soviets in Afghanistan in the 1980s. He added that he found it “easy for us to provoke and bait this administration.” If the Iraq war was a titanic mistake from the U.S. point of view, it was “a lifeline for al Qaeda and other jihadi groups, which were able to position themselves as the defenders of the Sunnis,” Lahoud later wrote. And bin Laden achieved this success by fooling the Americans into thinking he was much more threatening—much bigger and better-resourced—than he really was. It must be said that Bush started out well as a 9/11 president. Speaking through a megaphone at Ground Zero in New York two days after the attacks, when someone shouted, “I can’t hear you,” Bush responded spontaneously, “I can hear you. The rest of the world hears you. And the people who knocked these buildings down will hear all of us soon.” Bush followed that up by authorizing a devastatingly swift U.S. campaign that toppled the Taliban in eight weeks. That sent bin Laden and his lieutenants scurrying to their mountain hideout at Tora Bora, where the al Qaeda chief apologized to his followers for getting caught, as Gary Berntsen, the CIA officer in charge of the U.S. operation, recorded in his 2005 book, Jawbreaker. The kill-or-capture operation was going quite well. Vengeance for the deaths of nearly 3,000 people on U.S. soil was nigh. Then, in one of the most bizarre, inexplicable strategic diversions ever, the senior Bush team let “the people” who’d knocked down the buildings go. The Bushies ignored pleas from CIA officers and commanders such as Marine Gen. James Mattis to surround bin Laden and his lieutenants. “We could have had the entire al Qaeda command structure had we done that,” Berntsen told me in a 2016 interview. “The war could have been over pretty quickly.” Instead, Bin Laden and his group escaped. The Bush administration then went after someone who had nothing to do with knocking down those buildings, Saddam Hussein. Bush swiftly diverted to Iraq the Special Forces troops, Predator drones, and other resources involved in the hunt for bin Laden. The reasons for the turn to Iraq remain murky. All we really know for sure is that Bush never once held a cabinet meeting to ask whether it was a good idea. The best explanation may be hubris: Rumsfeld and other administration hawks (like his deputy, Paul Wolfowitz) were eager to reassert U.S. power. They didn’t consider Afghanistan to be much of a real war; in their view, bin Laden was a secondary target next to Saddam. “There’s a feeling we’ve got to do something that counts—and bombing some caves is not something that counts,” as Newt Gingrich, then a member of Rumsfeld’s Defense Policy Board, put it to me in late 2001. All they accomplished was to expose the vulnerabilities of U.S. power, an outcome that will rank Rumsfeld, Wolfowitz, and company among the biggest bunglers ever to hold high U.S. office. Twenty-five years later, what stands out is the missed opportunity posed by that horrible day. The silver lining of 9/11 was a wave of international sympathy for the lone superpower. (“We are all Americans,” France’s Le Monde newspaper memorably proclaimed on its front page; even U.S. adversaries like Iran gave condolences.) Washington also enjoyed almost unlimited support around the world in pursuit of its mission to hunt the murderers down. This was no “clash of civilizations,” nothing like it. It was a straightforward task: Wipe out a vicious—and really fairly minor—insurgency against our civilization and the U.S.-led postwar world order. This sort of terrorism provided, as the Yale scholar Charles Hill wrote at the time, a “natural bonding agent” for melding “the international system of states” ever closer. Consider the fact that, even as Washington found little support for its incursion into Iraq, it gathered more than 40 countries together to help try to stabilize Afghanistan as part of the NATO-led International Security Assistance Force. Oddly, pop psychology may explain the whole post-9/11 strategic catastrophe better than anything else. Bush’s father, President George H.W. Bush, had once deftly used the United Nations and the careful invocation of international law to build a coalition against Saddam in the Gulf War. For his son, 9/11 was an opportunity to build on that legacy. But George W. Bush, insecure and eager to do his father one better, openly defied advice from his father’s close aide, Brent Scowcroft, not to invade Iraq. Bush squandered that opportunity to a mind-boggling degree. Too many Republicans and Democrats (as well as many media pundits) endorsed his actions. No president has recovered since. Nor has the nation. Michael Hirsh is a columnist for Foreign Policy. He is the author of two books: Capital Offense: How Washington’s Wise Men Turned America’s Future Over to Wall Street and At War With Ourselves: Why America Is Squandering Its Chance to Build a Better World. item.title: Who Wears the BRICS Crown?
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 2.61
Who Wears the BRICS Crown? India and China compete to shape the bloc’s agenda moving forward. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at what to expect at this year’s BRICS leaders’ summit, the legacy of 9/11 a quarter century later, and the Houthis’ lightning offensive on the Red Sea coast. Vying for Influence In a world long dictated by U.S. hegemony, who leads the other side? That is the issue defining this weekend’s BRICS summit, as the leaders of Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, and other member countries gather in New Delhi to discuss what a counterweight to Washington’s influence should look like. Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at what to expect at this year’s BRICS leaders’ summit, the legacy of 9/11 a quarter century later, and the Houthis’ lightning offensive on the Red Sea coast. Vying for Influence In a world long dictated by U.S. hegemony, who leads the other side? That is the issue defining this weekend’s BRICS summit, as the leaders of Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, and other member countries gather in New Delhi to discuss what a counterweight to Washington’s influence should look like. BRICS was established in 2009 as a direct response to the U.S. dollar’s dominance in international trade as well as Washington’s leverage over the United Nations and what was then the G-8. But the bloc’s ability to make significant headway has long been stymied by internal dissent, especially between India and China. This weekend, New Delhi and Beijing will jockey for dominance over the bloc’s agenda going forward. On Friday, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi set the mood for the two-day summit by agreeing to strengthen his country’s special relationship with Russia. According to India’s foreign ministry, Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin discussed the Russia-Ukraine and Iran wars as well as vowed to continue negotiations over defense and energy issues. India is the second-largest buyer of Russian oil after China. New Delhi previously vowed to increase bilateral trade with Moscow from nearly $70 billion in 2025 to $100 billion by 2030, despite repeated U.S. threats against countries that trade with the Kremlin or continue to purchase Russian crude. At the same time, New Delhi has managed to maintain its close ties with Washington in a way that most other BRICS governments, including Beijing, have failed to do. Meanwhile, experts say Chinese President Xi Jinping will aim to push his own agenda during what will be his first visit to India in seven years. Over the weekend, he is expected to hold a sidelines conversation with Modi to discuss a long-running border dispute, opportunities for greater Chinese investment, and their shared roles in the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation. He is also likely to push India on its massive trade deficit with China, as Beijing is New Delhi’s biggest business partner. But dissent between the bloc’s two wealthiest nations will not be the group’s only schism. The U.S.-Iran war—and Tehran’s attacks on U.S. allies in the Persian Gulf—has also increased tensions among the group’s members. During a BRICS foreign ministers’ meeting in May, also held in India, the bloc failed to come to a consensus on how to address the conflict. Then in August, the United Arab Emirates (a BRICS member) suspended all trade with fellow member Iran over its continued attacks on Emirati soil. Despite the theme of this year’s summit being “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation, and Sustainability,” BRICS nations may find it difficult to achieve the level of collaboration needed to craft a cohesive message amid growing internal disunity. Today’s Most Read - Top Signs You’re Heading for a Quagmire by Stephen M. Walt - How to Survive in a World Without Rules by Hal Brands - How Could Iran Happen? An Autopsy. by Ariane Tabatabai and Julia Curlee What We’re Following Remembering 9/11. Friday marked the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks on the United States, considered the deadliest foreign assault on U.S. soil in history. Seven moments of silence were observed at a memorial ceremony in New York City to mark the times when hijacked planes crashed into the World Trade Center, the Pentagon, and a field in Pennsylvania. The silences also recognized when both New York City buildings collapsed as well as all those who later died from cancer or other illnesses from inhaling toxic dust in the attack’s aftermath. More than 2,900 people were killed, including hundreds of first responders, on Sept. 11, 2001, and at least 9,500 others have died from 9/11-related diseases. “Twenty-five years on, it’s still hard to grasp the significance of 9/11 because it remains a moving target,” FP columnist Michael Hirsh argues. The attacks led then-U.S. President George W. Bush to launch a “war against all those who seek to export terror and a war against those governments that support or shelter them.” A quarter of a century later, the United States continues to contend with the legacy of that global war on terrorism, including the fallout of its disastrous withdrawal from Afghanistan and the continued fight against Iran and its proxy groups. “We will never, ever forget,” U.S. President Donald Trump said at a separate ceremony at the Pentagon on Friday. “That’s why we fight today. We don’t have a choice.” He thanked active service members fighting in the Middle East for “working right now to ensure the world’s No. 1 sponsor of terror—the Islamic Republic of Iran—will never, ever have a nuclear weapon.” Major Houthi victory. Houthi rebels in Yemen seized control of several strategic Red Sea islands and port cities on Friday, solidifying their grip on the Bab el-Mandeb strait. “Everything that was under our control on the western coast has fallen,” said a military official with the internationally recognized, Saudi-backed Yemeni government. That includes the Houthis’ takeover of Perim Island, the Greater and Lesser Hanish Islands, and Zuqar Island as well as the coastal Yemeni town of Dhubab. Fighting between Houthi and Saudi-led forces has escalated in recent weeks, as the Iranian proxy group has carried out a lightning offensive on Yemen’s Red Sea coast. On Thursday, Houthi rebels claimed the critical port city of Mokha in a major blow to Riyadh’s military efforts. However, Friday’s victories may be even more detrimental to Saudi Arabia’s ambitions in the country, as it gives Iran leverage over another crucial waterway. Iranian control over the Strait of Hormuz has severely hampered the global economy, disrupting supply chains, raising oil prices, and injecting greater insecurity into the region. With the Bab el-Mandeb now under the thumb of an Iranian ally, experts expect these problems to only grow. Still, Tehran confirmed on Friday that it would meet with Iraqi and Gulf state representatives in Oman on Monday to resume negotiations on reopening the Strait of Hormuz to commercial traffic. Eroding democracy. A Hong Kong court sentenced three local activists to prison on Friday in a case seen as symbolic of the city’s declining democratic freedoms since Beijing imposed its strict national security law in 2020. Lee Cheuk-yan, Chow Hang-tung, and Albert Ho were convicted this year of inciting subversion under that law by organizing annual vigils to commemorate China’s 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre. All three individuals were leaders of the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China and have been in custody for years. “Even when the defendants believed their agenda of ‘end one-party dictatorship’ might breach the constitution and the national security law, they acted recalcitrantly after the national security law took effect and vigorously promoted their cause,” the three-judge panel wrote. Both Lee and Chow had pleaded not guilty; they were given a seven-year and seven-year, three-month sentence, respectively. Their loved ones confirmed on Friday that they planned to appeal. Ho, however, pleaded guilty and was therefore given a reduced five-year, two-month prison term. What in the World? The far-right Alternative for Germany party won a state election on Sunday but fell short of the majority needed to form a government without a coalition. If the party succeeds in coalition- building, it would be the first far-right party to lead a German state since when? A. The fall of the Berlin Wall B. World War II C. The Soviet consolidation of East Germany D. The Weimar Republic Odds and Ends When road rage threatens to get the best of you, Kenyan street performers are ready to help. Acrobats, jugglers, and other entertainers have recently taken on Nairobi’s busy roads by performing for motorists stuck in the capital’s notorious traffic jams. “There are no opportunities for us that we can go to,” street acrobat Jackson Okoth told The Associated Press, referring to Kenya’s high unemployment rate. “So we like it when we are here because it keeps us busy and it keeps us fit also.” And the Answer Is… B. World War II The rise of the far right in Germany signals the end of German postwar democracy as we know it, John Kampfner argues.
