item.title: Discarding an Old Map and Seeing Africa With Fresh Eyes
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 2.56
Discarding an Old Map and Seeing Africa With Fresh Eyes The continent offers solutions to some of the West’s most vexing problems. Since the advent of social media a couple of decades ago, hardly a week has gone by when I haven’t noted, often with a smirk or a shrug, some poster’s belated discovery of a long-known fact: The most commonly used cartographical representations of the world drastically understate the size of southern land masses, especially Africa, giving it an appearance far short of its true dimensions. Now, even the United Nations seems to have caught up. With one notable holdout, the United States, a recent vote by that body to recommend that future mapmakers correct this distortion has brought this somewhat obscure factlet out of the shadows, prompting a renewed wave of online commentary. Since the advent of social media a couple of decades ago, hardly a week has gone by when I haven’t noted, often with a smirk or a shrug, some poster’s belated discovery of a long-known fact: The most commonly used cartographical representations of the world drastically understate the size of southern land masses, especially Africa, giving it an appearance far short of its true dimensions. Now, even the United Nations seems to have caught up. With one notable holdout, the United States, a recent vote by that body to recommend that future mapmakers correct this distortion has brought this somewhat obscure factlet out of the shadows, prompting a renewed wave of online commentary. The cynic in me briefly objected that no measure by the United Nations can alter the conditions of life on the world’s second-largest continent or any other objective facts. Indeed, a vote such as this may not even ensure that the publishers of school textbooks and online atlases change their graphical representations of the world. But my skeptical reflexes soon gave way to a more positive sentiment. In an era when the Trump administration has repeatedly gone out of its way to signal its lack of consideration for Africa and to demean its people as well as the continent’s large diaspora, this move toward what might be called map justice seems like the sign of a dawning recognition: After more than seven decades since the start of its independence era, the continent is finally becoming a place that the rest of the world has to reckon with and, indeed, increasingly count upon. Acknowledging Africa’s geographic size goes hand in hand with the spreading understanding of the continent’s ballooning demographic weight in the world. Somewhat predictably, politicians in the West are behind the curve, still devoting remarkably little intellectual and policy capital to what will be one of the biggest drivers of global change for the remainder of this century. In fact, what little attention they do devote to Africa is of a largely reactionary nature. In the case of Europe, this means trying to figure out how to raise ever-higher dikes to hold back feared tides of African migration. The United States of President Donald Trump takes this one step further, actively pursuing means of deporting Africans, as well as dumping citizens from non-African countries on a continent publicly scorned as a “shithole.” Eventually, though, the West will learn that this isn’t just futile—it’s also harmful to its own interests and counterproductive. Just as drawing up maps in ways that graphically diminish Africa does nothing to reduce Africa’s true dimensions, actively shunning African migrants will do nothing to change the hard demographic realities that will radically shape our collective future. The wealthiest and most economically productive regions of the world, beginning with East Asia and including Europe, the United States, and Canada, share a grave, and as best we can presently understand, unsolvable problem: historically unprecedented fertility decline. China, which was recently surpassed by India as the world’s most populous country, is being slammed by this even harder. Many naïve techno-optimists seem to believe that the rapid advance of robots will offer a fix, replacing dwindling human labor with legions of automated and untiring smart machines. But even if this solves production issues, it does not reckon with the loss of human consumption, which drives every model of organized economic life on the planet today. In its simplicity, it also totally neglects vital questions about civilization: What are the essential ingredients of human society? The answer, I want to suggest, runs directly through Africa, but to see why, it helps to first look at the crisis now facing the world’s wealthiest societies from an entirely different direction. A question like this can seem overwhelming, especially in the confines of a column like this. Fortunately, it can be broken down into smaller and more easily digested pieces. Just in the past few days, headlines have been dominated by dire warnings about the runaway prowess of artificial intelligence, which some of its smartest designers say could soon escape human control and indeed eliminate us as a species. Even stopping well short of a doomsday such as this, it is already not hard to imagine AI rendering human intelligence, human ingenuity, and human management, along with much else, irrelevant. How do the rich countries of the world manage their bulging populations of elderly people? At some point, will they resort to stockpiling them in thinly staffed warehouses where they will be largely tended to by machines? What would doing so say about us? And if not, where would the workers required for a more humane treatment and social environment come from? One can flip this problem on its head to consider the other end of the human lifespan. In a world of radically fewer children, there will paradoxically be radically fewer people to engage with and look after them. Do we passively give in to the dehumanization of these environments? Do we rely ever more on computers and machines to engage with and supervise children instead of the far richer personal socialization that for so long has been dominated by full classrooms and peer-group activities? Already, there are villages in Japan that are grappling with this issue, and it is sure to spread far more widely in the decades to come. How, then, does this relate to Africa? Africa stands out as a kind of final frontier: a test of our fellow humanity that will measure the relative power of human selfishness and racial bigotry easily mobilized by far-right populists versus rational, collective human self-interest. This, too, deserves breaking down further. Just as relatively unconstrained, or so-called “free” trade has been understood since Adam Smith to strongly benefit both parties in international commerce, most economists today believe that liberalizing the movement of people across international borders broadly favors international growth, including in both the countries of origin and adoption. The work of Branko Milanovic and Lant Pritchett constitutes two prominent examples of this among many. What stands in the way of this is mostly prejudice, which is projected most of all toward people from the poorest parts of the world, and people of African descent, in particular. Each in its own way, both Europe and the United States are in the grips of this at present, with Germany’s ascendant far-right party, the Alternative for Germany, advocating the exclusion of migrants from the global south, and Trump publicly applauding. The anti-immigration populists seem unlikely to win out in the long term, and that is because the alternatives to embracing Africa more deeply, in both present-day economic engagement and in migration, will be so much more unpleasant for all but the most racially prejudiced among us in the rich world. I have limned some of the dystopian aspects of this just above. But there are other gauges of the growing importance of the continent that ill-informed politicians and racial holdouts have probably never considered. Africans are far less “foreign” than they imagine. Colonial rule and subsequent history have meant that people from that continent have been steeped in Western culture. More of them speak English and French than Europeans or Americans do. More Africans practice Christianity, too. With the sharp demographic rise of African youth, more Africans are capable and willing to produce the much-needed labor required by the West, along with the consumption that aging rich societies are rapidly losing. On a fast-urbanizing continent, where school attendance and university enrollment are booming, so is African intellectual output. By itself, a new map of the world clearly won’t change any of this. The question is whether the door is finally being pried open to let the rest of the world see Africa with fresh eyes and a new sense of our collective interests in mind. Howard W. French is a columnist at Foreign Policy, a professor at the Columbia University Graduate School of Journalism, and a longtime foreign correspondent. His latest book is The Second Emancipation: Nkrumah, Pan-Africanism, and Global Blackness at High Tide. item.title: Why Germany Isn’t Punishing Russia Harder
item.description:
Source: FP Foreign Policy Score: 2.35
Why Germany Isn’t Punishing Russia Harder Domestic politics constrains Berlin’s ability to respond to an attempted drone attack. Amid an escalating Russian sabotage campaign against Europe, Germany’s measured response to one recent attack is ringing alarm bells for many. But with rising populism at home and fears of escalation, it may be the best the country can offer. In early August, Germany discovered an explosive-laden drone near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig Airport. Last week, Germany formally accused Russia of being behind the attempted attack, and in turn shuttered a Russian diplomatic mission, ramped up travel restrictions for Russian nationals, closed a Russian cultural center, and urged the EU to slap additional sanctions on Russia. Amid an escalating Russian sabotage campaign against Europe, Germany’s measured response to one recent attack is ringing alarm bells for many. But with rising populism at home and fears of escalation, it may be the best the country can offer. In early August, Germany discovered an explosive-laden drone near a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig Airport. Last week, Germany formally accused Russia of being behind the attempted attack, and in turn shuttered a Russian diplomatic mission, ramped up travel restrictions for Russian nationals, closed a Russian cultural center, and urged the EU to slap additional sanctions on Russia. Russian President Vladimir Putin has denied involvement, accusing Berlin of planting evidence against Moscow. But Western officials have said the alleged attack is tied to a “broader pattern” of nefarious behavior from Moscow across Europe—involving drones, sabotage, cyberattacks, and disinformation campaigns—that is meant to sow discord and confusion among Ukraine’s allies. “This was an attack using military-grade material, carried out by Russian operatives on EU soil. And we will not tolerate it. We stand in full solidarity with Germany,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Monday. “Leipzig marks a new escalation on European soil, directly attributed to Russia. But it is part of a broader pattern of increasingly dangerous incidents.” Instances of Russian sabotage and other forms of interference in Europe have risen sharply since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, with some of the most dramatic attempted plots targeting Germany. These include the planned assassination of a major German arms CEO, the planned assassination of a German drone company CEO, and a plot to send mail bombs via a German parcel carrier. Germany’s response has appeared relatively muted. For instance, in the case of the reported Russian plot to assassinate Armin Papperger, the head of Germany’s largest arms company, Germany announced no specific punishments for Russia, and then-Chancellor Olaf Scholz made no direct comment. Many commentators have slammed Germany’s response to the attempted drone attack in Leipzig. “If every time Germany is attacked by Russia it does nothing[, then] Putin the bully will keep doing it,” wrote former British Defense Secretary Ben Wallace on X. “The German response so far reminds me of pre-2022,” Liana Fix, a senior fellow for Europe at the Council on Foreign Relations, told Foreign Policy. “It does not rise to the moment of Russian hybrid campaigns.” A more robust response from Germany might include seizing the ships that Russia uses to evade energy sanctions, as other countries are already doing, Fix said. Germany could also take action in the intelligence sphere, such as launching offensive cyberattacks—which would legally require sign-off by parliament. At least some of those efforts may be in the offing, Fix said, but could be difficult to trace due to their sensitive nature. Retired Lt. Gen. Doug Lute, who served as U.S. ambassador to NATO from 2013 to 2017, said many of the responses from Europe to Russia’s hybrid or gray-zone attacks have “been simply the most mild response, and that’s been to reveal them publicly, to disclose them, to bring them out into daylight.” It’s clear such responses have been “insufficient,” Lute said, but the “closing of diplomatic facilities by Berlin is a step in the right direction” and marks a “stronger” reaction than “most of the previous episodes.” Meanwhile, any German response to Russia must factor in the rising power of far-right and -left parties, which have taken pro-Russian stances, as well as the plummeting popularity of Germany’s pro-Ukraine leader, Chancellor Friedrich Merz. In April, Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) polled at 28 percent, while Germany’s far-left party, Die Linke, polled at 11 percent. For comparison, Germany’s current chief of the ruling parliamentary coalition, the Christian Democratic Union, polled at 24 percent. The AfD also won its first state election last week, a major victory for the party. Many AfD and Die Linke voters do not see Russia as a threat. “Intelligence information and plausibility are not evidence,” wrote Die Linke parliamentarian Lea Reisner, in critique of the German government’s assertion that Russia was behind the attempted Leipzig Airport attack. “The current escalation is highly dangerous.” And despite broad support for Ukraine in Germany, many fear nuclear escalation, which Russia has proved willing to manipulate. “This nuclear angst is still there in Germany,” Fix said. Still, some Western officials view Germany openly accusing Russia of coordinating this attempted attack as a significant development in and of itself—particularly from the perspective of Baltic countries such as Estonia, which continue to face disruptive drone incursions tied to the Ukraine war. Germany was “very clear” in stating that there’s direct evidence that “Russia was behind this attack,” and it’s important that it was officially designated an “attack,” Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna told Foreign Policy. “This is the change I saw from the German side,” he said. There’s been a narrative that the “Baltics are next” and that it’s “somehow only our concern that Russia is provoking and organizing different attacks,” Tsahkna said, but it’s now “public for everybody in Europe that Russia is attacking Germany and attacking many other countries as well.” However, Tsahkna conceded that it’s “hard to say” what the “proportional” response should be, adding that it’s “clear that we are not going to organize” the same “kind of attacks” against Russia. The Baltics, which share land borders with Russia, have long expressed impatience over the broader Western response to the Kremlin’s hybrid attacks. The West “needed to respond already years ago,” Tsahkna said, emphasizing that Putin has been “turning on the heat” to test regional unity and NATO. “Putin is a master of playing with fears,” he added, and “the fear of escalation” is something he’s been using for years. One action Germany declined to take in response to the alleged attack was to invoke Article 4 of NATO’s founding treaty, which allows members to consult allies “whenever, in the opinion of any of them, the territorial integrity, political independence or security of any of the Parties is threatened.” This is a rare step that’s only been taken nine times since NATO’s founding in 1949, but it does not immediately lead to further political or military responses. Yet Article 4 was invoked twice in September 2025 alone in response to Russian drones and fighter jets violating the airspace of Poland and Estonia. In late September 2025, after the Article 4 consultations, NATO warned Russia it would employ “all necessary military and non-military tools to defend ourselves and deter all threats from all directions.” That same month, U.S. President Donald Trump said NATO countries should shoot down unauthorized Russian aircraft that enter their airspace. But even after such steps and warnings, Russia continues to be linked to an escalating series of provocative incidents across Europe. Between its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and February 2026, Russia conducted 151 hostile operations in Europe, according to a report by the Netherlands-based International Centre for Counter-Terrorism released earlier this year. Between August 2024 and February 2026 there were 144 reported drone sightings over a dozen European states, according to a July report from the London-based International Institute for Strategic Studies. The report concluded that “it is highly likely that the Kremlin conducted a UAV campaign over Europe.” As the problem metastasizes, European leaders are also struggling with precisely what to call it. Germany has said it’s not at war with Russia but the target of “hybrid warfare.” The situation has sparked debate over whether such terminology falls short in terms of describing the issue and has contributed to a lackluster response. There’s a growing push for Russia’s actions to be labeled as state-sanctioned terrorism. “We need to name it as it is, and state-supported terrorism is a very precise thing, and we know how to act and how we deal with other terrorist acts,” Tsahkna said. “Putin understands only the clear messages and actions.” EU foreign-policy chief Kaja Kallas last week also said the failed attack “has all the hallmarks of state-sponsored terrorism,” while conceding that there’s still an open question about what to do about it. The use of the word “terrorism” by NATO allies marks an “interesting escalation,” said Lute, noting that the only time Article 5 was ever invoked came after the 9/11 terror attacks on the United States. But in terms of defining the problem, Lute said it’s especially important for NATO to stop treating Russian hybrid attacks on a “one-off” basis and “compile the record.” “There’s power in accumulating them and assembling them into a package so that you can see the breadth and depth and the persistence of the attacks,” Lute said, adding that there could also be more steps taken at NATO headquarters, ranging from table-top exercises to consultations with key allies, to send a signal to the Kremlin that the alliance is not sitting on its hands. “We’ve progressed far enough along this spectrum towards armed conflict, towards armed attack, that NATO has got to be seen as more active and not passive,” Lute said. “People say these kinds of political responses are not important because Putin is continuing,” Tsahkna said, but the Russian president “is very carefully watching what we do, how united we are.” Join the Conversation Commenting is a benefit of a Foreign Policy subscription. item.title: AI Is Changing the Rules of Entrepreneurship
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 6.20
Summary. Today, a single individual enabled by AI can—at very low cost—perform many activities needed to establish a startup quickly and in parallel: generating product ideas, simulating Almost two decades ago, the entrepreneur and author Eric Ries launched a methodology for the “lean startup.” In this approach, a new business could be launched with just capital, a minimum viable product, a team, extensive discussions with potential customers, and a process of repeated pivoting as the startup scaled. The lean startup approach combined Toyota’s lean manufacturing method with Stanford professor Steve Blank’s approaches to customer development. Because founders typically had few resources at their disposal, the lean approach took hold.

item.title: AI Is Blurring the Line Between Sales and Marketing
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 5.74
Summary. Agentic AI is blurring the traditional boundaries between marketing and sales, even as most companies continue to deploy the technology separately within each function. That approach misses an For years, aligning marketing and sales has been one of the most persistent priorities in commercial leadership—and one of the hardest to achieve. Agentic AI is changing that.

item.title: Research: How Curveball Questions Can Surface the Insight You’re Looking For
item.description:
Source: Harvard Business Review Score: 5.24
Research: How Curveball Questions Can Surface the Insight You’re Looking For Summary. Traditional “tough” questions often elicit polished talking points rather than candid answers. A more revealing approach is the curveball: a question that is closely tied to what We’re all taught to ask tough questions. Interviewers are coached to use open-ended prompts to get beyond rehearsed answers. Managers press for specifics when employees speak in generalities. Journalists and negotiators follow up when someone evades the point. The aim is the same: to uncover information the other person may be reluctant to reveal.
