Officials with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration are still investigating the processed iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms that was linked to the outbreak. Two months ago, epidemiological information collected by the CDC found that thousands of people had become ill after eating Taco Bell meals containing shredded iceberg lettuce between June 22 and July 20. The supply at the eateries was traced back to a Taylor Farms facility in Central Mexico. In mid-July, the company — which also operates as Taylor Fresh Foods — removed the outsourced lettuce from the U.S. market and issued a voluntary recall of potentially contaminated products. Despite outperforming other fast food chains and posting impressive same-store sales, the Mexican-inspired chain Taco Bell has taken a hit after being linked to Cyclospora. A sample of lettuce from Taylor Farms de Mexico did at one point falsely test positive for the cyclosporiasis parasite. However, FDA officials said the false positive did not change the course of the outbreak investigation, “or the overwhelming epidemiological data supporting the ... voluntary recall by Taylor Farms.” According to the CDC, cyclosporiasis is rarely fatal. The two people who died during the outbreak were both from the epicenter state, Michigan, and may have had underlying health conditions that made them vulnerable to the gastrointestinal illness and dehydration that can come with the disease. Officials say at the peak of the outbreak, before the recall, more than 1,000 infections occurred in a single day. By August, fewer than 2 infections were occurring per day, on average. California was not a part of the multistate outbreak. However, the state public health department did see an uptick in cyclosporiasis cases. Michigan health authorities were in touch with Taco Bell’s parent company, Yum! Brands Inc., about cyclospora weeks before the company officially alerted consumers. Between Jan. 1 and Aug. 21, there were 336 confirmed and probable cyclosporiasis cases in California, the state health department reported. Of those, 65 were domestically acquired, meaning infected people became ill either in the state or after traveling within the United States. Two of these individuals traveled to an outbreak-affected state, ate at a Taco Bell and became ill. The rest became ill after traveling internationally. The California Department of Public Health said the high number of cyclosporiasis cases in the state could be attributed to: - An increased awareness of the illness due to national attention on the outbreak, leading to an increase in testing - Overall improvements to the department’s surveillance and data-collection methods - An increase in cases in people who traveled to areas with outbreaks, whether international or domestic Food safety experts said identifying the source of a foodborne illness such as cyclosporiasis is a challenge because public health investigators need to analyze multiple pieces of evidence from available public health data, follow a potential food source through the supply chain and test samples of potentially contaminated food.

item.title: California's largest alcohol distributor agrees to pay $12.5 million in bribery investigation
item.description:
Source: LA Times Score: 4.85
California’s largest alcohol distributor agrees to pay $12.5 million in bribery investigation - Click here to listen to this article - - Southern Glazer’s Wine and Spirits will pay $12.5 million under a non-prosecution agreement. - The company admitted employees, including California-based executives, spent years bribing grocery and other alcohol retailers with cash, gift cards and luxury trips. The country’s largest wine and spirits distributor has entered into an agreement with federal prosecutors to resolve allegations that its executives and employees bribed alcohol retailers for favorable placement of certain products. Southern Glazer’s Wine and Spirits LLC, headquartered in Florida, will pay $12.5 million to the U.S. Treasury and step up efforts to comply with federal and state laws, according to the non-prosecution agreement signed Thursday by representatives of the company and the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of California. In exchange, the Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau has agreed to take no action against the company for the conduct involved in the investigation. In the agreement, the company admitted that employees provided improper payments and benefits to alcohol retailers for years, including cash, gift cards, luxury goods, resort stays, golf trips and airfare. The employees concealed the actions using third-party vendors and false invoices. California is Southern Glazer’s Wine and Spirits’ largest market, and the scheme included several of the company’s California-based executives, including multiple vice presidents, according to the agreement. “Southern Glazer’s employees tried to distort the wine and spirits market in California through bribes and other improper conduct and in the end it was the consumer that lost out,” U.S. Atty. Craig Missakian said in a statement. The company also agreed to continue cooperating with the government in criminal prosecutions related to the matter. “This conduct does not reflect Southern Glazer’s values, culture, or standards and it will not be tolerated,” said Wayne E. Chaplin, Southern Glazer’s president and chief executive, in a statement. A federal grand jury, in March, indicted five former Southern Glazer’s employees on conspiracy to commit bribery and obstruction charges, alleging they worked to bribe grocery store alcohol buyers and conceal the bribes with falsified financial documentation. A salesman for a Napa winery was also accused of bribing the head alcohol buyer for a large national grocery store chain. Last year, a wine buyer for Albertsons was charged with commercial bribery and conspiracy for allegedly accepting lavish vacations, luxury watches, gift cards and other bribes in exchange for carrying certain wines. Two executives at wine supplier Deutsch Family Wine & Spirits who provided kickbacks to that wine buyer pleaded guilty to commercial bribery in a scheme worth $360,000. Times staff writer Suhauna Hussain contributed to this report.

item.title: In-N-Out makes tweaks to buns, salt and ketchup. Can you taste the difference?
item.description:
Source: LA Times Score: 4.77
In-N-Out makes tweaks to buns, salt and ketchup. Can you taste the difference? - Click here to listen to this article - In-N-Out Burger this week announced several menu changes in line with a recent push to reduce use of artificial dyes and processed ingredients. The beloved California-born chain said it had recently removed sesame flour from its buns in 10 states, replaced iodized salt with sea salt in its seasoning packets and changed its ketchup recipe last year to use real sugar instead of high-fructose corn syrup. The company said the changes were part of an effort to provide “the freshest, highest-quality food possible.” The removal of sesame flour appears to address growing sesame allergies, although the company did not explain its rationale for the change. People with sensitivities to the seed have long been vulnerable to reactions from accidental exposure because regulators have not required labeling of the ingredient. Labeling rules tightened in 2023, but, counterintuitively, they caused big commercial companies to add sesame into products in order to comply rather than go through a more complicated process of ensuring trace amounts weren’t present in other ingredients. In-N-Out added sesame flour to its mixture in 2024. The recent change reverses that decision. The changes elicited strong praise from some and criticism from others. “Weirdly stoked on the sea salt option,” one Instagram user wrote on In-N-Out’s social media post about the changes. “Our bodies actually need iodized salt,” another user wrote. Iodized table salt is mined from underground deposits, processed to remove other minerals and fortified with iodine, which is important for thyroid health and proper hormone production. Sea salt, meanwhile, refers to salt extracted from ocean water or lakes. It’s typically less processed, with larger, irregular grains, and retains other minerals. According to the Mayo Clinic, sea salt is frequently promoted as being healthier, with less sodium than table salt, but in fact they have “the same basic nutritional value.” Last year, the company changed its popular strawberry shake and signature pink lemonade recipes to remove red dye No. 40, a synthetic additive used to give foods and drinks a bright red hue. The recipe changes come on the heels of an announcement by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, which asked companies to more quickly remove red dye No. 3 — a similar synthetic food coloring.

item.title: 'Relief is coming': Hot, humid weather will finally break in Southern California
item.description:
Source: LA Times Score: 4.50
‘Relief is coming’: Hot, humid weather will finally break in Southern California - Click here to listen to this article - - After days of record-breaking heat and brutal humidity, Southern California will finally get a break. - Starting Friday, a cooling trend will shave degrees off daily highs through at least Sunday. - By Sunday, coastal highs should sink into the upper 70s, and inland areas can expect highs in the 80s. Friday will finally mark the start of a cooling trend in Southern California, coming days after brutally hot temperatures and abnormally high humidity broke several local records and caused health and safety concerns across the region, particularly at schools and homes without air conditioning. “The relief is coming,” National Weather Service meteorologist Bryan Lewis said Friday morning. “In general, things are going to start to feel a lot better.” The last remaining heat advisories from the weather service are set to expire Friday evening for most of Los Angeles, Orange and San Diego counties, as well as for the Inland Empire. It’s been hot in SoCal, but at least it’s a dry heat. Wait. It’s not dry — at all. Locals’ favorite summertime cliche has been brutally terminated by the worst humidity we’ve ever seen. Heat and humidity on Friday are expected to fall from peaks on Thursday, with highs across the region dropping 4 to 8 degrees, forecasts show. That trend will continue through the weekend, with Sunday highs likely a few degrees below normal for this time of year. “By Saturday, generally we’ll see temperatures on the coast right around the upper 70s, and then further inland, right around the mid-80s, even lower 80s,” Lewis said. “And then even cooler Sunday.” Lewis called it “a pretty big swing” from temperatures this week. Highs along L.A. County’s coast soared into the 90s on Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday this week, while inland valleys recorded highs hitting the triple digits. Nighttime offered little relief in most areas, and scientists believe the humidity may have been the highest ever experienced in the Southland. “The sticky tropical air will finally exit the region by this weekend,” the weather service wrote in its Friday forecast. “Marine layer clouds will likely return to many coastal areas.” Forecasters also say the high surf and rough ocean conditions that rattled coastlines from Malibu to San Diego over the last week are expected to calm. “That swell from former Hurricane Marie has died off,” Rich Thompson, a National Weather Service meteorologist, said. Beach conditions “should be pretty normal.” Still, the effect of those strong, high waves continues to come to light. Laguna Beach on Friday joined a growing list of Southern California cities that have declared a local emergency in the aftermath of the storm, which transformed beaches and damaged dozens of beachfront properties. In Laguna Beach, officials said unrelenting swells have caused widespread coastal erosion, pulling “a significant amount of sand off our beaches” and damaging a parking lot at Aliso Beach, the city wrote in a statement. The city also confirmed damage to the sea walls in front of six oceanfront homes on Ocean Way and Lagunita Drive, “yellow-tagging” them to ensure ongoing caution. Dana Point declared such an emergency earlier in the week, after more than a dozen homes were damaged by strong surf, as did Malibu, after a massive sinkhole formed at a beachside home. And experts say the more-typical ocean conditions and temperatures may stick around. Officials are sounding alarms about the potential health impacts related to this week’s oppressive humidity and intense heat, that’s only expected to rise, across Southern California. “It honestly seems like it will stay cooler than normal for pretty much the entire area this weekend, and for the first part of next week,” Lewis said. “Pretty nice compared to what we did see the last few days,” he added. “That was pretty brutal.”

item.title: The surprising reason California survived record summer heat without blackouts
item.description:
Source: LA Times Score: 4.22
The surprising reason California survived record summer heat without blackouts - Click here to listen to this article - Californians just made it through the hottest August on record without having to endure any rolling power outages. And, as the Southland continues to sweat its way through record-setting heat and humidity this week, there have been no widespread calls to reduce energy. In fact, the state has not issued a Flex Alert since 2022, and it has not implemented rotating outages since 2020. Over the last few years, California has quietly but dramatically increased the resiliency of its electrical grid through a significant expansion in battery energy storage. These batteries hold onto solar energy captured during the day, so it can be sent to the grid as demand peaks in the evening and morning, when most people are at home running air conditioners and other appliances. During the August heat wave of 2020, the California Independent System Operator, which manages the flow of electricity for most of the state, declared a Stage 3 Emergency and hundreds of thousands of households lost power in rolling outages. At the time, the system had less than 100 megawatts of battery storage available, according to system spokesperson Jayme Ackemann. Today, it has more than 17,000 megawatts available. “In about five years, we have vastly increased the amount of battery storage that is available to us,” said Ackemann, “and that is great news.” Batteries that pair with clean solar and wind energy or just bolster electrical grids in general have completely taken off and are making a big difference on the California grid. According to Ackemann, the system seeks to add 20,000 to 25,000 megawatts of battery storage capacity by 2045 — the same year it has set a goal of achieving carbon neutrality. That means the state would remove as many carbon emissions from the atmosphere as it emits. Hitting that goal will require increasing the supply of renewable energy and transitioning away from the use of natural gas, which supplies roughly a third of the state’s electricity. In recent years, California has steadily grown the share of electrical power generated by renewable sources — such as solar, wind, geothermal and hydropower — which bolstered the resiliency of the grid by increasing the overall amount of energy available. An uptick in people installing rooftop solar panels has provided an additional power boost, Ackemann said. In May, California became the first known large-scale power system in the world to have relied on more than 50% solar power for an entire month. “California has had a wealth of solar growth in the last five years,” said Abby Lestina, an analyst at Grid Status, a group that tracks electricity supply and demand in U.S. power markets. “It makes sense that they would reach this goal.” New batteries to store solar electricity and low demand in May both contributed to high percentage of electricity that came from solar. California’s grid is also now integrated with electrical systems across much of the Western United States. This means that if there is an extreme heat event in Southern California, energy from a cooler area such as the Pacific Northwest can be imported to help meet regional demand. All of this has collectively helped the state’s electrical system weather this year’s long-lasting heat. “We passed our highest peak of the year Wednesday with more than 50,000 megawatts of demand on the grid,” said Ackemann. “While we were very carefully monitoring the grid, we were confident that we were going to make it through the day.” That high is close to the all-time peak demand record of 52,061 megawatts set on Sept. 6, 2022. Continuing to strengthen the resiliency of the state’s electrical grid is important as extreme-heat events become more common due to climate change. While California recorded the warmest average daytime maximum temperature on record in August, the planet as a whole tied with July 2023 for the Earth’s hottest month on record. In Europe, more than 35,000 people have died from heat during a string of record-setting heat waves, often due to a lack of air conditioning. After enduring a record-shattering heat wave this spring, Southern California continued to break temperature records this week when Long Beach and Anaheim reached a blistering 107 degrees and Escondido hit 112 degrees. The state must also continue to amp up its energy supply in order to ensure it can meet the growing electrical demand posed by AI data centers. Though the days of urgent pleas to reduce power use in the hopes of preventing major outages appear to be largely over in California, local utilities still employ public safety power shutoffs. These are proactive, temporary electricity shutoffs to prevent high-voltage power lines and equipment from sparking wildfires during red flag weather conditions. In addition, there are unforeseen circumstances that could prompt the use of Flex Alerts and rolling outages in limited areas. A wildfire that destroys energy generation facilities during a significant heat wave, for example, could cause enough capacity loss to generate the use of these tools, said Ackemann. Extreme heat can cause electrical equipment to fail, leading to temporary, unplanned outages, as took place in San Diego this week. “But because we have a much stronger grid today and because we have a much more geographically diverse grid,” said Ackemann, “we have a much stronger ability to navigate those kinds of unexpected incidents.” Times staff writers Blanca Begert and Hayley Smith contributed to this report.

item.title: Evacuations lifted as crews gain upper hand on fire that threatened homes, Getty Center
item.description:
Source: LA Times Score: 4.03
Evacuations lifted as crews gain upper hand on fire that threatened homes, Getty Center - Click here to listen to this article - All evacuation warnings around Brentwood were lifted as crews gained the upper hand on a brush fire that ignited Wednesday afternoon along the 405 Freeway, threatening homes, a university campus and the Getty Center. The blaze, dubbed the Getty fire, grew to around 25 acres before forward progress was stopped shortly after 6 p.m., according to the Los Angeles Fire Department. The fire was reported around 4:30 p.m. and appeared to have ignited near the Getty Center parking lot at 1200 Getty Center Drive, the Fire Department said. By about 5:30 p.m., it had grown to 20 acres. The fire prompted the closure of the Getty Center, which will remain closed on Thursday to give firefighters easier access to the area, the center said in a post on X. The Getty Villa, located about 10 miles from the Getty Center in the Pacific Palisades, was not affected by the fire and will be open normal hours. Aerial footage showed flames burning along a hillside. Firefighters were fighting the blaze on the ground and by air. Around 6:30 p.m., the Fire Department reported that ground crews had made progress, working amid heavy smoke and steep brush on the west side of the 405 Freeway while aircraft continued to make water drops. No injuries were reported and no homes damaged, authorities said. The Fire Department issued evacuation warnings for two zones near the Getty Center, said spokesperson Lyndsey Lantz. The evacuation area was roughly bounded by Promontory Road to the north, Sunset Boulevard to the south, the 405 Freeway to the east and Bundy Drive to the west. The warning encompassed the Getty Center as well as Mount Saint Mary’s University. Around 8:40 p.m., authorities announced they had lifted the two warnings, though crews were set to remain on scene until the fire was fully contained. The fire came as temperatures across large swaths of Southern California climbed over 100 degrees, with temperatures feeling 5 to 10 degrees hotter due to high humidity, according to the National Weather Service’s Oxnard office. Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said on X earlier in the day that she had been in touch with fire personnel and that the Los Angeles Police Department was ready to assist firefighters with evacuations if they were needed. Debbie Ream, a spokesperson for Mount Saint Mary’s University, said the school’s Chalon campus for undergraduate students canceled in-person classes around 5:30 p.m. The campus is near the Getty Museum and was within an evacuation warning zone. The school had encouraged visitors and commuters to leave and told the roughly 400 students who live on campus to prepare to shelter in place, Ream said. The fire along the Sepulveda Pass did not appear to affect traffic on the 405 Freeway. In January 2025, a fire erupted in the same area amid red flag warnings. The fire burned 40 acres and prompted authorities to briefly shut down the freeway. Times staff writer Sandra McDonald contributed to this report.

item.title: At the Nicolas Cage sinkhole in Malibu, El Niño fears alter the good vibes mood
item.description:
Source: LA Times Score: 3.52
At the Nicolas Cage sinkhole in Malibu, El Niño fears alter the good vibes mood - Click here to listen to this article - As the waves bashed the coast this week, boulders smashed into the piles of Mitchell Leib’s Malibu home, plucking them like a “guitar string” and shaking his house. That, along with news of a massive sinkhole opening up about seven miles away, has the man worried about the house he’s lived in for 10 years. Standing outside a shopping center in Malibu on Thursday afternoon, Leib, 67, checked a tide chart to see when the water would be low enough for him to even be able to see the damage to his house. After days of high tides and the remnants of Hurricane Marie battering his home, Leib said his wife has asked if they can sell the house and move elsewhere. He’s not entirely opposed. “We’re looking to have peace and quiet in our lives,” Leib said. “Not fear.” Fear is exactly what was struck in some Malibu residents since early Tuesday, when the sinkhole opened up in front of a beachside property owned by actor Nicolas Cage. By the day’s end, the hole was about 25 feet deep and 30 by 60 feet wide. Most residents on the street have been ordered to evacuate, with seven homes red-tagged due to hazardous conditions and an additional 24 red-tagged because emergency vehicles wouldn’t be able to access them in an emergency, city officials have said. Not everybody appears to be quite as worried as Leib, or at least not everybody is showing it. Former Malibu Mayor Andy Stern’s house was one of those ordered to evacuate because emergency vehicles can’t access it. Stern, who is a real estate agent, said he thinks the sinkhole down the street was a one-off incident caused by a combination of a burst water pipe and the waves, and not something that is necessarily a harbinger of unsolvable problems to come. The city of Malibu said the sinkhole was “caused by coastal erosion from high waves and tides associated with Hurricane Marie,” adding that the city is “preparing for potential strong storms, high surf, heavy rain, mudslides and coastal erosion this winter associated with forecast El Niño conditions.” The Malibu residents who live near the beach but up on higher ground are concerned for their neighbors and for the coastline as a whole. Jo Giese was in her home on the phone with her insurance company for an unrelated reason Thursday when she thought it wouldn’t hurt to ask whether her policy covered a sinkhole swallowing her home. Not that Giese thought there was much of a chance — she and her husband live in a house on a cliff above the ocean. Still, she couldn’t help but wonder, given those ordered to evacuate included two of her friends. Giese said she has been monitoring the work contractors have been doing. She saw a long line of concrete trucks headed that way a few days ago, and a contractor told her the concrete was to fill in the hole. When she went to see the hole for herself, it appeared unchanged, and a contractor told her that the concrete had been washed out to sea. Malibu City Manager Joseph Irvin previously said construction and repairs would take about four weeks. Leib hasn’t decided yet what all of this means for the future. “Is this just a one-time event, or what we would call ‘normal?’” he said. “Or is this really a reflection of a greater problem?”

item.title: Driver dies after his car goes through guardrail, falls into Grand Avenue gap in downtown L.A.
item.description:
Source: LA Times Score: 3.09
Driver dies after his car goes through guardrail, falls into Grand Avenue gap in downtown L.A. - Click here to listen to this article - A man died early Friday in downtown Los Angeles after his car smashed through a guardrail on upper Grand Avenue and fell into a gap dividing the road, landing upside down on the street below, according to authorities. The incident occurred around 2:30 a.m. near 4th Street, according to the Los Angeles Police Department. The man — the driver and sole occupant of the car — was traveling north on Grand Avenue and veered off the roadway and through a guardrail, authorities said. The vehicle overturned and fell about 40 to 50 feet below, according to authorities. The driver was pronounced dead at the scene by the Los Angeles City Fire Department. No other injuries were reported. Investigators spent the morning trying to piece together the incident. Video from news service OnScene showed officers peering down at the car from above on upper Grand Avenue, where a section of guardrail was missing. Debris was scattered across the roadway and Grand Avenue was temporarily closed and reopened later Friday morning. The investigation into the crash is ongoing.

item.title: Will Hayden Panettiere's death uncover a supplier like Matthew Perry's 'Ketamine queen'?
item.description:
Source: LA Times Score: 3.05
Will Hayden Panettiere’s death uncover a supplier like Matthew Perry’s ‘Ketamine Queen’? - Click here to listen to this article - Federal authorities probing the death of actor Hayden Panettiere are focusing on where the drugs and medications that played a role in her death came from, echoing similar probes that resulted in charges for suppliers in the deaths of Matthew Perry and Mac Miller. Drug Enforcement Administration agents and local investigators have questioned several people about the circumstances of her Aug. 16 death, focusing on potential controlled substances and medications tied to her demise inside a Greenville, S.C., apartment, according to sources familiar with the probe. Paramedics and police found Panettiere in cardiac arrest, according to the Greenville County Coroner’s Office. Dispatch audio recordings from Broadcastify.com reference a possible overdose and CPR in progress. Narcan was reportedly administered by paramedics who arrived, and after efforts to resuscitate her, she was declared dead at 2:31 p.m. Her death echoes that of actor Matthew Perry and rapper Mac Miller, both of whom succumbed to overdoses. In their respective cases, prosecutors secured convictions for the people who supplied Perry with ketamine and Miller with cocaine and oxycodone pills laced with fentanyl. Perry’s demise in his hot tub led to his assistant, two doctors, a producer and a woman dubbed the “Ketamine Queen” pleading guilty. The Greenville County coroner, in the wake of Panettiere’s death, conducted an autopsy but has not made a formal finding on the cause of death and toxicology results are pending. Panettiere lived in Los Angeles, but her boyfriend, Brian Hickerson, is a Greenville native, according to authorities. A police report outlined the initial response from police who arrived at the scene. The report states that Hickerson and his brother Zach Hickerson were with Panettiere inside an apartment when the 36-year-old actor died. According to the police report, Brian Hickerson showed an officer “a bag of medications HAYDEN is currently on.” Several areas of the report were redacted, including statements from the brothers about what transpired as they called 911. Kenneth Iwamasa, who made $150,000 a year as a live-in assistant to Matthew Perry, is sentenced to 41 months in prison for his role in the actor’s death. The officer who authored the report, Matthew Bryan, wrote that he recorded an interview with Brian Hickerson on his body-worn camera, and observed Zach Hickerson being “very emotional” while first responders tried to revive the actor. Brian Hickerson became emotional after she was declared dead, Officer Matthew Bryan wrote. Later, he said that authorities obtained video of three individuals coming and going from the apartment from the complex’s security, which helped detectives with a search warrant. Sloan Ellis, a South Carolina attorney for Hickerson hired in the wake of Panettiere’s death, said in a statement, “Hayden’s death remains under investigation, and it is important to allow that investigation to proceed. As has been publicly reported, police confirmed there were no signs of foul play. Out of respect for Hayden’s loved ones and the ongoing investigation, there will be no further comment at this time.” Sources familiar with the probe have met with DEA agents about the actor‘s death, according to People magazine and TMZ. Hickerson was arrested multiple times on suspicion of domestic violence against Panettiere, beginning in May 2019 in Los Angeles, though the charges were later dismissed when prosecutors couldn’t secure a material witness. Following an eight-count criminal indictment in 2020 that covered multiple violent incidents over the previous year, Hickerson pleaded no contest in April 2021 to two felony counts of injuring a spouse or girlfriend. He was sentenced to 45 days in county jail along with four years of formal probation, ordered to attend mandatory domestic violence classes, and received a five-year protective order.

item.title: L.A. Fire Department ambulance involved in collision; 3 fire personnel injured
item.description:
Source: LA Times Score: 2.93
L.A. Fire Department ambulance involved in collision; 3 fire personnel injured - Click here to listen to this article - A Los Angeles Fire Department ambulance that was taking a patient in serious condition to a hospital collided with another vehicle on Wednesday afternoon, authorities said. The Fire Department said there were five total patients at the collision scene at Boyle Avenue and 4th Street in Boyle Heights. Three were Fire Department personnel. One of the patients was already in serious condition prior to the crash, said Lyndsey Lantz, a spokesperson for the Fire Department. They were being taken to a nearby hospital when the collision happened shortly before 2 p.m. near the 300 block of South Boyle Avenue. The Fire Department personnel and one other individual reported minor injuries, according to authorities.. No details on the type of vehicle involved were available, but images from KTLA showed the ambulance alongside a red four-door sedan with front-end damage. Lantz confirmed all five people involved in the crash were adults but was unable to share further identifying information.

item.title: Heat sets new records as oppressive humidity strangles Southern California
item.description:
Source: LA Times Score: 2.82
Heat sets new records as oppressive humidity strangles Southern California - Click here to listen to this article - Punishingly hot temperatures coupled with drastically high humidity Wednesday, making the weather feel even more intense than during previously blistering days, with real relief not expected to arrive until Friday. Temperature records were set across California. Santa Barbara set a record for the day with a high of 96 degrees; Oxnard, 98; Camarillo, 99; Santa Maria, 103; Long Beach and Anaheim, 107; Santa Ana, 108; and Escondido, 112. To the north, San Francisco International Airport reached a record-breaking 94; downtown Oakland, 97; and San Rafael, 104. Downtown Los Angeles hit 105 degrees, tying the record for the calendar day. And due to the extra humidity, temperatures felt 5 to 10 degrees hotter, according to the National Weather Service office in Oxnard. “This humid heatwave is no joke!” UC climate scientist Daniel Swain said in a post on X. Public health officials warned that the unusually high temperatures and humidity raised the risk of heat-related illnesses, particularly among older people and those with medical conditions. Wednesday’s highs were “extreme heat warning temperatures regardless of the humidity,” said Bryan Lewis, meteorologist with the National Weather Service’s Oxnard office. “But that humidity certainly adds to the discomfort and the ‘real feel’ heat.” The sizzling temperatures are brought on by a combination of a strong upper-level ridge of high pressure coming from Arizona and an offshore flow coming from the north and east. This one-two punch raised temperatures about 8 degrees higher than normal in areas south of Point Conception and a whopping 10 to 15 degrees higher in those to the north. At least three individuals have suffered injuries and have needed to be rescued this summer at Ocean Beach’s Sunset Cliffs, leading police to ramp up enforcement as locals debate the merits of safety versus a need for a youthful rite of passage. Forecasters said there would be little relief for Southern Californians when the sun went down as temperatures would remain uncomfortably warm at night. Experts said the higher-than-normal humidity is brought by the remnants of former-Tropical Storm Marie and warm temperatures coming from the ocean. Lewis said dew point temperatures were projected to be in the 70s for most of Los Angeles and Ventura counties. The higher the dew point rises, the greater the amount of moisture in the air, according to the National Weather Service. Generally, a dew point of 55 or less feels comfortable, while 65 or higher can feel oppressive. The National Weather Service office in Oxnard, which issues forecasts for Los Angeles County, doesn’t keep historic records for dew point or relative humidity, he added. “But from my recollection, we generally sit somewhere between the mid-50s to maybe the low 60s,” Lewis said. “Even if it’s a 10- to 15-degree difference in dew point, it’s pretty drastic.” Tarik Benmarhnia, a climate change epidemiologist at Scripps Institution of Oceanography at UC San Diego, said it’s a misconception that there is a biological process that makes people in different parts of the country more acclimatized to some climates. Instead, he said, it’s really about differences in lifestyle, housing and landscape. “That’s why in Miami, Florida and New Orleans, for example, this is normal heat [to those residents] and society is more organized according to this type of heat event,” he said. “So that makes [those communities] more resilient.” In California, many homes and rentals don’t have air conditioning because it historically wasn’t needed thanks to the area’s Mediterranean climate. Extreme heat warnings are in effect until Thursday for a majority of Los Angeles County — from the Malibu coast, to the San Fernando Valley and all the way south to the Palos Verdes Hills. The humidity makes this heat much more dangerous than previous heat waves, according to Los Angeles County public health officials. Strong surf across Southern California this weekend blasted through a seawall in Long Beach, caused a massive sinkhole at a celebrity’s Malibu home and damaged several Dana Point homes, among other issues. Public health officials say all residents should limit their outdoor activities during the afternoon, seek air-conditioned spaces, and take lots of breaks. Residents are advised to check on those at high risk for heat-related illness, including people with preexisting conditions, older adults, pregnant women, children and anyone without access to air conditioning. Unsafe weather conditions can create an added heat stress by forcing a person’s body to adjust to maintain a stable core temperature, said Dr. David Eisenman, a professor at the David Geffen School of Medicine and UCLA Fielding School of Public Health. A person’s body is working to maintain 98.6 degrees and if it gets hotter and more humid outside, the body has to work harder to maintain that stable temperature, he said. The moisture in the air prevents the body from efficiently sweating, which is needed to regulate the body’s temperature, Benmarhnia said. If the body’s system isn’t functioning properly, there is a risk of dehydration, heart strain and overheating, he said. To aid the body in getting as close to stable temperature as possible, Eisenman said people can practice “skin wetting” by keeping as much bare skin continuously damp as possible. Use a spray bottle, for example, to mist water directly onto a person’s face, neck and forearms, he said. Repeat every five to 10 minutes to keep skin visibly wet. People can also soak their clothing in cold water or apply an iced or chilled damp towel to their body. Forecasters say temperatures should drop by 5 degrees on Thursday, but the high humidity will continue to loom through the day. By Friday, Lewis said, the region will experience another cooling trend — with temperatures dropping another 5 degrees — but the bigger relief will be the decreasing humidity that will probably” be a lot closer to what we normally expect in terms of that amount of moisture in the air.” “Friday is when we’ll start feeling it, and we’ll also start to kind of lose some of that really humid tropical air,” he said. Times staff writer Rong-Gong Lin II contributed to this report.

item.title: Order to build thousands of housing units on the VA's West LA campus stands on appeal
item.description:
Source: LA Times Score: 2.60
Order to build thousands of housing units on the VA’s West LA campus stands on appeal - Click here to listen to this article - The U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals on Friday upheld a federal judge’s order requiring the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs to build 2,550 units of housing on its West Los Angeles campus. A two-paragraph order denied the VA’s request to have the entire 9th Circuit review a three-judge panel’s rejection of its appeal. “No further petitions for rehearing will be entertained,” the order said. “It’s a really good day,’ said Mark Rosenbaum, the lead attorney in the class action case filed on behalf of disabled veterans. “It’s a tribute to all the veterans who stood up to their government and demanded it honor its commitment to the men and women who sacrificed for their nation and found when they came home that their government would not stand up for them,” Rosenbaum said in a statement. Rosenbaum, of the civil rights law firm Public Counsel, said he expects U.S. District Judge David O. Carter to quickly schedule status conference to set a compliance timetable for the government. The VA did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The 2022 lawsuit alleged that the VA discriminates against disabled veterans by not providing housing on campus near the medical services they need to access. It also challenged the VA’s leases of portions of the 388-acre campus to non-veteran interests, including UCLA and the private Brentwood School for athletic facilities. In his October 2024 final judgment, Carter ruled those leases invalid. He ordered the VA to create up to 750 units of temporary housing in 18 months and an additional 1,800 permanent units over six years, all in addition to 1,200 units ordered in the settlement of a previous lawsuit. Later that month, hoping to get some housing built before the rainy season, he ordered the VA to secure a contract within three weeks to install at least 100 modular units, some on the parking lot of UCLA’s Jackie Robinson Baseball Stadium. The VA appealed, and the 9th Circuit panel stayed the order. After oral arguments in the spring, the three judges issued a complex decision affirming Carter’s finding of discrimination but overruling his order invalidating UCLA’s lease for its baseball stadium. In the Friday order, the three-judge panel unanimously rejected the VA request for an en banc hearing. A judge requested a vote on that decision, and it failed to receive a majority, the order said. Three judges who were not on the panel all appointees of President Trump, dissented in 57 pages of argument characterizing Carter’s ruling as whimsical and judicially flawed. “We have no business ordering the VA to build thousands of housing units on a whim,” they concluded. “This is not the Ninth Circuit Court of Appropriations.” Rosenbaum praised the ruling, which came on the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks, as a bright spot on a sad day. “There are lots of ways to address what happened on 9/11,” Rosenbaum said. “This is one of the really good ways. Now the hope is the government will comply with the order, end veteran homelessness, get this out of the courtroom and get the veteran off the streets.” Rob Reynolds, an Iraq war veteran who has spent years assisting homeless veterans seeking housing and services on the campus and testified on their behalf in the trial, said the timing of the ruling was “deeply significant.” Sept. 11, 2001, was the day he and thousands of fellow veterans decided to join, Reynolds said. “Twenty-five years later to the day, this ruling is a reminder that the country’s obligation to those who served does not end when the war does,” Reynolds said. “The West Los Angeles VA has been mismanaged for decades, and court oversight is necessary to ensure the VA finally follows through on its obligations to our veterans. “My hope is that the VA does not appeal this case to the Supreme Court, because any further appeal would only delay the oversight needed to ensure that happens.”

item.title: Killing of Catalina Island's mule deer has begun, official confirms
item.description:
Source: LA Times Score: 2.46
Killing of Catalina Island’s mule deer has begun, official confirms - Click here to listen to this article - - Pepe Barton, the Catalina Island Conservancy’s director of communications, confirmed that the controversial shooting and culling of roughly 200 of Catalina Island’s invasive mule deer “is underway.” - The conservancy announced last year that it would use contracted hunters to shoot the invasive deer over four to five years as part of an ecosystem restoration plan. The controversial shooting and culling of roughly 200 of Catalina Island’s invasive mule deer “is underway,” local officials confirmed to The Times on Wednesday afternoon. The Catalina Island Conservancy, the private nonprofit land trust tasked with protecting most of Catalina’s 48,000 acres, previously announced the project it deemed “limited deer removal” was scheduled to run from September through October. Pepe Barton, the conservancy’s director of communications, confirmed that work had begun this week, shortly after legal challenges to stop the culling were shot down. The conservancy was authorized to start killing deer in early September under a permit issued by the California Department of Fish and Wildlife. The conservancy announced last year that it would use contracted hunters to shoot the invasive deer as part of an ecosystem restoration plan. A judge tentatively rejected a request for a temporary halt to the eradication of all mule deer on Catalina Island. Meanwhile, a Los Angeles County supervisor has asked the governor to step in. These hunters, a unit of up to a dozen trained professionals employing rifles and bound by state regulations, are expected to kill the island’s non-native mule deer on the ground over four to five years. About 200 deer are anticipated to be killed from September through October. The culling is part of an opening phase that will test whether any other tools, methods or equipment are needed when crews expand the process next year, Barton told The Times earlier this month. The history of deer on the island dates back to the 1920s, when they were brought to Catalina for sport hunting, Barton said. Shortly after their arrival, the deer population exploded to about 2,000. The deer have wreaked havoc on native species as they eat fire-resilient chaparral and other native plants, according to the conservancy. ‘Why are mule deer deemed less worthy than cougars? Don’t we teach our children that all animals have a purpose on our planet?’ writes an L.A. Times reader. That loss has made way for invasive annual grasses that ignite more easily, increase erosion and leave less water to soak into aquifers, Barton said. The deer also reduce habitat and food sources for native birds and mammals, such as the endemic Catalina Island fox, Barton said. A legal challenge to halt the hunting brought in L.A. Superior Court in March by the Safari Club International, the California Rifle & Pistol Assn. and the Coalition to Save Catalina Island Deer, was denied last week. The contingent challenged the California Department of Fish and Wildlife’s decision to exempt the paid-hunter plan from the California Environmental Quality Act. The plaintiffs alleged the department relied on documentation that “is the product of a biased, closed-off ‘process’ that ignored valid concerns raised by the public.” A nonprofit proposes to eliminate Catalina Island’s deer population using contracted hunters, saying the nonnative animals heighten wildfire risk by eating native vegetation. A Superior Court judge Sept. 1 tentatively denied the plaintiffs’ request for a preliminary injunction, saying there would be no irreparable harm to let the deer eradication plan begin because the process starts with a “pre-removal assessment” while the “actual eradication phase is not set to occur until June 2027.” But on Thursday, a final ruling denied the request to halt the initial phase of invasive mule deer removal. L.A. County Supervisor Janice Hahn long opposed the eradication, ever since a previous plan called for sharpshooters to take aim at the deer from helicopters. She called on Gov. Gavin Newsom to step in and revoke hunting permits as recently as last month. “These deer have become beloved to many of the islanders, as well as the thousands of tourists who descend on Catalina Island every year,” she told The Times last month. As for the deer carcasses, some of the meat will feed endangered California condors, bald eagles and foxes. Staff writer Lila Seidman contributed to this report.

item.title: Heat warning extended for San Diego County as some temps surpass 100
item.description:
Source: NBC 7 San Diego Score: 4.77
Heat alerts warning of dangerous weather conditions are in effect for each of San Diego County's climate zones through Thursday as a stifling heat wave peaks. The heat warning was extended through Thursday evening for San Diego's coasts and inland valleys, where dangerously high temperatures could be as much as 10-15 degrees above average. Inland temperatures reached triple digits again on Wednesday, while coastal temperatures reached 90s, according to NBC 7 Meteorologist Greg Bledsoe. In Escondido, the hottest place in the county Wednesday, a high of 112 degrees shattered an old record for this date of 104. That record was set in 1893, according to Bledsoe. Gillespie Field airport in El Cajon unofficially hit 108 degrees just a little before 1 p.m. Wednesday, Bledsoe said. San Diego County's mountains are under a heat advisory through Thursday at 8 p.m. Showers are still possible over the mountains each afternoon, but chances will drop as the week goes on. Local Out in the boiling desert, an extreme heat warning is in effect through Friday at 8 p.m. The weekend will continue to cool. We should also see more morning marine layer clouds, and cooler overnight temperatures. More seasonal temperatures will continue into next week. Adding to the discomfort is excessively high humidity stemming from a mix of monsoonal moisture and heat rising from warmer-than-usual ocean temperatures, according to the National Weather Service. Much of the county continues to feel muggy and the mountains saw some afternoon thunderstorms this week. Tropical storms hundreds of miles away, like the recent Hurricane Marie, can also increase humidity. "The effects of Marie have faded but the monsoonal flow has returned. So, we’re not really getting much of a break from the humidity," Bledsoe said. While some relief will come Thursday and Friday, lower humidity and cooler temperatures are not likely to come before next Sunday, according to the NWS. SDG&E power outages The extreme heat also prompted San Diego Gas & Electric to carry out some unplanned outages across the county. Within 24 hours between Tuesday and Wednesday, SDG&E had 29 unplanned outages. A blackout struck at about 1:30 p.m. Wednesday, knocking out power to 8,719 SDG&E customers in Del Dios, Green Valley, the Lake Hodges vicinity, Poway, Rancho Bernardo, Rancho Penasquitos and San Pasqual, according to the utility. Service was expected to be restored to the affected areas by late afternoon on Wednesday. "Community members out there with this type of temperature, they’re going to start using the A/C a little bit more, fans, and that on top of appliances that they already use. That’s going to put strain on the grid," SDG&E spokesperson Humberto Gurmilan said. San Diego Fire-Rescue Department responded to a power line down last night on Jamacha Road near Sacramento Avenue on Wednesday morning. Hundreds of people in the neighborhood were out of power till around 2 a.m. Omar Osorio said he returned home after six hours in the hospital with stomach pain. His illness was aggravated by a night without air conditioning. “My home it was super hot, no AC at all, it was really bad,” he said. His neighbor David Orosco has six people total living under his roof. Many of them were sleepless in Spring Valley Tuesday night. “Everybody was out here just trying to cool off, it was cooler outside then inside the house," Orosco said. A Chula Vista power pole caught fire Tuesday night because of what appeared to be a power equipment malfunction. The California Independent Operator coordinates the power grid to make sure electricity supply matches customer demand in real time across 80% of California. Until then, SDG&E recommends conserving energy by minimizing the use of appliances during peak hours. If you are impacted by a power outage, SDG&E recommends visiting their website to get updates on restoration. Hottest first pitch ever at Petco Park Wednesday's temperatures broke the record of the hottest first pitch ever at Petco Park in downtown San Diego, according to the Padres baseball team. Despite the extreme temperatures, the Friar Faithful still showed up in droves to support their team. Cooling off during the heat The NWS issues these warnings because heat illnesses increase during periods of extreme heat. Residents are urged to drink plenty of fluids, stay in air-conditioned rooms and stay out of the sun. San Diego County released tips and advisories on avoiding heat-related illnesses here. Never leave pets or children unattended in vehicles. "Car interiors will reach lethal temperatures in a matter of minutes," the NWS said. Dozens of locations across San Diego County act as "Cool Zones," providing a space where residents can seek relief from the heat for free. See the list here.

item.title: Seeing more bugs? San Diego's warm weather may be to blame
item.description:
Source: NBC 7 San Diego Score: 4.67
Hot and muggy weather in San Diego County may be contributing to increased activity from ants, mosquitoes and other insects, according to local experts. Eric Middleton, an entomologist with UC Cooperative Extension, said higher temperatures and humidity can affect insect behavior. Mosquitoes reproduce faster when temperatures are hot and humidity is high, while ants may head indoors as outdoor food and water become harder to find. “We have things like ants where when it gets hot and then it gets dry, so especially, you know, about this time of year, they run out of food and they run out of water outside. And so people are most likely to really notice ants when they start coming inside,” said Middleton. The activity could continue into the coming months if warm weather persists, entomologists said. For homeowners dealing with mosquitoes, Middleton said reducing standing water can help prevent them from reproducing. “So with mosquitoes, one of the biggest things, they need water. in order to reproduce. So making sure that you empty out sources of standing water in your backyard,” said Middleton When it comes to ants, keeping a home tidy and limiting their access to food can help. Middleton also recommended checking for possible entry points. Local "You want to make sure that they don't have easy access into your house. You want to check, you want to call or seal areas like around window sills or places where the ants might be coming in. You also just generally want to stay tidy.” Ants and mosquitoes are not the only insects showing increased activity. Leah Taylor, A UC Master Gardeners of San Diego County representative said beetles are also appearing later in the year. “We’re seeing a lot of beetles later in the year than we have before. Look for those green fig beetles because our fruit is on the trees and it’s falling off. It’s hot, it’s ripening fast, so that attracts insects,” said Taylor. People with questions about insects or other pests can contact the UC Master Gardeners of San Diego County through its hotline at 1-858-822-6910. “We are able to provide you with all sorts of strategies, if you’re dealing with insects, dealing with pests,” said Taylor. The group also invited people to ask questions in person at its Saturday fall plant sale at Balboa Park and encouraged visitors to bring photos or other information that could help identify their pest problems. “Come ask those bug questions you need answers to, bring photos, your phone, whatever. Tell us where you’re at and we’re happy to provide any resources and information.” This story was originally reported for broadcast by NBC San Diego. AI tools helped convert the story to a digital article, and an NBC San Diego journalist edited the article for publication.

item.title: NCTD suspends coastal rail service for the weekend for maintenance
item.description:
Source: NBC 7 San Diego Score: 4.56
The North County Transit District will suspend all coastal rail service this weekend to perform routine maintenance, transit officials announced Friday. The closure, which will take place Saturday and Sunday, will pause all Coaster service between San Diego and Oceanside. Regular service is scheduled to resume Monday morning, according to the NCTD. Transit officials said weekend closures take place periodically throughout the year on a predetermined schedule to allow construction crews to work safely on and along the rail line. The downtime enables workers to complete preventive maintenance improvements and advance major construction efforts. No passenger or freight trains will run during the closure. However, test trains, construction vehicles and equipment will remain active along the railroad right-of-way and on the tracks over the weekend. Officials advised residents to remain alert and cross rail lines only at designated crossings. More information on the weekend closures is available at GoNCTD.com/Alerts.

item.title: Average San Diego County gas price tops $6 for first time since June
item.description:
Source: NBC 7 San Diego Score: 4.35
The average price of a gallon of self-serve regular gasoline in San Diego County topped $6 for the first time since June 3 Friday, from rising 2.2 cents to $6.017. The average price has increased 23 of the past 24 days, rising 33.5 cents, according to figures from the AAA and Oil Price Information Service. It has increased a little over a dollar since the start of the joint U.S., Israel war on Iran in February, which sent oil prices higher and drastically accelerated increases at the gas pump. "Oil prices are now near or over $100 a barrel due to continued supply concerns related to the Middle East conflict, and that has pushed up pump prices locally and nationally," said a representative from the Automobile Club of Southern California in a statement Thursday. The national average price rose for the 11th time in 12 days, increasing from almost two dollars to $4.295, which is about a dollar above last year's prices. The national average price has increased a little over a dollar since the attack on Iran. "The national average is increasing during a season when gas prices typically go down due to lower gasoline demand," according to the AAA, formerly the American Automobile Association. Local The national average price is at its highest amount this late in the calendar year, according to Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, which provides real-time gas price information from more than 150,000 stations.

item.title: Carlsbad declares local emergency to stabilize bluffs ahead of El Niño
item.description:
Source: NBC 7 San Diego Score: 3.85
The City of Carlsbad declared a local emergency over an unstable coastal bluff along South Carlsbad Boulevard, allowing officials to move more quickly on stabilization work amid concerns about erosion and upcoming El Niño conditions Thursday. The area of concern is a stretch of Carlsbad Boulevard between Palomar Airport Road and Island Way, where cones blocked off portions of the unstable cliffside. For longtime residents and beachgoers, the erosion has become increasingly noticeable. “Every day I start my day with a nice walk. If there is beach, I walk down there,” said Mary Johnston, who has been taking daily walks along South Carlsbad Boulevard for two decades. Johnston said the coastline looked different when she first started walking there. “It was pretty much the same, but it had more beach,” she said. The city said it has been working closely with the California Coastal Commission and hired geotechnical experts to investigate the stability of the bluff and roadway. Those experts recommended immediate action. Local “We understand this is a heavily traveled roadway, and maintaining its integrity is essential to protecting public safety, as well as property and our coastal environment,” the Carlsbad city manager said in a statement. The stabilization plan called for placing large boulders, each weighing between four and eight tons, along the bluff to create a sloping wall extending approximately 190 feet. Work could begin as early as next week, according to the city. Officials warn the project could affect traffic in the area while construction is underway. For people who have watched the coastline change over the years, the deterioration is difficult to see. “I’ve been coming to this beach for like 20 years, and it’s just so sad to see,” one beachgoer said. Johnston said she worries about what could happen if the stabilization work is delayed. “It’s going to take a long time to go through the Coastal Commission and everything they have to go through,” Johnston said. “In the meantime, this road is going to cave in.” The local emergency declaration is temporary and will remain in effect until Sept. 15, when the Carlsbad City Council can decide whether to confirm it. If confirmed, the emergency declaration would then need to be reviewed by the City Council at subsequent City Council meetings until the City Council ends the local emergency, according to the City of Carlsbad's site.

item.title: Dog missing for nearly three years reunited with family after microchip scan
item.description:
Source: NBC 7 San Diego Score: 3.48
A dog missing for nearly three years has been reunited with his family after being found abandoned at a safe sleeping site, officials announced Thursday. Humane Law Enforcement officers responded Tuesday evening to a call about an abandoned dog at the Jewish Family Service Safe Sleeping site at 2209 Kincaid Road, according to the San Diego Humane Society. After securing the animal, officers scanned him for a microchip. The scan came back positive, revealing that Colby had been registered and reported missing since Sept. 27, 2023. Officers worked to confirm contact details and reached Colby's family around 9:30 p.m. The owner immediately woke her children to share the news that Colby was coming home. Because the family had not owned a dog for nearly three years, the owner spent the night and the next morning gathering supplies. Colby arrived flea-infested with a possible skin infection beneath matted fur. The SDHS medical team provided grooming, a bath, vaccines and a wellness check to ensure a comfortable homecoming. On Wednesday afternoon, Colby reunited with his owner, Cindy and young Gregory. The family opted to have Colby neutered before bringing him home Thursday afternoon upon learning the humane society encourages spaying and neutering. Animal welfare officials emphasized that microchips work, but keeping contact details current and filing missing pet reports remain essential. Local To learn more about microchipping pets, go to sdhumane.org/microchip.

item.title: Before 9/11, 3 Pentagon hijackers spent time in San Diego
item.description:
Source: NBC 7 San Diego Score: 2.24
The quotes in this article are from archived interviews gathered by NBC 7 in September 2001. Three of the hijackers aboard American Airlines Flight 77 had ties to San Diego, including two who lived in Clairemont and Lemon Grove, worshiped at a local mosque and sought flight training at Montgomery Field before the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks. In the days after the attacks, FBI agents searched San Diego neighborhoods as investigators examined the local connections of Khalid Al-Midhar, Nawaq Alhamzi and Hani Hanjour. “We have reason to believe that three of the individuals on board the plane that crashed into the Pentagon had ties to San Diego, that one of them might have been a pilot, and they may have lived here,” an FBI spokesperson told NBC San Diego on Sept. 14, 2001. During the investigation that followed, “This place was swarming with FBI agents,” a San Diego resident told NBC 7 at the time. Agents searched the Parkwood Apartments in Clairemont, where al-Midhar and Alhamzi had lived shortly after arriving in the United States. “They seemed very polite. They said 'Hi' when they were leaving,” a Parkwood neighbor told NBC 7 at the time. The two later moved into a Lemon Grove home owned by a Muslim leader they met at the Islamic Center of San Diego. “He opened his house for those who claimed they were students. They turned out to be murderers and terrorists, unfortunately,” a man at the Islamic Center told NBC 7 while the investigation unfolded. One neighbor recalled learning that the men had been living nearby. “Me, personally, I like freaked out. Freaked out knowing they're anywhere around the country, much less right in your own backyard,” the Lemon Grove resident told NBC 7. Al-Midhar and Alhamzi also sought flying lessons at Montgomery Field. At one point, they specifically said they wanted to learn how to fly Boeing aircraft. “They came here to learn how to fly, but they wanted to fly larger planes. We didn't have the larger plane, so we just took them for an intro flight, a short flight, and that's about it,” Fred Sorbi, of Sorbi's Flying Club, explained to NBC 7 shortly after learning of the attack. The men did not conceal their identities while they were in the area. They used their real names to pay rent, open bank accounts and buy a used car. The car was later found at Dulles International Airport after the attacks and is still kept by the FBI as evidence today. 25th Anniversary of 9/11 The San Diego connection also raised a significant question: What did the FBI know about the men before Sept. 11? According to a 2005 report released by the U.S. Department of Justice, Office of the Inspector General, that looked into the bureau’s handling of intelligence information prior to the attacks, the men had even lived with an FBI informant. The informant did not notice anything about them that indicated they were plotting an attack. Still, the review found the circumstances should have drawn greater scrutiny from agents, possibly leading to information that could have given investigators an earlier lead. The report also said that although the FBI had identified counterterrorism as a priority in 1998, the San Diego field office continued to make drug trafficking its priority in 2001. Adding that the FBI, according to the report, took few steps to ensure San Diego and other field offices were aligned with the bureau’s stated counterterrorism priorities. Hanjour, the third hijacker with a San Diego connection, was already a trained pilot when he arrived in San Diego in December 2000 to meet one of the other two men. It was a short visit. Within days, Hanjour and the other man left together for Arizona, where Hanjour resumed his flight training. “He was a weak pilot, but we had no idea, of course, that he was this kind of person,” the man who helped train Hanjour in Arizona said to NBC 7 at the time. Al-Midhar, Alhamzi and Hanjour later boarded American Airlines Flight 77, which crashed into the Pentagon on Sept. 11. More than 180 people aboard the plane and on the ground at the Pentagon were killed. For people in San Diego who learned the hijackers had spent time in their neighborhoods, the discovery shattered a sense of security. “It’s frightening now. It makes us start looking behind our back, and start looking, and that's sad,” a Lemon Grove neighbor told NBC 7. Overall, the FBI responded to more than half a million leads, conducted more than 167,000 interviews and processed more than 150,000 pieces of evidence. Present day FBI San Diego Field Office response FBI San Diego acknowledged the extensive examination of the two hijackers’ time in San Diego, along with “systemic pre-9/11 shortcomings,” according to a statement sent in response to NBC 7. It also addressed that the two men happened to be living with an FBI San Diego source who “had not observed nor reported conduct by either man that raised concerns about a possible connection to terrorism.” The statement continued to add: “Since 9/11, the FBI has adapted its investigative and administrative policies and procedures to better address the ever-evolving terrorism threat landscape and implemented significant changes to enhance our ability to detect and disrupt potential terrorist plots. Central to that transformation has been strengthening collaboration and timely information sharing among federal, state, local, Tribal, territorial, and international partners, recognizing that no single agency or investigative method can provide a complete threat picture. Thanks to these lessons learned from 9/11, we are faster, more coordinated, and better equipped to disrupt threats before harm occurs. In 2025 alone, we made more than 700 counterterrorism arrests and disrupted 640 planned attacks.” Lastly, they reaffirmed the bureau’s commitment to building on progress and protect the nation. This story was originally reported for broadcast by NBC San Diego. AI tools helped convert the story to a digital article, and an NBC San Diego journalist edited the article for publication.

item.title: Mortgage Rates Today, Friday, September 11: Just Below 7%
item.description:
Source: NerdWallet Score: 4.50
We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence.
