item.title: The U.S.-Canada trade war is creating a headache for auto-parts makers
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: World Score: 2.89
The U.S.-Canada trade war is creating a headache for auto-parts makers The U.S. and Canadian auto industries have been tightly woven together for decades. But the latest tariff flareup between the two countries may complicate that. Think of that sticker on the windows of new cars breaking down how much of the vehicle's content comes from the U.S. and Canada. From a manufacturing point of view, content from both places has long been considered deeply intertwined. But the U.S. and Canada failed to reach a new trade deal this summer, and the trade war between them has escalated quickly. In August, the U.S. enacted new tariffs on aluminum and steel, and President Trump has also threatened 50% tariffs on Canadian vehicles, auto parts and steel effective on Jan. 1. On Tuesday, Canada enacted retaliatory tariffs on a variety of U.S. goods — including on American steel and aluminum. All of this puts the auto manufacturing industry in a jam. For major U.S. carmakers, analysts say, the tariffs introduce uncertainty as companies determine whether to adjust their supply chains in the long run, or to absorb new costs in the short term. But for the smaller businesses that supply those big companies with thousands of parts — think bolts, or the steel rods for steering wheels — the tariffs could spell bigger, more expensive trouble. " It's really, really damaging to the industry and to the financials of the industry. It makes planning for things very difficult," says Dan Hearsch, global co-leader of automotive and industrial at the consulting firm AlixPartners. For these companies, he says, the new tariffs follow years of chaos — the aftermath of Covid supply chain shortages, the start-and-stop ramp up to making more electric vehicles, the need to grapple with pre-existing tariffs. "It's one more thing, on top of the one more thing, that was on top of the one more thing, that was on top of the one more thing," Hearsch says. The U.S. and Canada's auto relationship The U.S. and Canada started weaving their auto supply chains together in 1965, when they signed a pact with a goal of consolidating their auto industries and expanding their combined market. The pact removed duties on auto products or equipment crossing the border when they are made of at least 50% of U.S. or Canadian content. Their trade relationship deepened with the 1994 North American Free Trade Agreement, which included Mexico and removed many duties between the three countries, as long as they contained a certain proportion of North American parts. The 2020 United States Mexico Canada Agreement, which revised that deal, included a requirement that auto content be 75% North American to be able to pass borders without any tariff. For the auto industry, the free flow of many goods meant that components could be assembled in plants in each country, and ultimately combined in another. The auto supply chain grew into a single ecosystem. "I've often described it like an omelet" with ingredients from all three countries, says Jim Jarrell, president and CEO of Linamar Corporation, a Canadian manufacturing company that handles both auto and agricultural products. "Think about a casting that starts in Mexico and that gets sent into the U.S. to get processed. That part then jumps over to Canada to get further processed," says Jarrell, referring to a molded piece of metal. "Then we ship it back into the U.S. sub-assembly, to get it finished and assembled," Jarrell says. "And that story is, quite frankly, not unusual," he continues. "That is actually how the industry works." Linamar Corporation has a roughly equal number of plants in the U.S. and in Canada, but they also have plants in Mexico and in Asia, Jarrell says. And each of them make slightly different things, Jarrell says, making it potentially difficult to alter those supply chains in response to new tariffs — or the threat of additional tariffs in January. To alter where or how parts are made would mean re-evaluating entire supply chains, Jarrell says. "So it's a lot of cost and time." Aisin Corporation, one of the world's largest transmission makers and suppliers, is based in Japan, but does about 20% of its business in North America, and often moves materials back and forth as their supply chain warrants it. " We've always looked at North America as totally North America, not Canada-specific or U.S.- specific," says Chuck Sanders, the executive vice president for the company's North American division. " When there's rapid changes or new tariffs that are introduced suddenly," he continues, "that kind of creates chaos on the business." Shifting production means moving jobs around. That's a problem both the company and its workers would like to avoid. "We want to continue the business so they have a long-term future with us," Sanders says. The effect on the auto-part supply chain Cars are made with tons — literal tons — of steel and aluminum, and with thousands of parts. How many? It depends on when you stop counting. For instance, take a steering wheel. There's a metal rod, often padded in leather or vinyl. Then there are sensors, an airbag, an instrument cluster with "lots of dials and things that move," Hearsch from AlixPartners says. In that steering wheel system, he says, "There's probably 50 to 100 different parts coming from all over the world." Manufacturers occupy different tiers within the automotive supply chain. "Tier one is a supplier that delivers a part or a system to the automaker," Hearsch says. Think of a headlamp, for example. " A tier two is a company who makes something that goes to a tier one" — the smaller pieces that make up a headlamp, he says. And then a tier three company feeds parts to tier two. Any of these components might be made from raw metals like steel and aluminum, which could have been subject to tariffs when they were first imported to North America. Now, those components could be subject to additional tariffs as they repeatedly move across the border. For now, many auto suppliers are taking a watch-and-wait stance. Bosch and Magna, two of the biggest suppliers to North American companies, emailed NPR statements saying that they are monitoring the situation and its potential effects, particularly on customers. The Motor & Equipment Manufacturers Association trade group also wrote in an emailed statement that it's "concerned by the continued escalation of trade actions between the United States and Canada." "The vehicle supplier industry has built deeply interconnected North American supply chains over decades, and policies that increase costs or create barriers ultimately weaken the competitiveness of the entire region as we face challenging global competition," the statement continued. That global competition comes from the makers of Chinese electric vehicles, which are becoming increasingly popular, says economist Sue Helper, who studies the auto industry at Case Western Reserve University. Like Hearsch, she says the uncertainties of the post-Covid supply chain and the transition to EVs, as well as potential disruptions from AI, make it hard for automakers to decide when to make changes to their supply chains, so they "don't make the wrong investment and don't jump too soon or too late," she says. "So it's a really difficult time. It's always a tough business, but it's particularly tough right now." "The challenge is that the automotive industry does not move at the speed of politics," says Sean Tucker, an editor at Cox Automotive, an automotive services and technology provider. It takes time for automakers to reconfigure their supply chains — or decide whether they should, since tariff policy could change under a future presidential administration. If Canada and the U.S. do manage to disentangle their supply chains, Jarrell of Linamar says, it could cost years — and a lot of money for auto-parts makers. "The more uncertainty there is, obviously the harder it becomes to invest and grow in a confident way," he says.

item.title: Why gains by Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen could push gas prices even higher
item.description:
Source: NPR Topics: World Score: 2.35
Why gains by Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen could push gas prices even higher DUBAI, United Arab Emirates — A tenuous yearslong truce in Yemen unraveled further this week as Iran-backed Houthi fighters pushed out Saudi-backed Yemeni forces along a key stretch of Red Sea coastline, consolidating their control of a vital shipping route. Statements by the Houthis and a rival Yemeni commander, who's cited by The Associated Press, said Friday the Iran-backed group had taken control of the port city of Mokha, just north of the Bab el-Mandeb strait, and captured the barren island of Mayun, also known as Perim. Videos circulating online and broadcast by Arabic news channels show Yemeni army forces and allied militias melting back and leaving their vehicles for the Houthis to seize. A statement by the Houthis said its fighters had expelled Saudi-backed troops from six districts in the governorates of Taiz and Hodeidah, and freed prisoners along the way. Senior Houthi leader Mohammed Bukthi told NPR the attacks on Saudi-aligned forces and ships are in response to the kingdom's years-long blockade of Houthi-held areas, which he said had led to deaths from hunger. "Yemen will not be silenced as Saudi Arabia and its allies are free to navigate these waters while Yemen isn't able to do so in the Red Sea," he said. Bukthi called it a "blockade for a blockade" and said the aim is to pressure Saudi Arabia to end its airstrikes and military campaign. He said the Houthis are not attacking international shipping through the Red Sea, and focused only on Saudi targets. Oil prices climb as Gulf wars intensify The fighting in Yemen, and the Houthis' targeting of Saudi oil carriers around that waterway, coincided this week with another exchange of fire in the Persian Gulf between the United States and Iran. As a result, the price of Brent crude — a global metric for oil prices — shot up Thursday over $108 a barrel briefly, before settling Friday around $105. The London-based research firm Capital Economics says the fighting on both sides of the Arabian Peninsula raises the risk of even further energy price hikes in the coming weeks. Loading... AAA says gasoline prices in the United States are up by more than 34% from last year at this time, averaging nearly $4.30 a gallon on Friday. Diesel, used for farming and trucks, is up by more than 63% from a year ago to nearly $6.06 per gallon. Meanwhile, data from maritime analytics firm Kpler, and cited by multiple news outlets, shows Saudi Arabia exported just 3.2 million barrels a day last month, its lowest level in more than a decade. Saudi oil rerouted after attacks in key waterways Higher oil prices help Gulf Arab producers like Saudi Arabia offset the sharp fall in their energy exports, but they still face growing budget deficits, in part due to Iranian attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, which was Saudi Arabia's main gateway for exports. Loading... To avoid the Strait of Hormuz, Saudi Arabia had been rerouting its crude through an east-west pipeline leading to the Red Sea near Bab el-Mandeb as a fallback measure to keep oil flowing during the U.S. war on Iran. An image from Europe's Copernicus Sentinel-3 satellite program, examined by NPR, shows a fire near the western end of the pipeline this week as Houthis targeted the kingdom's energy infrastructure. Later Friday, the Saudi Energy Ministry confirmed attacks on the pipeline had occurred on Thursday, forcing a "precautionary suspension." Iran says Oman will host a meeting on Monday with Gulf Arab countries, as well as Iraq, to discuss a plan that could allow ships to pass through the Strait of Hormuz with Iranian permission. There's also discussion of possible service fees being paid to Oman and Iran — an idea the U.S. rejects. Saudi oil takes longer route as waterways are choked off Saudi Arabia is one of the world's biggest oil producers but its carriers are now being choked off by closures to its tankers in the Bab el-Mandeb and Strait of Hormuz waterways. Saudi Arabia is also a key stabilizer of energy prices in OPEC, but with its exports curtailed by the two conflicts and other Gulf Arab producers struggling to get oil and gas out, countries around the world are digging into emergency oil reserves to plug the gap, leading to higher prices. The Houthi attacks on shipping have forced Saudi Arabia to use a much longer and costlier route through the Suez Canal to the Mediterranean Sea and around Africa in order to reach buyers in Asia. Houthis and Saudi forces trade attacks The Houthi takeover of the Yemeni port city of Mokha comes just days after the group fired missiles and drones at four regions of southwestern Saudi Arabia. The group says the attacks were in response to dozens of Saudi airstrikes on Yemen, including one that killed civilians at a prison. The Saudi Energy Ministry said the Houthis struck Saudi oil facilities, sparking fires that halted operations on Tuesday. Saudi Arabia said more than 70 people were wounded in the attacks. The renewed fighting in Yemen comes 11 years after Saudi Arabia first led a coalition of Arab countries into war in Yemen to roll back a Houthi takeover of the capital, Sanaa, and reinstall Yemen's government to power. More than a decade later, the Houthis still control Sanaa. The deadly fighting in recent days for control of Mokha and other areas of Yemen's western coast has displaced at least 18,500 people, according to the United Nations' International Organization of Migration. It says families are fleeing with nothing and arriving at humanitarian sites that already lack emergency food stocks and shelter supplies. Abu Bakr Bashir reported from the U.K., Ahmed Abu Hamda contributed reporting from Cairo and Geoff Brumfiel contributed from Washington, D.C.

item.title: Door locks tested with a 100-pound battering ram: Consumer Reports
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.98
Door locks tested with a 100-pound battering ram: Consumer Reports A door lock that looks secure can still fail a real kick-in test. Consumer Reports tested locks that held up and some that did not A door lock that looks secure can still fail a real kick-in test, no matter how many smart features it packs in. Resistance to kick-ins, lock picking and drilling can vary widely between locks, whether they're basic deadbolts or feature-rich smart locks. Consumer Reports tested door locks across several categories, identifying standout picks worth buying and others that fall short on basic security, so shoppers know exactly what they're getting. Kwikset Juno 991J15SMTCP Credit: Kwikset Priced at $58.10, the Kwikset Juno 991J15SMTCP is a standard, non-smart deadbolt. Consumer Reports named this its top pick among standard door locks, and found it holds up well when someone tries to kick it in straight out of the box. CR found it scored high for resisting lock picking, rounding out a strong overall security profile for a conventional lock. Testers noted its one weakness is vulnerability to a cordless drill attack, though this is a common limitation shared by standard deadbolts generally. Yale Assure Lock 2 YRD450-WF1-BSP Credit: Yale The Yale Assure Lock 2 YRD450-WF1-BSP costs $249.99 and works with Apple $AAPL Home and Bluetooth connectivity right out of the box. Consumer Reports named this its top pick among WiFi smart locks, and found it holds up against kick-ins and cordless drill attacks. CR found it very easy to set up, connect to WiFi and control remotely, and noted it comes bundled with a Yale WiFi module and a sensor that tracks whether the door is open or shut, a combined $80 value included at no extra cost. Testers said this module adds remote control through the Yale Access app, voice assistant integration with Alexa, Google $GOOGL Home and Samsung SmartThings, unlock alerts, an access log and a way to generate and hand out digital keys and passcodes. Eufy Smart Lock Touch & WiFi S230 Credit: Eufy The Eufy Smart Lock Touch & WiFi S230 costs $179.99 and includes a fingerprint scanner for one-touch unlocking. Consumer Reports rated this the leading option in its fingerprint smart lock category, and found it earns strong scores in brute-force tests for kick-ins and lock picking. CR found it manages a decent drilling score despite not being a fully keyless model, and rated it strong for checking on the lock remotely and for how easily it goes in. Testers noted this lock also includes a touchscreen keypad for PIN entry, auto-locking, an access log and voice control through Amazon $AMZN Alexa and Google $GOOGL Home. August WiFi Smart Lock AUG SL05-M01-G01 Credit: August The August WiFi Smart Lock AUG SL05-M01-G01 costs $177.99 and connects directly to WiFi without requiring a separate adapter. Consumer Reports singled this out as the leading pick among retrofit smart locks, and found it earns high scores for letting a user unlock the door from afar, check its status remotely and get it installed without much hassle. CR found it rated very good for security add-ons, rounding out a strong overall test performance for a retrofit-style lock. Testers noted this lock includes auto-locking and unlocking, an access log, electronic keys, a door open and close sensor, and voice control through Amazon $AMZN Alexa, Apple $AAPL Home, Google $GOOGL Home and Samsung SmartThings. Delaney 345001 Credit: Delaney The Delaney 345001 costs $51.16 and is a standard, non-smart deadbolt. Consumer Reports found this lock ranked at the bottom of its ratings, earning poor marks for its ability to resist drilling, lock picking and kick-ins. CR found this weak performance held true across all three of its major security tests, not just one isolated weak spot. Testers said shoppers looking to spend around this price point have better options available for the money. Defiant Round Matte Black Smart Wi-Fi Deadbolt Powered by Hubspace Credit; Defiant The Defiant Round Matte Black Smart Wi-Fi Deadbolt Powered by Hubspace costs $83.47 and connects to Home Depot $HD's Hubspace smart home system. Consumer Reports found this lock offers plenty of genuinely useful smart features, but ranked at the bottom of its ratings for basic physical security. CR found it simply doesn't withstand forceful attacks such as kick-ins, drilling and lock picking, despite its smart-home conveniences. Testers said this lock illustrates a real tradeoff shoppers should watch for, since smart features don't guarantee a door lock can actually keep an intruder out.

item.title: 10 signs a neighborhood is about to get more expensive — and how to spot them early
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.76
10 signs a neighborhood is about to get more expensive — and how to spot them early The clearest signs a neighborhood is gentrifying show up years before prices do, from new coffee shops to rezoning votes A neighborhood rarely jumps from affordable to expensive overnight. The change shows up first in small, physical details: a new espresso machine behind a plywood counter, a permit notice stapled to a porch railing, a transit map that suddenly includes a stop that wasn't there last year. Real estate agents, urban planners and longtime residents have tracked these patterns for decades, and the sequence repeats across cities with remarkably little variation. Independent businesses tend to arrive first. National chains arrive last. By the time a Starbucks $SBUX or a Whole Foods opens, prices have typically already started to climb. Spotting the signs a neighborhood is gentrifying before they become obvious matters for more than curiosity. Renters priced out of one area can use the pattern to plan a move before costs rise again somewhere new. Buyers hunting for a starter home can use it to find a neighborhood on the way up instead of one that has already peaked. Small business owners weighing where to open a shop can use the same signals to lock in a lease before commercial rents follow residential ones upward. No single indicator guarantees a price surge, and few neighborhoods show all 10 signs at once. Taken together, though, they form a reliable early warning system that has held up in cities as different as Boston, Seattle and Portland, Oregon. Some signs are visible on a single walk down the main commercial strip. Others turn up only in public records: building permits, zoning agendas or transit funding announcements that most residents never think to check. This list covers 10 of the clearest and most consistent signals, arranged roughly in the order they tend to appear, from the earliest and subtlest shifts to the changes that only show up once a neighborhood's transformation is already underway. Read side by side, they offer a way to see the shift coming before it shows up in the asking price. Independent coffee shops open on empty storefronts Credit: R Matt Hoffman / Unsplash A wave of small, independent coffee shops opening in a neighborhood is one of the clearest early signs that prices are about to climb. Coffee shops require less capital and shorter leases than most retail concepts, so they tend to move into a block before national chains, or even most residents, notice the neighborhood is changing. Research backs up what real estate agents have long suspected. Harvard Business School research using Yelp review data, co-authored by economist Michael Luca, found that when a new coffee shop opens in a zip code, it predicts a rise in home prices of roughly half a percent within a year. Zillow's often-cited 2015 analysis went further, tracking homes within a quarter mile of a Starbucks $SBUX: those properties appreciated 96 percent between 1997 and 2014, compared with 65 percent for the typical U.S. home over the same period. The chains arrive after the shift has already begun, not before it. Starbucks' own site-selection process looks for walkable blocks, nearby upscale businesses and residents with rising disposable income — the same conditions independent coffee shops respond to months or years earlier, with far less research and far less money on the line. By the time a familiar green awning appears, the neighborhood has usually already passed through its first wave of change. The signal worth watching is not the arrival of a chain but the appearance of a new, locally owned café in a spot that used to sit empty, or in a storefront that housed something else entirely: a check-cashing outlet, a laundromat, a shuttered diner. A single new coffee shop on a quiet block rarely means much on its own. Two or three opening within the same year, especially clustered near a commercial corridor that previously had little foot traffic, is a stronger and earlier signal than almost any other item on this list. It shows up on a walk through the neighborhood well before it shows up in a listing price. Artists and small studios move into old industrial buildings Credit: Canva Images When artists and small design studios start renting cheap loft or warehouse space, it usually marks the first stage of a neighborhood's transformation, well before developers, galleries or retailers show any interest. The pattern has a name: urban sociologists call it the SoHo effect, after Manhattan's SoHo neighborhood, where artists moved into vacant cast-iron warehouses in the 1960s and 1970s because the buildings offered cheap, oversized space that no other tenant wanted. Sociologist Sharon Zukin documented the pattern in her 1982 book "Loft Living," describing how artist communities functioning as informal urban pioneers made industrial neighborhoods feel desirable to developers, who later converted the same buildings into housing aimed at a wealthier population with no connection to the original arts scene. The same sequence has repeated in Williamsburg in Brooklyn, the Pearl District in Portland, Oregon, the RiNo district in Denver and the Arts District in Los Angeles, among many other former industrial corridors across the U.S. Artists need cheap square footage more than any other amenity, so they gravitate toward buildings and blocks that mainstream renters overlook: former factories, printing plants, rail-adjacent warehouses. Their presence makes a once-overlooked area feel distinctive, which draws the coffee shops, bars and small boutiques that cater to a similar audience, which in turn draws developers who see underused industrial land as ripe for residential conversion. The earliest version of this signal rarely shows up in real estate listings at all. It shows up in local arts council grant announcements, artist open-studio events, or leasing notices for former factory space aimed at "creative" or "maker" tenants — records that often surface in city business journals or commercial real estate filings years before a single residential unit gets built. A neighborhood with a growing cluster of working artist studios in converted industrial space, especially one that previously had almost no residential population at all, is worth watching closely over the following five to 10 years. A city announces transit funding before a line opens Credit: Zoshua Colah / Unsplash Property values near a planned transit line often start rising the moment funding is approved, not once the line opens, which means this signal shows up years before construction even begins. University of Minnesota researchers Jason Cao and Shengnan Lou studied the Green Line light rail extension connecting Minneapolis and St. Paul and found that most of the increase in nearby home values happened before a single train ran. Home values near planned stations rose to about $9.20 per square foot higher right after the Federal Transit Administration approved full funding in 2011. By the time the line began carrying passengers in 2014, values had climbed to about $13.70 per square foot higher, then held roughly steady once service started. That timing runs counter to how most people assume transit affects property values. It is easy to picture a new station raising nearby home prices once it opens and commuters start using it. In practice, the bigger jump tends to happen earlier, once a funding agreement removes the uncertainty over whether a line will actually get built. Buyers, developers and investors treat a signed funding agreement as close to a guarantee, and they price that certainty into nearby land almost immediately. The size of the effect varies by city, by station and by how far a property sits from the platform, and not every station sees a meaningful bump — some research on Seattle's light rail expansion, for example, found mixed results across different stations along the same line. Still, the broader pattern holds across enough cities to make transit funding votes worth tracking. City council agendas, regional transit authority board minutes and Federal Transit Administration funding announcements are all public and typically searchable online, and they surface long before construction crews or a ribbon-cutting ceremony do. For a reader weighing where to buy, a transit line that has just secured funding is generally a more useful signal to act on than one that has already opened, since a meaningful share of the price movement may already be reflected in listings by the time trains start running. Home renovation permits start climbing Credit: hans middendorp / Pexels A jump in permits for additions, gut renovations and major remodels is one of the most concrete, checkable signs a neighborhood is changing, because permit filings are public record months before any work becomes visible from the street. When property owners invest serious money renovating existing housing stock rather than simply selling it, that decision reflects confidence that resale or rental values are about to justify the expense. Permit data is tracked by city building or planning departments, and most mid-size and large U.S. cities now publish this information as searchable open data online, updated far more often than home price indexes or rent reports, which typically lag actual market conditions by a month or more. A meaningful signal looks less like a handful of scattered repair permits and more like a cluster: multiple kitchen and bathroom remodels, home additions or full renovations filed within the same few blocks over a relatively short period, rather than permits spread evenly and thinly across an entire city. Individual homeowners upgrading a single kitchen tell you little. A concentrated spike across dozens of properties in one section of a neighborhood, especially older housing stock that previously saw little investment, tells you a great deal. Permit data has an advantage that most of the other signs on this list lack: it requires no interpretation of foot traffic, no reading of a company's site-selection strategy and no guessing about future zoning decisions. It is simply a record of money already committed by property owners who have decided this specific block is worth the expense. Checking a city's permit portal for a particular zip code or neighborhood boundary takes a few minutes and often reveals a shift long before it becomes visible anywhere else, including before rents move enough for tenants to notice, and well before any real estate listing mentions the neighborhood by name. A national grocery chain like Whole Foods or Trader Joe's moves in When Whole Foods, Trader Joe's or a similar specialty grocer signs a lease in a neighborhood, nearby home values have usually already started rising, and they tend to keep appreciating faster than the surrounding market for years afterward. A Zillow analysis found that homes located in zip codes with a Whole Foods or a Trader Joe's appreciate at roughly twice the pace of the median U.S. home. An earlier and more granular study, conducted in 2007 by the real estate research firm Johnson Reid using hedonic pricing models, found that a specialty grocer added an average of 17.5 percent to nearby home values, with the effect ranging from six to 29 percent depending on the specific market — a bigger boost than the study found for bookstores, bike shops or gyms in the same neighborhoods. The mechanism resembles the one behind the coffee shop signal, but it operates on a different scale. Whole Foods has reportedly targeted areas with roughly 200,000 people living within a 20-minute drive and a college-educated population, meaning the company's own site-selection research has effectively already identified the demographic shift a reader might otherwise have to piece together from scratch. A grocery lease signing is, in that sense, a confirming signal rather than a purely original one: by the time a national grocer commits to a 10-to-15-year lease, its real estate team has already concluded the surrounding population can support premium prices. The detail worth tracking closely is the "coming soon" phase, not the grand opening. Lease signings and permit filings for a specialty grocer typically become public through commercial real estate trade press or city permit records well before construction starts, and regional or smaller specialty grocery chains often follow the same pattern in markets where the two biggest national names have no locations yet. Trader Joe's, whose real estate process is notably slower and more selective than Whole Foods', often signs a lease years after a neighborhood has already begun changing, which makes a Trader Joe's opening more of a later-stage confirmation than an early signal, while a Whole Foods lease can arrive earlier in a neighborhood's trajectory. Rents are already rising in the neighborhood next door Credit: Tobias Wilden / Unsplash Gentrification tends to spread outward from an already-expensive neighborhood into whichever adjacent area offers the closest substitute at a lower price, so rising rents just across a street, a park or a rail line are often the clearest warning that a neighborhood is next. Demand does not disappear once a neighborhood becomes unaffordable to most renters and buyers looking for a bargain; it simply relocates to the next comparable option. Renters priced out of one area typically want the same things they valued before: similar housing stock, similar commute times, similar walkability and similar access to transit. The neighborhood immediately next door, provided it shares those features and offers lower rent, is the most obvious destination, which is why urban change tends to move block by block and neighborhood by neighborhood rather than jumping randomly across a city. The clearest version of this signal appears at what might be called soft boundaries: a street, a park or a transit line that separates two neighborhoods without functioning as a real barrier to movement, the way a highway or a river often does. Rents on one side of a soft boundary tend to catch up with rents on the other side faster than two neighborhoods separated by a harder physical divide, because renters and buyers can simply walk or bike across the line without changing their daily routine. Tracking this signal means comparing rent listings in a target neighborhood against its most similar, immediately bordering neighborhood, not against the city as a whole. A gap that has been narrowing steadily over the past year or two, particularly if the more expensive neighborhood shares a soft rather than a hard boundary with the one being watched, suggests the same forces are likely to arrive next door before long. Two rent-tracking tools make this comparison easier than it used to be: Zillow's Observed Rent Index and Apartment List's rent estimates both break out data by zip code, which allows a side-by-side comparison of a target neighborhood against its immediate neighbor rather than against a citywide average that can mask exactly the local gap that matters. New bike lanes and protected sidewalks appear Credit: K / Pexels Cities that invest in new bike lanes, wider sidewalks or a pedestrian trail are often building for the neighborhood a place is becoming rather than the one it currently is, and property values near that new infrastructure tend to rise faster than the surrounding area. Indiana University's Public Policy Institute studied the effect of Indianapolis's eight-mile Cultural Trail, a protected bike and pedestrian path completed in 2013, and found that assessed property values within about 500 feet of the trail rose 148 percent between 2008 and 2014, an increase of roughly $1 billion. A more recent analysis puts the trail's total contribution to assessed property value near $3 billion, and found that retail space along the route had grown by 39 percent since construction began, with food and beverage sales nearly double the citywide average per square foot. Infrastructure investment like this rarely happens at random. City planning departments typically direct new bike lanes, protected crossings and pedestrian trails toward corridors that already show signs of new investment interest, whether that is new housing construction, business openings or a rezoning proposal already moving through city council. In that sense, new pedestrian infrastructure functions the way a Starbucks $SBUX lease does: it both follows an existing trend and accelerates it, since a safer, more walkable street draws exactly the kind of foot traffic that supports the restaurants, shops and cafés covered elsewhere on this list. City transportation departments generally publish multi-year capital improvement plans listing planned bike lane, sidewalk and trail projects well before construction begins, and these documents are usually available through a city's public works or transportation website. A newly funded trail or protected bike lane heading toward a specific corridor is worth noting years before the concrete gets poured. Not every city builds something as ambitious as an eight-mile trail. A smaller-scale version of the same signal shows up in dedicated bus lanes, new pedestrian lighting or a streetscape redesign for a single commercial corridor, and the underlying logic, that cities direct scarce infrastructure dollars toward areas they expect to grow, applies just as much to a six-block streetscape project as it does to a marquee trail. Chef-driven restaurants and bars open before the chains do Credit: Masood Aslami / Pexels A cluster of new, independently owned restaurants and bars — especially chef-driven concepts distinct from what previously existed on that block — tends to open years before any national chain arrives, and its appearance is a stronger, more capital-intensive confirmation of change than a single new coffee shop. Opening a full-service restaurant or bar requires far more money, a longer buildout and, in most U.S. cities, a liquor license that involves a public approval process. That extra cost and friction means restaurateurs willing to sign a lease in an overlooked corridor are making a bigger bet than a coffee shop owner does, which makes their arrival a more reliable signal that the underlying shift is real rather than a passing flicker. National chains, by contrast, generally wait for a market to prove itself before committing, since their real estate teams need enough comparable sales data and foot-traffic history to justify a location to corporate leadership. Liquor license applications offer a public, trackable version of this signal that is worth checking directly rather than waiting to see a restaurant's sign go up. Most city and county alcohol licensing boards require a public hearing before approving a new full liquor license, and the resulting records and meeting agendas are typically searchable online months before a restaurant opens its doors. A rise in the number of new full liquor license applications filed for addresses in a specific commercial corridor, compared with the same corridor's history over the previous several years, is a leading indicator that shows up well before diners do. Commercial rents in a corridor tend to climb once several independent restaurants and bars have opened and proven a customer base exists, which is part of why this signal tends to arrive later in the sequence than a new coffee shop, but well before national brands. Investors start buying homes and paying in cash Credit: Pavel Danilyuk / Pexels A rise in the share of homes bought with cash rather than a mortgage, particularly by investors rather than owner-occupants, often means professional buyers have already concluded a neighborhood is undervalued relative to where they expect prices to go. Institutional investors, house flippers and small-scale landlords track data most residents never think to check: job growth patterns, permit filings, transit funding votes, zoning proposals and school enrollment trends, often months or years before a typical homebuyer notices anything has changed. Paying in cash lets an investor close a sale in days rather than the four to six weeks a conventional mortgage usually requires, which matters in a competitive market and lets professional buyers outbid people who need financing approval. A rising share of cash sales in a specific zip code, particularly one that previously had very few, suggests professional money has already priced in a shift that has not yet reached most listings. The effect is not uniform across every market or every year, so the signal is more useful compared against a neighborhood's own recent history and against its surrounding county than treated as a fixed benchmark. Most county recorder or property assessor offices publish sales records that note whether a given transaction was a cash purchase or financed with a mortgage, which makes this data checkable at the source rather than something that has to be estimated secondhand. A related and separately trackable pattern is house flipping: homes bought and resold within a year or two rather than held long-term. Data on flipping activity is available through some county records and through services such as ATTOM Data Solutions, though flipping volume varies significantly by market and by year, and a single data point in one direction is far less meaningful than a sustained rise over several consecutive quarters. The city rezones the area for taller buildings or mixed use Credit: Daniel Romero / Unsplash A zoning change permitting taller buildings, more housing units per lot or a mix of residential and commercial use is one of the strongest and most concrete signs a neighborhood is about to get considerably more expensive, because it directly raises what a developer is legally allowed to build, and land value follows that new legal ceiling almost immediately. Rezoning, sometimes called upzoning when it increases allowed density, changes what a given parcel is worth on paper before a single shovel goes into the ground. A lot that previously supported only a small single-family house can suddenly support a multifamily building with several times as many units, and buyers, sellers and developers price that new potential into a sale almost as soon as the change becomes official, not once construction finishes years later. City planning departments typically hold public hearings and publish proposed zoning map amendments months, and sometimes years, in advance of a final vote, and these records specify exactly what is allowed to change, down to the individual block or parcel. That level of detail sets rezoning apart from the more indirect signals earlier in this list: a new coffee shop or a rising rent next door suggests change is coming, while an approved zoning map amendment states, in writing, precisely what can legally be built and where. Rezoning proposals are usually tied to a broader comprehensive plan update, a transit expansion already working its way through the approval process, or a citywide push to add housing near job centers, so the timing often lines up with several of the other signs on this list rather than appearing on its own. Checking a city planning department's website or attending a public rezoning hearing, months before any new building appears, remains one of the most direct ways to see a neighborhood's future price already being decided.

item.title: Best local neighborhoods to visit in the worlds ten busiest cities
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.76
Best local neighborhoods to visit in the worlds ten busiest cities Local neighborhoods in the world's busiest cities reveal more about daily life than any skyline photo, from Tokyo's Yanaka to Mexico City's Coyoacán 10 cities carry more daily human traffic than any others on the planet, and no two show it the same way. Tokyo moves tens of millions of commuters through its rail network before most offices open. Dhaka packs a population built up over centuries into a river delta city that was never designed to hold it. Cairo, Mumbai, Beijing, Shanghai, Delhi, Mexico City, São Paulo and Osaka round out this group of megacities, each one shaped by its own mix of history, geography and migration. Most visitors budget their time around the same handful of landmarks: the Bund in Shanghai, the Gateway of India in Mumbai, the pyramids outside Cairo, Shibuya Crossing in Tokyo. Those places earn their reputations. But they say little about how residents actually spend an ordinary afternoon. The neighborhood level is where a city's food, architecture, commerce and daily rhythm actually show up. A visitor can walk through it in an hour or two, rather than photograph it from a bus window. This list picks one local neighborhood in each of the world's busiest cities. Each one was chosen for what it reveals about the city around it, not for a single photogenic view. Some, including Coyoacán in Mexico City and Yanaka in Tokyo, are old towns absorbed into an expanding metropolis that kept their own identity anyway. Others, including Vila Madalena in São Paulo and Tianzifang in Shanghai, grew out of one specific era of urban history and turned into creative districts almost by accident. A few, including Old Dhaka and Islamic Cairo, are the original core that the entire modern city grew from, centuries before either one became a megacity. None of these are secret finds. Locals in each city already treat them as a natural stop for a free afternoon. Nearly all are reachable by public transit rather than a long taxi ride. What follows is a practical rundown of what to expect in each one and why it developed the way it did. Each slide also covers what makes the detour worth it. Yanaka is the old Tokyo neighborhood the 20th century mostly skipped Credit: Nakaharu Line / Unsplash Yanaka survived the 1923 earthquake and the World War Two firebombing that leveled most of central Tokyo. It still has narrow lanes and low wooden buildings instead of high-rises. That accident of history makes it the clearest picture left of what pre-war Tokyo actually looked like. The neighborhood sits between Ueno and Nippori stations. It grew up around Yanaka Cemetery, a large graveyard laid out in the 1870s that doubles today as a quiet, tree-lined park where locals walk and cycle. Temples line the surrounding streets in unusually high numbers. That density is a legacy of an Edo-period practice of relocating many of the city's temples to this hillside district to cut fire risk in the crowded center. Several of those temples, with their wooden gates and small shrines, stay open to visitors at no charge. The main shopping strip, Yanaka Ginza, is a narrow street lined with small shops selling grilled skewers, senbei rice crackers and used kimono fabric rather than chain retail. It has become known for cats, both real ones that wander the street and a scattering of cat-themed goods in shop windows. That detail draws its own steady stream of visitors on weekends. The street stays busy through late afternoon and quiets early, so a visit before sunset gets the fullest sense of daily foot traffic. Yanaka works best on foot, ideally paired with the neighboring districts of Nezu and Sendagi. Together the three share the same pre-war character and are known collectively as Yanesen. A walk through Nezu Shrine, with its tunnel of vermilion torii gates, fits naturally into the same afternoon. This area was never rebuilt after the war, so the scale stays human: two-story buildings, streets never widened for cars, and a quiet unusual for a city Tokyo's size. Spring brings cherry blossoms along the cemetery's central path. Early evening light on the wooden shopfronts of Yanaka Ginza is a reliable, uncrowded alternative to the more famous old-town strips near Asakusa. Hauz Khas Village pairs a 14th-century reservoir with Delhi's café scene Credit: Zoshua Colah / Unsplash Hauz Khas Village sits around the ruins of a reservoir built under the Delhi Sultanate in the 13th century. Today that same ground holds one of the city's densest clusters of independent boutiques, galleries and restaurants. Few neighborhoods anywhere pair a medieval monument with a contemporary nightlife district this directly. The reservoir's name means royal tank. It was built under Sultan Alauddin Khilji to supply water to the walled city of Siri. Decades later, Sultan Feroz Shah Tughlaq restored the tank and added a madrasa, a mosque and his own tomb along its edge. Those structures still stand inside Hauz Khas Deer Park, open to the public and free to enter. Deer graze in enclosures nearby, and the ruins themselves are unfenced enough to walk through slowly rather than view from behind a rope. Around this historic core, the urban village known as Hauz Khas Village grew out of a settlement of the same name. Since the 2000s it has filled in with low buildings converted into design studios, small fashion labels and multi-cuisine restaurants. Many have rooftop seating that looks out over the lake and ruins at once. The mix of eras is direct: a diner can sit on a terrace built into a 20th-century house, looking down at a 700-year-old tomb lit up for the evening. Weekday afternoons are the quietest time to see the monument itself. The surrounding restaurants and bars get busiest after dark, especially on weekends. The narrow lanes are best explored on foot, since the village has little real space for cars once you're inside it. Several of the country's most established independent design labels got their start here rather than in Delhi's larger malls. Many still keep their original storefronts in the village today. Tianzifang shows Shanghai's French Concession at its most unpolished Credit: Canva Images Tianzifang is a maze of narrow lanes built from 1930s shikumen housing, tucked off Taikang Road in the southern part of Shanghai's former French Concession. It is now filled with independent galleries, small workshops and cafes rather than the concession's original residents. It is also the least redeveloped version of this architecture left in the city. Shikumen, meaning stone gate, describes a housing style unique to Shanghai. It fused a Chinese courtyard layout with the stone doorframes and brick construction common in Western row houses of the same period. Tianzifang's version, a shikumen complex originally called Zhicheng Fang, went up in 1933. It sat in a middle-income section of the French Concession, distinct from the grander avenues built for the concession's wealthier residents. Renovation of the lanes into a commercial district began around 2000, driven largely by artists and small business owners rather than a single developer. That history is part of why the layout still feels improvised rather than curated. Walking Tianzifang means ducking through alleys barely wide enough for two people to pass. Laundry still hangs to dry above doorways, and small workshops sell handmade jewelry, calligraphy and vintage clothing. Cafes and bars occupy former living rooms, often with the original tile floors and stone doorframes intact. The district connects easily to nearby Sinan Road and the Xintiandi area, another former shikumen block, though Xintiandi has been rebuilt to a far more polished, gentrified standard. The nearest metro stop is Dapuqiao on line nine, a few minutes' walk from the main entrance on Taikang Road. Weekday mornings run noticeably quieter than weekend afternoons, when the narrow lanes fill with both tourists and local shoppers. Because Tianzifang grew organically rather than through a single restoration project, its shops turn over more often than a typical retail street. Specific stores are worth treating as temporary, even when the surrounding architecture is not. Old Dhaka's Shakhari Bazar is the historic core the modern city grew from Credit: Canva Images Shakhari Bazar is a single narrow lane in Old Dhaka lined with shops run by Hindu artisans. For generations they have made shakha, the white conch-shell bangles worn by married Bengali Hindu women. The lane sits inside Old Dhaka, the original 17th-century city founded as Jahangirnagar under Mughal rule, and it remains a working example of a neighborhood defined by a single trade. The lane runs close to the Buriganga River and to Ahsan Manzil, the pink-domed former residence of the Nawabs of Dhaka, completed in 1872 and now a museum. A 10-minute walk connects the two. It passes through streets that still carry the layout of the Mughal and later British colonial city, rather than the wider grid found in modern Dhaka. Buildings here rise just two or three stories, with narrow facades and ornate colonial-era detailing that has largely disappeared from the rest of the capital. Old Dhaka as a whole is organized around a handful of historic market lanes. Each one is historically tied to a single craft or good: Shakhari Bazar for conch-shell work, Tantibazar for the city's gold trade, and Kumartuli for potters. Nearby Chawk Bazar remains one of the city's oldest general markets and turns especially busy during Ramadan, when its food stalls draw crowds from across Dhaka. Sadarghat, the river terminal a short walk south, adds constant boat traffic to the area's daily rhythm. Morning is the best time to walk Shakhari Bazar itself, since the lane is narrow enough that foot and cart traffic can back up by midday. The shell-carving work is done largely by hand, using techniques passed down within families. Several shopkeepers are willing to explain the process to visitors who stop and ask. The lane sits inside a UNESCO-recognized heritage zone, alongside sites including the Armenian Church and Ruplal House. It rewards slow walking over a fixed checklist, with river views from Sadarghat as a natural place to end the visit. Vila Madalena is São Paulo's street art and bar district Credit: Dominiquemel16 Ramos / Pexels Vila Madalena is a hillside neighborhood in western São Paulo known for Beco do Batman, an alley covered in rotating graffiti murals. A concentration of bars, live music venues and independent galleries makes it the city's main destination for nightlife outside downtown. The neighborhood began as a modest residential area in the Pinheiros district. It shifted toward its current identity in the 1980s and 1990s, as artists and students drawn by cheap rents opened studios and small venues. Beco do Batman got its name from an early Batman mural painted in the alley decades ago. The space has functioned since as an open, informal gallery, where street artists repaint sections over time rather than preserve any single piece permanently. The result changes from one visit to the next, which keeps it a working gallery rather than a fixed monument. Streets around Beco do Batman hold a dense mix of bars, some occupying converted houses with rooftop terraces, alongside boutiques selling Brazilian design and secondhand records. Live music runs heavily toward samba and MPB, Brazilian popular music, particularly at small venues that book local acts several nights a week. Weekend evenings bring the heaviest crowds, with sidewalks outside popular bars filling well past midnight. Weekday afternoons show a much quieter, more residential side of the same streets. The neighborhood connects directly to Pinheiros and to Vila Beatriz, both reachable from Vila Madalena metro station on the yellow line. Saturdays add a long-running organic and craft food market held in a nearby square, drawing a mix of neighborhood residents and visitors. The area is genuinely residential alongside its nightlife function. Daytime visits reveal a calmer, tree-lined side of Vila Madalena that its bar-heavy reputation tends to obscure. Small parks and quiet side streets sit just a block or two off the main strip. Coyoacán is Mexico City's best-preserved colonial-era neighborhood Coyoacán is a cobblestoned former colonial town, absorbed into Mexico City's southern expansion. It is best known as the longtime home of painter Frida Kahlo and the site of Leon Trotsky's final residence and assassination. Its two central plazas, Jardín Centenario and Plaza Hidalgo, stay closed enough to traffic that walking is the only practical way to see it. Hernán Cortés used Coyoacán as his base immediately after the fall of Tenochtitlan in 1521. The area kept a separate civic identity as a town outside the capital for centuries afterward. That history is part of why its architecture and street plan still read as distinct from the rest of Mexico City. The Museo Frida Kahlo, widely known as La Casa Azul for its cobalt-blue exterior, occupies the house where Kahlo was born, lived with muralist Diego Rivera, and died in 1954. It remains the neighborhood's single busiest attraction, and timed-entry tickets are worth booking well in advance. A short walk away, the Museo Casa de León Trotsky preserves the fortified house where the exiled Bolshevik leader spent his final years and was killed in 1940. Watchtowers and bullet-marked walls, installed after an earlier assassination attempt, still stand on the property. Between the two museums, the neighborhood's central plazas host a coyote-shaped fountain, a nod to the area's name, believed to derive from the Nahuatl word for a place of coyotes. Saturdays and Sundays bring the heaviest foot traffic. The plazas turn into an informal market for handicrafts and street food, including quesadillas and elote sold from carts around the square. Weekday mornings offer a quieter version of the same streets, better suited to viewing the colonial-era facades and colorful house fronts nearby. The neighborhood connects easily to San Ángel, another former colonial town a short trip south. Pairing both districts makes for a single afternoon focused on Mexico City's pre-metropolitan history. Al-Muizz Street is a walkable timeline of Islamic Cairo's architecture Credit: Faqih Abdul / Unsplash Al-Muizz Street is a one-kilometer pedestrian corridor through the walled core of historic Cairo. It is lined with mosques, madrasas and merchant houses built continuously from the Fatimid dynasty's founding of the city in the 10th century through the Ottoman period. UNESCO listed the surrounding district, known as Islamic Cairo, as a World Heritage Site in 1979. The street runs between two surviving city gates, Bab al-Futuh in the north and Bab Zuweila in the south. Both were built in the 11th century as part of the original walled city's fortifications. Along the way sits the Qalawun complex, a mosque, hospital and mausoleum built in 1284 by Sultan Qalawun. It stands in the Bayn al-Qasrayn section, once the site of two Fatimid palaces and long the street's most prestigious address. Restoration work beginning in the late 1990s repaved the street, restored dozens of monuments, and lowered surrounding buildings to keep the historic skyline visible. Al-Muizz Street sits directly beside Khan el-Khalili, Cairo's best-known bazaar, so the two are usually visited together. The bazaar handles shopping and food, while the street itself carries the architectural weight. Evening is widely considered the best time to walk it, since the street lights up and its daytime crowds thin out. Al-Azhar Mosque, founded in 970 and still an active center of Islamic learning, sits just off the street's midpoint and stays open to non-Muslim visitors outside prayer times. Because so many monuments sit within a single kilometer, the street rewards a slow, unhurried walk rather than a rushed pass toward Khan el-Khalili. Several smaller buildings, including preserved merchant houses like Bayt al-Suhaymi tucked down side alleys, charge separate small entry fees and keep shorter hours than the main street. Checking individual opening times before setting out avoids arriving at a locked door. Few other places on earth pack this much surviving Islamic-era architecture into a single stretch of road. Beijing's hutongs near the Drum and Bell Towers show the pre-skyscraper capital Credit: Andy Wang / Unsplash The hutong neighborhoods clustered around the Drum Tower and Bell Tower, just north of Beijing's Forbidden City, are narrow alleyways lined with single-story courtyard homes called siheyuan. This residential pattern dates back to the Yuan dynasty and once covered most of central Beijing. Nanluoguxiang, the best-preserved of these alleys, runs roughly 800 meters north to south. It has been continuously inhabited since it was laid out under Kublai Khan's Yuan dynasty capital in the 13th century. Its narrow lanes branch off into smaller hutongs on either side, many still residential, where courtyard gates and stone thresholds survive from the Qing dynasty. The main alley itself has filled with cafes, boutiques and snack vendors catering to visitors. The nearby Drum Tower and Bell Tower were first built in the 13th century and rebuilt several times since. They once announced the time to the entire city, and both remain open to visitors willing to climb their steep staircases. Houhai Lake, a short walk west, adds a different texture to the same district: a shallow, willow-lined lake surrounded by bars and restaurants that stay open well into the evening. Pedicab operators offer guided rides through the surrounding hutongs. Unlike Nanluoguxiang's daytime shopping crowd, Houhai's business runs heavily toward nightlife, especially in summer, when outdoor seating along the water fills up after dark. Large sections of Beijing's historic hutong network were demolished during the city's rapid development from the 1990s onward. That makes the surviving cluster around the Drum and Bell Towers one of the more complete examples left inside the city's second ring road. Early morning is the quietest time to walk the smaller residential lanes branching off Nanluoguxiang. Local residents there still hang laundry, play chess on stoops and run small corner shops largely unchanged by the tourism next door. Visitors interested in the architecture, rather than the shopping, generally get more out of these side alleys than the main commercial strip. Bandra is Mumbai's converted-bungalow beach suburb Credit: Prabhas Sah / Pexels Bandra is a former Portuguese fishing village turned upscale Mumbai suburb, known for its converted colonial bungalows, beachfront promenade and concentration of independent cafes. It remains one of the few parts of the city where a visitor can walk several kilometers along the water without a highway in view. Portuguese colonizers held Bandra from the 16th century until the Marathas took it in the 18th century. Two landmarks from that period still stand. One is Bandra Fort, a small hilltop fortification also called Castella de Aguada. The other is the Basilica of Our Lady of the Mount, better known as Mount Mary Church. Its annual September feast draws large crowds from across the city, regardless of religion. The fort's viewing platform looks directly out over the Bandra-Worli Sea Link, the cable-stayed bridge connecting the suburb to South Mumbai. Pali Village and Chapel Road, both within Bandra, hold clusters of early 20th-century Portuguese and Goan-style bungalows with sloped roofs and small front gardens. These are increasingly rare in a city where most residential land has gone to high-rise construction. Many of these lanes have also become an open-air canvas for street art, with murals commissioned as part of organized public art projects covering compound walls throughout the neighborhood. Linking Road and Hill Road carry the bulk of Bandra's shopping, from street-side stalls to independent fashion boutiques. Bandstand Promenade, running along the Arabian Sea, gets busiest around sunset, when residents from across the suburb come out to walk. It passes close to several homes belonging to Bollywood actors, a detail that draws its own steady stream of visitors. Weekday mornings offer a quieter version of the same promenade, better suited to seeing the fort and church without crowds. Bandra functions as a genuine residential suburb rather than a single attraction, so its side streets reward slow exploration on foot more than a fixed list of stops. Shinsekai is Osaka's retro entertainment district Credit: Canva Images Shinsekai is a downtown Osaka neighborhood built in 1912 around Tsutenkaku Tower, modeled on the Eiffel Tower. It remains the city's center for kushikatsu, deep-fried skewers of meat, seafood and vegetables that originated in this specific district. The neighborhood's name means new world, a reference to its original design, which modeled the northern half on Paris and the southern half on New York's Coney Island. It even had an amusement park called Luna Park, which operated from 1912 until 1923. The first Tsutenkaku Tower stood 64 meters tall and briefly ranked among the tallest structures in Asia. It was dismantled in 1943 so its steel could be repurposed for the war effort. The current tower was rebuilt in 1956 and now stands 103 meters tall. It keeps the same silhouette, combining the tower shape of the Eiffel Tower with the base of the Arc de Triomphe. Janjan Yokocho, a narrow covered alley running south from the tower, holds the highest concentration of kushikatsu restaurants in the district. Pinball parlors and cheap izakayas nearby have changed little in decades. House rules at most kushikatsu counters bar double-dipping skewers into the shared sauce, a detail worth knowing before sitting down. Billiken, a pointy-headed folk deity of good luck adopted as the tower's mascot, sits on the observation deck. He is a common photo stop for visitors rubbing his feet for luck, a local custom rather than an official one. Spa World, a large bathhouse with Asian and European-themed floors, sits just south of the tower. The floors swap between genders on a monthly rotation, and the spa extends a visit into the evening. Shinsekai's retro character, with hand-painted signs and neon lighting largely unchanged since the postwar rebuilding, sets it apart from Osaka's newer downtown districts. It stays busiest after dark, when the tower is lit and restaurant lines run longest. Dobutsuen-mae station, on the Midosuji subway line, sits at the district's northern edge.

item.title: Consumer Reports' 3 favorite trash bags
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 5.16
Consumer Reports' 3 favorite trash bags A cheap trash bag can rip at exactly the wrong moment. Consumer Reports tested three options for tear resistance and value A cheap trash bag can rip at exactly the wrong moment, spilling garbage across a kitchen floor. Tear resistance against blunt and sharp objects, capacity and cost per bag can vary widely between trash bags that all promise not to fail. Consumer Reports tested three trash bags for durability and value, so shoppers can find one that holds up through a full bag of garbage without splitting. Simplehuman Custom Fit Liners Code Q Credit: Simplehuman Priced at $21.99, the Simplehuman Custom Fit Liners Code Q fit the average 13-gallon kitchen trash can, even though the brand designs them primarily for its own trash cans. Consumer Reports named this its top pick, and found it outperformed every other trash bag in this test, standing up to both dull impacts and pointed punctures better than the competition. CR found it withstood more weight before failing when filled with water than any other bag tested, though it eventually gave way at the base and opening once the water load reached 100 pounds. Testers noted this bag isn't indestructible, but its overall tear resistance set it apart from the other bags evaluated. Great Value Trash Bags Credit: Walmart The Great Value Trash Bags cost $12.47 and are sold under Walmart $WMT's in-house brand. Consumer Reports named this its pick for value, finding it inexpensive yet fairly strong compared with other bags tested. CR found every bag in this test eventually tore, but this one held out longer than most, particularly during a blunt object test that measured how well the plastic resisted puncturing. Testers said its low cost paired with above-average durability made it stand out among the bags evaluated. Reli. SuperValue 13 Gallon Trash Bags Credit: Amazon The Reli. SuperValue 13 Gallon Trash Bags cost $29.99 for the pack tested, working out to about 5 cents per bag. Consumer Reports found José Amézquita, the lead tester for this evaluation, called these bags cheaper than every other bag evaluated on a per-bag basis, and said they proved reliable despite the low cost. CR found the bags held up well in a blunt object test, though they fared worse than every other bag evaluated when tested against sharp objects. Testers noted these clear, spacious bags lack a drawstring, meaning anyone using them needs to be comfortable tying them closed with a simple knot, and Amézquita called them an excellent buy overall.

item.title: Property insurance faces a new test as disaster losses accelerate
item.description:
Source: Quartz Score: 4.74
Extreme weather is creating a more demanding environment for property owners, insurers, and communities. According to the National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI), the United States recorded 27 confirmed billion-dollar weather and climate disasters in 2024, resulting in a total cost of $182.7 billion. These events spanned a wide range of extremes, including severe storm events, tropical cyclones, wildfires, drought/heat waves, and winter storm/cold wave events. Over the last decade, cumulative losses from these disasters have exceeded $1.4 trillion, driven significantly by population growth, material wealth, and increased development in hazard-prone areas. These figures suggest that the financial consequences of extreme events may increasingly depend on how accurately the value of exposed property is understood before a loss occurs.

item.title: Ben Johnson: making drinks and other things
item.description:
Source: San Diego Reader stories Score: 4.08
“Two years to the day after our first shoot, we have wrapped production on Find Them, a rock and roll thriller,” says local author, musician, and longtime Casbah bartender (29 years this month) Ben Johnson. “Immeasurable thanks to the amazing crew and cast that navigated these often stormy seas with me. It’s been a fun and educational haul…so many stories to tell. This has been so fun and rewarding, working with so many awesome and talented people. Fuck yeah, San Diego music scene people!” With shooting on the film complete, it's on to post-production, "which has been underway for some time. I don’t do timelines, but I have a feeling this will be done fairly soon.” The movie trailer premiered in August at the North Park Film Festival. Johnson has been making movies since the mid-teens, as well as acting in short films co-created with Grant Reinero and Smoking Jacket Films, a local collective of musician-filmmakers. One of their projects was a 48-hour moviemaking challenge entry entitled Deadline, which he describes as “a Twilight Zone sort of short.” Johnson is also the writer and director of a 2021 rock and roll thriller called Fanboy, a film where he plays an unhinged drummer obsessed with joining Xenos, his favorite rock band. Local spots seen in the movie include the Ken Club, Whistle Stop Bar, and of course, the Casbah. The soundtrack includes San Diego bands such as Hot Snakes, Red Fang, and Johnson’s own groups The Long and Short of It (formed with his brother Tim while attending college in Santa Cruz) and Tourettes Lautrec. Entirely self-funded, self-created, and self-promoted, Fanboy ended up streaming on Amazon Prime and even enjoyed theatrical screenings at several SoCal moviehouses and drive-ins. “It was such a minimal expenditure for the film that the drive-in [screenings] really took care of all that,” he told the Reader. His promotional efforts for Fanboy included exposing the film to national bands that playing during his shifts at the Casbah. “I tell them, ‘Hey, this is about the world you live in, if you want to check out this movie.’ So, I have little stickers behind the bar with QR codes so they can QR it, and it goes right to my website where you can click a link to watch it on the web. That’s been successful, and uses that sphere of influence that they have. A couple of bands have reposted it so their fanbase sees that it exists. Grassroots is probably the most effective way for this movie to be marketed.” Among Johnson’s own band projects is Hostile Comb-Over, which originated as a three-piece metal act with all three members on vocals as well. Wha? is a goth-punk band he formed in 2012 alongside keyboardist Tracy Wooley (of Beehive & the Barracudas and Tourette's Lautrec), with Kaoss Pad and David Robles (the Marsupials). Owl Be Damned is his rock trio with singer Douglas Thompson (Low and Be Told, The Marsupials), which happens to be playing the Casbah on September 15. He also has a rapper persona known as Grammatical B. “This is my first foray into rap, after doing heavy rock and punk for the last 20 years,” he told the Reader after filming a video for a comedic song about ordering drinks called “Rules and Laws” at his workplace. “Shot at the Casbah, it’s me speaking - or yelling - at all those obnoxious people who just don’t get the art of ordering a drink.” As an author, Johnson (an avowed fan of sci-fi scribe Philip K. Dick) is the writer behind the 2014 book A Shadow Cast in Dust, subtitled “An Urban Fantasy Epic,” which mostly takes place in Golden Hill and concerns an “ancient order of web spinners, a silver knife, a detective, and a boy running from his captors through the canyons of San Diego with his new friends and special dog.” The book serves as part one of what ultimately became the Webworld Trilogy. The Webworld books have featured area locales such as Switzer Canyon and other outdoor landmarks. “Our detective, Clementine, tracks the monster that has gone through there, ending up at the huge drainage tunnel at the foot of Florida Canyon, one of the creepiest places in San Diego.” Don’t look for many local personality cameos, though. “I don’t base too many characters off real life...that said, there is a big nightclub doorman that resembles a certain poet of that description.” Johnson says he has always been a fan of narrative in songs, and writing a book seemed like the obvious next step. As he told the Reader, “Over time, my songs just started having a beginning, a middle, and an end and were trying to be little stories. That’s actually what thrust me into trying to write a book. I started writing little stories, and then two or three songs kind of go together in a story and then you’re, like, now I just wanna write a story. You can put a lot more detail into writing fiction than you can a song.” So far, writing, filmmaking, and even bartending is proving somewhat safer and less traumatic than playing live rock and roll or hip-hop. “I’ve been injured countless times on stage. My old band Tourettes Lautrec used to end each show with the guitarist flying into me behind the drums.” The same group played what he recalls as his “worst gig ever, New York City in 1999. I was too drunk to play and embarrassed the shit out of myself in front of 500 people. That was not incredible.”

item.title: John Cardner sold diapers at Kobey's Swap Meet
item.description:
Source: San Diego Reader stories Score: 3.89
John Cardner sold diapers at Kobey's Swap Meet Then he started Baby's Heaven, Knockaround sunglasses, Dreamweaver, then Mogi
Jon Carder, cofounder and CEO of Mogl, with Mojo
When Jon Carder became a multimillionaire at the age of 26, his mother thought he was a drug dealer. “For a good four years, she thought for sure I was selling drugs. I bought a Hummer as a tax write-off. I remember driving up to my parents’ house, and my mom’s response was, ‘Oh, no, you’re selling drugs! I knew it! No one drives cars like that!’ She found it very hard to believe that a young kid could make that kind of money. The whole internet thing didn’t make sense to her at all." Art student millionaire Carder’s first foray into business came as a 19-year-old Point Loma Nazarene freshman. He started out peddling diapers at the swap meet. Thank you, Matthew McConaughey “I didn’t have a lot growing up. I grew up in a lower-middle-class family. There were definitely some arguments about money. I always wanted to start a business to see if I could be financially free and not have to worry about those kinds of things.” ^^^^^^^^^^^ The Reader has started this series of its best stories from the past 52 years — 2600 cover stories and some remarkable interior features — to help make up for the loss of its physical edition, which was once large enough to hold whole oceans of print. These stories will feature all the original illustrations and photos (plus easy-to-read typography). ^^^^^^^^^^^ Working as a restaurant promoter handing out fliers off of Sports Arena Boulevard to pay for his college tuition, Carder noticed the abundance of pregnant women and mothers shopping at the nearby Kobey’s Swap Meet. “So, I said, ‘That’s my first business idea. I am going to sell baby products at the swap meet.’ Such a random and horrible first idea, I might add.” Knockaround conference room Carder didn’t have any start-up money, so he applied for two credit cards at the little booths set up on his college campus that lured students in with the idea of unlimited beer money. He ended up with two credit cards, a free pen, and a $2000 credit limit. “I spent it all on baby products. I drove around Ocean Beach and looked for distribution trucks. I found someone who sold baby products. I bought diapers from them for 10 percent cheaper than I could have at, like, Albertsons,” said Carder with a nostalgic chuckle. Knockaround shades The following weekend, he set up a table at the Kobey’s Swap Meet. It was a disaster. “My first Saturday sucked. It’s a $40 entrance fee. I think I made, like, $45. That’s $5 for eight hours of work. The next weekend was the same.” His last day at the swap meet, Carder got so desperate to recoup his investment that he started selling the diapers for the same wholesale price he paid for them. In the end, all he had left were baby products and 300 bucks. “I thought that I could just start a business and then — bam — I am living on the beach and everything is good! My neighbor told me, ‘What you need to do is sell your stuff on the internet. The internet is massive! It’s huge. It’s going to be the next big thing.’” Mogl sales gong That was back in the early 2000s. At the time, Carder was clueless when it came to computers. Instead of a laptop, his parents sent him off to school with a typewriter. The neighbor who offered the advice was a web developer. He took Carder’s remaining $300 and built him a website. “That first website was really bad. It was called Baby’s Heaven. The problem was, my web developer’s favorite color was purple and he was in a heavy metal band. It had this pearly gold gate in this black and purple landscape with a couple of clouds. It looked scary. I mean, you’d click on the gate and maybe dead babies were going to be there. Worst marketing idea ever! It was a disaster and no one was buying anything once we got the site live.” Employees playing in the Knockaround warehouse After changing the website color scheme to blue and white and researching how to drive traffic to his site, Carder emailed Huggies. “I noticed that Huggies didn’t sell diapers [on their website]. I sent an email to their customer service and asked if they would link to [Baby’s Heaven] since I sold Huggies diapers nationwide. That would never work now, but that was back in 2000. Two hours later they got back with me and said, ‘Sure, that sounds great, send us a banner.’ I didn’t even know what a banner was. Dan [the web developer neighbor] built this cute little banner with a baby with wings that said Baby’s Heaven. That was really my first start into business. I remember when they put the banner up, an hour later I got my first order. It was really an amazing feeling. I was dancing in the street and telling all my neighbors.” From there, Baby’s Heaven took off. His junior year of college, the company got so big that Carder dropped out of school. He had 15 employees (all friends) and an office in Ocean Beach. “As a 20-year-old kid, my life was Huggies diaper runs at Costco. Imagine a young college kid with one of those flat beds filled with Huggies diapers up to the ceiling. I would get the funniest looks from girls. They’d be, like, ‘Whoa. Gross, bro, use a condom.’ Guys would look at me, like, ‘Hey, man, hang in there.’ My parents were kind of confused. They thought it was like a cute side project that probably wouldn’t amount to much. But they let me do my thing.” When it came to running a business, Carder was clueless.
