Spiers: I think there’s already a kind of post-shame stance from a lot of the writing community that’s not really institutionalized. And I don’t think that matters as much. But I think if you’re talking about a news organization—where trust matters, the relationship with the reader matters—I think at the very least you owe the reader a disclosure that AI was used in the piece. And you know, I’m a contributing writer for The New York Times, and my contract explicitly states that I cannot use AI. Even for, you know, putting it in to copy edit anything; not allowed to do that. In fact, if even if I’m gonna write about AI, I’m supposed to get permission to use the tools first. So the Times is sort of at the exact opposite end of the, I think, restrictive side of what people are and aren’t supposed to do. But until Paul Gigot wrote this editorial, everyone I know at The Wall Street Journal was under the impression that you could not do your work with AI that way, either. So I think it may have some backfiring effect on them—that first of all. they’re going to get deluged with AI-written submissions. But also they’re going to have to clarify where that line is. And so far, they haven’t. Brown: Yeah. I think that there’s a few arguments I’ve seen emerging. And one I’m not entirely unsympathetic to is that if the writing is good, who cares? And like, I understand where that comes from. Like, I think it’s actually beholden on readers and critics and things to be like, That writing sucks. and I don’t care if a human wrote it or if an AI wrote it. And now it just so happens that the balance of the vast majority of AI writing is awful, and that you gotta be able to identify it. And I know that it puts a lot of pressure on readers, who are just inundated with all of this slop, basically. But it is a little bit like, we should be a little more critical of what we’re putting in front of our faces and absorbing. Warzel: I understand what you’re saying about having some—you know, you gotta put a little bit of an onus, too, on the reader to care about it. To vote with your eyeballs, etcetera. But to me, it feels like this is like a frustration that I have with the conversation around this op-ed. and around the feeling, too, from certain people who are just like: This is inevitable. This is where it’s gonna go. The internet is gonna flood with this stuff. So, like, we’re gonna look back on the hand-wringing about this and kind of laugh one day, right? It’s gonna feel super-quaint, all you people who are doing this. And that may be true. Like, that I may be on the losing end of this thing, right? Like everyone’s just gonna be doing slop stuff, and it’s gonna get more sophisticated, and we’ll figure out some way forward. But for me, there’s also—in any era of technological change, you actually need people who are going to protest it. Who are going to stand and thwart it and stop it and object to it. Because that’s also how we create the new norms for this stuff, right? If we don’t spend some time thinking about that and having some people actually push back, if nobody pushes back, then it just happens. And it happens however these companies want. Or whatever the, you know, the lowest common denominator of slop that can get published. I find I’m really frustrated by the idea that some of these institutions, like the whole point of being the institution is to stand up for, you know, institutional things. Spiers: Yeah, what’s crazy about this is that, first of all, it’s The Wall Street Journal doing it. Where you have one of the most, what business-side people would call “premium products in the space.” And you’re actively enshittifying your own product when what you’re selling is, you know, “the original thoughts of Stanley Druckenmiller”—not what he couldn’t be bothered to slap into a, you know, Google Doc himself, but produced via AI. Your value proposition, even on the business side, is eroded by that. So I think there’s a lot of short-term thinking about headcount and cost. That really, people are using AI in ways that are not necessarily additive at the expense of the long-term value proposition of their own products. Brown: I do wonder about this sometimes, because we’re in the media. And we exist in sort of a filter bubble of our own making, right? I’m like, do people in general audiences care that Druckenmiller uses AI? Does the 85 percent of people who do not care about writing and actually find writing a chore—that they don’t want to write a note about why they’re gonna be five minutes late; they’d rather press a button and have that happen for them—actually care that much? And I worry about that, because I care so much about writing. Spiers: I think you’re right, but I also think with newsrooms, we have a trust problem already. And I think the readers care if they think they’re being deceived. I don’t think they really care about, you know, the process of writing, or writing for its own sake. Warzel: I also think alongside the trust part of it, too, there’s an effort thing that I think is actually very real, that comes with the part of the trust. Like if people, you know, can’t be arsed to, like, do the work, and everyone else is like, That’s fine, yeah; just send that sucker through, right? There’s this idea of like—so where else do they cut corners? Teddy, you wrote a good piece earlier this summer that was titled “The End of the Working Writer.” And I want to get to that, but the piece was kind of kicked off or inspired, perhaps, by a post by Bloomberg’s Joe Weisenthal, who’s constantly posting on X. This post set off, you know, a debate online. And he wrote: “Unfortunately, I think in the near future, not using LLMs to write for you will be like someone refusing to use Google Maps for directions in a new city. A bizarre, idiosyncratic choice that’s just completely incomprehensible to the vast majority of people.” So first I just wanted to ask: Do you think that that prediction is right, here? Do you think that’s kind of where we’re heading? Brown: I think “the vast majority of people” might be a little bit of an understatement. I think that as adoption picks up for a lot of these tools, I do think those people who, again, don’t really care about writing that much in the process of writing, and view it as a chore they can replace with a few clicks or a few keystrokes. Yeah—I think that’s gonna be quite a lot of people are going to start acting that way. And it’s just ease of doing these sort of things. We’re interested in the process of writing for its own sake, and in a way to sort of unpack our own thoughts and think about the problems we’re trying to solve. But yeah—I unfortunately see this becoming a little bit more acceptable to just use these chats for writing anything you need. Warzel: Teddy, you mentioned earlier that you—and that’s part of this Substack post that you did—is that you used to do this kind of work. And a good bit of your argument in “The End of the Working Writer” is that the AI-and-writing conversation can get caught up in this, like, craft/artistic corridor—but that a lot of writing’s very utilitarian. It’s very technical, right? It’s this stuff: Press the button and say you’re gonna be five minutes late. Or it is this, you know, copywriting; you’re writing white papers, or product descriptions. Copy that’s gonna be used for search-engine optimization. Corporate speak. LinkedIn posts, Elizabeth, as you said. And since you did this kind of work, you argue maybe this conversation is not talking enough about how AI is changing that brand of writing. So tell me about the working writer a little bit—define it better for me, and what AI is doing to that category of writing. Brown: Yeah. I mean, it’s all writing that no one cares about, is really what it comes down to. But I did this work because it was well compensated, and I had to afford rent in New York. And this is my career for a long time. I think that what happens is that AI is very good at writing that doesn’t matter. All the things you were talking about—all those pieces of little pieces of internet copy that are not meant to actually be critically engaged with—AI is extremely good at writing those things. And so there are two forces happening. One is that people recognize that this writing is actually not worth that much anymore. And so they’re like, How can we do this for the smallest cost possible? And you have these enormous costs of AI integrations into technology companies generally, where a lot of the better-paid opportunities were. Daniel Kolitz had a great piece in The Baffler today that’s talking exactly about this. Like it is there is this sort of squeezing-out of what I compared to session musicians in music. It’s like—Well, if I don’t need to pay these four people to play the backing track for this commercial thing; I can just plug into Suno and get the same thing, basically. It’s like, Why do I need to pay them $10,000? And like, right. That was paying those four people’s rent for the next couple months. And so I really worry about this hollowing out a generation of writers who are, you know, sort of 10 years behind me, who don’t have these opportunities to work on writing that is not necessarily the most wonderful artistic, literary pursuit, but is a way to at least make a respectable living in a very expensive city. And now those jobs are just gonna be gone. Warzel: Let me just play devil’s advocate here. There are probably people who don’t live in New York City who are, you know, gonna listen in and say: Well, if it’s work that fundamentally doesn’t have any value, and it’s a good thing—like, what do we lose if we lose this? Brown: I think it’s a big question. Because I was thinking about this before I got on, and sort of the idea of like—why, if you’re gonna take the job away from like 50 farmers with using mechanical tools or something. It’s like, Well, should we not do that? Should we not advance past this in order to sort of create more? Why would we keep paying people to do this writing no one actually cares about? And I understand that argument, sort of, in the medium and long term. But in the short term, it’s doing actual material damage to people who are trying to feed themselves. Spiers: I just worry that AI is making everybody dumber. Brown: That too. Spiers: I think when you outsource the fundamental cognitive arsenal that you’re using to actually construct a good argument, or to make a piece of art, what happens to us as a society if everybody’s outsourcing that to AI models? I see this a little bit with, you know, I have an 11-year-old son in school. They’ve sort of—most of he and his peers all know how to use ChatGPT to ask a question. And it’s increasingly difficult for people in academic settings to get their students to do the rigorous work of sitting down and trying to think through an argument without these aids. And I think it may badly prepare students for the real world, where they may not have that assistance all the time. Or they may have to learn how to think through more complex things that are just gonna be far more difficult, because they haven’t developed that intellectual rigor that comes from having to work your way through things from scratch. Brown: I feel that as an adult. When I worked in tech, I was writing 3,000-page papers about really dense B2B-enterprise marketing strategies, or whatever. Warzel: The dream. Brown: Yeah, exactly. And I would get to the end, and it would go onto the website: I have no idea what I wrote about. I could not tell you one thing about that, because it was just all flowing through Claude. And all I was doing was editing line by line, and making sure it sounded good. But I could not tell you anything about what I actually wrote, which is weird. It’s a weird sensation. Warzel: This gets to—I wanted to get here, which is that the broader “we” doesn’t think of writing, I think, as a technology. But it is. It’s an amazing technology that allows us to put our ideas in other people’s heads, in this intimate, transformative way. And then there’s this question of what it does for us, right? So I wanted to read something from the publication Nature about what might be going on when we write, that I enjoyed, here. Which is that: “Writing compels us to think not in the chaotic, nonlinear way that our minds typically wander, but in a structured, intentional manner. By writing it down, we can sort years of research, data, and analysis into an actual story, thereby identifying our main message and the influence of our work. This is not merely a philosophical observation; it is backed by scientific evidence.” And so I wanted to ask you all, as writers: Is the act of writing thinking? Or is it something different? Is it just something that forces us to think so that we may write? And I wanna get your thoughts on this, because I think it’s necessary and useful to put a point on what we are losing cognitively when we outsource it. Spiers: I think it is thinking. It’s not the only form of thinking, but there’s plenty of research that kind of indicates that there are parts of your brain that are activated when you’re constructing something as a written sentence, versus other types of, you know, communicative expressions. There’s also a lot of anthropological history that indicates that when humans started developing language, it changed the way that they were cognitively structured. So I think if you remove that, I just think the additive benefits of it probably just go away, and their systemic effects on your cognition altogether. You know, maybe it gets replaced by something else. I don’t know. But, you know, I wouldn’t rule out the possibility that whatever we’re losing can’t be replaced in the future. But I think for right now, we know that it serves a purpose. And we don’t have anything to replace it. So that does concern me. Brown: I mean, of course writing is thinking. It’s thinking through issues, and trying to sort of figure out what you’re actually trying to say, or trying to write down. I mean, it is like it’s actively trying to entangle problems that you’re dealing with. Instead of being like, you can just use incredibly seductive tools like Claude and ChatGPT, ’cause you can just put in a problem and it gives you a solution. And I know that people will say you can have it challenge you, and you can turn things and press these knobs, and all this kind of stuff. But it is also outsourcing that path for you. Warzel: I’ve thought a lot about this, because I’ve had some people challenge me on the “writing is thinking” thing. Like, are you actually doing that? And I would say if I had to, you know, really be precise about it—maybe it’s not just the act of thinking. But there’s no other time when I can get myself alone in a space where I am forced to think in order to write on a micro, you know, sentence-by-sentence, piece-of-logic-by-piece-of-logic basis, right? Like, I am having to have an extremely honest conversation with myself. Of like: Did that make sense? Does that connect to this in a way? And I think when people say, like, “Yes, man, it’s such a good sparring partner.” Claude, ChatGPT—it’s so good at, like you said, coming up with a counterargument or, you know, taking down your straw-man arguments, whatever it is. I think, you know, maybe, that is true in some way. But I don’t think it’s as good as having to deal with the honesty of yourself—where you’re like, I have this idea in the back of my head. I need to communicate that on the page. Does what’s on the page match that abstract idea in my brain? And like frankly, I think the act of writing is reconciling that with yourself. And that ability to be alone, like it forces you actually to do a lot of—you know, people find writing so agonizing, sometimes, on the page. Because it’s like, you have to be honest with yourself. Like, Is that my actual idea? Is that, you know, is that any good? Is that worth anything? And that conversation, to me—that’s what I think we’re losing. Brown: Well, and the models themselves, I mean the learning libraries force any problem that you’re trying to interrogate through one of the chats to look only backward. They can only look at things that have already happened. And I think it limits the amount of novelty you can have in an argument. It limits the paths you can take with it. And I know that Silicon Valley’s very antagonistic toward interiority and introspection right now, but the only way you can get there is thinking about: How do I feel about this? What does this do to me? What am I curious about, and how does this make me feel? And that doesn’t exist in a learning library; that doesn’t exist in a chatbot. Spiers: Also just at a macro level, now that you mentioned that, I think Silicon Valley has a general anti-intellectualism orientation that sort of gets built into the tech. It’s: I don’t wanna have to, you know, use my precious brain cells on going through rigorous material that might be difficult. I’m gonna build a piece of software that’s gonna do it for me. And I think the long-term ramifications of that are just sort of bad for society. There’s a cult in Silicon Valley of trying to learn things very quickly, but without friction, you know? And I think if you take those things away, what you’re doing is something that kind of looks surface-level like intellectual development—but isn’t when you scratch the surface. It lacks the rigor, the complexity, all of that. Warzel: Ezra Klein had a phrase that I liked with this. Which is “the Matrix theory of the mind.” Right? With the idea that, like, some people see information as the Matrix thing, right? You just—you plug, you jack into the, you know, the Borg. And you upload the information, and like: Boom; I understand everything about Kant. Right? Like, I know how to, you know, fly this F-15. Whatever it is. And it’s like the actual process of learning tends to be extremely different. Which is, it’s just about how you, your brain grapple with material, with information, and you think. And I think it’s the disagreement that Silicon Valley has between one style of learning and the other. I wanted to bring up, though, the argument with all of this with AI-assisted writing. There are folks that have argued that there’s an accessibility issue here. That not all writers either could, you know, can afford to have human editing, or that some brains are requiring outside help or accommodations. Chatbots assist with this. And another way of saying this—without getting into a conversation just about ability or disability—is that not everyone can write well. And not everyone wants to write well. And certainly, most people aren’t professional writers. So how should we be thinking about these tools for a crowd of people that aren’t pros? Brown: I think there’s a lot of people who see writing as an intellectual costume they can sort of put on, and chat like these chatbots allow them to do that in a very seamless, frictionless way. I’ve been on the record saying this. I think there should be fewer writers. I think there are way too many people who call themselves writers, and should not be in the industry generally. I think there’s sort of—it’s flooded with that. It might be good in the long run, because people who are actually good at this might be able to separate themselves. Spiers: I think, also, it’s sort of—I think people have this simplistic idea of writing. That, you know, anyone can do it. Just because anybody can sit down and type and do a document, or most people can. But I can’t think of—there’s a whole range of other professional skills that if I said, I’m really bad at this, but I wanna be able to do it, people would look at me like I had three heads. Like, if I wanted to go play WNBA basketball right now, I’m 5’1” and 49. That’s not gonna happen, and there’s no number of tools that I could add to myself that would get me there. And so I do think, also, people do need to understand that writing is a specialized skill. You know, it doesn’t matter. I think if you want to do it professionally, that you’re good at it. If you don’t care about doing it professionally, no one’s gonna stop you from writing for your own enjoyment or writing on a blog. I mean that the internet has completely democratized that. You can publish at almost zero cost. Warzel: You expressed it perfectly—that there are so many other genres of things where if you’re like, I want to do this professionally, and I’m not good at it, the people are tough, right? But what’s interesting and frustrating about the conversation with writing is that we always seem to, culturally, regard it differently. Like clearly—writing is a craft. It’s an art form, but it’s also this thing that everyone does, right? Often in these quotidian ways as we’re talking about. And so I think it’s treated differently than other crafts. And what I was thinking about in this space was Hollywood and, you know, AI video-generation tools. Like the guilds in Hollywood go out on strike, in part because they want protections from the studios from AI, and standards. And for the most part, people don’t say, like, “In a couple of years, of the all the hand-wringing”—you know, like all these people are being precious. “They’re gonna look back on this and cringe at what they were doing.” And I think that’s because most people aren’t out there every day making movies and sending them to their boss, right? Like, the way that they write an email or a LinkedIn post. And so I’m wondering: Do you guys think that writing is more at risk than other creative crafts to AI because of its universal nature? Brown: I certainly think the large middle class of it is, for sure. In the same way that I think the large middle class of moviemaking or the large middle class of graphic designers are at risk. I do think there is a huge contingent of this sort of middle 80 percent of writers who have to make ends meet, not through prestige, legacy media outlets. And those are at huge amount of risk. Spiers: I think some of it, too, is just that the skill set that you use in writing—and all of the tools available to you, and all of the things that you learn—live entirely in your head. You know, if you’re a filmmaker and you have a wide set of skills, this also involves using things that people see externally as being highly technical. If you’re a writer, you’re using a laptop, which everybody has. And so the idea that there’s a barrier to entry to writing—people don’t kind of understand that. Because they’re like, Well, I could write something and put it on the internet, and what’s the difference? So I think anything that has a kind of zero barrier to entry, people tend to overestimate the ease of doing it. Warzel: I think we’re all trying to be mindful of, you know, we are in our bubble of “this matters to us.” So as writers, are there opportunities here? You know, like there’s a few excerpts of media that I’ve read where people just start like, you know, talking to the chatbot in the middle of the thing as part of it; it’s almost like a creative-fiction-y thing. I’m just curious if you all see the possibility for opportunities here that aren’t just, like, I’m kinda gonna give a very bland prompt and then get out, you know, a bunch of Claude lorem ipsum. Brown: There’s certainly—it’s an edge case for me. The sort of avant-garde being like, I think there’s people wanting to read your prompts about how you got something. I think that’s actually like a fascinating artistic case. Like, I don’t care about your writing. Show me what your prompt looks like—because that’s more interesting to me, because it actually shows what your thinking is. I think that what the most likely scenario for me. Or—I don’t know if this is most likely or sort of what I would prefer to happen, is that professional writing becomes more akin to vinyl collecting now. And that this is sort of—not a curiosity, but something for people who really care about it. And that they actually seek out, you know, good writing done by humans. Just because the flood sadly is already here. I don’t want to be too fatalistic, but it’s just gonna be the state of things where it’s just like: This is too easy. You know it’s too big. The tools are too entrenched. And this is sort of—we have to figure out ways to live with that. Warzel: Elizabeth, where do you fall on that? Spiers: I mean I think that you know, if we do end up in a scenario where we’re flooded with AI writing and it’s all crap, that actually makes people who can do things that AI can’t more valuable. Like, for example, AI can’t write jokes. It’s terrible at comedy. And partly because it doesn’t have a kind of meta-sensibility, it’s incapable of understanding the sort of intersection between absurdity and novelty, which is where humor comes from. So I’m not terribly worried in the short term. I think there is a possibility that we eventually end up with models that are good enough that they can produce novelty, and that they do produce interesting output. And then, I don’t know what happens. You know, I think we’ll all probably adapt to it in different ways. Right now I’m not thinking about that far ahead, about any of it. Warzel: I feel sort of both sides of this. Where, to me—I said this on a different podcast, but I’m a really bad emailer. In the sense that, like, no punctuation or caps or things like that. And I’ve always had— Spiers: A Jeffrey Epstein–style emailer? Warzel: Haha, yeah; I guess, yeah. Just a wonderful comparison to make there. But that’s, like, my email style, and it’s embarrassing, and it’s always been. And I’ve had people comment recently, like: “You know what, man. I know you sent that email. Because it’s hot garbage.” Like, Thank you. Thank you so much for not taking the time to— Spiers: It’s your stamp of authenticity. Warzel: Yeah, exactly. It’s authentic. And I see that, you know, more in responses to just my work, personally, and things like that. Like, people feeling that that level of craft as like, as a distinction, right. And so I feel like there is that way which, in the near term, it can really distinguish. But I just wanted to ask both of you to close out here. If you were made writing czar today and you could set some kind of lists of standards that you would like to see codified for professional writing. In terms of this technology disclosure, all that stuff. Like—what would be just a couple of your first steps? Just things that like, boilerplate, “This is the norm that we wanna impose around AI and writing.” Spiers: At minimum, I think disclosure has to be a norm. Like, you know, even if newsrooms get to the point where they decide every single contributor can use AI—including to construct an argument—not informing the reader I think is a mistake. Because then readers will easily assume that all of the work of the newsroom is outsourced to AI, and therefore it’s sort of commoditized and not that original. And I think it’s a trust issue. Brown: I think Elizabeth brings up a really good point, and the journalism thing is a perfect example of this. That there are those cracks in foundational trust for institutions. Listen, there’s a lot of trust issues generally, but putting yet another one into the dam is—it’s really difficult to sort of navigate ourselves away from. On an individual level, for writers, I mean, I hate to say it, but it just doesn’t have a place in my sort of toolkit as a journalist. By sort of filter, you know—Google searches. Sure, Gemini is in my life every day because it’s the top of the search bar. But just, after using it so much in my previous life, I have just sort of been like: This is actually quite freeing to do all this work myself again. And maybe that’s personal; maybe that’s sort of me going from one sort of hard side to the other. But there is something so rewarding about finding stuff out yourself. And I really love that part of reporting. Warzel: I think that’s a great place to leave it. Teddy, Elizabeth—thank you for coming on and talking about this weird place that we find ourselves in, with this strange typing thing that we started doing a long time ago, that now robots do. But thank you for coming on. Brown: Thanks so much, Charlie. Spiers: Yeah. Thanks for having us. Warzel: If you liked what you saw here, new episodes of Galaxy Brain drop every Friday. You can subscribe on The Atlantic’s YouTube channel, or on Apple or Spotify or wherever it is that you get your podcasts. And if you want to support this work, and the work of my fellow colleagues, you can subscribe to the publication at TheAtlantic.com/Listener. That’s TheAtlantic.com/Listener. Thanks so much, and I’ll see you on the internet. This episode of Galaxy Brain was produced by Hadley Robinson and engineered by Erica Huang. Denny Thomas edited the video. Our theme is by Rob Smierciak. Claudine Ebeid is the executive producer of Atlantic audio, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor. Learn more about your ad choices. Visit podcastchoices.com/adchoices

item.title: Postscript to American Ground: Unbuilding the World Trade Center
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic Score: 2.26
American Ground was originally an Atlantic series, and an attempt to respond usefully to the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001. As it became clear that the magazine was committed to a long and heavily charged project about the deconstruction of the World Trade Center ruins, I wanted to take some emotional distance from the tragedy, and to approach the narrative as if I were looking back on current events from several decades into the future. The result would be, I hoped, like a “history in the present tense.” It was a formulation that came often to mind as I proceeded. My unwillingness to participate in the public displays of grief was partly just personal. But I also believed that the emotionalism surrounding the site, though at its origins genuine and necessary, had grown into something less healthy—an overindulgence, sustained by political forces and the media, that rather than serving as a catharsis only deepened the social anguish. And I thought that if American Ground was to have lasting value, readers should not be manipulated; they would bring their own feelings and thoughts to the text. My job was to observe for them, not as an “objective” journalist or an earnest encyclopedist, but more openly in the first person, as their agent on the ground. I spent six months immersed at the site, usually seven days a week, and another five months writing. I witnessed many sad moments, particularly when accompanying some of the families of the dead who came to contemplate their loss—but I did not write about that, because their grief was private, or should have been, and it was not my subject. My subject was construction, or more precisely deconstruction—the dismantling of the tangled steel and concrete, and all that this entailed. Now, nearly two years after the World Trade Center collapses, I still believe that the only way to communicate the essence of the cleanup, including the complexity of the emotions involved, was to maintain the narrative’s detachment. In American Ground the idea was to catch a glimpse of America itself, or of a certain slice of it at a certain time—unruly, unscripted, and in action. In the mix lay the bad as well as the good, but the book turned out to be hopeful—even celebratory—and all the more so because it wasn’t trying to be. Judging from the overwhelmingly positive response that followed publication, the narrative detachment did not diminish the book’s meaning to readers, or its emotional impact. But the responses ran the other way, too. Some readers interpreted my refusal to embrace heroic imagery as disrespectful of the dead, or fundamentally biased against firefighters. They were also angry because the book mentioned looting at the site by firemen as well as by policemen and construction workers, and in particular described a confrontation that broke out when a crushed fire truck was discovered with new blue jeans inside. The street demonstrations in New York that followed the publication of American Ground were local, union-driven affairs, but when some of the press picked up on the story, American Ground became “controversial.” In New York I was asked by reporters if I found the reaction surprising, and I answered no. I had seen and described these very same emotions in action on the pile, as the ruins were known. Moreover, the emotions were not unusual. Solidarity with a group, the possessive embrace of disaster, a sense of privilege, the searing or bittersweet sensation of sorrow—to various degrees most of us have known these feelings. I knew that the protesters had been through a tough and disorienting experience—the deaths of friends, co-workers, and in a few cases family, followed by the distorting glare of publicity and hype. Now time had moved on, but the feelings remained strong. I had written that the cool-blooded engineers had needed to learn a lesson—that the various emotions at the site had to be accommodated if the larger community was to function and the work was to proceed. America is a dynamic mess, not a dictatorship of rationalists. Now I was learning something, too, about writing nonfiction. “History in the present tense” can be so fresh that it’s alive—and still very raw. The book was becoming a small part of the story it told. But the book was always just a partial history. Had a calm and open conversation been possible, I would readily have admitted that the account was biased in a particular way—in its emphasis on the deconstruction job. That is not to say that it was biased in favor of one group over another. When I first arrived at the site, I had warned Department of Design and Construction Commissioner Ken Holden and Mike Burton, the construction “czar,” that my presence represented a risk to them, because I would write about the project’s failure—if such it proved to be—as readily as I would write about the project’s success. Though I ended by admiring both men for their performance at the site, for many months this was not a sure thing, any more than success itself was guaranteed. Indeed, some of the principal construction men (and Burton in particular) were taken aback by the candor with which I described their motivations and work. But for better or worse I certainly did pay more attention to the construction leaders than to anyone else. They were my subject, and this was no secret. From the very start I saw their role as interesting and forward-looking, in part because their challenges all lay ahead. That was the premise of my initial approach, and of the book that resulted, which, as the subtitle indicates, is about the “unbuilding” process. I wanted to tell the story fully, and this sometimes required me to grapple with implications and cross-connections, most significantly the extraction of the dead and the increasingly volatile social dynamics on the pile. But whenever possible I avoided straying into unrelated areas, of which there were many. It has been suggested that I must have been glad to be the only writer with free access to the inner world of the Trade Center site, but the opposite is true. There was obviously more happening there than I alone could know or describe. More important, exclusivity is a cheap trick; transparency is good for everyone, and I would have preferred it. The presence of the daily press would have served the useful role not only of informing the public but also of clarifying the participants’ views of themselves. It is worth remembering that the Trade Center site was an intensely chaotic place. A huge number of worthy efforts were being pursued in all directions and almost spontaneously, in many cases with admirably little direction from above. For the first few weeks there must have been two dozen chiefs, each doing good work and believing to varying degrees that he or she was the one in charge. Certainly there was room for a variety of experiences and impressions. Volunteers working in the food lines would have had a very different view from that of the telephone-repair people, the National Guard, the police officers at the perimeter gates, or the sanitation crews working ferociously to clean up the surrounding neighborhoods. All of them would correctly have seen their roles as necessary for the functioning of the whole. But I was not writing about them. I would hardly have mentioned the firemen either, had they not played such a pivotal role in the process of the unbuilding. Despite what the public believed, after the search for survivors ended, and the dust and smoke suppression was taken over by civilian water crews, the firemen’s role was not primarily physical. Beyond the increasingly careful raking of fine debris, and the immediate handling of human remains, which others could have done, the firemen’s position was largely symbolic. Their presence was crucial nonetheless, a forceful reminder of the human consequences of the attack, and of the importance of keeping people’s emotions in mind; it was also, as I have described, a source of friction and resentment on the pile, and ultimately a political challenge to the progress of the deconstruction. But in the climate of the times in New York, even short and neutral descriptions of any role or action that was not “heroic” constituted dangerous territory. The demonstrators’ anger was real, and though it often seemed based on misunderstandings of the book, it also grew from a fundamentally different view of the Trade Center experience. This was to be expected, and there will surely be other, different versions, in print, of the story that I told. In the meantime, the demonstrating firefighters legitimately wanted to register their opinion that American Ground was wrong and unfair. I was doing my job, and they were doing theirs. They chanted and held up signs for the cameras, inflated a giant plastic rat (a well-worn union prop), and went home. Heavily involved in these demonstrations was a group, small but vocal, that organized a campaign to have the book withdrawn and destroyed. Among others, its members included civilians who in the aftermath of the terrorist attacks had volunteered at the site, or in other ways had come into close contact with the firefighters, and had embraced their humanity and grief. They called themselves the WTC Living History Project, and announced their ambition to record and publish the oral history of this important event in the national experience. First, though, they fought against what they perceived as the injustice of American Ground. They organized e-mail campaigns against the book, disrupted public events, impugned my motivations, accused me of plagiarism, and pored over the text for factual errors. They found of course people from the site who were willing to dispute some of my observations and perspectives, and they called into question some of my information. They circulated to the press a long electronic document in itemized form, in which they attempted to lay out their case. Predictably, they had a more heroic “united we stand” view of the Trade Center site than did I. Again, all of this generated publicity, especially of the local television and tabloid kind. It was reassuring to know that before publication, American Ground had been heavily vetted by The Atlantic’s rigorous fact-checking department. For five months, two veteran checkers had gone over the text full-time, verifying statements and descriptions, reading and rereading primary documents, and cross-checking details, often with multiple independent sources. Typically, with the campaign against American Ground under way, The Atlantic did not retreat into a hostile posture but called its readers’ attention to the Living History Project’s compendium (which was posted on the internet) and published angry and critical letters, along with some admiring ones. With an eye on the specific points raised in the various accusatory documents, it also undertook an extensive review of the earlier fact-checking. I was very sure about the essence of what I had written. But despite the enormous effort that had gone into getting the details right, it was not unlikely that factual errors had slipped in. American Ground is a tight book, but a long and complicated piece of reporting. The publication of the paperback edition has offered the opportunity to make a few corrections. For example, the office into which Peter Rinaldi and Frank Lombardi escaped after the 1993 bombing was not associated with Brown & Root, as I had written, but rather with what was then the independent law firm of Brown & Wood. But the really striking result of the fact-checking review was that on item after item, the accusations proved to be incorrect. As might be expected, there were gray areas. The emotional state of the American Airlines flight attendant Betty Ong was described one way in initial press accounts and another way in some later ones; tapes of Ong’s phone call have not been made public. In the paperback edition, I have omitted any reference to her emotional state. Often the discrepancies involved not just sources and perceptions, but time frames. I was accused, for example, of underestimating the size of the Fire Department. Well, the Fire Department when? We stuck with the obviously approximate number (14,000) that the department itself had given to us as the most relevant count for the period in question. Time and again there were fundamental misunderstandings by the book’s critics, either of the site or of the text. In a passage about Mike Burton’s difficulty in ceding power as the work matured, I had written that “by the spring” the construction company Bovis had taken over day-to-day management of the job. The critics countered with a January 1 date, confusing the moment when Bovis became the sole “prime” contractor (initially a paperwork and billing rearrangement) with the much slower process of gaining significant operational control. One of the peripheral points of contention by the Living History Project was that there had never been, as I had written, an attempt (presumably by workers with a cutting torch and heavy tools) to break into a huge Bank of Nova Scotia vault containing gold and silver, underground in the old H&M Railroad station at the site. I knew that the bank had denied an attempted theft at the time, even as the bullion was being urgently transferred to another location; police thought otherwise, and said so to the press. Now in the Living History Project document, a Port Authority police lieutenant was cited as saying that there had been no sign of an attempted break-in. Later, to the press, he wondered why no one had spoken to him. I was in the vault several times, and heard about a break-in attempt firsthand from the police and others standing guard there, some of them with shotguns. I was also told about it by an independent engineer who had a supervisory role in helping with the removal of the bullion, and by city and Port Authority officials who were directly involved. Contemporary newspaper reports in The New York Times and elsewhere refer to an attempted break-in. In the end there seemed to be no good reason to change the text. As noted, these criticisms and more were posted by the Living History Project on the internet, and some were offered up at the public demonstrations and to the press. I responded repeatedly to the more important points, but tried to avoid sinking into the swamp of confused allegations and misinterpretations, many of them based on erroneous and perhaps naive assumptions. Some of American Ground’s critics seemed to be unacquainted with the concept of “spin,” or with the notion that people in nominal positions of authority might not know what was actually transpiring on the ground. In the free-for-all of the pile, the titular authorities often didn’t even know that they didn’t know. In such circumstances, there were frequent discrepancies between official reports and reality. One genuine error that did emerge pertained to the early dispute between Port Authority police officers and firemen over whether to free a dead Port Authority policeman’s body by expeditiously amputating his leg. Though the book’s description supports the firemen’s view that amputation was the right thing to do, I wrote, “The police pointed out—correctly—that no dead fireman would have had his leg cut off.” Information received later suggested that there were cases I was unaware of in which firemen’s bodies had indeed been freed through amputation. As a result, in the paperback edition the sentence now reads, “The police maintained that no dead fireman …” The rest of the passage is unchanged, however. The Port Authority police officers were indeed angry because they believed that the firemen were interested only in searching for their own. The officers’ view was too crude to be fair, and I described it as such. But there is no doubt that for an astonishingly long time (months), the various categories of the dead were treated with different levels of ceremony and respect. The denial of this pattern was among the more audacious criticisms of American Ground. The differential treatment of the dead constituted one of the most glaring realities of the Trade Center site, and it exacerbated the tribal resentments that occasionally erupted into fights. I wrote about looting at the site in a few passages. I was told about it first by policemen on the pile soon after I arrived. The looting started before the South Tower fell, as I wrote, “with the innocuous filching of cigarettes and soda pop,” and it rapidly spread and became more ambitious in the hours and weeks afterward. It involved firemen as well as other groups at the site. This was an open secret on the pile, well known to people there, as well as to more distant police and city officials, and to some reporters. After the campaign against American Ground began, a number of eyewitnesses came forward (including police officers, city officials, construction workers, and reporters) and privately offered me their moral support. A few went further and offered, if need be, though tentatively and with trepidation, to go public in the book’s defense with personal accounts of the acts that they had seen. I thanked them, but because I still hoped that the book would not become the carrying horse for this particular topic, I turned them down. I included what little I wrote about looting because the looting was pervasive, and it affected working relations on the pile. To have glossed over it would have been dishonest, and would have required me to omit descriptions of some of the most significant social challenges that faced the project. It’s obvious that only a small number of people engaged in the looting. But their actions greatly exacerbated the frictions on the pile, and for that reason became a necessary part of the story. As for the specific misdeeds, I never felt they were pertinent to my subject. In the story of the deconstruction it was the tribal perceptions of the misdeeds that counted, whether right or wrong. But that point was lost in the din of controversy. In tabloid reduction, American Ground became simply “the book that accuses the firemen of looting.” The most controversial passage turned out to be the description of an argument that broke out on the pile when jeans from a retail store were found in a fire truck that had been crushed and buried under the pile. One of the book’s critics, a professional writer independent of the Living History Project but with ties to firefighters, put considerable effort into reconstructing that fire truck’s final moments on September 11, to make the case that jeans from a retail store (apparently the brand was Structure, not Gap, as I had been told) had essentially become enmeshed with the truck as it was hammered down through shopping arcades rather than having been placed in the truck before it was buried. A reconstruction of the truck’s fate had no bearing, however, on the story I was telling in American Ground. That story was strictly related to the emotional and divisive social dynamics of a day in late fall, three months after the towers came down. It was not an account of whatever happened or did not happen on September 11, and it was certainly not intended as an exposé of the last moments of the fire truck’s crew. Nor was it the report of a rumor: Detailed descriptions of the argument, and the immediate context in which it took place, were provided to me shortly afterward by multiple independent eyewitnesses. These were people well known to me, who for months had proved to be reliable and steady sources, and who held important jobs on the pile. The reactions of the construction workers seemed to me to be unnecessarily provocative—as my description sought to make clear. But the argument over the jeans did not come out of nowhere. It occurred against the background of differential treatment of the dead, as well as of extensive looting in which firemen were known to have been involved. By placing the episode after these subjects had been explored, casting it in the past tense, and deliberately suppressing the identities of those involved, I tried to keep narrative attention focused on what mattered: a growing threat to the social order on the pile, which seemed to me to be a more important subject than looting, and certainly more pertinent to the unbuilding. I made that point explicitly a few sentences later: “The site would never stand united, as sloganeers said it should.” That said, it is clear that the passage has been misinterpreted by some of the public, including people beyond the book’s critics, as an accusation. One reason is that in the course of the campaign against the book, pieces of the episode were frequently torn from context and acquired a life of their own as printed snippets and disembodied sound bites. But misinterpretation may also be due to my unintentionally ambiguous choice of wording. The construction “It was hard to avoid the conclusion that … while hundreds of doomed firemen had climbed through the wounded buildings, this particular crew had been engaged in something else entirely” can be read as my own assessment, rather than, as was intended, the explanation of an assessment by others who were preconditioned to construe it that way. Therefore in the paperback edition I have added at the start of the sentence the phrase “In their eyes” to clarify my meaning. The World Trade Center site was an extremely complex place, loaded with emotion and political symbolism, full of action and confusion, with many interpretations possible. Having restricted my view to the engineering and deconstruction process, I wrote about it with complete candor, expressing my opinions openly, as I always do. I realized that the approach I took might offend a certain number of people who subscribed to different views—including the essentially two-dimensional one that has received so much publicity, and depicts the Trade Center project in maudlin and “heroic” terms. I do not perceive the project that way—and did not when I was there. More impressive, I felt, was another sort of American greatness that emerged at the site—a complex weave that included diverse acts and motivations, and also a culture of improvisational genius that seemed enormously encouraging about the future. There was no need to engage in propaganda. I wrote about the Trade Center with the assumption that candid descriptions would serve the subject best. When you buy a book using a link on this page, we receive a commission. Thank you for supporting The Atlantic.

item.title: Why Are So Many People Listening to a Podcast About Living in a Convent?
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Culture Score: 3.56
At a convent in Ann Arbor, Michigan, the bell chimes every day at 5 a.m. Then the 40 or so women who live there year-round—Dominican Sisters of Mary, Mother of the Eucharist—head to the chapel. Their day begins with an hour of prayer, followed by Mass. At 7 a.m., they have breakfast together, in complete silence. Many of them head off afterward to teach at nearby Catholic schools—sisters, unlike nuns, are not cloistered—while the novitiates stay behind to study at “the motherhouse,” as they call the convent. On some days, one of the women—Sister Miriam Holzman, who started living there 20 years ago—turns to a new item on her schedule: podcasting. Back in February, Sister Miriam started hosting Dominican Sisters Open Mic, a weekly show in which she and her fellow sisters discuss topics such as scripture, the saints, and day-to-day convent life. Sister Miriam told me that when the podcast started, she hoped it would encourage listeners to “go deeper in their spiritual life, no matter what their background might be”—Catholic or not, religious or not. The show seems to have resonated outside Catholic circles. Clips of the sisters playing the ukulele and describing an Ultimate Frisbee match have gone viral on TikTok. As of late August, their account on the platform has more than 275,000 followers and more than 8 million likes. The podcast has been featured in The New York Times and on the Today show. Listeners seem to be especially drawn to the sisters’ cheerfulness. They laugh frequently and have an easy way of interacting with one another. “Their laughter seems so stress free,” one commenter observed. Another said, “Sisters, I also want that regulated nervous system laugh.” In a post liked by more than 5,000 people, one listener asked, “Why does being a nun seems so fun even though I’m not religious?” Sister Miriam said that the show’s popularity may be connected to the overall trend of people seeking wellness content online. “People are looking for balance, and so are we,” she told me. “We want wellness too.” Their fixed routine—prayer, study, work, fun—minimizes unnecessary distractions. But the sisters aren’t just offering wellness advice or preaching self-optimization. Their search for balance includes trying to become a particular kind of person in body and soul, and noticing traces of transcendence every day. In one podcast episode, Sister Miriam talked about how, when she struggles to focus or when obligations and to-do lists intrude on her mind, her consistent schedule reminds her that in that moment, she is precisely where God wants her to be. “Which is such a gift,” she said. “I don’t need to be planning the rest of my life.” Resisting the pressure to multitask or worry about the future seems to help the sisters prioritize prayer, a pillar of their Dominican order. At midday, the sisters meditate on the essential Christian belief that the all-powerful God took on human form in the person of Jesus Christ. Later in the afternoon, they recite the Liturgy of the Hours, a set of reflections on the Psalms and Gospels. Many of the sisters have said that after years at the convent, these practices spill over into the rest of their life—when they pray for a passerby at the airport, perhaps, or let out a sudden “Come, Holy Spirit” or “Jesus, I trust in you” at difficult points of the day. Prayer, a sister concluded in one episode, “expands your vision of reality.” It has allowed her to notice “the dew on the grass, or the sunrise on the way to work.” As evening approaches, the sisters return to the motherhouse. They pray the rosary and have dinner together as one of them reads aloud from a recent papal address or a biography of a saint. Then out come the Trivial Pursuit boxes and guitars, the bicycles and Frisbees. As with prayer, recreation time together is fixed in their schedule. It’s not optional. The sisters don’t watch TV during it, nor do they scroll on phones. For all the joy that the sisters display on the podcast, they are also open about the sacrifices involved in convent life. They seldom see their families. Their daily lives downplay individuality: Their sleeping quarters, called “cells,” are designed to be interchangeable and are minimally arranged with a bed, a dresser, a table, an image of the Virgin Mary. Adjusting to the 5 a.m. wake-up call can take years. And like all of us, the sisters are prone to stress and worry. The contentment that the sisters seem to have despite these challenges may be partly explained by the documented benefits of engaging in religious practices. Clay Routledge, a social psychologist who studies sources of meaning in people’s lives, told me that prayer’s “cognitive and motivational power” can make people more attentive. He added, “It focuses your attention on something; it takes you off of these other distractions and worries, and helps you pay attention to what you care about.” In a 2016 study, psychologists at Georgia State University found that prayer motivated very religious students to “invest a greater amount of mental energy in the performance of everyday tasks.” A study from 2012 found that praying for others made participants feel more satisfied about making sacrifices for others—about living, in other words, a less self-oriented life. Starting at 8 p.m., after their evening prayer, the sisters spend the rest of their night in complete silence. Sister Miriam told me that during this time she likes to pray about both the difficulties of the day and the things she’s grateful for. Another sister said that she sometimes walks up a nearby hill, notices the twilight sky, and thinks of her Creator. Then she returns to the motherhouse, ready for the next morning’s bell to chime.

item.title: Misunder­standing Norman Rockwell
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Culture Score: 2.75
In 1976, as the country commemorated its bicentennial, an aging Norman Rockwell, then at the tail end of his career as America’s preeminent illustrator, painted his last magazine cover, Liberty Bell (Celebration). It was a tender—and notably low-key—tribute to national unity that doubled as a capstone for his body of work. For a decades-long stretch in the mid-20th century, the illustrator’s memorable images of smiling families and gentle, small-town interactions had filled the pages of national magazines, serving up a portrait of American life that was upbeat, idealistic, and reassuring. It’s a vision that has felt far away amid this year’s celebrations, once again, of the nation’s birthday. But the Rockwellian vision of America has felt distant for a long while. That distance is why we have songs such as Lana Del Rey’s “Norman Fucking Rockwell.” It’s why the phrase like a Rockwell painting is often deployed, not simply as a descriptive but as an implicit critique of naive civic optimism. And it’s why Rockwell has served as enduring grist for artists who, although they have been influenced by his visual iconography, have at the same time been compelled to give voice to some of the more disturbing impulses that have shaped the American psyche. No one did this more compellingly than David Lynch, the director who, over and over, turned Rockwell’s depiction of American innocence on its head. Lynch liked to recount in interviews a comment that a sound mixer on one of his films had once made to him: that his work was “like Norman Rockwell meets Hieronymus Bosch.” The filmmaker wanted to take Rockwell’s attractive but brittle surfaces, break them open, and plunge us into something deeper and darker. Understanding Lynch, in other words, is a way of understanding Rockwell. In particular, it’s a way of understanding one of the tragic effects of Rockwell’s influential vision: It’s so relentlessly benign and so morally pristine that it’s impossible to live up to. It’s an albatross slung over America’s shoulders. Early in Lynch’s masterpiece Mulholland Drive, which turns 25 this year, is a scene that doubles as one of Lynch’s many loving homages to Rockwell. The bright-faced, wide-eyed Betty (played by Naomi Watts) has arrived in Los Angeles, where she wants to become a movie star. On the flight over, she befriended an older couple, who walk with her through the airport. “Well, it’s time to say goodbye, Betty,” the old lady says. “It’s been so nice traveling with you.” “Thank you, Irene. I’m so excited and nervous. It was so good to have you to talk to.” “Remember, I’ll be watching for you on the big screen.” “Okay, Irene. Won’t that be the day!” They part, whereupon a look of horror cavorts across Betty’s face: Her bags are no longer at her feet! “My bags!” she says aloud. But her panic lasts only a moment. The Rockwellian universe is briskly restored: A friendly cab driver is putting her luggage in the trunk of his taxi. “Where to?” he asks. Only now, having toyed with us, does Lynch signal that everything we have just witnessed—the “kindness, comedy, and forgiving tristesse” that the critic Dave Hickey rightly saw as a hallmark of Rockwell’s sensibility—has been subject to a menacing undertow. Lynch returns us to the old couple, now leaving the airport inside a black limo. Strapped snugly into their seats, they’re reminiscent of overgrown children; their old heads swivel back and forth in slow motion like laughing clowns’, and their twinkling smiles suggest something just short of psychopathy. Their grins are so unkillable, in fact, that what they most powerfully recall to me are the faces that crowd around the Thanksgiving table in one of Rockwell’s most famous images: Freedom From Want. This is one of four paintings he made from 1942 to 1943 to illustrate the “Four Freedoms” laid out by Franklin D. Roosevelt on January 6, 1941, when he provided the moral framework for America’s involvement in World War II. (The other three are Freedom of Speech, Freedom of Worship, and Freedom From Fear.) If you look closely at Freedom From Want, which is on permanent display at the Norman Rockwell Museum, in Stockbridge, Massachusetts, you see first how utterly brilliant Rockwell was. Perhaps most striking is how monochromatic large parts of the painting are. There’s the opaque white tablecloth, a white apron, and translucent white curtains—but within all of that white is an astonishing level of variety. The round plates are glossy. The creased tablecloth is matte. A silver tureen is so shiny that it gleams white. The transparent water glasses cast silvery reflections with white highlights. And those curtains are gauzily radiant. It’s a bravura display. Is it also somewhat stiff and sepulchral? It is! And this could kill the whole painting, except that against this almost fanatically pure still life, Rockwell—following the same principle of contrasts at the heart of Lynch’s aesthetic—sets the sparkling, animated choreography of the family. Cut off from their bodies by the picture’s vertical edges, their love-flushed heads lean in, drawn together by high spirits, humor, and the same intergenerational respect Lynch wanted us to feel between Betty and Irene in Mulholland Drive. Rockwell studied faces closely, including his own in the mirror. (That’s him smiling out of the painting’s lower right corner, like Lynch popping up as a hard-of-hearing FBI chief on Twin Peaks.) Good illustrators use facial expressions to convey action and consequence. Rockwell always sought maximum expression. Here, your gaze ping-pongs back and forth across the table, involuntarily weaving a lacy web of loving rapport. Still, the intensity of their expressions starts to feel uncanny. The teenage boy at the far end of the table has a smile so impeccably amiable that you idly wonder whether he might ever have lost his temper. At which point the pigtailed girl next to him, who stares straight at the viewer, starts to convey something latently demonic. Next to her, you notice with a start, is a wrinkled and waxy, almost clawlike hand, which presumably belongs to the venerable paterfamilias who stands at the head of the table, but which is cut off from his body by the platter carrying the turkey. If it’s easy to imagine the whole scene as a movie, slowed down, subtly sinister—like the scene with the grinning retirees in Mulholland Drive—that’s because Lynch’s work so effectively gives the lie to Rockwell’s. In the good-humored and reassuringly rational world that Rockwell constructed, there was no such thing as evil. His portraits of everyday life included pratfalls, minor moral lapses, and some genuine pain, but the arc of history was always bending the right way. In its fundamental integrity, Rockwellian America was as immaculate and charismatic as that Thanksgiving table. What is clear today is that the strain, so many decades on, of trying to make America conform to Rockwell’s softly arcadian image is too great. It’s a burden the nation cannot collectively handle and probably never could—which is why it continually demands forms of cultural release. These, over the years, have come in the form of not just Lynch’s creations but also novels such as Portnoy’s Complaint and American Psycho, and films such as Apocalypse Now. All are explosions of irrationality designed to release us from the whole Rockwellian racket and to renew our connection to darker truths. It’s not that Lynch’s take on America was any more real than Rockwell’s. It’s that his films expressed the absurdity of trying to make actual life match the illustrator’s gorgeous yet finally intolerable image of pleasantness and perfectibility. Since Rockwell’s heyday, this image has loomed over America like an impossibly kind, wise, and accomplished parent—and like a silent rebuke. On your way to the Norman Rockwell Museum, you may pass through the nearby town of Stockbridge, where Rockwell lived for a quarter century. He lovingly rendered its Main Street in a Christmas Eve scene painted in 1967, a year that also saw the Summer of Love, the release of Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band, and another 100,000 American troops sent to Vietnam. Fifty years ago, during the nation’s bicentennial celebrations (and two years before Rockwell died), Stockbridge staged a parade of floats with tableaux inspired by the illustrator. The procession, in which 2,000 people participated, was attended by more than 10,000. No other American artist has ever received such a tribute. The most extraordinary room at the Rockwell museum is always the basement gallery, which is festooned with the artist’s Saturday Evening Post covers—more than 300 of them. Rockwell first walked into the offices of the mass-circulation weekly in 1916, carrying a portfolio of his artwork. His timing was excellent: This was near the beginning of a great era in illustration, when advances in printing technology transformed large-scale color illustration into an essential aspect of communication. His talent was quickly rewarded. Within four years, Rockwell had become the Post’s leading illustrator. By 1925, he was known around the nation, and before the Depression was over, he had been all but canonized—America’s leading “Painter-Patriot,” as his biographer Deborah Solomon wrote, its paragon of picture-making. Rockwell achieved his status by painting small-town America. “I do ordinary people in everyday situations, and that’s about all I do,” he said in his 1960 memoir, My Adventures as an Illustrator. He was so successful, and so much better known than just about any other American artist, that people had great sport comparing him with his avant-garde peers in the art world. (This reputation gave rise to some amusing images: Rockwell’s The Connoisseur, from 1962, for instance, shows a portly, fastidious-looking man in a light-gray suit standing in front of a parti-color splatter painting in the manner of Jackson Pollock. When he saw The Connoisseur, Willem de Kooning, Pollock’s friend and rival, quipped that the illustrator had done it better than Pollock.) But Rockwell never pretended to be other than he was: an artist paid to make images in service to stories. Content to be called an illustrator, he was nevertheless unsure about the difference between what he did and fine art. His confusion was legitimate. Illustration, after all, is not inherently better or worse than any other style of art. Rembrandt was, to a large extent, an illustrator, a visual artist involved in the challenge of dramatizing Biblical stories; so was Winslow Homer, and not just in his magazine work. Narrative art is difficult for the obvious reason that it’s hard to show cause and effect (the core engine of narrative) with a single image frozen in time. The illustrator’s art lies in implying both cause and effect, so that a story—with its conventional, if artificial, movement from obscured buildup to crystalline consequence—unfolds in the viewer’s mind even as the image remains static. At this, Rockwell was brilliant. Still, professional illustrators are usually beholden to the directives of those who publish their work. In Rockwell’s case, this meant 47 years following the dictates of the Post, a magazine that sold 2 million copies a week and was avidly read by many more people. For decades, it also had an abhorrent policy (against which Rockwell chafed more and more until he finally severed ties with the magazine) of not depicting Black people except in subservient roles. After he left, Rockwell felt freer to address civil-rights-era issues, especially desegregation, which he did in such celebrated paintings as New Kids in the Neighborhood and The Problem We All Live With, his depiction, for Look magazine, of Ruby Bridges being escorted by federal marshals to her previously all-white school. To see the Post covers gathered together is to discern a cumulative, if highly prejudicial, portrait of America spanning more than four decades. Was it a portrait that helped America understand itself? Despite its cheesiness, and notwithstanding the Post’s appalling racism, I think it did—not just because Rockwell was so good at what he did but also because he was an artist in whom humor, grace, and loving appreciation easily commingled. These attributes were tethered, moreover, to a larger civic-mindedness. His best paintings are not only ingeniously constructed and brilliantly colored—they’re also richly humane. Stories are connected to our curiosity about how the world works, and for Rockwell, this curiosity was rooted in everyday life. “The commonplaces of America are to me the richest subjects in art,” he wrote in 1936. “Boys batting flies on vacant lots; little girls playing jacks on the front steps; old men plodding home at twilight, umbrellas in hand—all of these things arouse feeling in me. Commonplaces never become tiresome. It is we who become tired when we cease to become curious and appreciative.” Rockwell’s portrait of life in America is certainly kitsch. (Kitsch, Milan Kundera wrote, is “the absolute denial of shit, in both the literal and figurative sense of the word”; it “excludes everything from its purview which is essentially unacceptable in human existence.”) Still, his vision has had an enduring afterlife. Inevitably, its narrative potency—in particular its appeal to nostalgia—has been exploited across the political sphere. A Forbes columnist writing in 2012, more than three decades after the illustrator’s death, described the GOP primaries that year as “a process by which the candidate who demonstrates the most willingness to bring back Norman Rockwell’s America wins.” In 2020, shortly after he was elected, President Biden posted on Instagram a Hollywood ad agency’s reimagining of Rockwell’s United Nations mosaic, The Golden Rule, populated (in both the original and the adaptation) by a diverse group of Americans. And last year, President Trump’s Department of Homeland Security posted—without permission, prompting uproar—several of Rockwell’s paintings (including Salute the Flag and Working On the Statue of Liberty) to its social-media account. But it is not just this country’s politicians who are in Rockwell’s thrall. The painter’s affable pictorial rhetoric has cast a spell over holiday celebrations, modes of patriotic display, civic relations, even family relations. He was such a powerful image-maker that he created prototypes—ideals, really—of how life ought to be. And his work leaves a lingering sense that, if you want to be a happy American, you must (consciously or otherwise) reenact Rockwellian rituals. What Rockwell visualized was, of course, suffocatingly narrow. The critic Robert Hughes once called it “a dream world of small-town America.” In this America, Hughes wrote, “kids did not snort angel dust and get one another pregnant; they stole apples and swam in forbidden water holes but said grace before meals. All soldiers were nice boys from next door; all politicians were benevolent or harmlessly bumbling.” Big cities were subject to the roiling forces of unchecked capitalism and the blights of anonymity, rootlessness, and exploitation. Small towns, in Rockwell’s view, provided antidotes to all this. (He died well before the peak of deindustrialization and the first wave of the opioid epidemic.) They offered daily connection, neighborly interdependence, and, always, the lubricant of good humor (qualities that oiled Lynch’s twisted soap opera, Twin Peaks, too). To say that Rockwell’s America never existed is not to say that Rockwellian virtues do not exist; they do, all around us, every day. It’s only to acknowledge that the starched-white fiction these virtues cumulatively illustrate is by now so stained and sullied that just trying to keep up the pretense can trigger a kind of collective hysteria. The psychic pressure of trying to live up to an impossible ideal deeply interested Lynch. It produced his bifurcated visions of Rockwellian naivete and raw malevolence. In Rockwell, a diner is a place where a policeman can buy a runaway boy a milkshake before taking him home to his parents. In Lynch’s Mulholland Drive, Winkie’s Diner is where a tormenting nightmare becomes atrociously real. The night after I returned from Stockbridge, I rewatched Lynch’s Wild at Heart, his bizarre, hilarious, and very disturbing spin on Bonnie and Clyde. A lot of the action takes place in Big Tuna, a kind of anti-Stockbridge in the Texas badlands where evil thrives. The rusty, fish-shaped sign on the edge of town has been defaced with an expletive. The film’s main characters, Sailor and Lula (Nicholas Cage and Laura Dern), are deliberately cartoonlike, avatars of innocence transplanted to a context so malignant that it eats away at their mutual infatuation. When Lula picks up Sailor from prison, she brings him his favorite snakeskin jacket. “Did I ever tell you that this here jacket represents a symbol of my individuality and my belief in personal freedom?” he declares, like a third-grader reciting the Pledge of Allegiance. “About 50,000 times!” answers Lula, with no hint of a rebuke, only adoration. But that Rockwellian earnestness is no match for a setting corrupted by a hit man, a depraved mother, and the sniggering malevolence of Willem Dafoe. When Sailor confesses to having once worked for the man who murdered her father, Lula becomes pensive: “It’s just shocking,” she says, “when things aren’t the way you thought they were.” Rockwell expressed a similar sentiment before he died. It had been his idea to paint the Four Freedoms. He first took the proposal to the United States Office of War Information, where it was rejected, but after the paintings were published in the Post and received a huge response (60,000 letters were sent in by readers), the OWI reversed course and printed 2.5 million posters of the paintings, which the agency used to sell war bonds. In 1977, near the end of his life, Rockwell said: “I really believed that the war against Hitler would bring the Four Freedoms to everyone. But I couldn’t paint that today. I just don’t believe it. I was doing this best-possible-world, Santa-down-the-chimney, lovely-kids-adoring-their-kindly-grandpa sort of thing. And I liked it, but now I’m sick of it.” Lynch saw and loved Rockwell’s America—really loved it, as a child loves their parents—but something compelled him to break its surface and turn it violently inside out. This was a psychic and an artistic reaction, which is very different from a civic or political one. Maybe what America has to do with Norman Rockwell, as all children must eventually do with their parents, is figure out how to love him and leave him at the same time.

item.title: Why Wendell Berry Didn’t Worry About the Future
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Culture Score: 2.63
Wendell Berry was not an easy man to reach. When I wanted to interview him for this magazine in the spring of 2015, his publicist warned me that a press request would take some doing. Berry didn’t have a cellphone. He didn’t use email. He didn’t even have a computer. He wrote most of his drafts by hand during the day, without electric light. And he definitely didn’t make himself available to any old reporter who wanted to talk. I knew this already, of course. Berry, who died on Monday at the age of 92, lived a life defined by acts of radical abstention. He said no emphatically and often; principled refusal was a central theme of his writing and the lore that surrounded him. The publicist spent the better part of a week trying to reach Berry on my behalf. This involved multiple phone calls to his farmhouse, in Henry County, Kentucky, where Berry and his wife, Tanya, had lived since the mid-1960s. Wendell spent most of his time outdoors, the publicist explained, so he often simply wasn’t around to hear the landline ring. After a while, though, she told me that she and Berry had managed to connect, and that he would consider my request. He asked that I write him a letter about the article I had in mind, which I emailed to the publicist so she could print it out and send it to him by post. A few weeks later, I received a voicemail from a number I didn’t recognize. “Hello, Mr. Fassler,” said a voice that was deep and hoarse with age. “This is Wendell Berry.” A giant of Luddism was speaking out of my iPhone. He asked me to call him back. When we spoke, he told me in a warm, genial way that I was out of luck. “I’m just so covered up with work,” he said, “and I can’t tell if it’s because I’m just busy or because I’m old.” But he’d thought a bit about my letter. I’d asked him to take part in “By Heart,” a series in which authors discussed the passages from literature that had most shaped their writing and outlook. He said that his forthcoming book, Our Only World, contained a section that the magazine might adapt in some way. It hinged on some verses from Jesus’s Sermon on the Mount, as described in the Gospel of Matthew: “Take no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.” He asked me to read that section of his book, and to call him back once I had so that we could talk. So I did. And I’ve been thinking about its message ever since. I was surprised, at first, that Berry felt so drawn to this specific moment from the Bible. Jesus’s instruction to not worry about the future seemed at odds with much of what Berry had written. Many of the social and environmental problems that Berry railed against were really problems of short-term thinking, including the pursuit of quick profit, the extractive poisoning of the land, and the love of cheap thrills over deeper, more hard-won pleasures. “Think not of tomorrow” seemed to better describe the ethos of Berry’s longtime nemeses: coal-industry strip miners, big agribusiness, the global financial system. It was also an odd choice for someone who seemed so concerned about the excesses of modern life. Berry struck me as someone who absolutely would fixate on the general worsening direction of things.
