Fretting about the future is a favorite preoccupation of the conscientious. Berry occasionally admitted to his own worried state of mind on the page, including in one of his best-known poems: “When despair for the world grows in me,” he wrote, “I wake in the night at the least sound / in fear of what my life and my children’s lives may be.” Nevertheless, in the part of his book that he asked me to read, he wrote, “Taking thought for the morrow is, fairly predictably, a waste of time.” He insisted that what we call “the future” is a flimsy and insubstantial thing at best—a phantom we obsess over that never really arrives, or never arrives in the way we imagine. “Most of the bad possibilities I have worried about have never happened,” Berry wrote. “By taking thought for the morrow we have invested, and wasted, a lot of effort in preparing for morrows that never came.” Obsessing about the future, he argued, also has devastating moral consequences. It allows people to avoid engaging with the urgent realities of the present. I don’t know whether Berry, given his extremely offline lifestyle, ever learned about doomscrolling—the way social media can serve as a collective orgy of dread. But he’s right that, when people become too obsessed with a future that may or may not befall them, they tend to turn their back on the moment they’re in. “The time is coming when it will be too late to save the world. Oh, oh, oh,” he wrote, lampooning the handwringer in so many of us. “If that is the way our minds are afflicted, we and our world are dead already. The present is going by and we are not in it.” As I see it, this was the core purpose of Berry’s work: He dared his readers to live in a way that honors the situation at hand, at this very second. That mandate suffused everything he wrote about. He exhorted readers to enjoy the food on their plates, to bear witness to the places that surround them, and to revel in shared experience with the people in their orbit. Honoring the present was a joyful thing for Wendell Berry. It was also a form of rewarding but very difficult work. It meant slow, careful deliberation about the things he was willing to let into his life, whether that was a new piece of technology or a request from a journalist. And it meant searching for ways to disentangle himself, by turns and sometimes painfully, from destructive systems. The moral goal of a human being, he often argued, should be to do less harm right now. When one of his most famous essays, 1987’s “Why I Am Not Going to Buy a Computer,” resulted in astonished and outraged letters from readers, Berry replied by writing, “I did not say that I proposed to end forthwith all my involvement in harmful technology, for I do not know how to do that. I said merely that I want to limit such involvement, and to a certain extent I do know how to do that.” This response boils down to a simple, radical worldview: We must seek to understand the harms caused by the systems we’re implicated in, then strive to become less reliant on them. Berry was no purist. He understood that no 20th- or 21st-century American can live a wholly blameless life. He lamented needing to drive a truck, the unavoidable, occasional use of gas-powered equipment on his farm. He knew that his ancestors had enslaved their fellow human beings and that he, in direct and indirect ways, had benefited from that obscene bondage. “I am owned by the blood of all of them,” he wrote in an early poem, “My Great-Grandfather’s Slaves.” “We cannot be free of each other.” Moral blamelessness isn’t possible. But Berry’s larger point was that people should strive for something better, here and now. As he put it in Our Only World, with his trademark aphoristic brilliance: “Maybe we could give up saving the world and start to live savingly in it.” This reframes Jesus’s “sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof” as a simple, clarifying injunction: Forget the future, and work toward what is good today. I did speak with Berry a second time. We talked a little while about the Sermon on the Mount, but I didn’t get him to agree to a formal interview. I could tell he wanted to help me, to be a sport. Still, I sensed something else nagging at him: the irresistible presence of the now. He was here, living on this Earth. He had land to tend to, animals to care for, a wife to love, books to write—more than 50 of them, by the end. Maybe someday, in some dimly glimpsed future, he would find some more time to talk with me. But right then, at that moment, there was just too much to do.

item.title: The Met’s Other Failure
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Culture Score: 2.59
The Metropolitan Museum of Art’s announcement this week that it is canceling next year’s exhibition on the fashion of John Galliano perhaps shouldn’t have come as a surprise. From the start, Galliano was a controversial pick for the museum’s Costume Institute, which launches its new show each year with the splashy Met Gala. In 2011, he lost his job as creative director of Dior after a video surfaced of him making a drunken anti-Semitic rant; later that year, a French court found him guilty of the crime of making anti-Semitic and anti-Asian insults. The New York Times also recently described claims that Galliano had made anti-Semitic comments during an outburst in 2019. (Through a spokesperson, Galliano denied the 2019 episode.) But not long after his Dior exit, Galliano—who has always traded on his bad-boy image while producing clothes of astounding beauty and theatricality—was welcomed back into the industry. After so publicly hitting rock-bottom, the designer, who said addiction to drugs and alcohol led to the rants, apologized and went to rehab. Maison Margiela then hired him. Celebrities such as Zendaya wore his designs; this year, the fast-fashion retailer Zara announced a partnership with him to great excitement. Anna Wintour, Vogue’s global editorial director and the Met Gala’s chair, also happens to be his longtime friend and champion. In the process of planning the Met show, Galliano, Wintour, and Andrew Bolton, the Costume Institute’s curator, consulted with Jewish leaders, and the exhibition itself intended to—as the museum initially announced in July—explore how the designer’s “derogatory conduct” had “fundamentally altered his career and public reception.” Those efforts did little to assuage wider public opinion. Museum donors threatened to pull funding; the speaker of the New York city council called the choice of Galliano a “serious mistake.” On Monday, the museum released a statement saying that the show “will not proceed as planned.” It was, Wintour said in the statement, “the right decision.” It is also a blow to the museum and its reputation that could have been avoided. For most of the Costume Institute’s 80-year history, it has followed an unofficial rule: Don’t do a solo show about a living designer—because such an exhibition could be seen as a form of advertising instead of scholarship, especially if the designer has curatorial input. Although such shows are now commonplace, the Met’s fashion wing has always prided itself on “setting the standard” for conservation and collection, and has devoted only two exhibitions to living designers: Yves Saint Laurent in 1983 and Rei Kawakubo in 2017. Both were controversial exceptions to long-standing norms intended to separate cultural analysis from commercialism. Putting on a museum exhibition of Galliano’s work, even while interrogating his past behavior, was always going to be ethically dicey because the designer still stands to benefit from the publicity and prestige that the show bestows. This saga suggests that the Costume Institute, and perhaps all fashion museums, should forgo retrospectives of living artists—and revisit why rules discouraging them were necessary to begin with. Museums have been routinely collecting and displaying clothes as a branch of the decorative arts since the 19th century, but early fashion exhibits typically featured only historical dress. Contemporary fashion was considered insufficiently artistic, and highlighting it was seen as overly promotional. But as fashion designers became household names in the 1960s, more contemporary pieces found their way into thematic exhibitions. Usually, the items were in shows featuring the work of several designers, including at the Met, which minimized the appearance of endorsing a particular label. The Costume Institute, which opened to the public in 1946, didn’t devote an entire show to an individual living designer until 1983, when Diana Vreeland—a former Vogue editor in chief—curated a retrospective of Yves Saint Laurent’s work in honor of his label’s 25th anniversary. Saint Laurent was involved in the exhibition and attended the opening fundraiser, both of which were underwritten by the firm that had long designed his textiles. The decision was contentious. Critics argued that it canonized a designer whose work had not yet stood the test of time, while blurring the boundary between art and advertising. The general public, though, was clearly captivated: The show drew more than 125,000 visitors in just its first month at a time when the average Met exhibition drew 500,000 visitors a year, Women’s Wear Daily reported. Despite its popularity, the experiment was not repeated under the next curator, or the next. Indeed, the Times later reported that the Costume Institute had adopted an “unofficial policy” of not doing monographic shows on living designers due to the “charges of commercialism” that the exhibition drew. Designers, however, took note of the public’s growing interest in fashion heritage and realized that their own histories could be a valuable source of design inspiration and cultural capital. In 1987, Dior created an archives department; most major fashion labels followed. Fashion-industry archivists started competing with museum curators to buy back their own vintage pieces at auction. Some fashion houses founded their own museums. Others turned their archives into touring exhibitions, large on spectacle and light on scholarship. By no coincidence, over the course of the 1990s, fashion studies gained traction as an academic discipline. “Suddenly, fashion was about identity, the body, gender, power, and visual representation,” Valerie Steele, a fashion historian and curator, wrote in Reinvention and Restlessness, a book created for an exhibition at the Museum at FIT. Fashion not only explained the past, the thinking went, but also expressed the ambitions and anxieties of the present. But the mingling of intellectual analysis and business interests hasn’t occurred without debate: Privately owned objects aren’t subject to the same strict conservation requirements as museum artifacts. And as museums started borrowing archival pieces directly from fashion houses, sometimes a designer’s “cooperation” with an exhibition stretched to input or approval—another ethical gray area that can compromise curatorial objectivity and authority. The ethics of fashion exhibitions got even more questionable in 2000, when the Guggenheim mounted a show about the Italian designer Giorgio Armani. The museum, which does not collect fashion, received a $15 million donation from the designer; the move was widely viewed as a transparent quid pro quo. “It’s all very well for an art gallery to declare the equality of ‘high’ and ‘low’ art forms, and to enjoy the boost in attendance that may bring,” one critic wrote at the time, “but the challenges and risks of shows like this can outweigh any benefits.” Whether they’re focused on pants or paintings, museum exhibitions don’t just publicize and promote the work of living artists; their imprimatur actually raises its market value. The Armani show had the distinction of prompting a museum-industry trade group and the IRS to update their ethical guidelines on corporate sponsorship to encourage greater transparency. Still, shows about living designers—produced with the help of those designers—became more common, and eventually they lost much of their stigma. For many years, in fact, the Met was one of the few holdouts. Its policy changed only when Bolton became curator in charge in 2016 and announced a show on the Japanese designer Rei Kawakubo. Bolton, according to a Times report, explicitly “wanted to challenge the idea” that museums couldn’t do monographs on living designers, and wanted to “demonstrate that ‘fashion is a living art.’” Kawakubo’s involvement was crucial to the museum’s show; every piece came from her archives, and that year, she served as the honorary chair for the Met Gala. Galliano, with his past behavior, complicates the ethics equation even more. Museums, of course, regularly exhibit works by artists with unsavory pasts—but, crucially, those artists are usually dead. They can no longer personally profit or walk the red carpet on opening night. And unlike fine art, fashion is built in to everyday consumerism. Few people can afford to leave a museum and buy a Basquiat. Many more can pop over to Zara for a piece from Galliano’s forthcoming collection. The art of fashion may be too enmeshed with the business of fashion for the two to ever be completely untangled. But museums can easily forestall self-inflicted scandals such as the one at the Met by not putting living designers on precarious pedestals. In the announcement of the show’s cancellation, Wintour called the move “John’s decision”; many news outlets subsequently reported that the designer “bowed out” or “withdrew” from the exhibition. This framing casts the news as Galliano’s noble self-sacrifice, and distances Wintour and the Met from the whole sorry affair. It also inadvertently highlights the conflict of interest central to this kind of show. An ethical, independent museum exhibition could have gone on without its subject’s participation. Or, better yet, it would not have sought its subject’s input in the first place.

item.title: A Great Novel Becomes a Bad Show
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Culture Score: 2.33
For many readers, the career of the novelist Bret Easton Ellis is the standard for mainstream literary stardom. The biopic writes itself: While still a college undergraduate, Ellis strikes it big with his debut novel, 1985’s Less Than Zero, an unsentimental stenography of disaffected, privileged young adults in swanky Los Angeles. It’s soon adapted into a movie starring Robert Downey Jr. and James Spader, which itself bears little resemblance to the book. Nevertheless, Ellis’s renown skyrockets. By the time he turns 30, he’s seemingly done it all: published multiple best sellers (American Psycho, The Rules of Attraction) filled with materialistic ennui, cheap sex, and lurid death; been mythologized as part of a literary “Brat Pack” alongside writers including Jay McInerney and Tama Janowitz; rubbed elbows with celebrities of the music and film worlds; made lots of money (for a writer, at least); and become addicted to drugs. Regardless of how you felt about his work—and readers had all sorts of opinions—his success couldn’t be denied. “If you were not a supporter of the Brat Pack, you simply had to accept us anyway,” he writes in his 2005 novel, Lunar Park, which is narrated by a semifictional version of himself. Such white-hot notoriety was rare in his time, and it’s rarer now. While a book can become a hit in many ways, you’re only young once—and though we’ve all been told about the virtues of writers who labor away unappreciated until they finally get their moment, it’s hard not to be a little envious of the ones who’re able to enjoy their spoils before knee pain sets in. It didn’t matter that, when I finally read Less Than Zero after college, I thought it was a relic best left in its era—the work of a poser trying too hard to convince readers of his secret depth. Ellis’s early works felt too significant, too settled, for me to really say much about; disputing him would have been like arguing with a redwood tree. His reputation as a hedonistic provocateur made the release of his 2023 novel, The Shards, somewhat of a surprise, at least to me. On its face, The Shards is an autofictional murder mystery starring a teenage version of Ellis who, at the start of his senior year of high school, suspects that a new classmate is responsible for a series of gory killings around the school’s ritzy Sherman Oaks neighborhood. Novel-Ellis is working on an early draft of Less Than Zero, drawing from his own party-heavy lifestyle. The sensationalistic violence and substance-fueled navel-gazing—all of that sounds like a typical Ellis novel. Yet The Shards is not celebratory or defiant. It’s narrated by a much older Ellis, who looks back on his youth with regret and shame—about his closeted homosexuality, about his formative and long-dead teenage friendships—and rips apart his own mythos from the inside. Parts of The Shards read like they could have used a more punitive editor—it’s a little long, and Ellis describes himself as “keyed-up” a few too many times. Yet the book’s hefty length—594 pages in hardcover—is conducive to novel-Ellis’s obsessiveness as he combs through memories for hidden meaning and tries to identify each emotion he felt during this chaotic time period. “The facts from that fall were receding from memory but being seventeen actually became clearer to me emotionally,” he writes. “I realized I had needed this distance of forty years to finally begin writing the book.” Now, he suggests, he can admit that Less Than Zero was indeed an act of mimicry—that he’d copied that book’s numbed affectation from a classmate. The cynicism of his early work had put me off, but here he seemed weary enough to let down his guard and, perhaps, tell a version of the truth. The Shards has now been adapted for FX by Ryan Murphy, whose campy and provocative shows (Glee, American Horror Story, Feud) have helped define TV in the 21st century. In many ways, it’s a natural match. Murphy’s eye is consistently drawn to beauty, and to the machinations and aspirations of the rich. And though his scripts can be plenty outlandish, he knows when a performer should play it straight. The early episodes seem to preserve much of Ellis’s plot. We begin by meeting Bret (played by Igby Rigney), an aspiring novelist and senior at the prestigious Buckley School in Sherman Oaks. Bret has recently started dating Debbie (Hayes Warner), a bottle-blond socialite; along with another couple, Susan (Kaia Gerber) and Thom (Graham Campbell), they constitute a glamorous foursome. Beneath this picturesque front is a more complicated reality. Susan and Thom may look like the perfect prom queen and king, but she’s grown restless in their relationship. And while Bret is quietly in love with Susan, he’s also been hooking up with some of his male classmates and wondering how to take advantage of the fact that Debbie’s father, Terry (Wes Bentley), a well-connected (and seemingly gay) movie producer, appears interested in giving him his big break. These delicate dynamics are unsettled by the appearance of a mysterious new transfer student, Robert (Homer Gere), who looks like he walked right out of an Armani advertisement. Bret is transfixed by his new classmate and is convinced that he’s seen Robert before, at the movies, where he made an indelible impression. But Robert becomes strangely defensive about the encounter, and insists that Bret must have made a mistake. His denials and secretive behavior lead Bret to suspect that Robert is connected to the Trawler, a yet-unidentified serial killer who’s been targeting local teenagers. Bret’s obsession with proving his guilt slowly spins out of control. Gruesome deaths, a pulsing ’80s soundtrack, dramatic conversations about people’s hidden motivations—it should be fun, and it sometimes is. As Robert, Gere conveys an alluring darkness; you can’t take your eyes off him, and neither can the show’s characters. Gerber’s Susan is beautifully nonchalant, a quality that propels her into Robert’s arms. (Gere and Gerber are the respective children of Richard Gere and Cindy Crawford, who used to be married.) And Jordan Roth is ridiculous but memorable as Steven, Terry’s assistant, who seems to be manipulating everyone behind the scenes. Yet Murphy makes a subtle tweak that changes The Shards completely. The novel is told from the first-person perspective, which allows an older Bret to constantly remark on the described action with the benefit of time and perspective. Here, that framing device is snipped entirely. Bret still narrates, but voiceover-Bret is not Bret Easton Ellis, the middle-aged author of American Psycho who’s now looking backwards. It’s just Rigney, who plays young Bret, speaking from a vague near future, and sometimes obnoxiously. “Kids today have it fucking easy,” he sneers, which is new writing. The elision of this metafictional narration is paired with a lot of new plot. Ellis co-wrote the first two episodes before being sidelined in a reported power struggle. (He has not promoted the show on his personal Instagram, nor did he appear at a glitzy launch party in July.) The other episodes depart drastically from the book’s structure. Murphy tacks on stray storylines: a dance competition on an American Bandstand–type local TV show, for instance, and a kidnapping plot involving a foulmouthed classmate who has what seems to be a form of Tourette’s. One episode has the characters monologuing at one another in Shakespearean verse while dressed in costume. The add-ons are tonally confusing and parceled out inconsistently. Some moments are played for show-stopping drama, only to be immediately abandoned. Other confrontations have the taste of corny reality TV, and the ’80s references are often played for laughs. A blunter way of saying this: The new stuff is awful, and a waste of time. The show expands Bret’s outer world at the cost of his inner life (and screen time, as Rigney disappears for long stretches), but that outer world isn’t very interesting. The novel’s emotions have been strip-mined, leaving only the surface tensions of vain teenagers. Many TV adaptations of literature miss the mark, because the visual medium isn’t always well suited to novelistic storytelling, which can be both wide-angled and highly internal. But this misfire bears a particular irony. Since Less Than Zero, Ellis has been trailed by critics saying his work is shallow and trades in shock value. The Shards show unfurls as if all of those put-downs were true, as though the book is little more than a collection of unsettling murders, great outfits, and hot people being mean to one another. Two comments about the making of the show—both from that launch party—reveal something about what went awry. The first comes from Murphy, speaking about what drew him to the book: “I knew the songs, I knew the clothes, I knew everything because I had lived it. It was my time.” The second is from Roth, speculating on the show bringing about a trend revival: “Love Story got us our ’90s nostalgia, and Shards brings us our ’80s nostalgia.” The former comment is Murphy viewing The Shards as his story, not Ellis’s—a tricky approach for a book that’s so explicitly personal. The latter is, I think, deeply cynical about the point of a show like this. Even when The Shards invites us to laugh at its characters, it does so through the prism of “Weren’t the ’80s crazy?” The emotions are blustery, but not intimate; the narration has been edited for cool concision. In the book, novel-Ellis narrates about Robert: “The boy aroused something primal in me that I had never felt before—I wanted him immediately, I needed to be his friend, I had to make contact, I had to see him naked, I had to own him.” In the show, this confessional surge has been drastically pared back, keeping Bret’s messy feelings at a distance. Regret and shame, the novel’s animating sentiments, are not sexy; I’m sure the actors had more fun overindexing on the ’80s of it all. The end result, though, is the transformation of a great novel into a bad show, one that Murphy wants to run for two more seasons. Let’s hope not. Although Ellis is often nitpicky about adaptations of his work—he’s never come around to the wonderfully caustic movie version of American Psycho—he’s right to distance himself from this one. “It was nothing like the book,” Bret narrates in both the show and the novel, after coming out of a screening of The Shining. “I felt cheated.” It’s quietly tragic that the same thing has happened here. When you buy a book using a link on this page, we receive a commission. Thank you for supporting The Atlantic.

item.title: Why Lonnie Bunch Is Leaving the Smithsonian
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Culture Score: 2.24
This story was updated at 6:12 p.m. ET on September 8, 2026. Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch plans to retire from the institution at the end of this year, bringing to a close a tenure marked by unprecedented pressure on the museum complex from a White House keen on controlling how to tell the nation’s history. After a person with knowledge of the situation confirmed the departure to The Atlantic, Bunch addressed Smithsonian employees at a town hall this afternoon, telling them, “I may be going away, but I’m still going to be a pain in the ass to some people.” The crowd of staffers, who spilled out of an auditorium and into an overflow room at the Hirshhorn Museum, clapped and cheered, even as some likely wondered: Why now? In conversations with intimates, Bunch, who became secretary in 2019, has been floating his retirement since at least the beginning of this year. But the increased attention from the White House surely made stepping down an even more delicate decision. Bunch, who is 73, tried to deflect any notion that his departure was Trump-related, telling staffers, “I now realize that I’m old as dirt, and it’s time for the next chapter in my life.” He also suggested that the timing may have been influenced by his wife, Maria Marable-Bunch, who recently retired from the National Museum of the American Indian. “The Smithsonian represents more than a career to me; it’s been an integral part of who I am,” he said. “I think about during the many years here, I met the love of my life, who’s retired and told me I better retire soon.” Bunch emphasized at the meeting and in an email to staff that his next chapter will allow him to “continue to protect the integrity of the Smithsonian and to champion the importance of a history that illuminates and symbolizes the complex story of our nation,” though he did not offer further details. One Smithsonian staffer, who requested anonymity because they were not authorized to speak on the record, told us that while “as a secretary, he has to be very polite and decorous,” Bunch can be noisier outside the institution. Still, that will likely come in a measured form, characteristic of Bunch. As the staffer put it: “He’s not a real bomb-thrower, usually.” The person described the secretary as an exceptionally popular leader among staff: “He’s one of the rare people in Washington everyone seems to like. Well, except, you know, certain people, obviously.” Bunch’s exit will leave the Smithsonian, which is largely federally funded, with a vacancy at the top as it faces escalating efforts from the Trump administration to influence its work. Bunch, known to be diplomatic and evenhanded, had largely staved off the White House’s encroachment over a tumultuous 18 months in which the administration issued executive orders and letters criticizing the museums and threatened to withhold funding. In July, President Trump signed an executive order calling for signage to be added to the exterior of the National Museum of American History warning about what the administration claims is an inaccurate and partisan telling of history. Smithsonian leaders have countered that telling the American story fairly and accurately means discussing its complexities too. In a news release, Bunch said: “There is no place like the Smithsonian—it has been one of the great loves of my life, and I am extraordinarily proud of what we have accomplished together. I leave with pride and sadness, gratitude and joy, and with enormous confidence in the people who will carry this remarkable institution forward.” The chair of the Smithsonian Board of Regents, Franklin D. Raines, thanked Bunch for his service and said the institution’s governing body will be “focused on ensuring stability during this time of transition.” He said that the Smithsonian would soon announce an acting secretary and begin a search for Bunch’s successor. “There are some very strong internal candidates,” Kim Sajet, the former director of the National Portrait Gallery, told us today. Before becoming secretary of the entire Smithsonian, Bunch was the founding director of the National Museum of African American History and Culture, which has been widely praised for its powerful handling of the darkest chapters of America’s past. In Bunch, the Smithsonian had at its helm an advocate for its continued independence. The first historian and the first Black leader of the 21-museum complex, he spent nearly 38 years in roles across the institution. His departure has increased anxieties about the institution’s future. “As the only Secretary of the Smithsonian to come from a background in history, he was well positioned to understand—and to defend—the discipline when history itself is under attack,” a former colleague of Bunch’s, who worked with him for years, texted us after the news. “His eloquent defense of history, grounded in a deeply rooted cultural understanding of the American story, will leave a leadership vacuum and the Smithsonian will be ever more vulnerable,” the colleague, who requested anonymity out of fear of reprisal from the administration, went on. In a way, Trump and Bunch exemplified a primary tension facing not only the Smithsonian in this moment but the field of American history more generally. Trump’s call for a feel-good, Founding Fathers–forward telling of American history is somewhat at odds with Bunch’s biggest achievements: the dramatic reevaluation of whose story has a place on the National Mall and how the country faces the harder parts of its past. Bunch will leave the institution just as it seeks to hold off a threat against the very work that defines his legacy. One of the most dramatic illustrations of that tension occurred in May 2025, when Trump announced that he was firing Sajet, even though he had no authority to do so. The Board of Regents affirmed Bunch’s authority over hiring and firing, though Sajet ultimately resigned from the National Portrait Gallery in June, saying that the dispute had become a distraction for the institution. Sajet, who now leads the Milwaukee Art Museum, told us she still misses the Smithsonian and has watched with dismay as the pressure that came for her first continues to bear down on her former colleagues. Through the changes, Sajet said that she and Bunch have remained in close touch. “I think it’s one of the loneliest jobs in the world to be in the head of a large institution like that,” she said. Sajet said Bunch’s background as both a historian and a museum director made him well suited to steer the Smithsonian through periods of turmoil—including the racial-justice reckoning after George Floyd’s murder and the pandemic. “I know that you believe that your legacy is building the National Museum of African American History and Culture,” Sajet recalled telling him. “But I’d like to suggest to you that you being the secretary at this particular moment in time is really important.” She said she believes those same qualities carried him through the Smithsonian’s showdowns with the White House, adding that he’s labored to maintain the institution’s unusual relationship with the federal government (all three branches are represented on the Board of Regents). “He’s tried very hard to maintain the respect for our elected officials, and I admire him for it,” Sajet said. Trump’s attacks at times seemed to directly target Bunch’s work. Last summer, the president came after the Smithsonian on social media, writing that it focused too much on “how bad Slavery was.” The two later met over lunch at the White House, a conversation that Bunch described as “the most stressful lunch I’ve ever had in my life.” In a December letter that the administration sent to the Smithsonian, the White House threatened to withhold funding if the museum complex did not comply with an order to send over a trove of documents about its work and comply with its demands to tell an adequately patriotic version of American history. Americans “will have no patience for any museum that is diffident about America’s founding or otherwise uncomfortable conveying a positive view of American history,” the letter said. This summer, the administration ordered the National Park Service to put up signs that would attempt to discredit the National Museum of American History. Throughout the pressure campaign, many have praised Bunch for sheltering the museums from the worst of it. Shanita Brackett, the current acting director of the National Museum of African American History and Culture, told our colleague Clint Smith earlier this year that Bunch has set an example in tough times. “What he’s taught us over the last 14 months is not to be afraid, not to run,” Brackett said. Bunch had become more direct in standing up for the institution in recent months, telling CNN’s Christiane Amanpour this summer that he believes “it’s our job to tell an accurate, complex, and truthful history,” and that “it scares me when people aren’t brave enough to face their history.” Still, Bunch’s legacy goes beyond holding the line between a beloved American institution and an overbearing president. Bunch first joined the institution in 1978, starting at the Air and Space Museum, and he later took on a number of roles at the American History Museum from 1989 to 2000, including associate director of curatorial affairs. After serving as the president of the Chicago Historical Society, he returned in 2005 to the Smithsonian to build the National Museum of African American History and Culture, which opened in 2016. Under his watch, two more museums were authorized by Congress: the American Women’s History Museum and the National Museum of the American Latino. Both have faced political roadblocks; the regents recently voted to open the Latino museum in a prominent building on the National Mall that the Smithsonian already controls in order for it to move forward without having to rely on Congress or the Trump administration to grant it a new site. At the town hall today, Bunch cited the plans for the new museums, the return of pandas to the National Zoo, and the celebrations for the country’s 250th birthday as among his proudest accomplishments. A show he co-curated, likely his final for the Smithsonian, was mounted at the Smithsonian Castle this summer, offering a subtle rejoinder to those who think history is a finished story, meant only for finding glory. The framing of this show for the country’s birthday, according to its introductory text, was Thomas Jefferson’s urging that the newly formed United States be a nation “in pursuit.”

item.title: The Terrible Movie That Chinese Audiences Can’t Stop Watching
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Culture Score: 2.17
One of the only compliments I can offer the new Chinese animated film Niu Lai is that it certainly qualifies as a film. There is sound. The pictures move. But beyond the basics of what makes a movie a movie, Niu Lai, which translates to “The Ox Comes,” contains little artistic merit. The plot, about a calf coming of age with the help of a leopard, a bird, and his mother, is thin, and the characters have been so nightmarishly rendered on a rudimentary computer program that they might as well be sleep-paralysis demons. Yet Niu Lai has become a bona fide box-office hit in China. Since a small distributor unceremoniously dumped it in theaters in early August, the film has become one of the most lucrative movies in Chinese history, making more than $7 million off a reported budget of no more than $500 and outperforming recent blockbusters such as The Odyssey and Spider-Man: Brand New Day. Much of its success is thanks to Chinese social media, where clips of it first went viral: Some users have embraced Niu Lai as a meme, purchasing tickets so they could ridicule the baffling work with an audience. Others have championed the project as anti-AI art, arguing that it deserves to be appreciated as a purely human creation. As flawed as Niu Lai may be, to the fans, it’s at least better than AI slop. I’m not so sure about that. Watching a bootleg version of Niu Lai felt painful but apt: What better way was there to see a jankily made film than in potato quality on my computer at home? Instead, what’s distinctly human about Niu Lai comes from everything around it: how it was made, how it became a sensation, and how it has inspired further creativity in turn. Theater workers have drawn posters by hand to help advertise the movie. Businesses have made plush toys of the bovine hero. Fans have donned cow masks for screenings, and although the film isn’t available in the United States, underground viewings have popped up in major cities. As such, Niu Lai is the rare passion project that has attracted audiences not because it’s so bad that it’s good, but because it’s an occasion to celebrate the ability to have an original idea at all. Never mind that the idea was apparently underdeveloped from the start. The first-time director, Xin Yumeng, explained in an interview that he wanted to write about an ox because that’s his father’s zodiac symbol; the year he began working on it also happened to be 2021, the year of the ox. Production took five years, as the then-29-year-old Xin and his mother, Sun Lifang, wrote the screenplay together and made up the entire crew and cast: Sun sang the theme song, and Xin animated the 86-minute film frame by frame on SketchUp, an architectural-modeling program. The process was grueling, Xin said, adding that he kept going in part because he saw the story as a way to inspire viewers to not tang ping, or “lie flat,” referring to a societal trend in 2021 where young people in China rejected overworking by cheekily glorifying the act of lying down. In some ways, the movie is a deeply Chinese phenomenon: Fuzzy cartoon characters tend to become popular in the country—Zootopia 2 is the highest-grossing Hollywood film ever released there—and the words niu lai could also refer to the coming of a bull market, which has led some Chinese stock investors to purchase tickets for good luck. Plus, Niu Lai’s threadbare plot is rooted in the principle of filial piety, as the titular protagonist learns to respect and care for his mother. The Niu Lai phenomenon also seems to embody a phrase that’s gained traction lately in China: huo ren gan, which, translated literally, means “alive-human feeling.” The film expresses this quality, but not only because Xin didn’t use AI to help create it. What makes Niu Lai stand out most is its unabashed sincerity. It is an earnest attempt to tell a fable about a naive cow, and the story of its making is deeply charming: Here is a mother-son duo, total outsiders to the entertainment industry, trying their best to turn their quixotic idea into reality. Making a movie anywhere requires overcoming so many hurdles that have nothing to do with art or creativity; there are budgets to be balanced and business expectations to be met. But Niu Lai is a modest reminder that any film simply begins with an idea and an irrepressible urge to see it through.

item.title: It’s Low-Calorie and Packed With Protein. Is It Healthy?
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Health Score: 4.06
Ice cream is one of life’s simplest and most enduring culinary pleasures. The first published recipe, which dates back to the 17th century, combined milk, water, sugar, and candied citron or pumpkin. By the early 20th century, companies were regularly adding stabilizers to their ice creams to prevent them from getting freezer burn and artificial dyes to give them appealing hues. But the core essence of ice cream—sweetened, frozen dairy—remained largely unchanged into the 21st century. Even Halo Top, the diet ice cream that surpassed Ben & Jerry’s as the nation’s best-selling in 2017, simply subbed in skim milk and artificial sweeteners to keep the calories down. Then came David. The protein-bar company has turned its attention to “frozen dessert,” which is, of course, more commonly known as ice cream, though the company can’t legally call their product that. Instead of being made with cream and milk, it comprises a “protein system,” a “structure system,” a “fat system,” and a “flavor system,” each of which is composed of ultra-processed ingredients such as whey protein isolate and “modified plant fat.” The only whole natural ingredients on the vanilla flavor’s label are water, salt, and vanilla bean. And yet, the treat’s basic nutritional stats are impressive: A pint has just 210 calories, less than 1 gram of sugar, and 30 grams of protein. Unlike diet ice creams of the past, it is rich and creamy. When the product launched on David’s website in June, it sold out in 28 minutes. (The company declined to tell me how many units it sold.) David’s ice cream is perhaps the most outwardly refined of a whole category of frozen desserts that are being deliberately packed with protein. These protein-ice-cream companies and others processing their way to a palatable nutrition label are making a bet on what Americans truly want from food. We (and our government) might have grown more skeptical than ever of industrially produced foods, but we also expect quite a lot from every morsel we consume. When I recently spoke with Brendan Niemira, the chief science and technology officer of the Institute of Food Technologists, he spent nearly two minutes listing qualities that Americans now desire: that food be tasty and safe, sure, but also low-calorie, high-protein, probiotic, full of omega-3 fatty acids, and so on. Last month, PepsiCo launched a powdered oatmeal drink, with 15 grams of protein, that dissolves in cold milk or water. It also makes a prebiotic version of Pepsi that contains 3 grams of fiber and does not taste like Metamucil. Kraft Heinz recently introduced a mac and cheese with 17 grams of protein and 6 grams of fiber, thanks largely to a “proprietary protein-and fiber-enriched pasta.” Nestlé offers a 45-calorie “pre-meal hunger support nutritional drink” that is composed almost entirely of industrially processed ingredients and that the company says helps people feel full sooner. At the Institute of Food Technologists’ annual conference earlier this summer, I feasted on “better-for-you BBQ pizza,” the crust of which was fortified with wheat-protein isolate, and watermelon-lime “satiety soda” that was spiked with corn fiber. I even ate frozen yogurt that starred a “network of cell-signaling peptides from the fava bean” and was supposed to help me recover from workouts. On paper, Americans are generally wary of such products: In a June 2025 survey, more than 60 percent of respondents said they believe that ultra-processed foods are addictive. And some experts worry that the ingredients such products depend on—emulsifiers, preservatives, and sugar substitutes—are somehow messing with our metabolism, such that the impressive macros of these products don’t provide the full picture of their healthfulness. (The FDA approves the safety of such additives, but that review process historically has focused on toxicity and, say, cancer risk, not metabolic effects.) Many believe that the manipulation of ingredients causes our bodies to react in unforeseen ways to the food we eat—that a manufactured “protein system” might not be beneficial in the way that, say, lentils’ protein system is. Or they note the simple fact that many UPFs—even those that may be high-protein, probiotic, or high-omega-3—still contain a lot of fat, sugar, and salt, which are clearly bad for us. Take PepsiCo’s SunChips Fiber, which launched in March. A 7-ounce bag of the chips—seven servings, according to the company, but honestly not that enormous of a snack—has 21 grams of fiber, most of what the FDA recommends an adult eat in a day. But it also has 910 calories. Even if these fiber-filled SunChips had fewer calories, UPF critics would point to the way they’re made—using an industrial process called extrusion, which essentially pulverizes grains into easily digestible morsels—as a potential danger. (Some researchers suspect that extruded grains spike insulin more than their unprocessed counterparts.) The problem is that the science around which processing steps and industrial ingredients might actually be harmful is still in its infancy. And it will struggle to catch up with the food industry’s innovation. Major food companies are regularly creating new processes for spiking foods with nutrients without making them taste like health foods. Nestlé’s “hunger support” drink, for example, uses something the company calls “whey protein microgels,” which help prevent the drink from getting too thick in the manufacturing process. David’s frozen dessert is so low-calorie and yet so indulgent because of that “modified plant fat,” a chemical called esterified propoxylated glycerol that is not absorbed by the digestive tract and was cleared for use in food by the FDA in 2015. (An earlier nondigestible fat, olestra, infamously flopped after people began reporting that it was causing them “anal leakage” in the ’90s; safety studies of EPG indicate that such leakage could occur with very high doses.) Scientists might be convinced that extrusion can make an otherwise healthy product like whole grains metabolically harmful. But what about “supercritical fluid extrusion” that—according to Frito-Lay, which patented the technology—uses less heat and thus can “deliver high levels of fruits or vegetables” in a still-crispy snack? Until experts can articulate precisely why ultra-processed health foods are a problem, we’ll all be stuck in limbo. Companies will continue offering ever more processed and refined health foods, made with shiny new ingredients and methods; meanwhile, some experts will continue warning Americans that we should not eat them, without being able to back those warnings up with data on the latest foods. Every time a new processed health food hits the shelves, anyone who visits a grocery store will have to guess whether this one will be truly healthy. In the face of some uncertainty, at least some Americans are, so far, turning to products such as David’s: The company sold $131 million worth of its protein bars in their first year on the market. Most Americans don’t actually need more protein in their diet, and certainly they could get it without spending about $9 on a pint of David. “This so-called ice cream looks to me a boondoggle for all concerned, save those selling it at, no doubt, extremely high profit margins,” David Katz, the founding director of the Yale-Griffin Prevention Research Center, told me via email. But David’s CEO, Peter Rahal, told me his detractors are Luddites. He argued that people need more protein than the daily recommended amount to “thrive,” and that having the option of a new diet ice cream on the shelf shouldn’t be controversial. “You want the full-fat, full-cream, full-sugar thing that has this amazing heritage, go for it. But if you want something that’s really close to taste and texture, that’s more advanced and more sophisticated, it should be there for you,” he said. (David’s product is so expensive, Rahal said, because of the cost of whey protein.) Clearly, some Americans see the world like Rahal does. When the craving for ice cream hits, a pint under 300 calories has its own appeal—even if it’s not ice cream at all.

item.title: Our Last Wi-Fi-Less Refuge Is Gone
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Health Score: 2.96
This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here. Until very recently, airplanes were one of the last places where you couldn’t count on having good Wi-Fi. Even the Amazon’s most remote villages have high-speed internet, but for years, the typical in-flight connectivity experience could have been best summed up by the aviation Reddit thread titled “WiFi horrible?” Now major airlines have started rolling out Wi-Fi that is both free and usable. In June, United announced that by the end of this year, nearly 1,000 of its planes would be getting high-speed Wi-Fi via Starlink, the network of low-Earth-orbit satellites owned by SpaceX. Other major airlines, including Delta, JetBlue, and Alaska, are partnering with either Starlink or its closest competitor, Amazon Leo, to offer better Wi-Fi in the next year or two. This new technology provides almost the same internet experience you’d get on the ground, Seth Miller, an airline-industry analyst, told me. This is not Wi-Fi that’s “good for an airplane.” It’s just … good. As technology conquers this final Wi-Fi frontier, air travel will never be the same. The fickleness that made in-flight Wi-Fi infuriating was also its own kind of luxury: Planes were a bastion of unreachability. And once that luxury is gone, we may miss it. Delivering the internet to a metal tube traveling at 500 miles per hour, 30,000 feet above the Earth, is so difficult because the tube is both far from internet sources and constantly moving. In the early days of plane Wi-Fi, aircraft had what were essentially giant mobile hot spots attached to their bellies, which would connect to cell towers on the ground. (This was Gogo’s in-flight Wi-Fi which, let’s be honest, never really Gogo’d.) For the past decade or so, major airlines have connected instead to satellites about 22,000 miles above the Earth, which provided Wi-Fi good enough to send an email (sometimes) but too slow for Instagram. The satellites that Starlink and Amazon Leo use travel much closer to the Earth and the plane, so they’re about 10 times less laggy, Miller said. With these connections, people can use social media, play online poker, and—in theory—Zoom, though many airlines still forbid or discourage video calls. This level of connectivity might sound like a win: Airplane travel is a cramped, chaotic experience; the least you might ask is for the ability to scroll through TikTok when the limited catalog of in-flight movies gets stale. The pitch, as Grant Milstead, the vice president of digital technology at United Airlines, told me, is that with faster, free Wi-Fi, the plane can become a “living room in the sky”—where, just like in a living room on the ground, people can have the TV on for entertainment, their laptop out for productivity, and their phones nearby for messages and social media. Some people are clearly embracing that reality: On a recent 10-hour flight, the guy next to me prepped a slide deck, listened to Spotify, and flirted over DM with someone I sincerely hoped was his girlfriend. But this level of connectivity also means that, on a plane, you can no longer be blissfully unaware of what’s happening back on the ground. Before Starlink, someone on a business trip might still decide to expense suboptimal Wi-Fi to keep up the pretense of working. But for the rest of us, “Sorry, I was on a plane” was one of the last socially acceptable reasons a person could be unreachable while doing nothing except eating Biscoff cookies. A plane ride meant hours set aside to watch movies, read, or doodle, free of guilt and earthbound demands. Instead of responding to a message from your mother-in-law, you could look out the window and see rivers transformed into green ribbons. While my seatmate worked on his slide deck, all I did was watch Top Gun and Top Gun: Maverick and slam Bloody Mary mix. It was glorious. The level of disconnection on a plane might have once been an inconvenience, but now people pay good money for enforced breaks from their phone. Sixteen years ago, when Starbucks started offering free Wi-Fi, this magazine declared, “It’s about time!” These days, many cafés withhold Wi-Fi and ban laptops as a selling point. At least 10 million people use the Opal app, whose premium tier costs $100 annually, to lock themselves out of distracting apps, while others pay $59 for the Brick to do the same. Subpar airplane Wi-Fi included this kind of detox with the price of your ticket. No one will argue that breathing stale air in a seat that offers 30 inches of leg room counts as a wellness retreat, and the research on how much dedicated tech detoxes actually improve well-being is mixed. Still, a disconnected plane ride “might create an opportunity to temporarily remove some of the demands that normally compete for our attention—email, work messages, social media, news, and notifications,” Lisa Walsh, a psychology professor who researches happiness at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore, told me. Flying was a rare, bounded period of time untethered from the world below. Whether or not someone might benefit from that time depends on how they spend it, Kostadin Kushlev, a psychology professor at Georgetown who studies technology and well-being, told me. A nice use of a plane ride might include actually talking to the strangers next to you (an act tied to well-being, he said), letting your mind wander (also linked to well-being), or even just really focusing on Top Gun (research has yet to link Tom Cruise to well-being, but you never know). Kushlev told me about how, during grad school, he once set aside a flight to journal about what he wanted from his life and future. “It really kind of changed my trajectory,” he said. Now, with enough to keep him busy on the plane, he said, “I don’t bother.” Of course, passengers don’t have to log into the Wi-Fi. But as fast connections become ubiquitous on planes, expectations may begin to shift. We already spend just about every moment of our life near our phones—at work, at the grocery store, at parties, at concerts, in bed, and, for the 75 percent of Americans who’ve copped to this, in the bathroom—where anyone can message us. Now people could easily expect a response while we’re hurtling through the lower stratosphere, too. (And if you don’t reply, people will know it’s because you wanted to eat Biscoff cookies and ignore them.) Connectivity also means the plane becomes just another place to be productive. Milstead, the United executive, told me that one of the company’s customers vibe-coded a website for his new business from the air. Meanwhile, people have already started complaining online about fellow passengers taking Zoom calls and Microsoft Teams meetings onboard. When your seatmate is leading a Q1 strategy session, staring out the window and daydreaming—one of the most distinct opportunities of flying—may seem like time wasted. If 30,000 feet is yet another place where Zoom meetings are unavoidable, it’s hard not to see a future in which we are nostalgic for the recent past when the Wi-Fi was bad. The early aviator Anne Morrow Lindbergh once wrote that flying is “a miracle that has nothing to do with any of its practical purposes—purposes of speed, accessibility, and convenience.” Instead, a plane ride was an opportunity to watch the familiar world grow strange. Most people who fly no longer treat the experience like a miracle, but now we barely need to notice we are up in the air. It’s just another place to check Instagram.

item.title: What Happened to Yoga?
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Health Score: 2.68
At a recent Pilates class, where I pumped and pulsed under infrared heat panels until my fingertips were sweating, I ran into a former yoga teacher of mine, our mats inches apart in the neon-lit room. Afterward, I said hi and told her that I hadn’t seen a yoga class that packed in a while. She shrugged. “Yoga,” she told me, “is dead.” She was being hyperbolic, of course—yoga is still plenty popular. In some ways, it’s more mainstream than ever. People practice it in airports, offices, prisons, schools. But her words illuminated something I’ve noticed: Yoga, it seems, is no longer the defining symbol of holistic health in America that it used to be. The decline has been building for a while. Yoga studios, which have long been plagued by razor-thin profit margins, took a hit during the pandemic. Independent studios closed; YogaWorks, a California-based chain, filed for bankruptcy. In September 2020, The New York Times asked, “Is This the End of the New York Yoga Studio?” Even after the fitness industry rebounded and people returned to in-person workouts, many yoga studios continued to struggle for all sorts of reasons—rising costs, increased competition from other workout styles, the decision by some students to stick with at-home practices established during the pandemic. On Reddit, teachers commiserated about low class attendance. In May, a beloved studio near my home in the Hudson Valley emailed a desperate plea for students to return, calling its current business “unsustainable.” Plenty of studios are doing just fine: Representatives from apps that track fitness attendance, such as ClassPass and Walla, told me that yoga remains one of the top choices at boutique fitness studios. But the data reveal something else, too. Many yoga studios are succeeding by offering less yoga. Walla’s “veteran” yoga studios, defined as those opened for more than three years, have cut yoga class supply by 25 percent this year. ClassPass said that in April, more than 40 percent of its yoga studios also had reservations for Pilates classes. Mindbody, another booking platform, said that the number of its yoga studios offering Pilates grew more than 20 percent from 2023 to 2025. On the yoga Subreddit, people frequently gripe about Pilates and sculpt classes bumping yoga from the schedule. Fitness trends come and go. But the workouts people choose also reflect the contemporary understanding of what it means to be well. For years, that meant yoga and its promise of stress reduction and mindfulness. In today’s world of fitness-maxxing and social-media-driven obsession over image, though, the cultural ideal seems to have shifted from inner peace to outward perfection. When yoga first came into vogue in the United States, physical fitness wasn’t the primary goal. During the countercultural movement of the late 1960s, many Americans were drawn to yoga because it was “exotic,” Andrea R. Jain, a religious-studies professor at Indiana University at Indianapolis and the author of Selling Yoga, told me. At the time, some people disillusioned with mainstream American religion and values were “looking for something radically ‘other’ than the traditions they had been brought up in,” Jain said. Yoga was a compelling answer: It originated in ancient India and is deeply intertwined with Buddhism, Hinduism, and Jainism. Practicing yoga was seen as a rebellious act, an alternative path to spirituality and enlightenment. Over the next few decades, yoga transformed from a fringe activity into a lifestyle empire. During the gym boom of the ’80s and ’90s, people became much more enticed by the practice’s physical aspects; the Los Angeles Times reported in 1987 that yoga was appealing to people burned out from aerobics and craving a gentler workout. In the mid-’90s, “integrative medicine,” a whole-person approach to health, became more widely accepted, and likely gave some of yoga’s messaging more credence. Celebrities also started endorsing the practice’s benefits. Sting appeared shirtless on the cover of Yoga Journal in 1995, one lithe arm wrapped around a leg; three years later, Madonna taught an incredulous Rosie O’Donnell how to do sun salutations and ujjayi breathing on daytime television. They touted deeper connections among their mind, body, and soul, and flaunted the strong bodies yoga had helped them achieve. Madonna told O’Donnell: “I don’t work out anymore. I do yoga.” In 2004, when I took my first class, the commercialization of yoga was well under way. The industry had spawned countless brands of yoga mats and athleisure, then franchised studios, and, eventually, Instagram influencers. (My mom, who practiced yoga in the ’70s and ’80s, recalls students using only towels or blankets, and wearing whatever comfortable clothes they already owned.) Soon, yoga became more than a workout—it was a lifestyle, at times even an identity. If someone said they were into yoga, the assumption was that they were healthy, spiritually minded, and self-aware. Many dedicated students (myself included) signed up for yoga teacher training, some without any intention of making a career of it but rather to further educate themselves in the practice. Etsy vendors sold hoodies that said namaste, a Sanskrit word commonly spoken at the end of a yoga class. And kitschy iterations such as goat yoga—in which playful farm animals tramp all over students’ backs—emerged, geared more toward entertainment than mindful practice. Yoga’s ubiquity, however, may have triggered its cultural decline in America. The most devout practitioners started arguing that the expansion had trivialized yoga’s spiritual roots. (One former instructor told me he used to teach brewery yoga—which, yes, involved beer; years later, the memory makes him cringe.) The perceived novelty of the practice, Jain said, was less important to young consumers who grew up exposed to more spiritual and religious diversity. In other words, yoga lost its cool. The practice has also developed a reputation for being a gentle workout that focuses on flexibility, characteristics that don’t align as well with recent fitness trends. In the past few years, more women have adopted strength training involving weights and resistance—especially those of a certain age who are bombarded with messaging about the bone and muscle loss that comes with getting older. Although anyone who’s taken a vinyasa class knows that chaturangas (sometimes called “yoga push-ups”) will fire up the triceps, yoga is not known for quickly building muscle mass. Suzanne Davis, a yoga-studio owner in Oregon, told me that adding lifting classes and wall-mounted resistance machines at her business was a “no-brainer.” Studios still need to pay rent, so they have to meet customers where they are, even if that place is no longer on a yoga mat. But wellness culture in general has changed too. Simply exercising and eating well is no longer enough—“biohacking” has become hot. Some of today’s wellness devotees wear continuous glucose monitors to clock blood-sugar spikes in real time as well as $400 titanium rings to track heart-rate variability and REM sleep. The goal: 24/7 self-improvement. Although people surely sign up for yoga to better themselves, the practice typically encourages them to do so slowly, with humility. Yoga tends to be about letting go of ego and striving, and about surrender—principles that don’t quite fit into a culture obsessed with optimization. This priority shift also mirrors what has happened with the body-positivity movement: A push to make peace with our bodies has been minimized amid the rise of GLP-1s, and many people have gone back to sculpting and shrinking. If skinny is unapologetically in again, fitness classes other than yoga might seem like a faster route to toned arms and a flat stomach. Of course, what people consider a well life could change again. In fact, this year’s report from the Global Wellness Summit, an influential industry conference, suggests that the interest in maximizing every moment has already peaked: “Optimization itself has become a stressor.” Laura Munkholm, the president of the fitness app Walla, told me she knows many people who have given up on tracking entirely. “People are shifting into a conversation of I don’t care what the numbers are. I just want to live well.” Apparently, wellness seekers are craving something restorative. As it turns out, I may have just the activity for them. When you buy a book using a link on this page, we receive a commission. Thank you for supporting The Atlantic.

item.title: Medicine Needs to Get Serious About AI
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Health Score: 2.52
For as long as ChatGPT has existed, Americans have been asking it, “Could that funny little spot on my toe be cancer?” And as AI has advanced over the past few years, doctors have begun to use specialized models to ask much the same questions in clinics. In the face of these developments, professional medical societies have presented a unified front: Doctors must always have the final say in clinical care. We disagree. As the medical societies allow, physicians’ enhancing their work with AI tools may be a perfectly good way to deliver medicine. (One of us—Khosla—has in fact invested in a primary-care start-up, co-founded by his son, in which doctors supervise AI assistants.) But for Americans to get the best health care possible, we need to be willing to experiment with models that put AI in control. This notion has caused a stir in the medical community. When we published a commentary in the Journal of the American Medical Association last month arguing that AI-only care could soon become superior to care provided by human physicians, the CEO of the American Medical Association denounced us as undermining the patient-doctor relationship. The organization’s position was unchanged: AI should be relegated to a supporting role in clinical care. It’s an argument that ignores the available evidence and could hold untold numbers of Americans back from better health. Much of modern medicine—including managing hypertension, determining the right treatment for many cancers, and addressing chemotherapy side effects—is largely algorithmic. A physician needs to ask a patient targeted questions, determine possible diagnoses, order tests to identify the correct one, offer a treatment plan, and adjust it depending on how the patient responds. That series of actions is steered by detailed guidelines from professional societies. Yet doctors—despite the best of intentions—make plenty of mistakes when following those steps. Studies indicate that up to 15 percent of American patients are misdiagnosed each year, leading to tens of thousands of preventable deaths. That’s why health-care providers have software that notifies them if they, say, prescribe a deadly dose of a drug. Any software that could practice medicine autonomously would be similarly specialized: not generic ChatGPT, but a model trained in medical knowledge with the appropriate guardrails to minimize risks and mistakes. Such a model could check for drug interactions more consistently and comprehensively than physicians. And it would be able to check in with patients much more frequently than human health-care providers do. Some AI models have already proved adept at such tasks. In one study published last year, expert physicians judged Google’s Articulate Medical Intelligence Explorer—a highly trained AI model for medical diagnosis and reasoning—as significantly better than human doctors at getting actors playing patients to open up. The “patients” revealed more about their complaints, along with their medical, family, and medication history, all of which can be crucial for an accurate diagnosis. In a 2023 study, patients with type 2 diabetes were randomized to have their insulin dose adjusted by physicians or autonomous AI. The machines got patients to a stable dose faster than human physicians, and their patients took their insulin more reliably and had less distress related to their diabetes. What about the physician-AI hybrids that medical associations are backing? Research on them is sparse, and more is needed. A 2025 review of 52 studies concluded that, on balance, such hybrids “neither outperformed medical AI alone nor surpassed the best of clinicians.” In at least a few of those studies, human-AI hybrids outperformed AI alone. But in those hybrid teams, the AI controlled the final clinical decision—the opposite of what the AMA and others have in mind. Medical organizations are not entirely closed-minded to the possibility of change. For example, last week the American College of Physicians published a position paper that allowed that “fully autonomous AI is possible,” but cautioned that its use should be infrequent and “limited to low-risk, low-complexity decisions, and always allow for bringing a clinician into the loop.” John Whyte, the CEO of the AMA, told The Atlantic that he was “disappointed” in the quality of the analysis in our JAMA commentary last month. He questioned the design of the studies we reviewed, many of which involved simulated situations with actors or a retrospective review of existing cases rather than real clinical outcomes, and did not follow patients for years or decades. We agree that longer-term, real-world studies are necessary; hopefully, once advanced AI medical tools have existed for more than a handful of years, results will begin to arrive. Whyte was enthusiastic about further study of physicians controlling AI tools, but only cautiously open to further exploration of autonomous AI in medicine, arguing that the latter would need to be highly regulated. Reasons exist, of course, to be skeptical of AI-driven medical care. In nine of the 51 studies we reviewed, human physicians outperformed the machines. But some of these tested older AI models or general-use AI models that weren’t trained on medical information and specific guardrails for patient care. Prominent physicians have also argued that real-life doctors are harried by 15-minute appointments and administrative burdens such as prior authorization. That is certainly true, but it is also irrelevant to many of the experiments we reviewed, which examined relatively hassle-free simulations of medical appointments. One of the most common objections to an AI-doctor future is that robots lack the human connection that patients need to build trust. The American College of Physicians’ recent position paper, for example, cited AI’s inability to make eye contact. But consider that doctors, too, can be robotic. In a Gallup survey conducted late last year, 21 percent of respondents said they had turned to AI because they had previously felt dismissed by a health-care provider. In the 2025 study of Google’s AMIE, patient actors reported that the AI was more emotionally supportive than the physicians were. In a systematic review of 15 studies comparing AI chatbots with physicians, 13 found that AI had significantly higher perceived empathy. Like human physicians, AI is not and never will be perfect. But isn’t the possibility of reducing fatalities caused by physician error—even by just a little—worth exploring? Instead of writing off a possible source of progress, the medical community should help answer the key questions raised by AI: How should researchers devise ethical, real-world situations to test autonomous AI models? How should governments and professional organizations regulate them? And how should medical education be reformed so that human doctors can continue to do what they uniquely can? Hundreds of years ago, doctors believed that disease was caused by an imbalance of “humors” in the body. Even after Louis Pasteur proved that bacteria caused infection and Joseph Lister introduced sterile surgical techniques, physicians cut patients to have them bleed out what ailed them, not bothering to clean the knife or their hands. But medicine progresses. Humans have learned from our past mistakes and created new drugs, procedures, and treatments to massively lengthen lifespan and improve quality of life. Today need not be any different. Doctors have been presented with a powerful tool that has the potential to improve care for millions of people. It’s their duty not to stand in the way.

item.title: Mothers for Sale
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Ideas Score: 3.25
This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here. When Shoshannah Roberts talks about the four babies she’s given away, she glows. “When I think about it now, it still feels emotional,” she told me. “Those moments are so magical.” For many women, the thought of handing over a newborn to someone else is almost incomprehensible—they feel a deep revulsion at a primal sundering. But for Roberts, acting as a surrogate four times is the most meaningful thing she has done with her life. “I’ve seen the parents hold their babies right away, skin to skin. I mean, like, raw,” she said. “Baby’s off me, cord is cut, and Mom is just holding her baby and sobbing. It’s amazing.” The first time I saw Roberts, who lives in Santa Barbara County, California, she was speaking at the Men Having Babies conference in downtown San Francisco. Men Having Babies does exactly what its name promises: The organization helps gay aspiring fathers find women who are willing—eager, even—to carry their children. For one weekend every year, more than 200 men from across California and beyond fill the ballroom at the Marines’ Memorial Club & Hotel and listen to panel discussions and keynotes, with a special breakout session for single dads. Since the legalization of same-sex marriage, male couples have become the big growth market for American surrogacy, but the practice is booming among aspiring parents—married or single, straight or gay—who can afford the cost of hiring someone else to carry their child. In 2024, 11,821 embryos were transferred to surrogates in American clinics associated with the Society for Assisted Reproductive Technology, up from 8,461 three years earlier, and the United Nations estimates that the global worth of the industry is almost $15 billion. Most surrogacy in America today is commercial, meaning that the carrier is paid, and gestational, meaning that the carrier has no genetic relationship to the child. Barely a week passes without another celebrity posing with their new baby on Instagram—perhaps in scrubs or doing skin-to-skin contact—and thanking their heroic surrogate. Kim Kardashian, Anderson Cooper, Meghan Trainor, and Chrissy Teigen have all used surrogates. Some celebrities, citing medical risks, hire a surrogate to take on the dangers of pregnancy for them. Others want more children than they can have biologically. Hilaria and Alec Baldwin had a sixth baby via surrogate five months after Hilaria gave birth to their fifth child. (She has since carried their seventh.) But just as paid surrogacy is becoming a more conspicuous part of American life, so, too, is the backlash. When the actor Lily Collins, then 35, announced the birth of her baby, Tove, and her “endless gratitude for our incredible surrogate,” she and her husband were bombarded with messages describing them as “human traffickers” and “baby buyers.” In the past year, multiple horror stories—fraudulent agencies, human trafficking, elderly parents who are unable to take care of a newborn—have emerged, complicating what is usually presented as an uplifting narrative. If your primary concern is reproductive freedom, most surrogacy stories will seem inspirational. But if you factor in the risks to carriers, or simply feel skeptical of unregulated commerce, your doubts will multiply. In my experience, many liberal Americans are surprised to discover that their country is an outlier in its enthusiasm for commercial surrogacy. In Britain, where I live, a ban on the practice enjoys substantial support among feminists, who worry about the power differential between paid surrogates and wealthy would-be parents. (Altruistic surrogacy, in which the surrogate carries a baby solely out of generosity, is less controversial and is permitted.) A recent UN report went even further, declaring that commercial surrogacy “constitutes the sale of children, which is a crime,” and that “surrogacy arrangements can amount to or resemble slavery.” In one recent scandal, Thai women who answered an advertisement for work as surrogates in the nation of Georgia had their passports confiscated and were coerced into donating their eggs. Several developing countries that have become hubs for surrogacy tourism have enacted laws to protect women from exploitation by wealthy foreigners. Thailand banned commercial surrogacy in 2015 after the “Baby Gammy” case, in which a surrogate was left caring for a disabled child. She alleged that she had become pregnant with twins and refused a request by the intended parents—one of whom was a convicted sex offender—to abort the twin with Down syndrome. Because so much can go wrong, every country in the European Union has banned commercial surrogacy. France’s centrist liberal president, Emmanuel Macron, has described the practice as “not compatible with the dignity of women.” Italy’s right-wing populist leader, Giorgia Meloni, has enacted one of the strictest anti-surrogacy frameworks in the world. Not only is domestic surrogacy banned, but any Italian citizen who brings home a baby born to an overseas surrogate risks jail and a fine of up to 1 million euros. Many other developed countries have either tightly restricted surrogacy or chosen, as Britain and Canada have, to allow only the altruistic version. Israel allows surrogacy but imposes a raft of conditions: The commissioning parents must not have more than two children already, must not have serious criminal convictions, and must be of the same religion as the surrogate. In general, Europeans think of Americans’ enthusiasm for paid surrogacy the way we regard their fondness for guns and capital punishment: inexplicable. The piquant difference, however, is that surrogacy is a cause of the American left rather than the right. Red states tend to have tighter limits on surrogacy. Louisiana, for example, restricts surrogacy to married heterosexual couples using their own sperm and eggs. By contrast, when New York legalized commercial surrogacy in 2020, LGBTQ activists hailed it as a triumph for “fertility equality.” The debate cuts across political traditions and defies easy categorization. When surrogacy goes well, the result is a happy family that would not otherwise have existed. When it goes wrong, however, it can do so in unpredictable and emotionally crushing ways. At its core, the ethical question is this: How much physical and emotional risk should individuals be allowed to take on in the name of a commercial transaction? California, the home of Hollywood and Silicon Valley, is the undisputed center of American surrogacy, and the practice there is infused with a distinct blend of crunchy vibes, social liberalism, and straightforward capitalism. Surrogacy costs in the state begin at about $150,000 for a single baby, according to promotional materials for a variety of agencies doing business there. The percentage paid to the surrogate varies widely. Many, many enterprises want to help make gay couples’ dreams of parenthood come true, and the Men Having Babies conference was underwritten by a number of them: IVF clinics, genetic-testing companies, and surrogacy agencies. If the sea of Zegna sneakers and stylish down jackets didn’t tell you that these guys have money, the brochures offering future fathers “white-glove service” and VIP packages made it clear. In the exhibitors’ hall, I passed an abundance of merch designed to reel clients in—candles bearing the instruction LIGHT ME WHEN MATCHED, onesies with I LOVE MY DADS on them, canvas bags with the legend DADDY VIBES, and my own favorite: multiple iterations of sperm-shaped stress balls.
