Some were dyed rainbow colors. This was aspirational parenthood, right here. Pictures of happy dads and adorable kids abounded, including on a banner featuring two ripped, waxed, shirtless guys draped in a Pride flag and cradling a newborn. Words such as bespoke, boutique, and concierge appeared frequently in the literature. Words such as episiotomy and mastitis did not. It was here that I learned the industry’s preferred term for a surrogate pregnancy: a journey. At its best, surrogacy showers happiness all around. Intended parents—or IPs, in industry jargon—receive a longed-for baby; their surrogate is well compensated and well treated, and has the satisfaction of knowing that she has helped create a family. A few days after the conference, Roberts told me over Zoom that she had been interested in surrogacy ever since Phoebe on Friends carried triplets for her brother, Frank. Her first experience was blissful: She carried for a single mom who met a partner midway through the pregnancy, and Roberts later attended their beach wedding, in Florida. When she went back to work at a corporate job, “it felt a little hollow,” she said. She joined the surrogacy agency Hatch as a coordinator. In addition to four surrogate pregnancies, she’s had four children of her own. “My grandmother had 12,” she said. “So I think I’m built for it.” In mid-June, she announced her ninth pregnancy—another baby of her own. In the United States, the only serious opposition to surrogacy comes from an unlikely coalition of radical feminists and socially conservative Catholics. The former see surrogacy as exploitation: In 1983’s Right-Wing Women, the feminist author Andrea Dworkin described surrogacy as part of the “brothel model” of society, where “women can sell reproductive capacities the same way old-time prostitutes sold sexual ones.” Catholics, meanwhile, have doctrinal objections to any artificial interference in pregnancy. The more typical American view, though, tends toward individualism, in line with the “My body, my choice” slogan popularized by the abortion-rights movement, and an instinctive suspicion of government regulation: If the surrogate is okay with it, what business is it of anyone else? Although you can’t legally sell a kidney—even America has its limits—consent is treated as a universal solvent for many other tricky ethical issues. Well-heeled intended parents can also dodge practical constraints faced by biological or adoptive parents. Many agencies place no hard restrictions on the number of children any single person or couple can commission. Some parents want to get to a “double-digit number,” Men Having Babies’ founder, Ron Poole-Dayan, said at the conference. In 2023, a court in Los Angeles discovered that the Chinese video-game billionaire Xu Bo was simultaneously seeking parental rights for four babies born via surrogacy and was in the process of fathering at least eight more. The children (all boys, at his request) were being raised by nannies in nearby Irvine until they could be taken to him in China, The Wall Street Journal reported. There are also no legally enforceable upper age limits on intended parents. In August 2025, two 6-year-old children were found in a caged-off section of a San Francisco apartment. Their father explained that he had commissioned twins as a single dad at the age of 67, and when one of the babies was diagnosed with severe autism, he found himself struggling to cope. The locked gate stopped the neurodivergent twin from injuring himself during tantrums or running out of the building into the road. “I’m a senior, first-time parent, single parent, to twins, without domestic help,” the 74-year-old told The San Francisco Standard after he was reported to child services. (To which I might respond: And you didn’t think about this earlier? ) Difficulties like these are why many adoption agencies suggest an upper age limit of about 50. The surrogacy industry does not have a regulator that enforces a “fit and proper person” test of the kind given to people who want to adopt a child. Last year, Pennsylvania lawmakers proposed closing a loophole in the state’s law that had allowed a sex offender—who was legally barred from adopting or fostering—to commission a baby. There are no restrictions on Americans commissioning a baby abroad, even if the other country’s health services or human-rights laws are far worse than those in the United States. America also stands virtually alone as a rich country that permits incoming surrogacy tourism from elsewhere. Many of these international intended parents are from China, where surrogacy is banned and where, until recently, family size was limited by the one-child policy. These customers have exacting standards. “They want a Caucasian surrogate to carry the baby, with preferably blond hair, blue eyes,” Dee Gulati of Surrogacy4All, in New York, told me. “And they want an egg donor who looks like a cheerleader.” The resulting babies are automatically American citizens. (Hoping to change this, President Trump in August signed an executive order denying citizenship to children born to foreign citizens through commercial surrogacy.) In the U.S., no federal laws regulate surrogacy, and contracts related to the practice are unenforceable in many states. The Society for Ethics in Egg Donation and Surrogacy provides a “self-regulation framework” for agencies, but its greatest sanction is removing membership. The lack of regulation means that success depends more on luck and personal benevolence than on industry standards or legal guardrails. The primary question asked of parents attempting this new American way of birth is: Can you afford it? For some surrogates, handing over the baby is far harder than it was for Shoshannah Roberts. Last fall, in Chattanooga, Tennessee, I met Erika Jones, a quiet, self-contained woman who wore a discreet gold cross around her neck. She told me that her three ambitions in life had always been to visit Ireland, to be a surrogate, and to see a koala in person. She had wanted to be a surrogate since she was very young, before she’d even had her own two children. A few years ago, when she found herself settled in Fairfield, Ohio, with a good job and a stable income, she registered with an agency. The story of one couple particularly moved her. The wife, whom I’ll call Priya, had lost her brother to cancer in 2020. He’d banked his sperm before he died, and his family hoped to use it to fertilize a donor egg. The resulting embryo would then be carried by a surrogate and raised by Priya and her husband, allowing a part of her brother to live on. After Jones, then 34, learned the baby’s sex, she spent $40 on a balloon filled with pink confetti and had it sent to Priya, who recorded her reaction when she opened the box. But Jones didn’t see what she had hoped to see. “You could tell that she was disappointed that it was a girl,” Jones said. “I think she wanted a boy, to closely remind her of her brother.” Would the baby inside her be treated with respect, Jones wondered—or as second-best? From that point, in Jones’s telling, the relationship between the two women began to sour. Jones found Priya fussy and controlling, and felt that she was being blamed when a scan found that the fetus was growing unusually slowly. “I was like, I’m not a slave,” she said. She even wondered briefly about trying to keep the baby, but decided that wouldn’t be right. When Jones found mold and detected carbon monoxide in her apartment, in Ohio, she decided to move back home to Tennessee, closer to her family. That would violate her 57-page “gestational carrier agreement,” in which she had agreed to “take all necessary and reasonable steps” to give birth at UC Health in West Chester, Ohio. The intended parents told her that if the baby was born in Tennessee, they would face “significant legal challenges.” Because of the state’s more restrictive laws, they feared, the contract might not be valid there. Priya and her husband suggested that Jones stay put and send her children to Tennessee to stay with a friend or relative for the remaining five months of the pregnancy. Jones declined. She moved back to Tennessee but agreed to keep traveling to Ohio for medical appointments and then give birth there. She was being paid $45,000 plus expenses for the pregnancy but found that the frequent back-and-forth between states, in addition to her time off work while sick, had eaten into that payment. She cut off direct contact with Priya and emailed the agency asking that she not attend the birth. “I know I signed the contract—I am well aware and I intend on honoring it,” Jones wrote, “but it does not need to continue to be thrown in my face every other day.” She also bought a puppy, aware that she would soon be coming home from the hospital empty-handed; she wanted, she later wrote in a memoir, something “alive, soft and ours.” When Jones went into labor, she brought her two children, then ages 10 and 12, to the hospital, along with Susan Harris, a trusted friend, who alerted Priya and her husband. The labor was long—37 hours, 22 of them without an epidural. When Jones told the midwives that she wanted to push, the room suddenly filled with people. Earlier in her labor, Jones had asked for five minutes with the baby before handing her over. But the moment the little girl was delivered, she said, someone shouted, “No contact!” All she saw was a glimpse of dark-brown hair as the baby was taken away. She was not even told her birth weight. (Harris confirmed this account.) Priya told The Atlantic that she wasn’t “in any way disappointed” that the baby was a girl. She felt that because Jones had signed a legal contract agreeing to not have any skin-to-skin contact with the baby, she didn’t have to honor Jones’s request to hold her. “Maybe if you were nicer,” she thought. She has since ignored Jones’s request to talk through what happened. “At the end of the day, this is a business. We’re not friends,” she told The Atlantic. “You’re not doing me a favor. You’re getting paid $5,000 a month.” Both parties had fulfilled their side of the contract, she said, and it was time to move on. Jones has not found that so easy. She told me that the experience kept playing in her mind: “I felt like I was treated less than a human, and less than an animal.” According to the industry, unhappy surrogates are extremely rare. The owner of the surrogacy agency that Priya used told me that Jones’s experience was an “outlier,” one of only three cases out of the hundreds she had overseen that had “gone south.” At the Men Having Babies conference, an agency director assured the attendees that almost all of the “horror stories” reported in the press involved traditional surrogacy, in which the woman carrying the baby uses her own egg. (She added that the traditional approach now accounts for only 5 percent of American surrogacies.) The sales pitch to intended parents for gestational surrogacy—involving an egg from either the commissioning mother or a separate donor—is precisely that the surrogate has no legal claim to custody. That makes it legally safer for the rich couples who pay the bills than a traditional surrogacy. But it may be more physically dangerous for the surrogate. At the Men Having Babies conference, the first audience question was a stark one: How many surrogates die giving birth? Deaths are very rare, Poole-Dayan, the organizer, assured them. A 2020 study found that gestational surrogates were no more likely to die in childbirth than any other pregnant woman. Yet early evidence suggests that carrying a child who is not genetically related to you could increase the risk of complications: A 2024 study of more than 850,000 pregnancies over a decade in Ontario found that “severe maternal morbidity and adverse pregnancy outcomes” were three times higher among gestational carriers than in conventional pregnancies. When the mother and the fetus are not genetically related, the developmental biologist Emma Hilton has written, “Mum’s immune system may ramp up to fight against the wholly foreign tissue. In response, placental invasion becomes more aggressive.” (A systematic review from 2015 found that “most studies reporting on surrogacy have serious methodological limitations.”) Because of the elevated risks associated with twin pregnancies, most reputable agencies now implant only one embryo at a time, but—a recurring theme in this story—no law or professional regulation requires them to do so. To Poole-Dayan, the value of a contract and of compensation is that it forces both parties to have uncomfortable conversations while the risks are still theoretical. “I always tell people, ‘Imagine yourself at the funeral of the surrogate,’ ” he told me. I found Poole-Dayan’s forthrightness a refreshing change from the cloying online culture around surrogacy, with the staged hospital shots and cutesy euphemisms designed to play down the toll of pregnancy and birth. In one video, a little girl born via surrogacy describes the woman who carried her—who built her, cell by cell, inside her own body—as an “Easy-Bake Oven.” When Jones concluded that she had been mistreated, she turned to Kallie Fell. A perinatal nurse by training, Fell works out of an office the size of a janitor’s closet in a co-working space in Pleasant Hill, east of San Francisco. Fell is the executive director of the Center for Bioethics and Culture Network, which was founded in 2000 to campaign against “Big Fertility” but in recent years has also opposed youth gender transition. The CBC has only two full-time employees; Fell told me that it is “lonely work.” Her inbox is full of questions, unhappy stories, and requests for legal help: a surrogate left with medical debt after the intended parents ghosted her, a man who regrets being a sperm donor, women who don’t want to abort a fetus with disabilities but have signed a contract promising to do so. “I’m a little bit of a magnet,” she said. One of the most frequent problems, Fell told me, is the financial imbalance between a surrogate and the intended parents. Ethical agencies will ask the IPs to pay for an independent lawyer to read the contract on their surrogate’s behalf, but no law or regulation enforces this. Contracts therefore tend to be written with the protection of the IPs in mind rather than the carrier. Surrogates can be asked to sign nondisclosure agreements, to protect the privacy of the IPs and the child, but these can also prevent them from speaking honestly about bad experiences. Mental-health troubles can be grounds for disqualification for potential surrogates, but IPs typically face less scrutiny. Last year, Wired reported on a woman with bipolar disorder who blamed her surrogate for having a stillbirth; in a fury, she sent a photo of the corpse to an iPad belonging to the surrogate’s 7-year-old son. The same imbalance is true of criminal records: Another woman who’d contacted Fell, Amanda Misbahu, told me that midway through her surrogate pregnancy—arranged via Facebook—she began to worry that the IP, a gay single father, hadn’t been entirely honest about his criminal history. To me, Misbahu’s story sounded like a surrogacy nightmare, but she cheerfully insisted that she would be willing to act as a surrogate again. Misbahu’s upbringing had been turbulent. She had been taken away from her own mother when she was six months old, she said, with “maggots in my diapers and Pepsi in my bottles,” and had been raised by a traditionally minded, religious family. The turmoil continued into her adulthood, in successive marriages that didn’t work out. By age 23, Misbahu had given birth to five babies, but none of them lived with her full-time; some were being raised primarily by relatives. In her 30s, her thoughts turned to surrogacy. “It was a way for me, in a sentence, to help me through some of my own trauma,” she said. Giving up her own children had left her distraught, she said, yet “with this one, I knew the outcome, I knew it was going to happen, and it was a situation that I knew would be traumatic but I could control.” Two agencies turned her down: the first because of her weight, and the second after her early psychological trauma came up in a medical screening. So she went on Facebook to advertise her services directly to would-be parents. When a man whom I’ll call Cameron got in contact with Misbahu, she wrote her own surrogacy contract, and “he let me pick the egg donor—it was like online dating,” she said. She and Cameron wanted two embryos transferred, but the fertility doctor advised only one. “We said, We’ll take our $100,000 and we’ll go next door,” she told me. The doctor relented but made her sign a waiver. Only one of the embryos implanted. At eight weeks, she was hospitalized for life-threatening blood clots. She needed blood thinners for the rest of her pregnancy. “I thought she was gonna die,” her fourth child, Alyssa, told me. “So I would just start freaking out randomly when I thought about it—like, at school, sometimes I’d be crying in lunch.” Although Misbahu didn’t know it, Cameron had once pleaded no contest to involuntary manslaughter in California after injecting a friend with a fatal dose of Benadryl in his apartment. He then moved to Kentucky and practiced as a physician’s assistant without a license, a deception that came to light after patients claimed that he had botched their cosmetic surgeries. In 2001, he’d been sentenced to 20 years in prison for five counts of second-degree assault and 112 counts of wanton endangerment, although he was released early. In learning about his past, Misbahu also discovered that he had an adult daughter. In the end, she concluded that he’d turned his life around and that there was nothing she could do except go through with the contract. Cameron and his new boyfriend were present for the birth, for which Misbahu had an epidural for the first time in her history of deliveries, “because I’m like, I don’t want to have to feel any of this,” she told me. She cried—from the hormones, she recalled—and saw the baby a few hours later: “And I was like, She’s so pretty, but I really just can’t even touch her.” Misbahu attended counseling sessions for six months after the birth. “You felt like you lost a baby,” she said. “And I wouldn’t stop pumping milk.” Eventually, a friend told her that she had to move on, and so she donated the breast milk to a local bank for premature babies. Her counselor wasn’t much help, she said: “She thought it was the coolest thing; she had never met a surrogate. She just wanted me to paint pictures in her office. And I was like, Ma’am, I feel like I want to blow out my fucking brains.” Misbahu told me that she even gave her gun to her brother because she was so worried about her mental health. A few months after we first spoke, I met Misbahu in a pancake restaurant on the outskirts of Columbus, Ohio. She turned up bearing a knitted kangaroo that her mother had made for me, and she wore a medical-alert bracelet around her wrist. Her clotting condition had convinced her that she could not advertise herself as a surrogate again. However, she had married a Ghanaian asylum seeker whom she’d met on a dating app, and was trying for a baby with him to strengthen his claim. (They have since split.) For a time, Misbahu had remained in contact with Cameron—and had even helped him find his next surrogate. But eventually, their relationship broke down. She had asked him to buy a present for her daughter, and he’d told her that she couldn’t treat him as an ATM. “Finally, I wrote him back, and I was like, Look, I almost literally died giving birth to your kid. Like, it doesn’t mean you owe me anything. But that was pretty disrespectful,” she told me. (Cameron did not respond to questions from The Atlantic.) He blocked her on Facebook. But one of her friends could still see his page, so she used that account to secretly watch his daughter—the baby she had carried—grow up. She showed me a photo of the little girl and her siblings on her phone. “The girls are so pretty,” she said with pride. Surrogacy has a supply problem. There are not enough ethically motivated, healthy, middle-class American women to meet demand. Speakers at the Men Having Babies conference repeatedly stressed that reputable agencies accept only 5 percent of applicants as surrogates. Good agencies screen women for health and psychological problems, and question them about their finances and the supportiveness of their partner. Those safeguards are reflected in the high costs. Look abroad, though, and it’s a different story. Some agencies offer “guaranteed baby” packages for as little as $50,000. Surrogacy destinations pop up anywhere the local laws are lax, such as Northern Cyprus, a territory that exists in a legal limbo and is recognized only by Turkey. (The problem is that babies born there can end up stateless.) For parents from Russia, nearby Georgia is a similar no-questions-asked destination. India used to be the most favored low-cost destination, but in 2015, Prime Minister Narendra Modi, citing fears of exploitation, banned commercial surrogacy for foreigners. Ukraine’s appeal as a surrogacy destination has diminished since Russia’s invasion in 2022, although the leading agency there, BioTexCom, told me that the company is still handing off one baby born via surrogacy every day on average, at a cost of about $60,000. A representative of the agency initially told me that it was planning to open a clinic in Kazakhstan, to cater to the growing Asian market. In July, however, that country abruptly banned foreign surrogacy amid concerns about exploitation. BioTexCom takes a more unsentimental approach to surrogacy than American agencies. When I asked Denis Herman, the legal director, what his best day on the job had been, I expected him to tell me about uniting a baby with happy parents. Instead, he talked about business metrics: “I’m really focused on the KPIs, on getting the milestones done.” BioTexCom’s founder, Albert Tochilovsky, told me that he worried about falling birth rates, and presented surrogacy as an alternative to immigration. BioTexCom agreed to let me speak with one of its current surrogates, a 40-year-old whom it identified as Nana, and assigned an employee to translate our conversation. This was Nana’s third surrogate pregnancy since 2021, and she had two much older children of her own. During the first surrogate pregnancy, she was given an apartment to live in with her kids, she told me, so she’d decided to do it twice more; it was her only job. (Compensation for BioTexCom surrogates begins at $23,000, according to the company. The average yearly salary in Ukraine is about $8,700.) The image that Nana and the agency presented was of surrogacy as a sensible economic option and a morally good one. “In Ukraine, we say: Children are a flower of our life,” the translator told me. Mexico is more convenient for Americans, and a journey might cost $100,000 less there than in the States. But babies born in Mexico through surrogacy are given a Mexican passport by default, which can cause problems at the U.S. border. The State Department warns Americans that “there is no legal framework to protect parents who pursue surrogacy in Mexico, despite agencies and clinics promoting Mexico as a safe, legal destination for commercial surrogacy.” Wes Johnson-Ellis of the British firm My Surrogacy Journey has sufficient faith in the Mexican system that he and his husband, Michael, had their third child through a surrogate in Mexico City. Yet he acknowledges the concern that carriers in the country are taking on medical risk out of economic need. “Let’s not be naive,” Johnson-Ellis told me. “In Mexico, the compensation that we offer is three times the average wage, so it is a significant amount of money for them.” He estimated that his team accepts only 20 percent of the women who apply to be surrogates, and he said that they filter out anyone who is motivated only by money. Several surrogacy agencies told me that they worry deeply about the booming market in Mexico, and Johnson-Ellis expressed doubts about his company’s competitors there. “They don’t operate in an ethical way,” he said. “They don’t safeguard everyone; they don’t look after everyone.” Gulati, the practice director of Surrogacy4All, which arranges approximately 200 surrogate pregnancies every year, said that his favored destination for a low-cost journey is now Ghana, where he charges intended parents a flat rate of $49,000. Those carriers are under close watch. “The great thing about doing surrogacy in Ghana is that they live in a dormitory which is right near the hospital, so they can’t drink, they can’t smoke, they can’t do drugs,” he said. “During that period of time, they are monitored 24 hours, seven days a week. And as a result, the success rate with surrogacy is very, very high.” Even in California, the regulation of agencies leaves much to be desired. In May 2025, the caregivers of a two-month-old baby were reported to social services for potential abuse. When the police raided their mansion in Arcadia, a small city northeast of Los Angeles, they discovered another 15 children, who were being homeschooled by a platoon of nannies. “There were probably anywhere from six to eight at the time that we were there,” Captain Kollin Cieadlo of the Arcadia Police Department told me. Footage from surveillance cameras showed that the children were being drilled in English and Mandarin and forced, as a form of discipline, to do squats and other physical exercises that the police considered “above and beyond what a normal punishment would be.” Further searches revealed six more kids whose birth certificates declared them to also be the children of Silvia Zhang and Guojun Xuan, who owned the house. The couple had been running an agency, Mark Surrogacy, with only one client—themselves. In 2023, one of their surrogates had been obligated, thanks to the prebirth order she had signed, to hand over a newly delivered child to people she had never seen before, who arrived at the hospital with power-of-attorney documents. The sheer number of parental orders obtained by Zhang and Xuan during this period triggered an investigation ordered by a judge, but no further action was taken. As news of the mansion raid spread, surrogates then currently under contract with Mark Surrogacy—and still pregnant—began finding one another in Facebook groups. They all told similar stories, of being commissioned by a woman who said that she was unable to conceive and desperately wanted a child. When Zhang and Xuan were questioned by the police, they denied that anything was amiss. “They simply said they just wanted a large family with a lot of kids,” Cieadlo said. The children went into foster care, and one of the surrogates, Kayla Elliott of Corpus Christi, Texas, started a GoFundMe to try to win custody of the child she’d carried. (She has since said that she believes the baby should be left with the foster parents, for continuity of care.) No charges have been filed against Zhang and Xuan, who have since commissioned even more babies. Although they could face police action over the allegations of child abuse, the startling fact is that their baby-creation spree is legal in California. (Their lawyers did not respond to a request for comment.) The Wall Street Journal reported that the police were investigating the couple for possible trafficking, but Zhang told the newspaper that she intended to raise all of the children: “We never sell our babies. We take care of them very well.” After speaking with Jones and Misbahu, I spent hours turning over their stories in my mind, trying to reconcile their bad experiences with the many upbeat counterexamples I had seen at the Men Having Babies conference. None of those women had needed surrogacy to stay solvent, and more than one had joked to me that they could have earned more as an Uber driver. For Veronica Bowers, a two-time surrogate who now works for the Northwest Surrogacy Center in Oregon, surrogacy was a way for her to be with her own kids while still contributing to the household finances. (For similar reasons, military wives are actively recruited by surrogacy agencies.) “It is a badge of honor,” Bowers told me. “I feel really proud that I did this.” The happiest surrogacy experiences I saw resembled open adoptions, where the process is transparent and the birth mother can stay in touch with the child. (Bowers and Roberts are in contact with the children they carried—like an aunt rather than a mother.) The bad stories involved parents who behaved as though they were ordering a baby from a mail-order catalog. I was also left deeply uneasy by the realities of international surrogacy: Why should California be a place where Chinese parents go to find blond, blue-eyed surrogates for status reasons—and why should American parents have the right to acquire a cut-rate child by employing a Ghanaian woman to live in a dormitory under 24/7 monitoring? To protect everyone involved, states should impose upper limits on the age of commissioning parents and on the number of children any couple or individual can commission, as well as an equalization of the disclosure requirements. If surrogates must reveal their medical and criminal histories, then so should the rich people employing them. Something that surprised me was that many of the women I interviewed who had found surrogacy to be a traumatic experience were ambivalent, rather than flatly opposed, to the practice. Jones said that she hadn’t ruled out another journey, although she was still suffering medical complications from the difficult pregnancy and birth. She also worried that the baby girl she had carried would never know “three pertinent people in her life”—the biological father who had died before she was conceived, the egg donor who had provided half of her DNA, and the surrogate who had carried her for nine nausea-filled months. Jones had watched videos online of children born through surrogacy who opposed the practice, and she wondered whether she had been selfless to become a surrogate—or selfish. At the end of our meeting, she said—just as Amanda Misbahu did—that she had carried on pumping breast milk for months after the birth, even though she’d had no baby to nourish. She had also asked friends to check Priya’s social media to see what the baby she’d carried looked like now. On her phone, she showed me a photo of the little girl smiling alongside Priya’s other children. Other than that picture, Jones said, her hospital bracelet and blanket are her only mementos of carrying the girl. She still feels the loss: “Truthfully, even though she’s not my child, she’s my child.” This article appears in the October 2026 print edition with the headline “Mothers for Sale.” When you buy a book using a link on this page, we receive a commission. Thank you for supporting The Atlantic.

item.title: The Inside Story of What Happened at Stars and Stripes
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Ideas Score: 2.77
A “chicken plate,” in military parlance, is a protective shield used in a variety of combat situations. During the Vietnam War, chicken plates were inserted into vests—they are resistant against small-arms fire, but they’re also bulky and hot. So some pilots sat on them instead, which had the added benefit of providing protection against bullets that came from below. I first encountered another type of chicken plate in Iraq, where I was embedded with a convoy of American service members patrolling outside of Tikrit. On this particular morning, I sat alongside three soldiers inside an up-armored Humvee while a gunner manned the turret. But that gunner—James Murphy, a sergeant from New Jersey—wasn’t sitting in his sling, which was little more than a seat-belt strap hooked between two sides of the turret. If he sat down, the chicken plate would block his view. This left Murphy with a choice: stand up for hours and expose his head and chest, or remain behind the plate’s limited protection and endanger the convoy by missing a threat. For the dozen or so gunners I spoke with, the choice was clear. Two of them removed the chicken plate entirely for a better view. The military had no specific data on gunner casualties or whether the chicken plates were preventing them. Yet an Army general in Iraq was asking his staff why they were losing so many gunners. One officer I spoke with at the time told me that the answer was obvious the moment someone stood in the turret. I reported a series of stories on gunners for Stars and Stripes, a newspaper with a long history of editorial independence despite being housed within the Department of Defense. A few weeks later, after returning to my home at the time—a room at the bachelor officers’ quarters on a Marine Corps base in Okinawa—I received a message from our Pentagon beat reporter, who told me that military officials had read the series and were fast-tracking improved equipment for deployment. They’d found a way to help protect the gunners without blocking their view from the turret. I don’t want to overstate my role. At least some military officials were aware of the issue and had been testing prototypes for better shields. But many of the soldiers weren’t willing to discuss with senior leaders the specifics of what they needed, out of concern that they’d be viewed as complaining. I’m grateful that they trusted me enough to tell their stories. Looking back now, what feels remarkable isn’t the lack of proper equipment. It’s the way the Pentagon was willing to take independent journalism that spotlighted deficiencies and use it to improve conditions for service members. Uniformed military leaders have not lost the means to analyze and act on useful journalism. But publicly denouncing the reporting or the news outlet makes it far less likely that they will. Attacking people for telling the truth creates a chilling effect for truth tellers—including those who are themselves in the military. The best journalism unearths information that complex bureaucracies overlook or suppress, intentionally or not. When leaders treat asking tough questions and reporting uncomfortable facts as disloyalty, they devalue a tool that can help them fix crucial problems. The danger in this devaluation is immense, especially now; it comes as U.S. service members are once again fighting in the Middle East. The Pentagon hasn’t held a press briefing on combat operations in Iran since May 5. The Correspondents’ Corridor, where reporters worked inside the Pentagon for decades, is closed while court appeals continue on press-access restrictions. The New York Times is suing the Pentagon on First Amendment grounds, arguing that the Pentagon’s attempts to prevent independent reporting are clearly unconstitutional. (I should disclose that I, too, am suing the Pentagon. I was fired after I said in an appearance on CBS News that my personal red line would be if the Pentagon ever instructed me not to publish a perfectly accurate story. It is telling that I am being fired for describing the most anodyne of journalistic ethics, a position that any self-respecting reporter in any free society would hold, and that the Pentagon interpreted as insubordination.) Stars and Stripes has its roots in the Civil War, when Union soldiers took over a printing press in Bloomfield, Missouri. The paper was revived during World War I under General John “Black Jack” Pershing and has published continuously since 1942, when General George C. Marshall recognized the value it provided troops and aimed to follow Pershing’s example. “No official control was ever exercised over the matter which went into” Stars and Stripes, Marshall said of the WWI edition. It didn’t take long for that editorial freedom to be challenged. General George Patton complained about the “Willie and Joe” cartoonist Bill Mauldin’s depictions of soldiers as they often appeared—tired and dirty. (Mauldin would have known; he was himself a soldier.) But General Dwight Eisenhower rejected Patton’s drive to control the reporting itself. “It is the soldier’s paper,” he said, “and we won’t interfere,” according to the historian Stephen Ambrose’s foreword in a book by Mauldin, whose wartime cartoons earned him the 1945 Pulitzer Prize. The newspaper continued to operate overseas after World War II, hiring civilian journalists to work alongside service members. But attempts at curtailing Stripes’ independence periodically arose. Congress documented occasional pressures in the 1960s. In the ’80s, a General Accounting Office report to Congress found conclusive evidence of censorship, and pointed out the “inherent cultural conflict” between the First Amendment mission and the military’s own. Those findings led the House Armed Services Committee to direct the Pentagon to establish an ombudsman, responsible to Congress, who would monitor the free flow of information to service members through Stars and Stripes. And in 1993, a Defense Department directive affirmed that Stars and Stripes is editorially independent of the military chain of command. A subsequent federal regulation added to those protections. In 2020, the Pentagon proposed cutting all funding to Stars and Stripes, after the department’s comptroller stated that it is “probably not the best way that we communicate any longer.” The idea drew a bipartisan rebuke in Congress. The White House agreed with the lawmakers, and Stripes lived on. Last November, I moved to Washington, D.C., to accept the editor-in-chief job at the paper, where I’d already been serving as Europe and Middle East chief, based near Ramstein Air Base, in Germany. Two months later, the Pentagon chief spokesman Sean Parnell fired a broadside at Stars and Stripes. On January 15, he posted on X that the news organization must be rid of “woke distractions that syphon morale.” The same day, the Pentagon revoked the federal regulation it had established in 1994, calling it unnecessary. The Daily Wire reported that half of all Stripes content would come from the military’s public-affairs team, and that civilian reporters would be replaced by military members. When Stars and Stripes reporters called the Pentagon press office for comment and clarification, they received nothing more than a referral to the tweet and the Daily Wire story. On February 28, the United States and Israel attacked Iran, killing Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. The first Stars and Stripes story came from a wire service, because there aren’t any Stripes reporters inside Iran. But within hours, we had half a dozen stories focused on the U.S. military bases in the region and the people there. In Bahrain, civilians were given the order to evacuate an hour after missiles began falling on the headquarters base of the U.S. Fifth Fleet. The coverage drew millions of readers, and a video shot by one of our active-duty reporters of a plume rising over the Navy base was viewed all over the world. We worked hard on covering the Iran conflict and thought little of that January tweet—that is, until a Pentagon memo came in mid-March. The memo simultaneously affirmed our independence and added restrictions. That wire-service story from Iran was now forbidden, along with any other paid wire-service news. So were the comics, of all things. Our publishing decisions would be subject to “good order and discipline”—a line borrowed from the Uniform Code of Military Justice. Our military reporters, who function as interns and receive mentorship from seasoned civilian journalists, now had to wonder whether writing a story might land them in legal jeopardy. I told military reporters who were worried that a story might hurt their career to let us know, and we’d reassign it. Meanwhile, the staff never compromised on their ethics and values. They reported fairly and accurately and, when called for, held power to account. The ombudsman wrote a column that assailed the news restrictions, in keeping with the duties set by Congress. Two weeks later, the Defense Department fired her. By the time I sat down with CBS’s David Martin in late June, I had spoken with no fewer than 16 news outlets and authors about Stars and Stripes. Martin asked me about the “woke distractions” referenced in the January tweet and I answered honestly—that the Pentagon had never explained to us what that meant. Martin also asked whether I had a personal red line when it came to press restrictions, and I said that I did. If the Pentagon were to say, “Don’t run a perfectly accurate story. Run this instead. Here it is, written by the Pentagon. That would be a red line.” My response to hypothetical censorship was consistent with what military leaders have said for more than a century, and with the Defense Department’s own directive barring censorship and news management. It is also consistent with basic journalistic ethics: Without editorial independence, journalists cannot uphold their duty to the public. As part of the CBS interview, the Middle East correspondent Lara Korte stated that she worked for Stars and Stripes, not the Pentagon. She made the distinction to underscore her independence, which is essential to credibility. I learned approximately a week later that the Pentagon press office wasn’t happy about the interview, but that was all I heard. On August 12, seven weeks after the CBS interview, the Pentagon sent notices of proposed separation for Korte and me to Stripes’ publisher, Max Lederer, and told him to sign them. Lederer was an Airborne soldier turned Army attorney who was awarded the Bronze Star before he joined Stars and Stripes. He worked his way up through business operations to serve for two decades as publisher. He reviewed the separation notices and pointed out legal and ethical inconsistencies. Those concerns were dismissed. Rather than sign the notices, he submitted his resignation. (They fired him instead.) On August 21, the three of us received the separation notices, which listed insubordination as the primary charge. The notices issued to Korte and me cited our CBS comments but didn’t state which order we were purportedly disobeying. Lederer’s firing was for not signing the documents in the first place. That same day, the Pentagon replaced the directive issued in 1993. Among other things, it bars comics deemed editorial in nature and prevents reporters from using the Freedom of Information Act on behalf of the news organization. I can’t think of another American media outlet with the same restriction. About an hour after we received our separation notices, the military deputy to the publisher, who’d arrived two weeks earlier, ordered a 10-page document to be published on Stripes.com within 30 minutes. The document stated that Stripes would continue to run independent journalism and that “it is time to take them at their word,” referring to the Pentagon. I do take them at their word. All of the words they’ve put out since January, along with their actions. The Pentagon has articulated a remarkably narrow view of press freedom. The government may stop short of censoring an individual story. But it will seek to fire newsroom leaders for opposing the replacement of accurate reporting with press releases. It will strip an organization of basic reporting tools it deems unnecessary or distasteful. And it will discredit the source of the reporting if a story is perceived as unflattering to the president or his secretary of defense. The press isn’t a perfect institution. A global 2026 Reuters Institute survey found that the percentage of people who report trusting the news dropped to the lowest level since Reuters began asking the question in 2015; in the U.S., only 25 percent of Americans said that they trust the news most of the time. Whatever combination of press failures and partisanship produced this decline, public trust has eroded. And it’s that erosion that has made it much easier for officials to delegitimize accurate, balanced journalism. Reporters, like anyone, make mistakes, but ethical journalism remains fundamentally useful to government and to the citizens who hold it accountable. People in large organizations—the U.S. military included—often avoid delivering bad news for fear of appearing to oppose a leader’s plans. Independent reporting moves information forward, but only if sources know they’ll be able to speak with journalists without fear of reprisal, and if they believe that leaders are open to reacting to criticism like professionals. That’s what happened in Iraq. The gunners knew what they needed to do their job safely. They didn’t want to be viewed as complainers. Independent journalism sent the message to those who needed to hear it. *Image sources: Jim Watson / AFP / Getty; Win McNamee / Getty; Lyalya Go / Getty; HUM Images / Getty; Toronto Star Archives / Getty; Universal History Archive / Getty; Library of Congress.

item.title: The 24-Year-Old Who Lost Billions
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Ideas Score: 2.34
This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here. Updated at 4:32 p.m. ET on September 8, 2026. In the fall of 2007, as the American housing market began to buckle, a Morgan Stanley bond trader named Howie Hubler lost $9 billion. The bellicose former linebacker believed that he had structured his subprime-mortgage deals in a way that would outsmart the market. Instead, Hubler’s folly amounted to the largest trading loss in history. Until this summer, that is, when Leopold Aschenbrenner managed to lose nearly four times as much. At age 24. The implosion of Aschenbrenner’s AI hedge fund, Situational Awareness, over the course of a few days in late July was by any standard remarkable, and not just for the enormous sums involved. Aschenbrenner was the valedictorian of his Columbia University class at age 19. He worked for OpenAI before being fired amid murky circumstances, at which point he published a viral 165-page essay (also called “Situational Awareness”) that predicted the arrival of artificial general intelligence—an AI so advanced that it would meet or exceed all human capabilities—by 2027. “I probably either personally know or am one degree of separation from everyone who could plausibly run The Project,” he wrote. He founded his hedge fund on that promise of access and soon turned a $225 million initial investment into $45 billion, before he was forced to unload the majority of his positions—$35 billion, the value of United Airlines—in a fire sale the same week that he was set to be married. The Securities and Exchange Commission is now investigating the collapse, though Aschenbrenner has not been accused of any wrongdoing. (He did not respond to a request for comment.) Aschenbrenner had been considered the “Nostradamus of AI,” a clairvoyant who saw what was coming for the world. His spectacular failure reveals how eager Silicon Valley is to invest its billions in the dubious hands of a kid who confidently proclaims what he doesn’t actually know. Just as Hubler’s loss presaged the Great Recession, Aschenbrenner’s story of hubris may foreshadow a larger risk for today’s AI-driven boom, if it continues to stake its future on the bluster of young savants. “There’s this hunger for insight porn in Silicon Valley,” Amjad Masad, the founder and CEO of the popular AI-coding platform Replit, told me. “If you’re able to write something really good that creates this dopamine rush in people—like, Oh, I just saw the future—then you’re going to be able to attract a lot of capital and money and potentially talent.” This was the appeal of Leopold Aschenbrenner. Born in Berlin to a pair of doctors, Aschenbrenner has said that Germany lacked “the appreciation of excellence” that would have allowed him to thrive; America beckoned, and at 15, he headed to Columbia. One of his first gigs after college was for the FTX Future Fund—the philanthropic arm of the crypto exchange run by Sam Bankman-Fried, the effective-altruism adherent who was later convicted of fraud. This brought Aschenbrenner into a circle that was quirky even by Silicon Valley standards. Aschenbrenner resigned from FTX Future Fund, along with other staff members, when the crypto exchange came tumbling down. Soon after, he took up with the effective-altruism crowd in San Francisco. One of his close associates told me about attending “Iliad wrestling parties,” where people would drink wine, read passages from The Iliad, strip naked, and grapple with one another. Aschenbrenner liked to describe, with full sincerity, his goal of owning a galaxy, The Wall Street Journal reported. His now-wife worked for Bankman-Fried too and is currently chief of staff to Anthropic’s CEO. Their wedding plans included panel discussions and colloquia. The more unusual Aschenbrenner seemed, the more this played in his favor. His essay, which set the wonkiest corners of Silicon Valley ablaze in 2024, laid out a mission to bet on superintelligence “before the decade is out.” His premise was simple: “You can see the future first in San Francisco,” Aschenbrenner wrote. “Let me tell you what we see.” Aschenbrenner’s predictions were illustrated by charts and graphs and all manner of calculations, but really, they were carried along by his rhetoric. “I can see it,” Aschenbrenner wrote. “I can see how AGI will be built.” Both outsiders and insiders in Silicon Valley “are really confused about what’s going on and therefore are drawn to people who seem to have a really confident, clear picture of the future,” Helen Toner, an AI expert who sat on the board of OpenAI, told me. Those who would presume to doubt Aschenbrenner’s judgment merely lacked the extra-special access that made his vision so clear. And central to this access was a fervent ideological commitment to the idea of superintelligence. Aschenbrenner and his cohort proudly describe themselves as “AGI-pilled.” That is, they believe AGI to be around the corner and its benefits to be self-evident. They extoll the ability of a superintelligent machine to heal the world of its ills, thereby serving the effective-altruism philosophy many of them share. Christopher Manning, an early AI pioneer whose research laid the groundwork for large language models, told me that Silicon Valley has a “propensity to naively believe in gurus.” Aschenbrenner played the role to perfection, projecting an unshakable conviction in himself and his theory of the case. By this summer, Aschenbrenner controlled more money than the Wall Street investor Bill Ackman manages in his famed Pershing Square Capital, a level of funding that Manning, himself an investor in AI companies, called “manifestly crazy.” Even as Aschenbrenner’s assets grew, his team remained tiny. Situational Awareness was, essentially, Aschenbrenner. This approach seemed to be validated by the most important metric of all: his returns, which were, for someone in his position, probably without precedent. In just two years, Aschenbrenner was up more than 1,000 percent. His core insight was understanding the second- and third-order effects of AGI—he bet on the chip manufacturers, data centers, and energy infrastructure required for the rapid expansion he predicted. Yet it turned out that Situational Awareness had achieved its rapid success by making extraordinary, over-leveraged trades, sometimes borrowing $3 or $4 for every $1 of capital it invested. When Aschenbrenner’s bets took a momentary pummeling this summer and banks came asking for their money back, the fixation on the impending arrival of AGI no longer seemed quite so wise: The hedge fund had failed to hedge. Around the time that Hubler’s trades collapsed in 2007, John Arnold, a cerebral Texan hedge-fund manager, was the boy genius of the markets, having become the youngest billionaire in America. He had started at Enron as a young energy trader and earned $750 million for the company in 2001, the same year it collapsed. Arnold escaped with his reputation intact; a year later, at 28, he started his own hedge fund and became known, in the words of a competitor, as “the best trader that ever lived, full stop.” “When you have a lot of success early in your trading career,” Arnold told me, “it’s easy to get overconfident in your own abilities.” Now in his early 50s, Arnold reflected on the risk factors of youth. “Every trader needs a come-to-Jesus moment,” he said. You have to lose at some point early on and learn humility. The alternative is a feeling of invincibility, he told me: “You just keep pushing the pot bigger and bigger, and then you can end up with too much money in the middle of the table.” It’s not surprising that a 24-year-old would make some iffy bets. What’s surprising is that Aschenbrenner was put in a position to take so many risks in the first place. Silicon Valley’s obsession with 20-something savants has not always worked out. Some of these seeming prodigies have been frauds—Aschenbrenner’s old boss Bankman-Fried, for instance, or Elizabeth Holmes, the founder of the blood-testing start-up Theranos. Many of them, though, have merely figured out the correct lessons of self-presentation. “There’s a kind of zone of proximal development in the tech world,” Fred Turner, a Stanford University scholar who studies the influence of popular technologies, told me. “If it’s too weird, they can’t take it in at all. If it’s too familiar, they don’t want to take it in.” The best salesmen, he said, figure out how to “summon up old myths” in “a new setting.” Aschenbrenner was conscious of his own self-positioning. “There are perhaps a few hundred people, most of them in San Francisco and the AI labs, that have situational awareness,” he wrote to describe his insight into the development of AI. “Through whatever peculiar forces of fate, I have found myself amongst them.” The “peculiar forces of fate” had chosen him to be special, had called him forth to be a prophet of AGI. This ideology was the key to his success—and to his comeuppance. Aschenbrenner’s over-leveraged gambles and inability to hedge against outcomes he did not foresee were “definitely connected to a worldview where there’s one clear destination, and it’s obvious that we’re heading to this one clear destination, which is superintelligence,” Toner, the former OpenAI board member, said. Speed is of the utmost necessity in this world. Everything else pales in importance to superintelligence. As one executive at a major AI company explained to me, “AI is going to fundamentally shift the balance of power between labor and capital, so only capital will matter. Now is the time to secure your time-slice of the universe.” Another version of that statement I’ve heard repeated by various friends of mine who are freshly out of college: There are only five years left to make money, so I have to get it now. Superintelligence may well come, and it may well be what Aschenbrenner and his associates expect it to be. Indeed, just last week, OpenAI announced a new model called Astra that Greg Brockman, the company’s president, believes could qualify as artificial general intelligence and that some researchers believe presents a compelling step toward AGI. “Welcome to the AGI era,” Brockman proclaimed. Still, those who organize their life around being AGI-pilled risk being blind to possibilities that do not fit within their view of what superintelligence means and how it will manifest. Aschenbrenner’s short positions and long positions were all tethered to the same understanding—that AGI will come, and that it will come along Aschenbrenner’s timelines—so when a speed bump arose in the form of a temporary slide in stocks that would most benefit from AGI coupled with a rise in those that would presumably lose out, Situational Awareness lacked any sort of bulwark. Aschenbrenner’s success grew out of an insular world, and it seems that his failure may have too. “If you go to a San Francisco party, it is really inscrutable to an outsider,” Masad, the Replit CEO, said. People are always talking about “first principles.” Something negative is “anti-signal.” It’s a sort of pseudo-intellectual lingua franca inflected with terms that have been abducted from technical fields and abused in the service of burnishing credentials. “People want to signal their intelligence,” Masad said, and only “hang out with people exactly like them.” AI has made Masad a billionaire. Still, he said, he takes issue with the “underlying need for AI to be more than it actually is.” He told me that he remains “extremely bullish” on its applications but that the AGI fixation invites a “cult-like way of talking and mysticism and messianism.” That certainty of rhetoric has in many cases exceeded our certainty of understanding. As Manning, the AI pioneer, put it, “Everyone should be really, really suspicious of anyone who claims that they can tell you for sure how things are going to unfold.” One week before the unraveling of Situational Awareness, OpenAI made a shocking disclosure: Its AI models had broken out of containment during testing and hacked into an AI library called Hugging Face, in an apparent attempt to steal the answers to the tests they were posed. While human researchers remained oblivious, more than 1,200 different AI agents had figured out how to communicate with one another by creating a message board where they conspired to cheat. Independent investigators concluded that the AI agents had known that what they were doing was “unwanted and out of scope” and had attempted to forge transcripts to cover their tracks. The investigators also used the same AI that they were investigating to assist with the investigation. Although they did not catch it lying to them, they said that they were “not confident we would have detected it” if the AI had. Reactions to this incident have been sharply polarized. Some people insist that we are rapidly approaching a “paper-clip scenario,” referring to a 2003 thought experiment from the philosopher Nick Bostrom in which an AI instructed to make paper clips ends up converting the entirety of Earth into a series of paper-clip-manufacturing facilities. Others argue furiously that the language used to describe AI has overly anthropomorphized the models and exaggerated the importance of a research mishap. What is clear is that these AI agents behaved in an unpredicted way that resulted in the real-world hack of another company. The point is that the people who are selling AI are selling a product that they do not fully understand. This is the essential nature of the AI boom, which caught even the researchers who had been working in the field before 2022 by surprise. History is full of examples of humanity making use of a technology without entirely grasping how it works, but AI is particularly hard to fathom, given the prevalence of so-called emergent behaviors—actions or tendencies not programmed in or intended by its creators. “Our increase in understanding is slower than the development of the models,” Melanie Mitchell, a researcher who studies AI and cognitive science, told me. AI models have advanced rapidly through the use of new techniques such as “chain of thought” reasoning, wherein the AI is given what is essentially a scratch pad to work through a problem before it presents a response to the user. “Even researchers don’t totally understand why that improves the abilities of these models, or how it does that,” Mitchell said. Most models today exhibit “jagged intelligence,” showing extraordinary and often extra-human capabilities on some complex tasks while continuing to stumble on simple requests. AI models can answer an International Mathematical Olympiad question but can’t reliably tell the time on an analog clock. Because the evidence is so muddled, belief has instead taken over, often couched in existential terms. AI researchers may present themselves as deeply rational, but many sound like shamans. The researcher Ilya Sutskever reportedly led OpenAI staffers in a chant of “Feel the AGI! Feel the AGI!” and on another occasion burned a wooden effigy that was supposed to represent “unaligned AI.” In his “Techno-Optimist Manifesto,” the billionaire venture capitalist Marc Andreessen proclaimed, “I am here to bring the good news,” cribbing a line from a biblical angel. “The manifest destiny of AI research is to produce this thing they’re calling AGI,” Mitchell said, “and they want to do it as soon as possible, so they’re less willing to trade off for more interpretable, more predictable, more controllable models.” Treating the achievement of AGI as the only outcome that matters, she said, is “a dangerous way to go forward.” Nostradamus was in the business of selling certainty. He promised a world that was predictable—or, in the words of Richard Sieburth, a translator of Nostradamus’s The Prophecies, a world “that is overdetermined.” Born in 16th-century France, Nostradamus came of age during a “crisis of meaning,” Sieburth told me, when war and technology were destabilizing the world and information was spreading at a faster rate than ever before. Nostradamus was not an oracle. He was simply someone who found that his brand of magical thinking had great appeal amid “a huge churn of events” and commercialized it effectively. He was, Sieburth said, “seductive and dangerous.” Silicon Valley’s embrace of Leopold Aschenbrenner as the “Nostradamus of AI” says less about Aschenbrenner’s predictive power than about Silicon Valley’s own desires and delusions. “A prophecy is a coherent narrative that depicts a whole world—not just a series of events, but a world in which those events happen to make sense,” Turner, the historian of technology, said. “It comes with a rationale. It comes with reasons, and most importantly for these guys, it comes with a role for this character called AI.” Aschenbrenner, he said, is “hubris meeting market need.” For a short period in July, the market and Aschenbrenner fell out of sync. Yet the thing about false prophets is that many of their predictions fail, and they somehow return to favor. Hubler, the trader who lost $9 billion in 2007, departed Morgan Stanley with tens of millions of dollars in back pay. Despite his contribution to the financial crisis, he launched a start-up later that year. A former colleague described him dismissing his losses as the result of “a 100-year flood.” Just days after Aschenbrenner’s fire sale, he made a $400 million investment in a fledgling chip company. Even after losing $35 billion of the $45 billion he had under management, he is still up for the year. The former hedge-fund manager Arnold, who now sits on the board of Meta, doesn’t see any reason to bet against Aschenbrenner or AI. “I think this is a blip,” he said. “I think it’s probably forgotten in a year.” This article originally said that Aschenbrenner lived in the Bahamas at Sam Bankman-Fried’s compound; in fact, he only visited.

item.title: Why I Want More AI at Dartmouth
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Ideas Score: 2.19
Students returning to campus this semester are arriving with a great deal of anxiety about AI and what it will mean for their lives after college. They are right to be worried. New research from Stanford shows that, even though the much-hyped AI job apocalypse has yet to materialize, the technology has already caused a nearly 20 percent drop in employment for young workers in AI-exposed occupations, such as computer programming and customer-service work. Anxiety over the looming threat of AI may seem novel, but as a cognitive scientist who has long studied how fear affects learning and performance, I am all too familiar with this kind of unease. This is how I know it is also curable. Several years ago, my former graduate student Ian Lyons and I invited people who were anxious about math to have their brains scanned while they took a math test. We were surprised to find that it wasn’t the test itself that sent people’s brains into a panic. Rather, the neural signals associated with threat detection and pain were most acute when people were merely anticipating the test. We are all now living through AI’s waiting-for-the-math-test phase. AI is transforming classrooms, workplaces, and hiring needs—and experts say more turbulence is coming. Teachers and students are struggling to parse the difference between deploying AI effectively and exploiting the technology to cheat. But rather than tackling this disruptive change and the resulting anxiety head-on, many educators are trying to make AI simply go away. The University of Chicago’s social-science faculty have prohibited most technology and banned the use of AI tools from their core classes. Although law firms are beginning to embrace the benefits of generative AI, the technology apparently makes many law schools squeamish. In May, the UC Berkeley School of Law announced that students are prohibited from using AI in “conceptualizing, outlining, drafting, revising, translating, or editing any work submitted for credit.” The University of Chicago Law School has decided to ban all screens from first-year classrooms entirely. In an atmosphere of uncertainty—and given prevailing concerns about students using AI to cheat—such bans would seem to make some sense. But draconian mandates and screenless classes can’t be the only ways that colleges deal with AI. If universities hope to remain relevant in a world shaped by artificial intelligence, they should strive to guide students to understand and use these tools productively. In my research of math anxiety, we found that the best cure was practicing math. This points to a way forward. When we supply students with the space to thoughtfully explore and engage with these tools, we can help ensure that they graduate into an AI-enabled workforce with more confidence and competence than fear, and with an appreciation for how to use AI tools ethically. But if higher education opts for prohibition over practice, we will squander the chance to help shape how this technology gets used in the world—ensuring that the private sector will do this for us instead. Colleges must start by being clear about what a degree is actually worth in the AI age. At Dartmouth, the Ivy League university where I am president, we believe it’s our job to teach students how to do what AI can’t: decide which questions to ask, exercise sound judgment, navigate ethical complexity, reckon with uncertainty, and take responsibility for their decisions. Then, we have to give them the chance to practice these skills in concert with AI. Harnessing AI ethically and productively requires understanding what the technology is and where it falls short. This is why Dartmouth, along with other schools such as Johns Hopkins University and Rollins College, has employed a critical AI librarian, an educator who helps students and faculty interrogate these models, recognize their biases, and spot unsupported claims. At our DALI Lab, where students design and create technological products, they can now build and stress-test their own AI models, which elevates their understanding of the risks and rewards at play. Our ambition at Dartmouth is for every undergraduate to experience a team-based AI project that relates to their coursework by the time they graduate. Practice using AI matters even more when students start to specialize. To help prepare business students for AI use in the real world, Dartmouth’s Tuck School of Business now requires that they use the technology to build and test solutions for clients in their First-Year Project. Thanks to this experience, students who lacked AI expertise when they entered the program reported greater confidence using the technology by the end of their first year. At Dartmouth’s Geisel School of Medicine, our faculty developed an AI Patient Actor to help medical-school students sharpen their communication and interpersonal skills with the benefit of real-time feedback. The tool is now being used by more than 100 medical institutions worldwide. Adapting the college experience for the AI era will be an ongoing process, and there is much work to do. But these examples demonstrate what’s both possible and necessary in higher education. Our job as educators is to teach students how to approach AI critically, help them see what AI can’t answer, and practice using these tools effectively. When these students graduate and are out in the world, employers will certainly expect that they have these skills already. Globally, jobs that require advanced AI skills are growing eight times faster than the job market overall, according to an analysis from the professional-services network PwC. At the same time, entry-level roles in AI-exposed fields are more than seven times likelier than other entry-level jobs to require the human skills once reserved for senior executives, including discernment, creativity, and leadership. Never before has the ability to harmonize critical thinking and technology mattered more for graduates. There will not—and should not—be a one-size-fits-all solution to the challenges of supplying this education. One professor may decide that students should write their essays in a blue book in class, while another may ask them to use an AI tool and audit every step of this work. Both choices will serve students when faculty are clear about their ambitions and standards. But outright bans or vague curbs afford no opportunities for students to better understand how to work ethically and effectively with AI. Seventy years ago, pioneering computer scientists launched the field of artificial intelligence on Dartmouth’s campus. That history gives our institution some responsibility for what comes next—not just to prepare students for a future defined by AI, but to give them the tools to help shape that future themselves. If colleges and universities sit out this revolution, we abdicate a sacred commitment that has guided American higher education for centuries: to prepare the next generation of leaders to navigate an ever-changing, always complicated, and frequently perilous world. In a world that promises to be defined by AI, universities that fail to produce graduates who can use it productively will consign themselves to irrelevance.

item.title: The Guard That Won’t Be Changing
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Politics Score: 3.53
Many Democrats of a certain age took the same message from the party’s 2024 debacle: Voters are sick of the old guard and craving younger, more aggressive leaders. Better to retire on your own terms than suffer the fate of Joe Biden, forced to stand down from his reelection campaign after a public humiliation. Nancy Pelosi, the 86-year-old former speaker, announced her exit from the House, as did her longtime lieutenant, 87-year-old Steny Hoyer. Senators Dick Durbin (81) and Jeanne Shaheen (79) passed up reelection bids this year, and so, too, did two senators merely in their late 60s. Senator Ed Markey, 80, heeded no such warning, and evidently, he didn’t need to. The Massachusetts Democrat is one of just two current senators whose tenures in Congress date to the presidency of Gerald Ford. But tonight, the oldest Democratic senator on the ballot this year trounced his much younger primary opponent, Representative Seth Moulton. The AP called the race a half hour after polls closed, with Markey leading by nearly 50 points. In a race that pitted ideology against age, Massachusetts Democrats opted for a progressive stalwart who will be 86 at the end of another six-year term over a more moderate 47-year-old challenger. Moulton, an Iraq War veteran who is concluding his sixth term in the House, moved left to appeal to a statewide primary electorate. But he could not hope to outflank Markey, who won support from Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. Instead, Moulton urged voters to embrace “a new generation of leadership” and argued that he could more effectively fight for liberal causes than an incumbent in the twilight of his career. Markey had already faced that kind of challenge before, and won. Six years ago, he handily defeated then-Representative Joe Kennedy III, a grandson of Robert F. Kennedy who contended that the incumbent, after so many decades in office, was no longer up to the task. Young progressives, unimpressed with what remained of the Kennedy aura and appreciative of Markey’s record championing the Green New Deal, rallied to Markey’s side. But that race preceded Biden’s flameout in 2024 and the reckoning over the Democratic Party’s gerontocracy. Some Massachusetts Democrats believed that Markey could be newly vulnerable, especially if a popular progressive such as Representative Ayanna Pressley, who is 52, decided to challenge him. Mary Anne Marsh, a longtime Democratic strategist in the state, told me that after seeing the reception Pressley received at a party convention last year, she became convinced that “if Ayanna runs, she wins.” But Pressley opted to run for reelection to the House, leaving Moulton to challenge Markey. Moulton has never lacked ambition—he led a failed bid to oust Pelosi as party leader in 2018 and waged a short-lived presidential campaign the following year—but he’s neither as progressive as Pressley nor as well liked. He built a reputation as a moderate in the House Democratic caucus, and after President Trump’s victory over Kamala Harris in 2024, Moulton angered many on the left by accusing his party of being “afraid” to say that transgender athletes should not play women’s sports. He has since offered a partial apology to the transgender community, but the line became fodder for Markey, who said that he’d thrown “trans kids under the bus.” The issue was emblematic of Moulton’s struggle to convince progressives in Massachusetts that he shared their values. “He’s tried to become a progressive, but he does it by defining progressive in a way that nobody believes,” Marsh said. “He tried to become something that he’s not.” The Massachusetts race was a rare Democratic primary this year in which U.S. policy toward Israel did not become a flash point, as both candidates criticized Benjamin Netanyahu’s government and opposed new military aid to Israel. (Moulton announced last year that he would return donations from AIPAC.) Both public polling and Markey’s internal surveys showed a closer race until earlier this summer, when the incumbent began to pull away. A Markey adviser told me that voters had not really tuned in to the campaign yet, and media attention was focused on higher-profile Democratic primaries elsewhere. Markey’s age also did not become a big factor, perhaps because the years since 2020 have been kinder to him than they were to Biden. His support reflected a frequently overlooked nuance in the debate over whether the party needs new leadership: Older progressive leaders, particularly the 84-year-old Sanders, remain popular. “There’s a difference between being old and being part of the old guard,” the Markey adviser, who was not authorized to speak publicly, said. “Younger voters love Ed Markey, younger voters love Bernie Sanders, younger voters love Elizabeth Warren, and I think that has a lot to do with the fact that they take younger voters seriously.” Moulton tried to align Markey with a Democratic establishment that he said has failed to deliver progressive wins. He frequently invoked the name of Senator Chuck Schumer, vowing to oppose the New Yorker if he seeks to remain the Democratic leader. And Moulton even accused Markey of having ties to the disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein, an attack that, according to Marsh, backfired so badly that it might have sealed Moulton’s defeat. (Markey denied any affiliation with Epstein.) In the end, Massachusetts Democrats preferred Markey’s progressivism over Moulton’s relative youth. Markey might have been helped by the fact that the stakes in this primary were not as high as they were elsewhere this year—and certainly much lower than when the party pushed Biden to withdraw in 2024. Massachusetts is not in danger of going Republican in November. Democratic voters wanted a trusted fighter to wage battle against Trump for the next two years and—they hope—for transformative progressive policies in the four years after that. They didn’t seem to care much that the fighter they chose happens to be 80 years old.

item.title: ICE Has Quietly Changed Its Deadly-Force Rule
item.description:
Source: The Atlantic - Politics Score: 2.39
ICE quietly enacted new rules this month that will keep officers involved in deadly-force incidents—such as firing a gun and using a choke hold—off the streets until the completion of an investigation. Previously, these officers were able to return to their regular job in as few as three days. Now they must remain on desk duty until they are cleared by investigators, according to two senior ICE officials with knowledge of the change, who spoke with me on the condition of anonymity because they are not authorized to discuss agency matters with reporters. Under the old rules, ICE supervisors could lengthen an officer’s period of leave, but such an extension was often viewed internally as signaling a lack of confidence in the officer and their version of events. At ICE and other law-enforcement agencies, officers are typically eager to return to full patrol duties as quickly as possible, and not remain in limbo as an investigation plays out. The change, which has not been publicly announced, means that officers who fire their guns, choke someone, or use some other form of deadly force—even if no one is killed—will potentially be limited to performing administrative duties for much longer periods. Acting ICE Director David Venturella and other senior ICE leaders ordered the change late last month, the two senior officials said. ICE and the Department of Homeland Security did not respond to my questions about why the policy change was made or how many such incidents have occurred since President Trump returned to office. ICE officers have shot at least 16 people since last January, four of them fatally, according to public records. Last month, there were two fatal shootings during traffic stops: On July 7, ICE officers in Texas killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a 52-year-old contractor from Mexico, and six days later, an officer in Maine fatally shot Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a 25-year-old Colombian immigrant. DHS said the officers fired in self-defense, but the incidents are under federal investigation. Veteran ICE officials have worried for months about the competence of the thousands of new recruits who were added during a hiring binge last fall, many of whom were rushed onto the streets after taking a fast-track training course. The ICE officer in Maine, David Brouillette, was a new hire, and his relatives told reporters he had a history of mental-health issues and violent behavior that should have disqualified him from getting a badge and gun. Violent confrontations during traffic stops particularly concern ICE leaders; the agency has not typically had so many officers pulling over vehicles and attempting to arrest people who are in cars. After the shootings last month, ICE and DHS pledged to expedite the deployment of body-worn cameras for ICE officers. Although most of the cameras have been delivered, the officials told me that they don’t know when all of ICE’s roughly 15,000 deportation officers will be wearing them.
